kinds.name: Command-line program
kinds.description: A program a person or an agent runs from a terminal, one command at a time.

kinds.name: Long-running program
kinds.description: A program that runs in the background under a service manager and is reached through a socket or a port.

kinds.name: Network service
kinds.description: A program that answers requests over HTTP for other programs or for a page.

kinds.name: Web application
kinds.description: Pages a person uses in a browser, built from components and served by a program of the product.

kinds.name: Library
kinds.description: Code other code imports: a package or a module with no program of its own.

kinds.name: Static site
kinds.description: Pages built ahead of time and served as files, with little or no code in the browser.

kinds.name: Cloud service
kinds.description: A service run on a cloud provider's managed functions, tables and queues.

kinds.name: Docs-only repository
kinds.description: A repository that holds Markdown, pages or nothing, with no program to build: its checks are the commit members and a members file that says so.

kinds.name: No identity
kinds.description: A program with no visitor, no grant and no sign-in: every view is public data, so the rules that assume a signed-in person do not bind it.

kinds.name: Static data
kinds.description: A page that reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: it has no live connection, no reconnect and no write, so the rules about a live server do not bind it.

rules.statement: A decision has a permanent id and one home the repo declares, a status, supersession links on both sides, and a link to the check that holds it or the word instruction; every cited id resolves, and one index test checks all of it.

reasoning.definition: Retired: decision records stay private; the public reasons are docs/reasons/. The text below is what the rule said while it was active. The repo declares one container for decisions: a file per decision (a MADR-style record with front matter validated against a JSON Schema), an entry in one append-only log amended only by dated sub-entries, or a numbered row in a design note with ids numbered across notes. Whatever the container, the invariants are the same: an id that is never reused, a status from a fixed set, supersedes and superseded-by links where a target that does not point back fails, and a check link or the word instruction on an accepted decision. A reversal is a new decision that marks the old one superseded; the old one is not edited away. Every decision id cited anywhere in the repo resolves, links are resolved by a link checker, and an accepted decision whose check file does not exist fails. One index test reads the declared container and checks all of this.
pros: Decision logs are prose files in each repo, so a decision cannot be found, superseded or tied to its check. Three target repos keep decisions in three different containers with the same invariants; the invariants are what a reader relies on, the container is not.

rules.statement: A structural change needs a ruled decision record before any code, with a machine-read header.

reasoning.definition: Structural means a new or split module, a new dependency edge outside an existing record's scope, a new shared package, a new element kind, an app-wide concern, a new library family, or a new gate tier or always-full check. If no door of the classification table (arch.structure.1) fits, the record is written and ruled before code. Only a ruled record may be named when gate configuration changes. A chart library is such a decision: the first project that needs one writes the record, with an earlier ruling as the recorded prior, and there is no ban and no pick now. A new rule, shared package or framework needs its change record, check and pack first.
pros: A structure that appears in code first becomes the precedent; the record makes the choice visible while it is still cheap to change.

rules.statement: The kind of change decides who rules it, and the decision record names who ruled.

reasoning.definition: Retired: decision records stay private; the public reasons are docs/reasons/. The text below is what the rule said while it was active. A new module, slot, shared package or check is ruled by the area lead. A new library family, anything that changes a recorded operator decision, or a change to the ten-domain list's foundation and business split is ruled by the operator through the engineering manager. The record carries its ruling header.
pros: A change ruled by the wrong person is not ruled; naming the ruler in the record is what lets a later reader trust it.

rules.statement: Every decision record lists each rejected alternative with the reason it lost, a rejected item with no reason fails, and a new module, repository or shared interface answers two questions in its change.

reasoning.definition: Retired: decision records stay private; the public reasons are docs/reasons/. The text below is what the rule said while it was active. Each decision, in whatever container arch.decisions.1 declares, has a Rejected part listing every alternative considered, each with the reason it lost beside it. A decision with no alternative says so in one line (none considered, and why the answer was forced). The index test of arch.decisions.1 fails a decision with no Rejected part and a rejected item with no reason. Whether the alternatives were real stays review. A seeded decision record with a single design must be flagged.
pros: Design it twice was written assuming hours per design; for an agent a second design costs minutes, and the first plausible design is what agents settle on. The rejected alternative is the part somebody later proposes again; without its reason the same argument is held twice.

rules.statement: An id is never the next free number taken on a branch: it is a slug, derived from content, or assigned by the landing step, and a reference to an id that has not landed is refused.

reasoning.definition: Two branches that each take the next number collide as surely as two edits of one line. Where an id has no public grammar (a decision, a note, a planned item) it is a slug, permanent and chosen once; ids already issued as numbers keep their numbers. Where it has one that must stay numeric and frozen (a rule id), the author writes a provisional form and the landing step allocates the number, rewrites every reference in the change and records the allocation in its own commit; until that exists, whoever dispatches the work assigns the number in the ticket. A number the host system already allocates (a pull request's) is safe. Counts that are ratchets are not ids: two changes moving one count meet on purpose, and the answer is to add them. Per-author ranges are not used, since they put the roster into permanent ids.
pros: Own measure: two changes took the same decision number in the same week, and the rulebook's rule ids and the fourteen ports are counters of the same shape.

sources.says: Change notes are fragments named by the change, not entries numbered in one file.
A proposed API addition is a file named by its issue, joined at release.

rules.statement: Imports run one way through named layers; a lower layer never imports a higher one, and the failure message gives the reason.

reasoning.definition: The layer order is fixed and written as a table in rule data: folder or package globs mapped to layers, and the allowed edges between layers. Entry code does not import storage code. Infrastructure code never imports application source. Shared kernels and libraries never import a module or the application shell. Inside a module the same holds one level down (pages above components, model and api). Each forbidden edge carries a message that names why the edge is forbidden. Breaches present at adoption sit in a baseline of one file per entry (one-file-per-entry) that only shrinks, and a baseline line that no import makes any more also fails.
pros: A layer that imports upward makes the layers unreplaceable and unreadable one at a time. In Go the layer test exists in two repos and the table counts breaches in four (7, 1, 1 and 1 at baseline). In the web stack the rule existed as a text rule (check-layers.mjs) in two repos, with no fault traced to a missed breach.

rules.statement: Import rules are enforced by a lint rule or a repository test, never by convention.

reasoning.definition: The lint configuration is generated from the same layer table as the layer test (files globs, list-mode, allow and deny lists, each with a reason) and a byte check of the rendered file proves it matches the table. One shared import-boundary preset ships with a few error rules and an empty list for later rules, and the layer check is one program every site imports.
pros: A rule that only a reader knows is not held; the lint rule is the part that keeps working when the author is an agent. Only one Go repo enables the lint rule today.

rules.statement: Every source file belongs to exactly one declared layer or element, a file in none fails, and the boundary checker counts the files it parsed against the tracked source files and exits as could-not-run on any shortfall.

reasoning.definition: Inside a module only the declared slots exist; a sub-module folder exists only if the module's manifest lists it. Configuration that is data sits outside every element and is read only by the kernel and the application element. A package that sits in no row of the layer table fails the layer test. The checker compares the number of source files it read with the tracked source files of the same kinds (from the version control index); a file it skipped, could not parse or never saw makes the run exit 2 (could not run), never a pass.
pros: A file outside every layer escapes every boundary rule, so the table says nothing about it. A checker that silently parses fewer files than exist passes the files it never read.

rules.statement: There are no import cycles between modules, across or inside a layer; a known cycle only leaves the list.

reasoning.definition: Cycles are refused between modules, between parts of one module and inside one part. A cycle found at adoption goes on a baseline that only shrinks. The Go compiler already refuses package cycles, so the Go side is held by the compiler and by the shared-library rule (arch.layers.7); the web stack needs a tool. Cycles that pass through .astro files are invisible to the stock tools, so a graph step extracts imports from .astro frontmatter and <script> blocks with the Astro compiler (@astrojs/compiler), joins them with the TypeScript module graph, finds strongly connected components and holds the count of cyclic groups from rising (shrink-only). The same graph serves the declared-edge check and the merge-candidate report.
pros: A cycle makes two modules one module that cannot be moved, tested or replaced separately. One web repo has 11 cycle groups (68 files) and another 3 (40 files), all legal under their gates; at the donor a reviewer found a test and storybook cycle that no script did.

rules.statement: A module is reached from outside only through its one public entry; no deep import and no relative path across modules.

reasoning.definition: A module exposes a few named entry files (public API, pages for the router, manifest, test helpers for tests on a declared edge) and nothing else is importable. The public entry (index.ts) re-exports no internal layer (handler, repository, action, core). No deep relative imports. A module that two or more modules need moves to the shared layer and moves back when one consumer remains (arch.shared.12). A module that must add something to another module's screen registers a typed contribution with the host and never imports upward; an optional dependency is reached only through such slots, and a direct import is allowed only downward along a declared edge. Route files (routes/**) only wire a page and are held to a thin-route line limit set in rule data. In Go, a package is importable from outside only through its exported surface, with internal/ guarding the rest.
pros: A deep import turns every internal file into a public API, so no module can change its inside. Boundary plugins fired on 10 of 10 Astro plants but have never been run on React.

rules.statement: No code imports another package's source or build-output paths.

reasoning.definition: A package is imported by its published name and exported surface, never by a path into its source tree or its build output. In Go there is no replace directive and no workspace file, and the public surface is listed per tag.
pros: A path into another package's source or output fixes that package's layout as a public contract and bypasses its versioning.

rules.statement: A module that others depend on stays extractable, so it imports no program package and reaches into no sibling module, checked against an allow-list.

reasoning.definition: A shared library package imports no program package. Each library package lists its allowed dependencies in rule data, and the closure of its dependencies must stay inside that list. The shared layer's core imports nothing from the domain modules (core/** imports nothing from domains/**; the entry re-exports no @core). Making the shared code a separate module makes a program import impossible at compile time.
pros: A library that imports a program cannot be extracted, versioned or reused. In the Go kit, 7 of 8 packages import no other in-module package and one imports 2, so the rule is cheap to hold.

rules.statement: A module imports another only along an edge declared in one graph; the graph is acyclic, foundation never depends on business, and a new edge is an explicit gated change.

reasoning.definition: The graph names modules or surfaces and their edges. A new edge is a one-line edit to the graph file whose commit trailer names it. The threshold at which this binds (6 modules) is rule data with its reason, not a repo's choice. Edges are checked against real imports, so a manifest's declared dependency list equals the cross-module imports found. In Go the layer table lists the allowed edges and a repo test checks them.
pros: Undeclared edges grow until every module can reach every other; declaring them makes each new coupling a visible decision.

rules.statement: The module graph is declared in one file, the layer check is one program every site imports, and boundary rules, test projects and structure checks are generated from that file, never hand-written or typed by hand.

reasoning.definition: The graph file is protected gate config. Each site passes its own parameter file to the shared check, and the lists the check uses are derived from the tree or from the graph file. A rule that names files by hand is a finding: a rule object holding more than 3 literal source paths fails (3 is a guess, ratcheted down from 19). A second copy of the shared check in a site's scripts folder is found by scanning for the shared file name and by a clone detector that ignores identifiers and literals against the shared source. A drift check regenerates and diffs the output.
pros: Two sites' layer-check scripts differ by 1314 lines; hand-typed lists drift from the tree and a copied check drifts from its origin.

rules.statement: Tests and stories obey the same import rules as code, production code never imports a test file or fixture, no stand-in kind is in non-test source, and no release recipe or config carries a test build tag.

reasoning.definition: A test cannot reach what its code cannot. Cross-module fixtures come from a testing entry on a declared edge. Specs and stories sit next to the file they test and no new __tests__ folder is added. In Go the compiler refuses an import of a _test file from another package, and the layer rules cover test files. A stand-in (a fake adapter, a test registry entry) is defined only in test source or a test-only package that production code cannot import; a test may register one (arch.ports.16). A build tag that exists only for tests never reaches a release: a test reads the release recipe, the release workflow and the build config and fails on any such tag.
pros: A production import of a fixture ships test data, and a test that reaches around the entry hides a coupling. A test tag in a release build ships the stand-in in place of the real adapter.

rules.statement: A package declared types-only exports no runtime value.

reasoning.definition: A shared vocabulary layer holds declarations only: in Go a shared types package has no init, no side effect and no mutable state.
pros: A runtime value in the vocabulary layer drags behaviour into every module that only wanted a type.

rules.statement: Every source file, test and story has exactly one owner, each module has at least one test and one story, and a module's declared dependency list equals its real cross-module (cross-domain) imports.

reasoning.definition: An owner is a module manifest, the application, the kernel or a library; tests outside the source tree belong to the tooling or infrastructure owner. In Go each package sits in one layer row and each shared package has a named owner; every package with logic has at least one test.
pros: Ownership and a truthful manifest are what let a change find its readers and a reviewer find who rules it.

rules.statement: Where a design says a part must stay separable, a subset binary that registers only that part is built in every gate run and fails when it links a forbidden package.

reasoning.definition: The design names the part and the packages it may not link. The gate builds a second binary that registers only that part and compares its linked packages with the forbidden list (supply.intake.2 holds the per-binary closure). The build runs in the local gate (make check and the pre-push hook), never only in a hosted job. A part's own trusted binary (a guest) is the same case: its link list is the proof of the trust line.
pros: A part declared separable stays separable only while something builds it alone; the first import across the line otherwise goes unseen until somebody tries to split it.

rules.statement: The layer table names a family of packages by folder pattern, and a package that joins a family is no new line in the table.

reasoning.definition: A pattern is a path with one trailing ellipsis (a folder and everything below it), not an expression (gates.registry.8). It appears on the layer row that owns the family and in the lists of what may import it, so a new adapter, context or tool under the family adds no line anywhere. A pattern is one reviewed edge (arch.layers.8): the layer tests and the import linter hold every package under it to the row. The table stays one file (arch.layers.9). A row that lists a package a pattern on the same row already covers is refused, so the table cannot grow back a line per package.
pros: Own measure: in three days a layer table was edited in 42 commits, and the entry rows' import lists took 10 hunks because each new adapter added a name to them. With a pattern for the adapter family the same lists take none.

sources.says: The linter reads one configuration file and has no include or extends, so the import rows it needs are generated from the layer table rather than split by the tool.

rules.statement: Core code knows nothing it does not own: every connection in or out of a program goes through an interface the core declares and an adapter implements, and the core imports only pure packages.

exemptions.reason: a shared package that wraps one thing is itself the adapter and declares that

reasoning.definition: This is ports and adapters. A connection is a provider, a runtime, the operating system, a store, the network, a child process or a terminal. The core directly imports only the standard library's pure packages, the shared packages that rule data names as pure, and its own core: no OS-specific file, no process-spawning package (os/exec) and no network package (net, matched exactly, so net/url and net/netip stay pure). Only an adapter imports those. Our own domains count the same way (an anti-corruption layer): one domain reaches another only through an interface the caller declares, so any domain of ours can be replaced by an open-source tool or a vendor. In the web stack a provider, data client, engine-specific browser API, analytics, payment or sign-in reaches a screen or feature only through a module we own that the provider's adapter implements, a feature imports no provider package, and a service of ours counts as a provider. A module imports a generated client only for a service its declaration lists; generated types are free. Raw third-party clients are reached only through one shared wrapper. A program need not ship for every OS or provider today, but its shape must leave adding one to an adapter. The rule holds with a single implementation, because the edge is the reason for the interface. A fake adapter is how the core is tested at unmanaged edges, and a managed store runs on the real engine. A shared package that wraps one thing is itself the adapter and declares that.
pros: Code that names a vendor or an OS in the core makes every later provider or platform a change across the program. In one repo a Mac port took 151 files, 19 of them in the command layer; in another a second runtime touches 15 files in 3 packages before the index.

rules.statement: A provider's name and its vocabulary do not appear in the core or command layer, a command reaches a provider only through the port and imports no adapter, and the programs and products a tool manages are named nowhere in its shipped source.

reasoning.definition: The command layer may import the port package and not the adapter folders. Outside a provider's adapter no identifier, string or JSON field name from the provider's own vocabulary (its name, its plan, quota or account terms) appears in the core or command layer; the check reads tokens, not just imports, and is proved with a planted name. Separately, a program that manages other software names none of it in shipped source: code, comments and help text. A word-list test reads every non-test source file and fails on a listed word; its exception map holds a path and a reason per entry and only shrinks. Tests and fixtures may name the managed software. The word list is data, so a new provider or managed product extends the list and not the rule.
pros: One repo has 13 command files importing the runtime adapter directly and 150 lines in 12 packages that name it. A name ban that counts only imports misses the provider's field names and plan words, which tie the core to one provider as firmly as an import, and a product named in a comment or help line is a product the next reader assumes is supported.

rules.statement: The number of files in each package that import a vendor SDK directly is reported, as the price of leaving that vendor.

reasoning.definition: A report only: counts come from the module's import lists and nothing fails. A commit that adds a provider is read with arch.measures.2.
pros: The count is the cost of replacing a vendor, shown before the replacement is wanted.

rules.statement: The core compiles for every operating system in the supported list, shipped or not, and holds no platform path literal and no OS tool name, with no exception list; a new use fails and the fix is a port.

reasoning.definition: Shipping is a release decision; shape is not. The list is linux, darwin and windows. An adapter path is outside the set. Compiling is not enough, because a path literal compiles everywhere: no non-test file in the core holds a string starting with a system root (/sys, /proc, /run, /opt, /etc), a home-relative system folder, or the name of an OS tool (a service manager, a log reader, a package manager). The path and tool lists are data, so a new platform adds its roots and tools to the list. There is no exception list for this rule: gates.exemptions does not apply, and the fix for a finding is a port. Paths reach the core from the platform's defaults through config. No platform path or syscall sits in the core, and no OS tool name or path outside the OS adapter. go build stops at a failed dependency and so can show a count that rises after a fix, so the check type-checks per OS, continues past failures and counts packages with their own errors, reading the package list from the dependency closure so an adapter reached through the core shows up. It proves compilation only, needs no limit and takes about two seconds.
pros: Four core packages of one repo fail on windows (ten over the whole repo); go build showed three of them and hid one. Two other repos have a machine or file package that fails on other systems.

rules.statement: The core does not learn the platform from a port: no platform field or name in a port, no core code reads a port's presence as a platform, a missing port is one stated absent value that only the capability layer tests, and a capability the machine lacks is answered by that layer as not on this machine.

reasoning.definition: No Platform, GOOS or OS-name field or string in a port struct that core code branches on; a platform name may be carried for a health or doctor report only, never for a decision. A port the machine lacks has one absent value, stated on the port package (nil in the machine value, or a named absent type), never a stub that pretends to work. Only the capability layer tests for that value; a nil or absent test on a port field anywhere else in the core is a finding. The capability layer turns an absent port into one answer, not on this machine, that every client shows the same way. A port does not carry the shape of the platform: a method or parameter that means something only on one OS or provider is a finding. A second adapter written before the port is frozen is the cheapest test of its shape. A missing port is nil, not a lying stub, and the port package holds its adapters per OS. The review asks what the port does when no adapter is wired and whether that is stated on the port. In the web stack the owned module's methods are domain verbs carrying domain values, and a failure crosses it as a typed value, never as text to match.
pros: One repo has 18 nil tests on port fields outside its port file; its Mac port took 151 files. Agents model the first platform they see.

rules.statement: Every external module and every external program is reached from exactly one adapter package per binary, which declares its binary name, socket, paths, headers, variables and field names, and a test with a shrink-only allow list fails any other importer or caller.

reasoning.definition: For each binary, one adapter package owns each external module (it alone imports it) and each external program (it alone runs it). Running a program means a name passed to the process-start or path-lookup call, resolved the way the compiler sees it: a literal, a constant, or a variable whose value comes from a constant or from the one adapter; a name from anywhere else counts as unresolved and fails. The adapter declares the program's binary name, socket path, HTTP paths, header names, environment variables and JSON field names, and they appear nowhere else. Names shared between two programs are declared once, in a package both import or in a contract file both check against; a header or path literal in two repos with no shared definition is a finding. The standard library's system-call extension module counts as the standard library. The allow list (module or program to its one package) only shrinks, so a new dependency is one new line and a planted second importer fails.
pros: One repo has 41 Go files and 7 site files naming its sibling program outside the adapter, and one finds the sibling's version by searching its help text. A rule that counts only literals lets a program name pass through a variable.

rules.statement: A shape crossing a language or program boundary has one source and a consumer-driven contract: the consumer lists the fields it reads, and that list is checked against the provider.

exemptions.reason: a shared package nothing else reads has no contract to keep
a program nothing else reads has no contract to keep

reasoning.definition: The list is checked against a golden or schema generated from the provider's types. A rename fails and an added provider field passes (a tolerant reader). When a generator lands, the generated type is the list and the check becomes that the generated file is current. The list is derived from the consumer type where possible. It runs when the provider lands, reading the consumer's list. An optional field counts as a miss unless an exception is recorded (66% of the trial list was optional). A list that shrinks without a reason fails, which also catches a shape widened to any. Routes through the consumer's general call path must be on the list, and an empty list on a live consumer fails. Where the consumer is in another language, a generated JSON Schema is the shared file.
pros: 193 of one repo's 195 tags and 38 of another's 46 are hand-typed again in TypeScript; names on one side only were 2 and 8. Against the provider the consumer reads 19 routes and 244 fields with 0 required misses and 9 optional ones, none a fault.

rules.statement: Domain modules inside one program import one another only through an interface the calling domain declares, with an independence contract listing the domains as data.

reasoning.definition: A direct import from one listed domain to another fails, including through the other's public barrel; the allowed route is a file under the caller's ports folder. In the web stack, UI contributed across modules whose host would import upward or sideways goes through a typed slot (home tiles, search providers, shell status, navigation, cache roots, record sections); a direct import is allowed only downward along a declared edge; a dependency marked optional is reached only through slots; typed route links are not imports. Moving the shared piece into a neutral package is the known way round, so a package imported by two domains goes on the review list.
pros: A public barrel is a door that the caller did not design and the callee can widen; making the calling side own the shape gives the stricter boundary. It costs more adapters and is weighed against the size of the domains.

rules.statement: Decision logic is a pure function from values to a decision; the shell reads through ports, calls it and applies the result; functions that take a port and also branch are reported.

reasoning.definition: Report per module the functions that take a port and also branch. There is no limit.
pros: A decision that needs no port shrinks the ports, makes tests need no doubles and stops each decision from growing a store dependency.

rules.statement: A port the target architecture names is declared before its first adapter, in one interfaces-only port package that the core and every adapter import, one subject per port with a handful of methods, and growth is a new adapter on an existing port; an in-program seam over code the core may already use needs a stated reason.

exemptions.reason: tested for by type assertion, not injected

reasoning.definition: Platform and edge ports are written up front from the target architecture, not discovered when a second implementation turns up, so moving from a simple adapter to a better one is never a refactor. They live together in one port package per program (slot interfaces may live in their slot package), so the whole platform contract reads in one place and one fake fills it; an interface for a platform or external edge declared beside its user is a finding. A port is a subject (machine, services, peers, storage), with a handful of methods, never one interface per function. The port package holds interfaces, the value types they carry and the absent value of arch.ports.5, and no logic. The limit on speculative seams stays for code inside the program: a wrapper around what the core may already use (a file read, the shared write helper) or a clock port needs a stated reason, and the second implementation or a design names it. Time is passed as a value or tested with the standard synthetic-time helper. A small optional capability a caller tests for by type assertion is not a seam.
pros: Three target designs fix their platform ports up front and reject interfaces beside their users, because a port found late is a refactor across every caller. The old limit (an interface only once a second implementation exists) still catches the failure it was written for: one repo has 89 interfaces, 14 with no production implementer, and the true failures were wrappers over pure code.

rules.statement: No dependency-injection framework; wire by hand in the entry point.

reasoning.definition: The banned list is rule data (the common wiring and container modules), and a module allow file that refuses any module not allowed makes the list not need to be complete.
pros: One wiring library is archived and no repo uses one; hand wiring in one place is what makes the composition readable.

rules.statement: The entry point is thin and its run function can be tested in process; package-level state exists only as a registry, the machine or the default paths, written once by the entry point before any read or goroutine, and any other mutable package variable is a finding.

exemptions.reason: has no main

reasoning.definition: A main function under 80 lines (the limit is data in the rule file with its reason, and is a guess) and a test of the run() function. Write-once state is allowed in three forms only: a plug-in registry, the machine value that holds the ports, and the default paths. Each is set by the entry point's files before any read and before any goroutine starts; a second write panics, and a read before the write panics. A test that swaps one restores it in a cleanup. Every other package-level variable that is not a constant, a sentinel error or a compiled pattern is a finding. A library has no main and sets nothing.
pros: One repo has 26 init functions. Entry files today are 62, 54, 21, 15 and 15 lines; one outside program has a 934-line main and would fail on day one. Two target designs need a registry and a machine value set at start; allowing exactly those, write-once and loud on misuse, keeps the ban on hidden mutable state without forcing every port through every call.

rules.statement: An app shell composes modules: one composition file is the only place that imports every module manifest, and the shell holds no module logic.

reasoning.definition: The shell holds the router, providers, auth screens and the composition file; its module list equals the graph file's list. It reaches a module only through that module's manifest, its pages (from the router folder only) or its public entry. In Go the program's main wires every package by hand in one place and imports no logic of its own.
pros: One composition root is the only place that knows every module, so a module can be added or removed in one place.

rules.statement: In a program with more than one client, every write from every client goes through one executor and one write port, only that executor and the store adapters import the write handle, and every outcome a caller branches on comes back as a typed result.

reasoning.definition: Every write is a registered operation (a verb) that the one executor runs through the one write port; a command, a route, an agent tool and a page all call the executor and never open storage for writing. A failure the caller branches on is a typed result value with its exit or status; an exception or panic past the executor means a bug. The import table names the executor package and the store adapters as the only importers of the write handle, so a second writer fails the layer test. A program with one client meets the rule by having one write path.
pros: Two writers that each open the store each grow their own checks, and the client that skipped one corrupts the data the other trusted. One executor is the one place a write is checked, logged and undone, whichever client asked.

rules.statement: A new library enters only as an adapter on a port that exists, and a new port lands in the target architecture document before its code.

reasoning.definition: A capability the program does not have yet is a new port, written into the target architecture first with its intended adapter. A new library or tool for a capability the program has is a new adapter on the existing port, so swapping it never touches the core. The change that adds the port's code cites the target document's section; a port in code with no section there is a finding.
pros: A library that enters without a port leaks its types into the core, and a port written straight into code has no design anyone agreed; both make the next swap a refactor.

rules.statement: A plug-in registry is the one place an implementation meets the core, only the entry point's files call Register, a plug-in brings its commands and checks through its port and the command layer mounts them without importing it, and a name clash refuses at start.

reasoning.definition: Slot packages hold a registry each. Only files under the entry point (cmd/<name>) call Register in non-test code; a test file may register a stand-in. A plug-in contributes commands, checks and routes through its port, and the command layer reads them from the registry, never by importing the plug-in package. Two registrations under one name stop the program at start with both names. A registry is write-once state under arch.ports.12.
pros: A plug-in the command layer imports cannot be removed without editing the command layer, and a name clash that one registration silently wins is a command that quietly changes meaning.

rules.statement: The port package declares which ports every platform must fill and which may be absent, and ships one in-memory fake that fills every port so the core's tests run on every operating system; a platform word in the fake is a port finding.

reasoning.definition: The required set is data on the port package; a platform adapter that leaves a required port absent fails at start and in its test. The fake fills every port, required and optional, and holds no word from any one platform (no tool name, path or OS name); such a word means the port carries the platform's shape. A port is extracted from the existing platform's callers first, and the next platform's adapter is written against the extracted port, not the other way round.
pros: Without a fake the core's tests run only on the platform the developer has, and without a declared required set a new platform learns what it must fill from crashes.

rules.statement: A consumer decides what to draw or run from the capability list the server publishes, never from a platform name, so a new platform edits one repository.

reasoning.definition: The server publishes which capabilities this machine has (from arch.ports.5's capability layer). A page, a CLI or an agent shows, hides or disables a feature by reading that list. A platform name may be shown to a person; a branch on it in consumer code is a finding.
pros: A consumer that branches on a platform name has to be edited for every new platform, in every repository that reads the server.

rules.statement: Data from a less-trusted peer reaches a decision only through fields declared decidable on its type, each naming the one decision it drives, checked by a syntax-tree test over the deciding layer with a planted read.

reasoning.definition: Every field of a type that carries a less-trusted peer's report is documented either as may decide, naming the one decision it drives, or as display only. A condition in the deciding layer reads only may-decide fields; a display-only field in a condition, a switch or a map key fails. Decoding of such data is strict (an unknown type or field is refused, sizes are capped), which the service and daemon parts hold.
pros: A peer that can set a field the core branches on can steer the core. Naming the decision per field makes every new field a choice, not a default.

rules.statement: An adapter reads another program's machine format where it has one, and never parses text meant for a person.

reasoning.definition: Where a program offers structured output (JSON, a stable record format, an API), the adapter asks for it and decodes it. Parsing a program's human text (tables, help text, version banners) is allowed only where no machine format exists, with the reason in the adapter and a pinned sample in its test.
pros: Human text changes between releases and locales without notice; a machine format is the part its authors promise to keep. One repo finds a sibling's version by searching its help text.

rules.statement: A program's entry point only wires: it builds the adapters, fills the ports and calls the core, and holds no logic, no type with behaviour and no direct operating-system work beyond what an adapter's constructor needs.

reasoning.definition: The entry point is a program's main package or entry file. Reading a flag, an environment variable, a path or the clock, spawning a process and opening a file are adapter work, so each is a port the entry point fills. A type with a method, a loop over domain data or a branch on domain data in an entry point is a finding. The size of the entry point and its run function being testable in process are arch.ports.12's; this rule holds what the entry point may contain.
pros: The organisation's own gate grew operating-system calls in its entry point, and no check fired, because the ports rule held the core and said nothing of the file that wires it.

rules.statement: Build, test and gate tooling, scripts and hooks are programs: every rule that holds a program holds them, with ports, one adapter per outside program and no platform literal; a shell step is a thin call or a declared adapter.

reasoning.definition: A script, a make recipe, a hook and a workflow step that reach the operating system, another program or the network are connections of a program like any other. A shell step is either a thin call to a program the repository builds, or an adapter declared in rule data with the one program it wraps. A platform literal (an operating-system name, a path or a tool flag that exists on one platform) in a shell step outside a declared adapter is a finding.
pros: The organisation's own gate grew shell with platform literals and no rule applied, because tooling was not counted as a program.

rules.statement: Code that touches an operating system lives only in the host layer, behind ports: no other package imports an operating-system package, reads runtime.GOOS or runtime.GOARCH, or carries an operating-system file name or build tag.

reasoning.definition: Retired for arch.ports.24, which has no host layer: a ruling moved what the layer held into the platform libraries. The text above is what the rule said while it was active.
pros: Each block of the organisation's first programs was built on one operating system and failed on the others, because the operating system was named in every block.

sources.says: Naming a file dns_windows.go will cause it to be included only when building the package for Windows
As events arrive from the outside world at a port, a technology-specific adapter converts it into a usable procedure call or message and passes it to the application.

rules.statement: A product names no operating system anywhere: no package imports an operating-system package, reads runtime.GOOS or runtime.GOARCH, or carries an operating-system file name or build tag, and the platform library that covers the need is the way.

reasoning.definition: A product has no host layer. What differs between systems is the platform libraries' knowledge, and a program reaches it through the library that covers the need, never through golang.org/x/sys, syscall, github.com/gofrs/flock or github.com/shirou/gopsutil, which stay inside those libraries. Three things mark a file of a product as a finding: an import of one of those packages, a read of runtime.GOOS or runtime.GOARCH, and a file whose name go build reads as one system's (_GOOS or _GOOS_GOARCH, before _test), or that ends in _unix or _other by convention, or that carries a //go:build line naming an operating system before its package clause; a Go file that cannot be read as far as that clause, or whose //go:build line go build refuses, is a finding too, never a pass. The register of libraries names the one package of a program that holds each need: its trust package (file-owner-and-mode), its peer package (peer-identity) and the one package of atomic-write, path-lock, app-folders, login-service and unix-socket-listen; machine-facts reaches the machine through the library the register names, in any package. A product's files that stand outside the rule today are rows of its exemptions file, one a file, each with its reason and expiry, and the rows only fall. A lint run reads the files of one system only, so the gate lints each system of its list by GOOS on the one machine it runs on.
pros: Each block of the organisation's first programs was built on one operating system and failed on the others, because the operating system was named in every block. A layer inside each product only moved the naming to one more place to keep right; one library owns it once for every product.

sources.says: A product imports no x/sys or syscall at all, the host layer included; that knowledge belongs to the platform libraries.

sources.where: f300ad376, os-host row and the exemptions held by the test
sources.says: gragas has no host layer: the os-host row spares no folder, and every file that names an operating system is held by a row of its exemptions file or its allowlist.
Naming a file dns_windows.go will cause it to be included only when building the package for Windows

rules.statement: Shared code lives in a small, named set of shared modules with one owner lane, and no other shared module exists.

reasoning.definition: The set is named in rule data: the shared library modules (for example one for plumbing and one for the terminal look) and any separate private package for design tokens. All of them have one owner lane. A package managed by agents, with the operator only advising, versions on its own semver and not in lockstep with the others. A scan of the module files across repositories finds shared modules outside the named set.
pros: Every extra shared module is another place a copy can hide and another owner to find. The shared module exists; its owner lane is a new platform lane that cannot be created until the roster change is allowed.

rules.statement: The shared package holds mechanism, not product knowledge; policy and domain words stay in the program, and the API is small functions and structs.

reasoning.definition: Domain logic, product sentences and a page's own layout stay in the project whatever the copy count. In Go an AST test over the shared module's identifiers and string literals runs against a deny-list of program and domain words (tool names from the workspace, domain words) and a scan finds repository names. The shared module carries no program's domain.
pros: A shared module with product words in it is a program in disguise; one shared style file (style.go) carried photo words. The shared kit has no repository names today.

rules.statement: A step copied into a second repository moves to the shared module, and the census count of copies only falls.

reasoning.definition: A census (the step-copies measure, a go test that regenerates the census and diffs it against the committed one) hashes every known shared step across the repositories and counts copies and versions; the count per step has a shrink-only ratchet. Clones across repositories are reported. Engines such as a clone detector are candidates. Copies found by hashing are also counted for design tokens and parts on the web side.
pros: One census found 42 hand copies (223,170 bytes) of what the shared UI module holds, and named a shared package for 31 of the 51 steps. Copies diverge silently.

rules.statement: A second copy found by shape is reported in the change, which either moves it or lists it as independent with a reason.

reasoning.definition: The clone detector runs with identifiers and literals ignored (a renamed copy shows 0 clones by default) with a minimum of 5 lines and 30 tokens; looser similarity and embedding modes exist and were not run. The report is advice; the gate is the ban on the primitive in arch.shared.8.
pros: A copy found only by name is missed once renamed; the shape is what repeats.

rules.statement: A copy that must differ is listed as independent with a reason and a removal date, and a copy that diverged is reported.

reasoning.definition: A census class named independent needs a named reason, and every allowed copy has a removal date that fails once it passes. A copy that diverged is reported when only one of its copies changed in 90 days (a git log per copy file); the next change to a diverged copy is blocked until answered. The count only falls. Clones not on the list fail. In Go the list is the shrink-only baseline file: one row per deliberate copy, with the path, a metric of lines, a ticket and the date by which it is zero. The divergence report reads the list of copies taken from another repository (arch.shared.6).
pros: 12 of 20 UI steps were independent copies in one census, and 14 independent steps in a Go census; without a reason list a divergence cannot be told from drift.

rules.statement: A file that must stay a copy is checked byte for byte against its origin in the gate, and a shared file reaches every consumer through a manifest of path and hash, and copies are counted by the step-copies census.

reasoning.definition: Root configs are byte-equal to the template and an edited one fails; a config read by meaning is validated by meaning (an .npmrc is last value wins, and the pnpm-workspace file is compared to the expected key map). Each holder has a manifest of path: sha256, a changed hash re-runs the readers, and the check sits inside the path agents take, with a per-repo ceiling that only falls. A repo copy of a canonical root file is diffed against the shared config package: each repo's copy is a one-line extends or re-export, a pre-push job diffs it, and a template update reconciles drift once the template exists. For a copy taken from another repository the list is one file with one row per copy: the path here, the original, what may differ and why. A repository test reads the list through the shared module's list reader and compares each pair; a difference the row allows passes and any other fails. The first rows are two test-isolation helpers copied from another program.
pros: One repo's drift check fails and sits outside the gate (7 of 25 whole-file entries fail); five versions of a pre-push hook exist in five repos; three byte-equal things were found in one census.

rules.statement: A shared rule or look changes once, in its package, and reaches projects by a version bump; it is imported, never copied.

exemptions.reason: no terminal output
no terminal output

reasoning.definition: No project holds a copy of the shared rule file or of a module file; declared differences (a program's own brand, banner art) stay allowed. A one-line wrapper is allowed and a 78-line copy is not. In Go the terminal look comes from the shared UI module, with no colour literal or escape string outside it and no terminal-detection package outside it (a program can still paint with raw escape strings through the formatting package or detect a terminal with x/term, which is not banned today).
pros: Only one program imports the shared UI module (30 non-test files); the others copy. Three byte-equal things and 12 independent steps were found in one census.

rules.statement: Every shared export that replaces a hand copy is protected twice: a ban on the primitive outside its owner with a shrink-only allow list, and an advisory shape rule that points at the export to use.

reasoning.definition: The ban is the gate. The shape rule is advice and does not stop a rebuild by itself, because a name search cannot find a copy (copies are called Put, replaceOnce or enqueue). The message names the export to use and old copies stay on a per-file count that only falls. The shape rule has a planted copy under a different name, its known bypasses kept as fixtures (a helper that makes the temp file, a file create call, a root rename, a method-value alias of the rename call, link-then-remove) and its measured rates beside it. Locking, atomic writes, paths and the daemon helper come from the shared module, not a local copy. An export without both halves is planned. A known bypass is a helper in a ban-free package that calls an allowed primitive. In Go the ban rows are not hand-kept: they are generated from the registry of arch.shared.15, one forbidigo or depguard row per primitive with the export in its message, and the exclusion list of each ban is the shrink-only allow list. The bans at adoption are the file-write primitives (rename, temp file, write file, create, open for write) outside the write owners; the digest primitives and the hex encoding of a sum outside the digest owner; the raw stat of a path outside the trust owners; running the version-control program outside its owners; and the golden update flag outside the one golden helper. The shape rule stays advice; the restructured copy it cannot see is made visible by the trailer of agents.discovery.6.
pros: 13 hand-written replace-a-file bodies sit outside the owner and 14 production files call flock directly; a name search found none of the copies and a clone detector found 0 clones; the shape rule flagged 1 of 6 planted forms of the atomic write and missed all five restructured copies, so per-export bans are the gate.

rules.statement: Each port and shared package's public surface is listed in one generated file per tag with a stability mark (stable, experimental, internal) on every export, held both ways against the code, and a change to the surface or a mark fails until a reason is recorded.

reasoning.definition: The listing is regenerated and diffed in the owner repository (for Go, a short doc listing per package); a test that the listing's tag equals the pinned version, and a program reads the listing for the version it pins. A surface is few, typed and closed. Every export carries one mark: stable (kept until a recorded break), experimental (said so at the export site too) or internal (not reachable from outside the package). The register and the code agree both ways: an export with no mark fails, a mark with no export fails, and an internal export reachable from outside fails. For a published web package the surface is its exports map with one subpath per unit, no root barrel on a package with more than one unit, and every entry resolving in the packed tarball. The reason must resolve to a ticket or a second case. Width per part is printed and does not gate because a limit would be a guess. The interface comment is a review question (see code.comments).
pros: The shared Go package's surface is 181 lines and 6.9 KB; the list read at the version one repo pins has no UI and no door entry. In the trial, 25 landings in one repo and 11 in another were real port changes. A surface with no stability mark promises everything to every reader; the mark is what lets an experimental export change without a break.

rules.statement: A new shared package or part enters the shared layer only when entry conditions hold: two live consumers, one concern, a named owner and a line in the generated listing.

reasoning.definition: For a web module: two or more consumers today; no single module's entity rule; imports only the kernel, generated types, the design system and packages; a named kernel package with a README naming its purpose, allowed imports and owner; a catalogue row and tests. For a shared part: published criteria, holds no single surface's rule, and the fan-in threshold (3 surfaces) is rule data with its reason, not a repo's choice. Test helpers go in a testkit package in the root module. Anything else stays in the program.
pros: A shared item with one consumer pays for the shared layer's cost and none of its value.

rules.statement: A piece moves up one step at a time (page, the site's shared/ folder, then a shared package), and stack-free code moves when a second project needs it.

reasoning.definition: Stack-free code moves on any framework. A part moves by the three-copy rule inside a site; across sites it needs a second live consumer on the same framework, after its fault has recurred. Domain logic, product sentences and a page's own layout never move. A new package or repository names the driver that a folder or namespace cannot meet (arch.structure.5).
pros: Skipping a step creates a shared package for something that has one user.

rules.statement: A shared item whose consumers drop to one moves back into that consumer, or names a second as a recorded exit.

reasoning.definition: A module two or more modules need moves to the shared layer; one that drops to a single consumer moves back. The structure check fails a shared item with fewer than two consumers. A step used by one program again returns to it, since a step moves up only on two holders.
pros: A shared item kept for one consumer is shared in name only.

rules.statement: A shared pattern, marker or behaviour-deciding value has one exported definition that others import.

reasoning.definition: A shared value or pattern is defined once in the shared module and copied byte for byte only by listing (arch.shared.6). A threshold or limit is a named constant in one configuration module, so the same number is not typed in two view files. The same value in two exported constants blocks until answered.
pros: Two copies of a pattern drift apart and the program silently splits into two behaviours; one threshold lived in four places in one repo.

rules.statement: A shared source has a named owner, one home, a stated version and a place to ask with a response time, named before it is called adopted.

reasoning.definition: Each shared repository has an owner file with the owner, home, version, ask channel and response time; the sync check verifies every shared dependency repository has a valid one at its pinned tag. The tokens package is managed by agents and the operator only advises.
pros: Two shared UI sources have no owner file; a shared source with no one to ask is abandoned the first time it needs a change.

rules.statement: Every capability that more than one package or program needs is one row in a registry, and the lint bans, the instruction block and the export listing's shared column are rendered from it.

reasoning.definition: The registry is one file, one row per line, sorted. A row has the capability, the owner package, the export, the shared module's package and export if it has one, the primitives the capability owns, a status (local, shared or later) and the tag since which it is shared. A repository test fails a row whose owner does not exist, a primitive with no rendered ban, a ban with no row, and a shared-module row whose export is not in the pinned tag's package listing. The owner column is held to the owners that the layer table already names, so the two files cannot disagree. A ban nobody can find is not read, and an instruction nobody enforces is not followed; one file is both, and the generator writes the ban rows into the generated part of the lint config and the instruction block into the agents' file. Removing a row narrows a gate, so the registry is a protected path.
pros: Own measure: the atomic write exists six times in one Go program and the digest of a file twelve times, each added by a builder who did not see the earlier one; the shared module's own instruction file states the second-copy rule, and nothing in this program enforced it.

rules.statement: A new concern lands in exactly one door of a classification table and the change names it; a program cannot grow its own folder for a shared concern.

reasoning.definition: The doors are an existing module, a new module, a shared package, a design-system part, a generated client, an app-wide concern, a new library and a new check. The change names the door in a trailer. If none fits, the decision record of arch.decisions.2 comes first. The concern table gives one owner per concern. An agent cannot create a plumbing folder in a service, and there is no util or common package.
pros: Without a table every agent invents a new place, and shared plumbing grows a private copy in each program.

rules.statement: An extension lands complete in one change: structure, rule, check with its plant, catalogue row, examples and docs.

reasoning.definition: One change holds the structure (from the generator), the rule rows, each new check with its negative test, the catalogue row, stories and specs, the scope-rules entry, and the rulebook and page update. In Go, growing the foundation is one change record adding the rule, its check, its plant and its grid cell together. A living example per state and a catalogue entry for a part belong to the same change.
pros: A rule without its plant or a part without its example is half added, and the half that is missing is the one a reviewer cannot see.

rules.statement: Splitting, merging or renaming a module needs a decision, and a move or rename commit changes no behaviour and no baseline count; editing comes in a second commit.

reasoning.definition: A move commit contains only renames at 100% similarity and import-path and package-clause edits; baseline keys are rewritten and counts left unchanged. A commit that marks itself as a move is checked, other commits are not. A move that lands before any behaviour change is the wanted result.
pros: A move mixed with an edit cannot be reviewed as a move, and baselines reset when a rename is not recorded. Not measured in Go; the web rule holds it for the UI.

rules.statement: A project declares its kind and its one framework and uses the stack the foundation lists for that kind; a package outside the list needs a written exception.

reasoning.definition: The framework value is read from the project's parameter file. A second framework is refused by the import-side rule in the web part. Which framework per kind follows the foundation's by-kind answer, which is a recommendation: only some project rulings bind their own artefacts.
pros: A stack the foundation did not list is a stack nobody maintains; the declared kind is what lets the right pack be applied.

rules.statement: A new module, package or repository names the driver that a folder or namespace cannot meet, because a logical split comes before a physical one.

reasoning.definition: Before a new package, shared library or repository is created, the change states the driver a folder or namespace inside the existing package cannot meet. A seeded change that creates a package with one importer must be flagged. A required field in the change template can be checked for presence only.
pros: Companies reported going back to a coarser split after paying for a physical split they did not need, risking a distributed monolith. New packages are free for an agent to make, so the question has to come from outside.

rules.statement: Things that change together live together, in the same folder shape across a kind of program, and the layout matches the template for that kind.

reasoning.definition: The folder-shape template for a kind says what folders must exist and which file kinds sit beside which; a missing or extra folder fails. Whether things belong together is judgement; the shape is mechanical. The Go program template is: cmd/<name> for each binary; under internal, core and core/api for the decisions and the operations every client calls; one port package holding the platform interfaces with its fake; slot packages that hold a registry each; adapters under host/<platform> and host/<tool>; door for the network front; config; cli/<group> for commands and cli/ui for terminal output. The import table between these folders is rule data read by the layer test (arch.layers.1), not prose. A new kind of program or a new language adds its own template under the same rule.
pros: A census of 20 UI steps found 3 identical and 12 independent; the same shape across a kind is what lets a check and an agent find things. Two Go target designs name the same folders for core, port, adapters and commands, and a template that does not exist (the rule pointed at one) holds nothing.

rules.statement: A package or module is a unit of meaning: no catch-all names such as util, common, helpers, types or misc, and the phrase describing it needs no "and".

reasoning.definition: The name deny-list holds util and common, the layer-type names helpers, types, models, interfaces and base, and the words other and misc, matched on the whole name. The names adapters, domain and port are the ports model's own and stay off the list. The word "and" in the description stays a review question: Go package names have no word breaks, and a substring match only gives false hits (standin-gate, standdown and ondemand all hit falsely).
pros: A run over 190 Go folder names in six repos found one hit, a package named base; the substring test for "and" hit three false names. A catch-all name invites everything.

rules.statement: A refactor of a path in live use starts only after a merged contract test of what its consumers read, and a refactor that moves code that touches the system (files, processes, the network) behind ports records a transcript of every command's output first, with each step's transcript diff empty.

reasoning.definition: Before the first refactor commit on a path a consumer reads, a contract test of the fields and answers that consumer reads is merged (arch.ports.7 holds the contract; this rule holds its order). A refactor that moves such code behind ports records, before it starts, the output of every read-only command, the status and health commands and every dry run, and each step of the refactor reruns them and shows an empty diff; a step with a diff is a behaviour change and is split out. The transcripts are committed beside the tests and replaced only by the change that means to change the output.
pros: A refactor without a pinned consumer contract finds its breakage in the consumer, after release. A port extraction touches every command at once, and only a recorded transcript shows that nothing a person reads moved.

rules.statement: A list that grows by one entry per feature is a folder of one file per entry, joined by a generator and held by gen --check; no feature edits a line another feature owns.

reasoning.definition: Commands, gate members, planned items, surface marks and the notes an index points at are the usual lists. Adding an entry is a new file, and removing one is a deleted file; the one table the program or a reader needs is rendered from the folder by a generator, sorted by a key in the entries so no order list exists. A cross-cutting rule over the entries ("every entry has two examples") is a test that walks the joined result, not a column each feature edits. A generated join still conflicts as text when two changes add neighbours, and the fix is to run the generator (gates.protection.5). An index is generated too (docs.freshness.1): a person reads it and nobody edits it.
pros: Own measure: in one repository a single new command edited a dozen shared files, and the run log of one working day shows each landing sending the queue back through a rebase and a full gate run. Surveyed projects avoid the same by putting each command in its own folder and walking the tree in a test.

rules.statement: A fact about a package, an export or a command (what it holds, why it imports what it imports, its stability mark) is written in that thing's own folder, and any central table of such facts is rendered from them.

reasoning.definition: The fact sits where the thing's own author already edits: what a package holds in its package doc comment, an answer about an import in a file of the package's folder, a mark beside the export or in a per-package file, a command's usage text in the command's own file. The central table, the layer document or the usage page is a generator's output, so a change to one package edits one folder and one generated row. A column of prose in a table that every package change edits is the sign of a fact kept away from its thing. A table row keeps what is true of the layer itself, in one line.
pros: Own measure: over three days one layer table was changed in 42 commits, and by changed line the paragraph each package says it holds took 92 lines, more than the lists of what may import what. Each package change edited a prose column that another package change also edited.

sources.says: Build facts about a package live in a build file in that package's own folder, not in one table at the root.
Who owns a directory is a file in that directory, inherited upward.

rules.statement: A template per kind lays down configs, scripts and gates, records its answers and version in a file, and a deleted synced file fails the sync check.

reasoning.definition: One template exists per kind of project. The sync tool writes the version and the source hash to a lock file, so a later update can replay it and so a vendored copy shows where it came from. The tool is one Go command in the same binary as the checks, not an external template engine.
pros: A template that does not record its version cannot be updated, and a project that has drifted from it cannot be told apart from one that chose to.

rules.statement: A new program, command, package, page, part or surface comes from a generator or golden example, and the gate accepts what it writes.

reasoning.definition: The generator scaffolds the folder, entry files, registry entry and test stubs, and one reference program is the first file an agent opens. The gate is a self-check that runs the generator into a temporary copy of the repository and then the lint, type check and layer rule over the result, which must pass. Hand-made files are allowed as long as they pass. A hyphenated name is a fixed plant. Come-from-a-generator cannot be forced; the mechanism proves only that the generator's output passes. In Go a scaffold creates a new program, command or package with a thin main and a gate-clean layout.
pros: A page generator failed one repo's own gate on a hyphenated page name. There is no Go scaffold or reference program, and an agent copying an old program copies its faults.

rules.statement: The template installer asks exactly three questions (name, version range of the shared package, runtime major) and has no yes or no switches for optional file groups.

reasoning.definition: Optional file groups are separate kinds, not switches, so two projects of one kind have the same shape. In the ruled Go form the questions become the kind pack and a module path.
pros: Each switch doubles the number of shapes a gate must accept.

rules.statement: On template update, files the repository owns are written once and left alone, managed files are rewritten, and a test checks that no byte-equal file is on the skip list.

reasoning.definition: The sync tool rewrites managed files and leaves repo-owned local fields; copies that must differ are listed as independent (arch.shared.5). A byte-equal file on the skip list is a managed file that was never updated.
pros: An update that overwrites owned files is not used, and one that skips managed files drifts.

rules.statement: Afferent and efferent coupling per package is reported, and a rise in a package's fan-out blocks until the change says why.

reasoning.definition: Report Ca, Ce and instability per package. A package created after adoption may not exceed a fan-out ceiling (a guessed number), and a package not in the baseline whose Ce exceeds it fails. The cheap cure is a facade package that re-exports, so a fan-out line alone is easy to pass; the answered form needs no guessed ceiling.
pros: In one repo the command package has Ce=43, the hook package 28 and the main package 25, and 3 of 325 edges run from stable to unstable.

rules.statement: A commit that adds a provider reports how many core files and folders it changed, and a change that touches core files blocks until answered.

reasoning.definition: On the change that adds a new case to an existing seam (a new adapter) report the files and folders touched outside the new adapter (git diff --name-only against the adapter globs), as a change-locality report. It reports the result of the seam, not its form, so renaming does not satisfy it. A decision-point alarm at a guessed level is optional.
pros: A new launcher took 6 files in 1 package in one repo and a second OS took 69 code files in 21 folders in another; this is the measured result of arch.ports.1.

rules.statement: Change coupling across a boundary is computed per ticket or pull request, and a pair that crosses a boundary without a visible link blocks a review until answered.

reasoning.definition: Group file pairs by ticket or pull request, never by commit (per commit it means nothing at an agent's commit rate); ticket ids on commits make it possible. A pair crossing a package or repository boundary with no import link is printed at land (ticket-grouped file-pair coupling, cross-language pairs read first). The numbers (confidence 0.5, 3 tickets) are guesses.
pros: It is the one history idea with outcome support that was not computed. The trial rediscovered a known seam.

rules.statement: A package is judged by its exported surface, not its size; a rise in a package's exported count blocks until the change says why, and no size line is set.

reasoning.definition: Report exported names per package at each tag from the generated listing of arch.shared.9, diffed between tags and printed. The count is read with the merge-candidate report of code.size.
pros: One repo's command package has 117 non-test files and 37,566 non-blank lines, which no size line would have caught early; the surface shows the cost.

rules.statement: A shared abstraction is watched after entry: releases that forced a consumer change, signature churn, option growth and callers using disjoint subsets.

reasoning.definition: Per-package release and consumer counts by release from the registry plus an exported-signature diff across tags. The question each report asks is whether this should be two packages, and whether all its callers change for one reason. There is no limit. A shared package past its churn baseline blocks until the owner answers. A shared part with fewer than 3 importing surfaces is listed as a candidate to move back.
pros: A shared abstraction is cheap to enter and dear to leave; option growth is the early signal that two uses have drifted apart, and agents add an option to a shared call rather than question it. Entry is gated by arch.shared.10 and nothing watched a package after it.

rules.statement: The repositories that release together and how far each consumer lags the newest shared version are reported; a forced-newest rule is itself a cause.

reasoning.definition: Release tags per repository joined with the shared-package pins. The unit is the release, never the day, because agent commit rates make day counts meaningless.
pros: A many-repo layout rests on pairs of repos not moving together; lockstep deployment signals a misplaced boundary. Independent deployability is what the layout protects.

rules.statement: A file per service lists the stores and event families it writes and the services each flow includes, compared with a scan of the writers.

reasoning.definition: The tool compares the file with the writers found by scanning write statements. Measure first, gate once the list exists. An agent cannot infer ownership from the code, so the list is what makes a check possible.
pros: Two seam cases of our own were this: no one could say which program wrote a shared store.

rules.statement: Code is clean under one formatter and one import-order tool, checked by the tool's output and not by its exit status.

reasoning.definition: One formatter and one editor configuration are used across projects. In Go the code is gofmt- and goimports-clean, and the check is that the formatter and the standalone import-order tool print nothing (the formatter's list mode exits 0 on findings, so the exit status is not read); the import-order check uses the standalone tool, not the lint runner's formatter, which measured 141 CPU-seconds cold. In the web stack formatting is one command and the format check is in the gate, with a class-order plugin in the shared config. A tree-wide formatting commit is made once, in a quiet window, and listed in the blame-ignore file.
pros: Unformatted code makes every diff noisy and every review slower; the floor items are cheap and run in every Go lint config. The one-time format commit has no blame-ignore row in Go today.

rules.statement: The language's vet and static analysis pass in the lint gate.

reasoning.definition: In Go the lint runner runs the vet analyzers at their defaults and the static-analysis suite (all of its correctness, simplification and style groups, with the six non-default style checks off), from one shared configuration pinned by version. In the web stack the equivalent is the type check and the lint gate named in the web part.
pros: These are the cheapest finders of real mistakes (a wrong print verb, a deprecated call); they run in six repositories today.

rules.statement: Files over a per-type line limit are reported without failing, and the count of files over a far larger limit is held from rising.

reasoning.definition: The reported lines (code 300, component 400, stylesheet 800) are guesses, and so is the gated tail of 1000 lines. A file over the report line prints; a file past the tail line fails when it is not in the committed baseline (one file per entry, shrink-only). Generated files, golden test data and end-to-end files are on a declared exclusion list. The donor's rule gated at 300 lines (counting non-blank, non-comment lines) with a shrink-only per-file override list that ships empty; our ruling demoted the 300 line to a report because no harm is shown and a ratchet with no partner rewards the cheap split. Splitting a file past the tail is free, which is why only the tail gates. The other side of this rule, a file split too far (a too-small split, which no instrument covers), is read through code.size.6.
pros: A size ratchet failed once in the estate (a file grew from 400 to 3,000 lines and still counted as one violation), so a one-sided count is known to be gamed. Over 300 lines: 62 files (11.4%) in one repo, 96 (26.0%) in another, 36, 44, 37 and 8 in the others; the standard library has 25.9% over 300 and 8.3% over 800. Over 1000: 5, 8, 4, 1 and 0.

rules.statement: Functions over 50 lines are shown as a measure beside the count of tiny single-use helpers, read per change, so a fall in length with a rise in helpers reads as no progress.

exemptions.reason: test bodies are long by design; the donor's cap does not apply to tests

reasoning.definition: A helper is any function of 20 lines or fewer, exported or not, with exactly one referrer by call or value. The count covers exported helpers and function values, because counting private call sites alone is beaten for free by exporting the helper, calling it from a dead branch or putting it in a table.
