A function over 100 lines is reported and fails nothing: length cannot tell a nest from a flat table, and cognitive complexity already holds every nest. 50, 100 and 20 are guesses. A function over 50 lines grows only after the change says why. The donor's rule failed a function at 50 lines (not applied to tests); that demotion is the ruling here. The review question beside it is whether the new function can be understood without opening its caller.
pros: Nine commits in one repo say they extract a helper to get under a limit, so the limit drives extraction. Over 50 lines: 3.1%, 3.7% and 7.9% of functions in three repos, 7.6% in the standard library; helper counts are 1311, 1056 (331 exported), 514, 415 and 401. In a sample of 24, about 4 were merge candidates.

rules.statement: The count of functions with cognitive complexity over 20 only falls, and a fall paired with a rise in the helper count prints as no progress.

exemptions.reason: tests are off in the tool configuration

reasoning.definition: The line of 20 is inherited, not measured, and is one line for Go and the web stack; the donor's line was 15 and is not used. The ratchet reads the pair per change: a fall in this count with a rise in the helper count of code.size.2 in the same change prints as no progress, so the baseline can lower only if the helper count did not rise. The count of over-limit functions is a per-function baseline, one file per function. A lint runner's new-from-merge-base setting flags every touched line of an old over-limit function, so the count ratchet is preferred. Existing debt in the web stack sits in the linter's bulk suppression file, which is the shrink-only baseline. Tests are off.
pros: At 20 with tests off: 94 functions in one repo, 91 in another, 48 and 33 in two more; 0 over 30 where the config holds 30. In a hand sample about 2 of 4 hits were worth splitting. A 160-line nest scores 143 and fires; a 159-line flat table scores 0; splitting a nest into two methods that share state still fires on both. Nine commits extract a helper to get under the limit.

rules.statement: Functions with many parameters take a struct or options object, and the parameter count only falls.

reasoning.definition: The Go limit is 6 for new code with the receiver not counted (a guess; no Go source gives one, and the revive default is 8); the web limit is 4, with a shrink-only baseline for existing debt. The cure the rule wants is the one that passes. The donor's cap was 3 parameters per function. The cheap cure is a variadic any, which the port rules catch at ports only.
pros: A long parameter list hides a missing type and makes every caller depend on the order. In the web stack 67 functions in one repo exceeded the limit of 4.

rules.statement: Size and complexity are watched as a trend and a hotspot list (churn times lines), reported and not gated, with a declared exclusion list and a window by release or ticket, never by days.

reasoning.definition: A hotspot report uses a declared exclusion list that takes generated files, registers, golden test data and end-to-end files, and states its window and its unit: by release, train or ticket, never by days, because agent commit rates inflate churn and make time windows meaningless (118 commits a day on one repo). After a squash the unit changes little, and splitting a hot file drops it off the list, so a file that leaves it has not shown it got better. A hot file carries a per-file trend (lines and indentation depth over its commits) before and after a refactor, so a fix is checked against history. A ratchet is used only where a number reaches zero in practice, such as files over 1000 lines not rising (code.size.1; one repo's numeric per-file file-baseline already does it). A size distribution (the 90th percentile) is reported as a trend. A diff size (a diff-size ceiling paired with a rework count) is reported beside post-land rework per ticket wherever a small-change rule exists, from the delivery record, with no limit.
pros: The top tenth of files by churn times lines took 46.4% of later fix touches in one repo and 30.2% in another, against 9.9% for a random tenth; lines alone gave 34.8 and 36.9, so the product is no better than its parts. A rerun did not reproduce the 46.4: the top tenth took 31.1, 30.7 and 25.9 against 9.8 random, and lines alone beat the product in two repos. Commit and ticket units share 18 to 20 of the top 20. Raw churn lists fill with generated files. The delivery stability findings with AI use are explained by larger changes.

rules.statement: A merge-candidate report lists modules with one importer that change with it, near-duplicate modules, ports with one implementation and private functions with one call site; it is report only.

reasoning.definition: A root or command module imports everything by construction, so it does not count as the one importer. Near-duplicates are found by token clones (renaming every exported name beats a name match for free). Interfaces with one implementation are listed when no second is named. No floor is set: a single call site is often right and floors misfire. A new merge candidate blocks until the change merges it or says why not. It is read beside code.size.2.
pros: Every size rule pushes towards splitting and nothing reported the opposite. Across six repos 93 packages had one importer, 33 changed with it, 31 of those on a command root, 2 left to read; a clone finder found about 9 clone pairs in one repo in 0.9 s.

rules.statement: Types are listed by method count, with no limit, so a god object that is under every file-size line is visible.

reasoning.definition: A small analyser counts methods per type, leaving out fakes. Grouping methods by the fields they use does not do this: it flags fakes and data records, a mutex used in every method hides it, and it missed a 49-method server. A type whose method count rises above its baseline blocks until answered.
pros: The types with the most methods were 49 (a server), 35 (a config) and 33 (a call type). Field cohesion tried flagged 49 hits across six repos, of which 1 to 2 of 12 in one repo were plausibly true.

rules.statement: Duplicated blocks only fall, measured across packages by a clone detector; no new clone is added inside a repository.

reasoning.definition: For Go there are two rows. The lint runner's detector (dupl) runs at 60 tokens and compares within one package only, as a tripwire. A standalone build of the same detector, pinned in the tool list like the other Go tools and built offline, runs over every non-test file at 60 tokens, so it sees across packages; its clone-group count goes to the measure output and to a shrink-only baseline row, at its count on the day of adoption and then at 0. For TypeScript a clone detector (jscpd) runs over the source roots with generated files ignored, and the clone count and the cloned-block metric are held by a shrink-only ratchet through one ratchet helper; its thresholds are 10 lines and 80 tokens. No Node tool is used where a Go one does the job in the Go gate. A clone found at adoption goes on the baseline.
pros: One Go repo has 82 source clones (1.25% of tokens); two web repos had 2 clones (0.26%) and 5 (0.15%). The lint runner's detector misses cross-package copies, so a cross-package detector is needed. The two reports' figures are not reconciled.

rules.statement: The duplicate-block check runs a second pass that ignores identifiers, with the same shrink-only ratchet, so a copy with renamed names is seen.

reasoning.definition: For Go, the standalone detector of code.duplication.1 is token-based and already ignores identifier names, so the renamed-copy pass is met by the engine at 60 tokens; the threshold goes to 40 once the 60 pass is clean. For TypeScript the second pass uses identifier matching in its consistent mode at 50 tokens and 8 lines beside the default pass; the blind mode lets any name match any other and matches too much. The default pass returns 0 clones on a renamed copy.
pros: Renaming every name defeats a name-based detector for free; the shape is what repeats.

rules.statement: Functions that do the same job written differently are looked for as advice when a package is added that overlaps a shared one; a semantic near-match to a shared export blocks until answered.

reasoning.definition: The optional mechanism is a clone tool's semantic mode (experimental, a 548 MB local model) or an offline embedding tool that lists pairs with the same intent and different syntax. A report from it is a hint, not a gate.
pros: Same job written differently is a semantic question; a text detector cannot see it.

rules.statement: No file nobody imports, no unused export (including in a shared package), no unused dependency and no unused path alias.

reasoning.definition: In Go the dead-code tool must print nothing, or print only lines on a committed list, because its exit status is 0 even with findings. The dead-code tool and the linter run for each system of the project's list, by GOOS, on the one machine the gate runs on, as one step. Tidying the module file leaves no diff. Both runs are in the local gate. In the web stack the unused-file finder follows the project's entry points (page routes, scripts, test files) with the framework plugins active (else .astro files report false unused), reports unused files, exports and dependencies as errors with a baseline of known ones that only shrinks; the lock holds exactly the declared dependencies. An unused export in a shared package fails.
pros: 27 lines of dead exports in one Go repo; 97 and 124 unused exports in two web repos. At the donor the finder caught unused exports at land on two changes. (An earlier version of this rule asked for a run per GOOS because a single run called the other system's code dead; a product now holds none, so one run suffices.)

rules.statement: No stub is left in shipped source: no not-implemented bodies and no placeholder returns.

reasoning.definition: A command that is not built refuses and says so; documents say what is built and what is only designed. A scan for stub bodies and placeholder returns in shipped source is the check; stub patterns include not-implemented errors and a typed empty value cast to the return type.
pros: A stub that compiles looks like a feature and fails at the first caller.

rules.statement: A project's own Go code has no //go:linkname directive, unless the project lists the file in an exemption with an expiry date.

reasoning.definition: A linkname binds a name to a symbol of another package by string, past the compiler's export rules and the linker's check of what a package may reach. The scan reads every non-generated Go file of the project's own modules for the directive, in test files too, and a hit outside the exemption list is a finding. The list starts empty; a row names the file, the reason and the date it ends, and a row past its date is a finding. The directive needs an unsafe import, but a scan for that import is not the check: the import has other uses and the directive can sit in a file that gosec passes.
pros: A linkname is invisible to the dead-code tool and to the compiler's export rules, and the standard library's linker now refuses new references to its internals, so a binding that builds today can fail on the next toolchain. The gap was found in the review of #650: no rule banned it.

sources.says: The linker now disallows using a //go:linkname directive to refer to internal symbols in the standard library (including the runtime) that are not marked with //go:linkname on their definitions

rules.statement: Identifiers follow the language's case convention and one table of verbs and shapes per layer, and do not stutter on the package name.

reasoning.definition: In Go names are MixedCaps and do not repeat the package name (a type UserStore in package user stutters; Store does not), underscores and initialisms follow the static-analysis style check. In the web stack identifier patterns are enforced per-layer (for example repository methods are find, list, create, update or delete) and names of classes, tokens and routes follow one table that the repo owns.
pros: A fixed table lets a reader and an agent guess a name correctly; a stutter and a free spelling make the same thing two things.

rules.statement: One file-name scheme is used, enforced by lint; names of files, folders and routes follow one table.

reasoning.definition: For TypeScript files the style is kebab-case with middle extensions ignored. In Go file names are a convention with meaning in suffixes, so the narrow part is enforced: lower case and the fixed layout under cmd and internal. Names of non-code files are checked by a name linter.
pros: A second spelling of a file name makes every glob and every search miss half the files.

rules.statement: Before a new name is written, the same name in other repositories is found.

reasoning.definition: Before naming or writing a helper the agent reads the shared module's listing and searches sibling clones; in the web stack the parts catalogue is queryable before a new part, and a second copy found by shape is reported in the change.
pros: An agent invents a name that already exists elsewhere and creates the second spelling.

rules.statement: One spelling is used for each concept across the public surface (paths, parameters, flags, JSON fields and terms).

reasoning.definition: A flag has one meaning everywhere, and documents match the registered flags and JSON fields. The glossary half, a product term defined once and a shared word set with one definition, is held in the docs part (docs.glossary.1 and docs.glossary.3).
pros: Two spellings of one concept make clients and docs guess which one is real.

rules.statement: A comment says why, not what, and none narrates the change; one question judges it.

reasoning.definition: The question: could someone who never saw the code write this comment from the adjacent lines? If yes it goes. A comment that states an interface contract may be longer than a function body, so the length clause is dropped from this rule. A regular-expression report for change-narrating words (now, no longer, previously, used to, changed, was) was considered and not run; false hits are expected. Agents narrate; the question fails narration without counting words.
pros: A comment that restates the line adds a second thing to keep in step with the code. A study of 60 Go bugs found no comment fault, so this is practice and an instruction.

rules.statement: A TODO, FIXME, HACK or XXX names an issue in one shared pattern; a bare one is refused.

reasoning.definition: The tracked form is TODO(#123). The first tier is a comment-node pattern check (it catches line and block-comment forms); the second tier checks that the named issue exists and is open. The Go lint runner's godox cannot test the named-issue form and was rejected; in the web stack the core no-warning-comments rule does not read an issue id, so every TODO fails, and the tracked form needs an expiring-todo rule or a small local rule.
pros: A TODO with no issue is a promise with no owner. Not measured: nothing checks that a TODO names an issue today (one bare TODO in one of six Go repos).

rules.statement: Commented-out code is refused, found by a lint check enabled by name.

reasoning.definition: In Go the check is gocritic commentedOutCode, enabled by name (a stock linter set does not enable it); a two-line commented statement pair beside a nolint line was not reported, so a short group can pass. In the web stack the sonarjs no-commented-code rule fires on some forms and misses others (a commented call chain such as // fetchAll(items.map(x => x.id)); and a commented if block), so it holds only some forms.
pros: Commented-out code is dead code that no tool tracks and that readers cannot tell from intent. Not configured in any Go repo; one source says no tool works.

sources.says: Provides diagnostics that check for bugs, performance and style issues.

rules.statement: Every exported name of a port or shared API has a doc comment stating its contract; elsewhere a doc comment is written only when it says more than the signature, and a comment one could write from the line below is a finding.

reasoning.definition: On a port, a shared package's surface and any other API a second program or package builds on, every exported name has a doc comment stating, where they apply, units, the meaning of nil, null or absent, ownership, invariants, ordering, what it mutates and what it throws or returns as an error. Presence and form there are a rule: in Go the lint runner's exported check over the port and shared-package paths (with its comments exclusion preset off, so it is not hidden) and the doc-comment form check. Elsewhere an exported name gets a doc comment only when it says something local, non-obvious and with no other home; a comment that restates the name or the line below is deleted. The content is review. A surface change of a shared part or port fails until a reason is recorded (arch.shared.9).
pros: Ports are where the reader cannot read the body; a contract that is not written is guessed. A doc comment required on every export elsewhere produces filler that restates the name, which three target repos ban.

rules.statement: Comment blocks stay short within the comment standard, cite a ruling once, carry no decoration lines or narrated history, and do not restate types or facts with a home.

reasoning.definition: A ruling id appears once per file with no prose; there are no decoration lines; doc comments restate no types; a comment id that is cited must exist. In Go inline comment groups over three lines only fall. A checker for comment-block length, decoration lines and restated ruling ids is built because no stock linter does it.
pros: Long, decorated and restating comments rot first and bury the few that carry a contract.

rules.statement: A disable comment carries a reason.

reasoning.definition: In the web stack a lint disable comment with no description fails; the Go counterpart is the nolint rule of the suppression concern in the gates part.
pros: A suppression with no reason cannot be reviewed or retired.

rules.statement: The error path returns early and the normal path stays unindented.

pros: A guard clause keeps the normal path at one level, so the reader does not carry the failure branch while reading the success branch.

rules.statement: The standard library is used where it already does the job.

reasoning.definition: The mechanical neighbours are linters that flag helpers the standard library now has (exptostd, modernize with go fix, usestdlibvars). They hold the common cases only; knowing that the standard library already does the job needs knowing the intent.
pros: A hand-written helper beside a standard one is a copy that will drift.

sources.says: A suite of analyzers that suggest simplifications to Go code, using modern language and library features.

rules.statement: A switch over an enum covers every case.

reasoning.definition: A default case counts as exhaustive in the tool's setting, and tests are excluded.
pros: A new enum value that no switch handles is a silent bug; the linter finds it at the switch.

sources.says: Check exhaustiveness of enum switch statements.

rules.statement: A long switch or if-ladder is table-driven, with the count of over-limit functions ratcheted.

reasoning.definition: Cyclomatic complexity counts every case, and the limit is 30 (a guess). Cognitive complexity scores a flat 159-line table 0 and a long switch +1 once, so it cannot see a long ladder; the cyclomatic count is needed beside it. The cheap cure, moving cases into helper functions, is caught only by the helper pair of code.size.3.
pros: One repo has 5 switches of 10 or more cases. A study of 60 sampled bugs found none with a long ladder as root cause, so this is practice.

sources.says: Computes and checks the cyclomatic complexity of functions.

rules.statement: A component has one reason to change.

pros: A component with two reasons to change is edited by two kinds of change and is the likeliest place for a merge conflict and a regression. No accepted metric exists for single responsibility (the lack-of-cohesion measure was dropped on Go for the same reason).

rules.statement: A value specific to one installation comes only from the loaded config: a literal of one in non-config, non-test code fails, and a default is the program's own neutral choice said once, never one installation's fact.

reasoning.definition: An installation-specific value is a service address, a path on one machine, a port, a container, host, network or household name, or any other fact true of one deployment and not of the program. It comes from the loaded config or is observed on the machine at run time. There is no literal service address or fallback beside the configured one. A default exists only as the program's own neutral choice (a documented port, a path under the platform's standard folders), declared once in the config package. Config is read in one package with a reader, a default and a doc row per key; a secret never comes from a flag. Variables are declared in a typed schema. A word-list check reads non-config, non-test source and the defaults, with the installation's known names, addresses and paths as a list kept outside the repository (supply.secrets.4 holds that list's handling); a hit fails.
pros: A hard-coded fallback address sends traffic to the wrong place when the configured one is missing. A default holding one installation's fact works on the author's machine and silently misbehaves on every other.

rules.statement: A test inherits nothing from the run that started it: its own home and temp folder, and no agent or git variables.

reasoning.definition: A repo test refuses to pass the parent environment to a child process unless the call is marked. Every test package calls one shared isolate function at start-up (a TestMain in Go). In a child's environment a nil value, the parent environment as a whole and an append to it are all findings; the environment comes from the isolate helper. The agent and git variables removed are every GIT_* variable and the agent-session variables; the analyzer is named testenv.
pros: A test that inherits the caller's home, git settings or agent variables passes on one machine and fails on another. Own bugs: 6 of 60 sampled bugs. One repo has the isolate helper; three others copy a client that passes the parent environment through.

rules.statement: Specs get their store from one helper that asserts isolation, so no two tests share data.

reasoning.definition: The helper hands each spec its own database, table or file and asserts it is empty at start. A test that reaches a store any other way fails the scan.
pros: Shared data couples tests through order and timing; one helper is the only place isolation is proved once. The reference practice has one helper per store kind; our Go side gets the same effect from a per-test home and temp folder plus shuffled order (tests.isolation.10).

rules.statement: Heavy test fixtures such as containers start once, in one place, and tests share them only through a helper with its own temp folder and no fixed port.

pros: A container per test turns a suite into hours; a container started anywhere is a fixed port and a leaked process waiting to happen. The real engine is the reference for managed stores (tests.doubles.1).

rules.statement: No test binds a fixed port; every listener asks for port zero or a path in the test's own folder.

reasoning.definition: In test files every listen address is the literal ":0", "127.0.0.1:0" or a path built from the test's own temp folder or testenv.ShortDir. Anything else is a finding: the check fails closed, because a scan for port literals alone passes a port from a constant, a config field or a built string.
pros: Two agents running the same suite on one host collide on a fixed port. Own bugs.

rules.statement: A Unix socket path in a test is at most testenv.SocketPathMax bytes.

pros: The operating system limits socket paths to about 104 bytes and a deep temp folder passes it; one of our programs failed at 153 bytes.

rules.statement: A test does not sleep to wait for an event; it waits on the event or uses a fake clock.

reasoning.definition: A sleep call in a test file is a finding on a shrink-only count per file; removal lowers the baseline. Where the runtime offers it, tests use its fake-time bubble (Go testing/synctest). Fixed waits that stay carry a written reason (tests.flakes.4).
pros: A sleep is a guess about speed that fails under load. Own bugs; counts in test files today: 48, 37, 34, 13, 5 and 4 across six repos.

rules.statement: A test reads the machine (child processes, network, home folder, clock, /proc) only in a named place, and that list only shrinks.

pros: A read of the machine is an input the cache and the selector cannot see (tests.selection.6) and the reason a test passes on one host only. Own bugs. One repo has the scan: 7 files, 121 listed reads.

rules.statement: Default tiers never change shared machine state, a test launches its own browser and database and never attaches to the person's, and no script kills a process by name; an opt-in tier that must touch the service manager does so only under names hashed from its own root and proves its cleanup, and a privileged system test seals the host first and proves the seal.

reasoning.definition: Shared machine state is the service manager, the terminal multiplexer, the real home, the real git config, the person's browser and profile, and any process the test did not start. In the default tiers a scan against a machine-writer list (launchctl, systemctl, tmux, git config --global, the real home, a kill or pkill by name) fails, fakes of those programs sit on the test's PATH, and the isolate helper (tests.isolation.1) gives each test a temp home as a backstop. A test that needs a browser or a database starts its own on a temp profile or a temp data folder. An opt-in integration tier (declared as in tests.admission.5) may register units with the service manager only under names that carry a hash of its own root; its cleanup removes them and then lists what is left under that hash and fails if anything remains. A system test that needs a privileged container first seals the host's devices, kernel settings and cgroups from the container, and a check run before and after proves the seal held.
pros: A test that registers a service, edits the real git config, drives the person's browser or kills a process by name damages the host it runs on; one repo's integration tests need root and write under a system folder. An opt-in tier that must touch the host is held to names it owns and a cleanup it proves, so a failed run leaves nothing behind.

rules.statement: One gate run uses a temp folder reached through a symlink, and the suite passes.

pros: Code that compares paths without resolving links passes on Linux and fails on macOS, where the temp folder is a link. Own bugs.

rules.statement: Tests run in shuffled order in the gate, and the printed seed replays a failure.

reasoning.definition: The shuffle flag is set once in the shared runner configuration and a scan asserts it is in the gate command. One seed catches about half of two-test order pairs, so the admission ladder (tests.admission.1) uses several seeds as separate runs; a count flag with a shuffle seed reuses one order for every repeat.
pros: A test that passes only in file order is not found by retries or double runs, which are banned (tests.flakes.1). Best practice, not measured.

rules.statement: The machine is a stated input: a verdict names the OS and host it ran on, and a result from one OS never satisfies a row that needs another.

reasoning.definition: A verdict names the machine and OS it ran on and the tree it was computed for; the land step refuses a verdict with none, or one for another tree. Skips are counted separately (tests.admission.5).
pros: Own bugs: 17 of 60 sampled bugs were machine-dependent. A verdict names the machine and OS it ran on, so a result is never read as another machine's.

rules.statement: A suite that shares module state between tests lists the tests that need isolation, each with a reason, and a scan looks for the hazard.

reasoning.definition: Turning off per-file isolation in the runner config is refused unless a needs-isolation list file exists. The hazard scan for module-level mutable state is a report.
pros: Sharing a pool is faster and breaks tests that mutate module state; eight specs failed on the donor's first run without isolation. The three tests the lead named were not on the list and only one was traced.

rules.statement: Each module's suite runs with sibling modules unresolvable, a suite that still passes with its subject deleted fails, and a module's tests make other modules' data only through that module's public commands or its own fixtures.

reasoning.definition: A module is a unit of the declared import table (the architecture part's layers). Its suite is run with every module it may not import made unresolvable, so a test cannot reach a sibling the code could not; how that is done is the language part's resolver form (ts.modules.5 for TypeScript; the Go form is held in the Go part). A separate drive deletes the module's own source and runs its suite: a suite that still passes loads nothing of its subject and is vacuous. A test that needs another module's rows creates them through that module's public commands or fixtures that module ships, never by writing its tables directly.
pros: A test that imports across modules passes for a module nobody could extract, a suite that never loads its subject proves nothing, and a test that writes another module's rows encodes that module's schema in a place its owner cannot see.

rules.statement: A test builds the repository, files and folders it needs in its own temp folder, and never reads an ignored file, another member's output, the checkout's own git folder, or another repository's checkout.

reasoning.definition: tests.isolation.1 holds that a test inherits nothing from the run that started it. This rule holds what a test may read from the tree around it: its own package's checked-in testdata and nothing a run writes. A test that needs a git repository makes one in its temp folder. A test that needs a built binary gets it from the package's shared setup (tests.runners.5). A test that needs another repository declares it and fetches it once in setup, or it is an opt-in member that skips with the exact command (tests.admission.5). A test that reads the checkout's own git folder fails in an exported tree and passes in a clone, which is two answers for one tree.
pros: Two tests of one project needed the checkout's own git folder, so every exported tree carried a failure that had to be explained away; four tests of another organisation needed sibling checkouts and failed rather than skipped, so a fresh clone was red.

rules.statement: A repo whose full suite fits its push budget runs it whole and uncached at every push, and a full run always satisfies the gate; where a repo turns selection on, a program picks the tests from what changed, prints what it skipped, and runs global checks whole.

reasoning.definition: Whole and uncached means every test of every package, with any result cache off (in Go `-count=1`), because a cached pass is a claim about a run that did not happen. A repo turns selection on by a declared setting in its gate config, with the measured whole-suite time that passed the push budget; without that setting the selection rules (tests.selection.2 to 15) do not bind and a selected run does not satisfy the gate. Where selection is on: it is by package in Go and by recorded reads in TypeScript; global checks (types, lint configuration, structure, size, vulnerability scan, tidiness) are never affected-only unless the tool is sound under caching: the rule table carries a scope field and the runner refuses an affected-only run of a global check. The plan prints the global list and the gate fails if one is missing from the run. The plan data is a protected path. Tests of the selector plant a failing package behind a changed one, and an unknown path selects everything (tests.selection.2).
pros: Selection is a tool for a suite too slow to run whole, and its only failure mode is a missed dependency. A full uncached run has no such failure and is the claim every target makes, so it is the default, and the selection rules are kept for the day a suite outgrows its budget.

rules.statement: A change the selector cannot place selects everything and says why, for tests and for journeys alike; selection never errs towards fewer.

reasoning.definition: Unplaced means a path in no class of the path-class table, a file no journey declares, go.mod and go.sum or the package lockfile, build and release files, a platform version bump, the journey map and the selector itself. The result names the path and the reason.
pros: Held today in two repos (6 of 6 unplaced paths select everything in one, 15 of 15 and 87 of 87 in the trialled selector); every other path is a guess.

rules.statement: Test selection counts every input a test has (files read, folders listed, modules loaded, programs run), and a test that reads files, globs or spawns programs declares those inputs.

reasoning.definition: A test that reads the file system, globs or spawns declares its inputs with a tag line naming a glob; a dynamic import is banned outside a declared list. A recorded-reads tracer (about 90 lines, about 200 with the selector, near-zero cost) records what each test actually reads. A read behind an unset branch is not recorded. The selector is proved on the TypeScript runner (0 of 69 missed) before any older-runner test file migrates. Globbing libraries covered are glob and fast-glob, as well as readFileSync, readdirSync, fs/promises, node:fs, import.meta.glob and the exec and spawn families. The tracer and selector together are about 200 lines. A non-literal import() is banned outside a declared list.
pros: 44 of 87 test files in one repo read the file system or run a program, so a selector that looks only at imports misses them.

rules.statement: A test whose inputs cannot be seen always runs.

pros: A test that spawns git or a shell reads things no tracer sees; one to two per suite.

rules.statement: A change to the selector, its map, its rules or the hooks selects everything.

pros: In one repo the reach map and the picker sit in the class that selects nothing, a hole held only by a unit test; a documented trade there and a disagreement with the donor.

rules.statement: A cached gate result is trusted only for units that read nothing the cache cannot see, and is keyed so it can be recomputed from the commit.

reasoning.definition: Packages that read the machine (the list of tests.isolation.7) run with the cache off. A cached result is keyed by the check, its command, the content ids of its inputs, the lockfile and the platform; it records whether it came from a run or from the cache.
pros: A cache hides a changed home folder, clock or process; the key must carry every input. Own measure: one repo's selector holds the machine-read list.

rules.statement: No test runs twice on the same tree; a run is proved by a record keyed to the tree.

reasoning.definition: The one exception is the bounded repeat of new or changed test functions at admission: one step of the one proof, able only to fail.
pros: A second run is either waste or a rerun-to-green. One repo keeps the tree-keyed record from the test JSON summary.

rules.statement: A skipped, todo or zero-test run is not a pass; a skip is named in the output and in the verdict, and nothing reports green for what it skipped.

reasoning.definition: The verdict has a not-run section naming each skipped step and its tier, and a schema check fails a verdict without one. A check that needs a browser or a slow tool is named by tier and never silently skipped. A gate fails closed on empty input: a glob that matches nothing or a run that finds zero tests fails. The runner proves it ran its full list.
pros: Green for a skipped step is a lie the next reader believes. Today one repo prints its plan and loses it; the tools already fail closed on empty globs (verified) but custom checks and name filters need the runner to close the gap.

rules.statement: Every unit a run skipped (a package or a journey) is proved skipped by a verdict that names the unit, the inputs compared with the change and the tree, and a skip with no reason fails.

reasoning.definition: A package's reason is that nothing it imports or tests changed, or that the tier is not due. The land step compares the skipped list with the full list and reruns one planted failing unit to show selection still works. A tag's record says whether its test suites ran selected or in full, and at most two tags pass between full runs. A skip counts as proved only once the oracle of tests.selection.10 has run. Each release prints the age of the last whole run; no weekly or other scheduled run is added.
pros: The rule says each skip is proved; without a per-skip record the claim is unproved. One repo records only counts of packages run, skipped and cached.

rules.statement: Applies only to a repo that turns selection on: its selector is judged against an oracle that deletes what tests read, runs everything and counts misses, at adoption, whenever the selector, its map or its rules change, and on every third tag.

reasoning.definition: A repo that runs its suite whole (tests.selection.1) has no selector and records nothing here. One pass runs the suite once per deletion, so it is a separate job outside the release time, run by dispatch at the release step and not on a schedule. The result prints the corpus size, because a smaller corpus is the known way round. It has run on script tests only, never on a browser grid.
pros: Selection has one failure mode, a missed dependency, and the oracle is the only check on it. The rule's "each skip proved" is unproved until the oracle runs; it learns dependencies from deletions only.

rules.statement: A browser-test selector that follows only the test files' imports never skips a test at land, and the flag that does so is banned.

reasoning.definition: The banned flag is the runner changed-only option, --only-changed, which follows import graphs only.
pros: The runner's changed-only flag selected 0 tests on a change to the site (trialled): the rule was a guide line and the lander ignored it.

rules.statement: Applies only where selection is on: a full no-cache run backstops selection at least every third release, the tag records whether it ran selected or in full, and a red locks further releases.

reasoning.definition: A repo with no selection runs whole at every push and records nothing here. At most two releases pass since the last full run. On a red the bad range is bisected, a lock file stops further releases until the miss is fixed or reverted, and each miss becomes a permanent fixture. The backstop runs on the merged tip or the tag, not after every land. A deliberate miss planted in the map must be caught by it.
pros: Selection is exactly as safe as its map is complete; the backstop is how a miss is found and turned into a fixture.

rules.statement: A release reruns the full gate unless a verdict for its exact tree exists, and where selection is on the scoped plan since the last tag is recorded in the tag.

reasoning.definition: The verdict is keyed to the tree hash and comes from a whole run of the gate (the push run or an earlier release run); a verdict for another tree, or from a selected run, does not count. Where selection is on, a tag with no recorded plan or no full-grid age is refused, the full grid runs when the last full verdict is older than a stated line (every third release), and each release prints the age of the last whole run.
pros: A release is a claim about one tree, so it either proves that tree or shows a verdict that already did. Where selection is on, the release is exactly as safe as the map is complete, so the plan is recorded with the tag.

rules.statement: The plan step stays cheap as tests multiply, and an index is built if it passes 2 seconds.

pros: Timed at 0.7 s over 8,700 synthetic tests; a fixed timing gate on a loaded host is the fault tests.flakes.4 forbids, so the number is read unloaded. A timing assertion on a loaded host is load-sensitive.

rules.statement: Page-scoped runs keep a receipt per page and check, holding the content hash of the closure and the green result, and a shared item selects every page.

pros: A design with no build; the web notes warned against building a planner.

rules.statement: A repository turns test selection on at push only when its whole push, run with members at the same time and tests in parallel, still misses its budget on a quiet host, and the owner decides it.

reasoning.definition: Until then every push runs the whole suite (tests.selection.1). When selection is turned on, the train candidate and the release tier still run whole, the run prints every package it skipped and why (tests.selection.9), the stamp records that the run was selected, and the oracle of tests.selection.10 runs at adoption. A path no map places, and the shared inputs (the module files, the selector, the build file, the tool list), select everything (tests.selection.2). The decision is the owner's and is recorded with the measured floor that led to it.
pros: Selection buys about 20 seconds on a 50 second push and trades a whole run at every push for a whole run at every train and release; the study recommends measuring the cheaper changes first.

rules.statement: A split of the gate by language (the TypeScript members only when the explorer or its lock changed, no Go member but the generators and the readers of the contract on a TypeScript-only change) is one row of the selection map and follows tests.selection.16, not a separate switch.

reasoning.definition: The split saves seconds on a Go-only change and minutes on the rare change that touches only TypeScript. It uses the same map, the same skipped-with-reason output and the same whole run at the train and the release as selection does, so it is decided with it.
pros: A second switch beside selection would be a second way to skip a test, with its own gaps; as a row of the map it is held by the oracle already.

rules.statement: Each journey declares what it exercises, and a change selects the journeys whose declared inputs it touches; every command, route or page has a journey.

reasoning.definition: End-to-end journeys of a CLI or a daemon (the built binary run script-style, an install and start under the init system, a request and its answer) and browser journeys declare their inputs: commands, routes, packages, config files, build inputs, source paths. A change selects the journeys whose declared inputs it touches or whose inputs depend on what it touched. The journey map is a file; the command tree (CLI) and the route table (daemon) are the complete list, and a test fails when a leaf command or route has no journey, a journey has no declared inputs, a journey sits in no entry or a glob matches nothing. A flow that spans CLI, daemon and page has one cross-program journey, run when any touched program changes; its declared programs list is the selector's cross-repo input. A consumer contract comes first, so a journey covers only what the contract cannot see. Unplaced paths pick all (tests.selection.2); the plan is printed and carries a hash and a freshness date per map entry. Every cross-service flow has a journey, run when any program it touches changes.
pros: Operator direction: end-to-end tests must be scoped. One repo's browser reach map selected 7 of 41 journey files for a one-card change; none of the repos declares inputs per journey, and the land step runs the whole acceptance suite.

rules.statement: The real built binary runs in a script-style test with its own home, temp folder and environment, and only the acceptance package and its sub-packages run it.

exemptions.reason: It has no binary to run.

reasoning.definition: A shared harness runs the binary (testscript-style or the shared UI test matrix) and one built-binary test exists per program. A program that is only a library has no binary and is exempt. A sub-package of the acceptance package is for a journey that needs a run of its own, as one that runs in a containment which wraps its whole test binary and so cannot hold the other journeys.
pros: Own measure: one repo has the acceptance package; three others carry drifting copies of the client harness. A harness each repo copies drifts.

rules.statement: A binary or page under a gate check records the tree and toolchain it came from, and a check on a stale or unstamped build is refused.

reasoning.definition: Go stamps the revision and the modified flag into the binary (build info); the script test asserts the stamp equals the tree under test and a missing stamp fails. A page build carries the same stamp.
pros: A gate that runs yesterday's binary proves yesterday's tree. The check is the stale-build plant, not the stamp itself.

rules.statement: Each journey declares a stated risk naming what a cheaper test cannot see, an owner and its place in a capped list; the cap is an alarm and not a limit.

reasoning.definition: A schema check on the journey list requires risk, owner and the cheaper-test reason, and fails a journey with none. Identical risk text across journeys is reported. The cap is a guess and only alarms. A cross-program journey lists its programs. A consumer contract comes first. An end-to-end journey records the risk it covers, an owner and why a cheaper test cannot see it.
pros: Journeys are the dearest tests and the rule that every flow has a journey grows the list by one per producer-consumer pair. Authoring is now free, so upkeep is the limit. One repo's journeys are 35 minutes serial for one family (not re-timed). Estate record: 39 journeys in the reference baseline, run only by hand.

rules.statement: An integration or journey test follows one longest path per scenario, and edge cases go to unit or contract tests.

pros: Agents write an integration test per branch unless told, and that is a structural cause of slow suites.

rules.statement: Journeys run on the shipped tree, with no internal stubs and in a development environment only, and leave nothing behind; every created marker is torn down, referents first.

pros: A journey with stubs proves the stubs; one that leaves records breaks the next run. Binds to the tree through the verdict (tests.selection.7).

rules.statement: A program that writes users' files is killed at many points of a write and recovered in a crash-injection run at release, with a short run at push.

reasoning.definition: The release run kills the program at a stated number of points across each write path and checks that every recovery leaves the old file or the new one and never a half. The push run kills at a smaller number of points chosen to cover every path once, and takes seconds. A program that writes no user file has no crash-injection member. The number of points is data on the member, and a path added to the write code adds its points in the same change.
pros: A torn write is found only by the kill that lands in it, and a run long enough to find them all does not belong in a push; the release already runs everything a release alone proves.

rules.statement: A screen is held to one golden width read by a person, and at the narrower widths to properties: no line wider than the screen, nothing cut off, the same rows in the same order.

reasoning.definition: The golden at the standard width is the oracle a person approved. At each narrower width a check runs the same command and asserts the three properties on its output, so a width adds a few lines of data and no golden file. A property that fails prints the width, the row and the measure. The widths are data on the check, and a screen that is new adds its rows to the standard golden only. A column a table leaves out and marks is not cut off only when the width forces it out: the lowest of the table's drop order, in that order, never the first column, and no more than the width leaves no room for.
pros: Three goldens of the same screen at three widths triple the review of every change and say the same thing three times; the properties catch the same breakage and never need a hand read.

rules.statement: The long crash-injection run at release is 400 kill points and 100 recoveries spread over several child processes, each with its own root; a program that writes only its own records takes atomic-write tests instead and is exempt from the crash members.

reasoning.definition: tests.journeys.7 holds that a program which writes users' files is killed and recovered at release with a short run at push. This rule holds the long run's size and shape. The points are split across children so the run uses the pool (gates.command.27) and each child writes under its own root, so a kill in one cannot touch another's files. A program whose files are its own records (a cache, a journal) proves atomic writes (cli.commands.23) and lists no crash member.
pros: The crash run of one project is 400 and 100 by ruling; run in one child it is a serial member that sets the release time.

rules.statement: A journey that needs a virtual machine, a container runtime or a device is a journeys member at release or on demand, skipped with its reason where the host lacks the runtime and listed every run; a container leg for a second platform is a release member, and the long or costly set is on demand.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.30 holds that a member says where it can run and that a skip is red at land and release unless a dated exemption names the machine. This rule places the journeys that need a machine the gate's host may not have: at release where the host has the runtime, on demand for the long set (gates.command.26), and never at push. A platform the project claims is proved by a run on it (gates.command.16); a container leg is one way to run one.
pros: Three projects of one organisation had journeys that need a virtual machine, a container runtime or a device, and each needed somewhere to say the host lacked it without a quiet pass.

rules.statement: Every new or changed test passes a machine-run admission ladder at land: it builds, passes in file order, passes under several shuffle seeds, fails against a break the tool chooses, stays inside its budget and passes a bounded repeat.

reasoning.definition: The land step selects new and changed test functions only. Seeds are separate runs, because a count flag with one shuffle seed reuses one order for every repeat. The break is a mutant in the changed lines chosen by the tool, not the author (comparisons, logic, constants, returns, removed statements); a change with no mutant site prints n/a, and the n/a share is reported as the third result, since n/a is otherwise a free pass. A browser journey takes a break written for its claim, not a mutant. The bounded repeat is the one exception to no test twice on a tree (tests.selection.7): one step of the one proof, able only to fail. Its bound, the seeds and the kill count are not set; any number would be a guess. Surviving mutants on changed lines in core logic and shared parts are reported. A test that mirrors the code passes the ladder, so review keeps that question. The browser-journey break is hand-written for its claim. The time limit is the per-package budget of the shared preset.
pros: Measured elsewhere: a published study admitted generated tests only if they built, passed repeatedly and added coverage, and about three in four built, 57 percent passed reliably and 25 percent added coverage; a scorer was tampered with in 39 of 128 agent runs (older models). Own bugs: 4 of 15 test drives in one organisation pass could not turn a test red.

rules.statement: A test with no assertion, or only tautological ones, is refused, a test that loops over cases, files or items asserts the loop ran at least once with a planted empty case, every guard has a test that sees it refuse, and each test carries one line on what breaks for a person when it fails.

reasoning.definition: A tautology is a literal condition (a log, a literal truth), a comparison of an expression with itself or an equality check of a value with itself, never any constant: a test comparing named constants across packages is a real drift test. The check follows helpers that take the test handle, contract packages and table function values to find an assertion. A single trivial assertion passes this row and the ladder's mutant break catches it (tests.admission.1). A loop over cases, files or items found at run time (a directory listing, a glob, a parsed list) asserts its count is above zero, and the suite holds a plant that feeds it an empty set and must fail. A guard is any code that refuses (a check, a validator, a permission test, a gate rule); each has a test that drives it to refuse and asserts the refusal. The cost line is one comment above the test, in the words of the person who loses when it fails, not a restatement of its name. No test is disabled, focused or commented out (tests.admission.5). How each language writes the shape (helpers, table names) lives in its language part.
pros: Agents are the likeliest authors of weak assertions, and an empty loop is the second way a suite goes vacuous: it asserts nothing and passes. A guard with no negative test is an opinion. The cost line says what the signature cannot: why the test exists. Trial on the Go side of the assertion check: 11 hits in 5,767 tests, 0 to 1 true; the false ones trace to contract suites, table values, helper processes and skip-only tests. Low yield, kept because it costs nothing.

rules.statement: A test can fail: its author shows it red against a deliberate break, and mutation efficacy on the diff in core logic and shared parts does not fall.

reasoning.definition: Mutation testing runs on shared code and core logic, on the diff only, with the threshold set in the tool's config file (a flag on the command line alone does not gate). The subjects of property-test laws are mutation tested. A program can repeat the break (a drive runner). Property tests also get an anti-vacuity check (tests.generated.3).
pros: Own bugs: 4 of 15 test drives in one organisation pass could not go red. One run on the Go side: 86.1 percent on the selector package (not re-run).

rules.statement: A test's expected value is a literal, the spec, a recorded sample of the real server or a generator with a stated invariant, never the code under test.

reasoning.definition: An analyser flags an assertion whose expected value is computed by calling the function under test or a copy of its expression, and a change that edits code and its expected literal together is flagged first for the reader (nothing sees output pasted in as a literal). Only the trivial form is mechanical. Tests are independent of the code they check: daemon samples, not mocks the agent also wrote.
pros: A test written against its own implementation verifies nothing (Khorikov); an agent will paste the code's own output in as the literal. Full independence cannot be checked, the cheap detectable form can.

rules.statement: In the default tiers a skipped, focused, disabled or commented-out test fails the gate, and a test whose precondition is unmet reports not measured, never a pass; an opt-in tier skips with the exact command that runs it and fails when asked to run without what it needs.

reasoning.definition: Default tiers are the ones the gate runs on every push and release. There a skip call, a focus mark, a disabled test or a commented-out test fails; a test that cannot run because a precondition is missing (a tool, a permission, a platform) reports the precondition as not measured in the verdict, and an empty list of cases is not a pass (tests.selection.8). An opt-in tier (real machines, root, a privileged container) is declared in the gate config with the command that runs it; when it is not asked for, each of its tests skips with that exact command in the skip message, and when it is asked for and its precondition is missing it fails, never skips. The skip count of the default tiers is zero; an existing repo that starts above zero holds a shrink-only count until it reaches zero. In Go the count is taken over t.Skip calls in _test.go files.
pros: A skip in a default tier is a test that silently stopped existing. Skips per test in our repos, raw and including environment skips: 102 of 1,645, 74 of 1,731, 68 of 1,020, 38 of 1,301, 25 of 271, 13 of 465.

rules.statement: A test edited in the same change as the code it judges is flagged to the reader with a reason line, not refused; a removed assertion, an added skip, a focused test and a loosened literal are listed first.

reasoning.definition: A real behaviour change also edits its tests, so the flag is for the reader. A changed oracle, golden or fixture on the protected list needs a non-author.
pros: Weakening a test is the cheapest way for an agent to get green; a diff scan makes it visible. The scan with the same list serves Go and TypeScript.

rules.statement: Tests changed in commits marked refactor or move, and surviving mutants on changed lines, are reported.

pros: A refactor that keeps behaviour leaves tests green; tests that fail on such a commit were testing the implementation.

rules.statement: A change that alters behaviour (a command, flag, exit code or UI behaviour) adds or updates a test, or says why not.

pros: A person-found fault becomes a planted check; nothing asks every behaviour change to carry a test.

rules.statement: A boolean switch (an exported flag, a boolean config key or a build constant) is tested for the value it does not ship, or carries a reasoned and ticketed exemption.

reasoning.definition: The rule covers an exported top-level boolean flag, which needs a spec or story naming the value it does not ship.
pros: A switch only ever exercised in its default state is dead code on one side.

rules.statement: A test name is a claim in plain English, and a table test names every case.

pros: Names are how a failure is read; a naming claim cannot be machine judged, only the presence of a case name can.

rules.statement: A managed store (one our own services own) is tested against the real engine, not a fake.

pros: A fake of a store proves the fake. One of our repos has no mock library at all. The reference practice starts a real database in one shared container (see the tool record).

rules.statement: Tests do not mock our own modules, and no mock library is a dependency.

reasoning.definition: Mock libraries (gomock, testify mock, mockery and the like) are banned in go.mod and imports. In TypeScript a module mock or global stub of a module in the repo is banned in test files by a restricted-import or restricted-syntax rule. A fake stands only as in tests.doubles.4, small and written by hand.
pros: Mocking our own code makes the test a copy of the implementation. Own measure: no mock library in any repo today.

rules.statement: A repo keeps a file in a protected path marking each dependency managed or unmanaged; a double of a managed one fails a scan, and a double of an unmanaged one uses literal recorded bytes and asserts no calls on queries.

reasoning.definition: Managed means a database or queue our own services own; unmanaged means a third-party API. A double stands only at an unmanaged edge, is small and hand-written, and carries literal recorded bytes. A call assertion on a query (as opposed to a command) is wrong; whether it is wrong is a review question. The file is a protected path, since marking a dependency unmanaged is the known way round. Recorded bytes are the second choice: where the unmanaged program offers a fake account or a local server, the test runs the real program against it (tests.doubles.5).
pros: Khorikov's line: mock only the edge you do not control, and do not assert on calls that are queries. The file turns a ban of named paths into a check per dependency.

rules.statement: A fake of a store exists only to inject a failure the real engine cannot cheaply produce, a contract test against the real adapter pins that failure, a fake serves its seeded rows and throws on any call it was not seeded for, and no fake returns a constant.

reasoning.definition: A fake answers from the rows a test seeded into it; a call whose arguments match no seeded row throws with the call it got, so a test that forgot to seed fails loudly instead of passing on a default. A fake whose method returns the same value whatever it is asked is refused. One contract suite per fake runs the same cases against the fake and the real adapter, and the failure the fake injects is one of those cases.
pros: A fake that drifts from the engine hides the bug; a contract test per fake proves it against the real one. A fake that answers an unseeded call with a default makes a test pass for a reason the author never chose.

rules.statement: Where a test needs an external program's behaviour it runs the real program against a fake account or server, and only where no fake account exists does it use recorded bytes; tests and stories use fakes generated from the contract, and hand-written network stubs are banned outside the generated folder.

reasoning.definition: The order of preference is fixed. First, the real external program, run against a fake account, a fake model or a local server it can be pointed at. Second, only where the program offers no such account or server, a double with literal recorded bytes at the unmanaged edge (tests.doubles.3), pinned by a contract test where the engine allows one (tests.doubles.4). A hand-written stand-in for the program's behaviour is never used. Generated mock handlers come from the spec, and a lint ban stops hand-written network stubs and per-feature fake harnesses outside the generated folder. In Go the equivalent of a generated fake is a small hand-written fake proved against the real one by a contract test (tests.doubles.4).
pros: A hand-written stub encodes what the author thought the server said, and recorded bytes freeze what it said once; the real program on a fake account says what it says today. Reference practice, one fake source for the whole repo.

rules.statement: Fixtures are the server's own output or held to its type in both directions, every enum member and nullable field has a sample, each supported platform has its own generated example set held exactly, and a test fails when an answer changes.

reasoning.definition: Fixtures come from the server side: its tests write golden JSON from the real encoder (an update flag run only in the owning repo, `-update`), and a check (`companion fixtures --check`) regenerates in memory and diffs (forward direction). In reverse, every golden path must be exercised by the demo world; the check lists golden paths absent from it and fails on a rise (shrink-only). A schema walk over the generated schema confirms a sample for every enum member and nullable field. A program that supports more than one platform keeps one example set per platform, written by one command from that platform's adapter or fake and held exactly; the answer for a feature a platform lacks is one shared body, not a copy per platform.
pros: Fixtures generated from samples run the wrong direction: goldens are the handler's bytes and the schema is a second check. Generators' defaults broke "null, never 0". Own bugs: 11, 6 and 6 faults across three repos. A single example set hides what one platform answers differently.

rules.statement: Fixtures, stories, docs, tests and shipped examples use made-up names only, for people, machines, managed software, networks and addresses, checked against an explicit stand-in list.

reasoning.definition: Every name of a person, machine, container, image, network, domain or account in those paths is on a committed stand-in list, and any other name in a name-shaped position fails. Addresses use the documentation ranges (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32, the example domains), never a real MAC or host. A second check compares every tracked file, commit message and branch name with a roster of real names kept outside the repository or as hashes, never in clear text; the check fails when the roster cannot be read, rather than passing on an empty list. In a public repository every author and committer email is a no-reply address, refused at pre-push.
pros: Real names recurred in fixtures twice (own bugs), and a real host, address or person in a public file cannot be taken back. A stand-in list catches the name nobody thought to put on a roster; the roster catches the known ones in places the stand-in list does not cover.

rules.statement: A failing test is never rerun to green, and a red suite is never accepted as the new normal.

reasoning.definition: No count above one and no retry step or loop in a gate script or workflow, and zero retries read back from the runner configs. The scan excepts the admission step by name (tests.admission.1). A count of one is required by tests.selection.6 and is allowed. A green test list with a non-zero exit is classified as an infrastructure fault before any rerun (tests.flakes.5). A red suite is never re-normalised: the suite is green or the cause is ticketed.
pros: Own bugs: one repo's rule. The donor reruns three times to prove a flake; this catalogue bans reruns and quarantines on first sight.

rules.statement: A result that is not reproduced is quarantined on first sight, ticketed and counted; the quarantined test has an expiry date, by which it is fixed or deleted, and the count and oldest age are reported per repo.

reasoning.definition: A quarantine with no clock is a way to delete a test without saying so. Quarantine is a shrink-only list that does not lock landing but blocks the next proof-debt credit until ticketed; the cap and the expiry follow the exemption rules of the gates part. A quarantine that is a separate suite is not covered by the skip rule. Applies to repos with a flaky-test list.
pros: Fowler names the graveyard: tests left in quarantine are not helping regression coverage, and his remedy is a limit on how many or how long. Neither the cap nor the expiry has a number: both are guesses until a real quarantine set exists.

rules.statement: Record, per test, how often it failed on a tree that later passed unchanged, and report the rate with the machine load at the time.

pros: In one study 78 percent of flaky tests were flaky when first written, so the first sighting is early. Load from parallel agents is a flake source people rarely count: our own swings of 22 and 40 percent in one measurement were load noise. An agent facing a red will rerun it, so the gate must write the record.

rules.statement: A test asserts counted work, never elapsed wall time; where timing is the point, it judges only on an undisturbed machine or as a ratio, and fixed waits carry a reason.

reasoning.definition: A time budget is measured by a script at low load. A loaded box gives no verdict, which is a bounded third result (an all-inconclusive run still locks). A scan for the wall-clock reading used as an argument of an assertion, with the remaining uses in test files on a shrink-only count; a wait deadline is legitimate and carries a marker or allow-list entry. A fixed-waits list and a flake counter exist beside it. Wall-time budgets are measured by a script at low load, never asserted in a test.
pros: Own bugs: 7 of 60 sampled bugs; one project fixed three cases, and 9 load flakes in 12 days read as waits, not pixels.

rules.statement: A green test list with a non-zero exit is classified as an infrastructure fault before it is re-run.

pros: Reruns of an infrastructure fault look like reruns to green.

rules.statement: No rerun closes a red: the hub may rerun a red proof once on a quiet slot as a diagnostic and logs both results, the first red opens the ticket whatever the rerun says, and a second red quarantines the test with an owner and an expiry.

reasoning.definition: tests.flakes.1 holds that a failing test is never rerun to green, and tests.flakes.2 holds the quarantine with its expiry. This rule holds the one rerun that is allowed and what it is for. The rerun is a measurement: run alone on a quiet slot, it tells whether load exposed the fault. Its green does not close anything. The ticket names the test, the load at the red and the two results. A second red of the same test, in any run, moves it to the quarantine list (gates.exemptions.4), with an owner and the date by which it is fixed or deleted. A quarantined race skips its test at push and nothing else: the member still runs, so no member leaves push over one test, and the skip line names the test, the ticket and the expiry. At release a race-kind row's test is not skipped, so the release proves the fix. The first implementation is the shared module's tier quarantine list.
pros: Reruns hide what load exposes: one project's journeys flaked at load 76 to 202 and only under load; 13 red journeys of another were 75 of 75 green alone, and each had a cause and a fix.

rules.statement: A parser of input the program did not write has a fuzz target with seeds checked in.

reasoning.definition: Every parser package listed in rule data has a fuzz function and a checked-in seed folder. Long fuzz runs sit at the slow tier: the changed parser packages on every tag, all of them at least every third tag. The presence check looks for a func Fuzz function and a testdata/fuzz folder in each listed parser package; whether a stateable invariant exists for pure logic is the review half (tests.generated.2).
pros: Practice with fuzz targets already in the repos: 25 in one, 2 and 1 in two others.

rules.statement: Pure logic with a stateable invariant (a formatter, a parser, a pure domain function) has a property test that generates its inputs.

reasoning.definition: A property-based test generates the inputs; fuzz targets for parsers are tests.generated.1.
pros: Generated inputs find the case the author did not write; a property is the stated invariant. The web catalogue has no row for pure UI logic such as formatters and parsers; the rule fits them.

rules.statement: A property test file ends with an anti-vacuity test that shows the generator can produce a failing input.

pros: A property over an empty or constant generator passes forever; the last test in the file proves the generator reaches the interesting inputs.

rules.statement: Each deployed API (a daemon's routes, a service's endpoints) is fuzzed against its own contract, and its responses are checked against the contract.

reasoning.definition: Requests are generated from the API spec and responses checked against it; the running service answers what its spec says. In our programs help and JSON are golden and the command tree is diffed with the last tag, but a daemon's answers are not yet checked against a description.
pros: A page or client consumes the contract; only the server can prove it holds. The web side does not own this check.

rules.statement: Output a person reads is held by a golden file, and the gate compares without writing; a golden a machine reads fails on any change, and one a person reads is approved by a person.

reasoning.definition: git diff --exit-code on golden files after the compare run; the golden helper never writes in gate mode.
pros: Own measure: one repo's goldens-check target; the shared golden helper is used by nobody outside the shared UI test package today.

rules.statement: Long fuzz runs happen on demand, for a new parser in the pull request that adds it, and never as a blocker of a push, a land or a release.

reasoning.definition: The seeds checked in under tests.generated.1 run as ordinary tests in every tier, in seconds. The long run, which mutates the seeds for minutes, runs when the owner asks for it, or when the hub asks the owner first, and a pull request that adds a parser asks for one run of it in its description. A long run that finds a crash adds the failing input to the seeds in the same change as the fix. Fuzz is not a release gate: a release does not wait for it and does not fail for the lack of it.
pros: A fuzz run of 14 minutes 38 seconds found two bugs in 260 commits, both while a parser was new; at the release it cost more than every other member together and found nothing.

sources.says: These entries are run by default with go test, whether fuzzing or not.

rules.statement: A size or depth cap on a parser is proved by the smallest input that crosses it, never by a large input, and an allocation or alias proof shrinks to the smallest size that still proves the cap.

reasoning.definition: tests.generated.1 holds that a parser of untrusted input has a fuzz target with seeds. This rule holds how its caps are tested. A test that feeds a large input proves the cap at a cost of seconds and under the race detector of tens; the input one byte over the cap proves the same thing in milliseconds. A proof that an alias bomb or a deep nest is refused is shrunk the same way. The seeds run in every tier and the long fuzz run is on demand (tests.generated.6).
pros: One project's alias-bomb proof took 23 seconds under the race detector and about 1 second once shrunk to the smallest input that crosses the cap.

rules.statement: Every parser of input the program did not write has a fuzz target with its seeds checked in, or is on a named exemption list that gives its reason, and the seeds run in every tier.

reasoning.definition: The program parses input it did not write when it reads config, a rulebook, a tool's output or a file a person edits. Each such parser has a fuzz function and a checked-in seed folder (tests.generated.1). A parser that cannot have a target, such as one that only wraps a library's own fuzzed parser, is named on a list in the project, one line each with its reason, and the list only shrinks. The seeds run as ordinary tests in the push tier and every tier above it; the long fuzz run stays on demand (tests.generated.6); the caps of a parser are proved by tests.generated.7.
pros: Fuzz found 2 bugs in 260 commits of one project, both while a parser was new; a parser with no target and no named reason is one nobody decided to leave unfuzzed.

sources.says: These entries are run by default with go test, whether fuzzing or not.

rules.statement: Each tier's wall time is recorded per run with the load beside it where the system gives one, and re-measured at each release, never on a timer.

reasoning.definition: The runner writes a times file per run with tier, seconds and the load, and per-package elapsed time from the test JSON; a schema test fails a summary without time and load. A timeout prints the load. The load is the load average where the system keeps one (go-proc load.Read). Where it keeps none (Windows: load.ErrNoAverage) the program records the CPU time of the run's own process tree (proc.Usage with proc.JoinTree) and says that is the figure, never an invented average.
pros: Whole suite 4 to 66 s wall on five repos under load, and the top three packages are 63 to 89 percent of the time in every repo (one sample). Own measure: 7 of 60 sampled bugs were time or load budgets.

rules.statement: Each tier has a whole-suite budget, a selected-run budget where selection is on, and each package a budget, written in one file; a budget is a ceiling with a measured floor, raised only with a new floor measurement in the same change, and a budget that is passed or a package whose time rises tree after tree fails or is flagged.

reasoning.definition: Each budget line holds the ceiling and the floor it was set from (the measured time, the date, the machine and its load). Lowering a ceiling needs nothing. Raising one is refused unless the same change replaces the floor with a new measurement on the stated machine, and the new ceiling stays within the stated margin of the new floor. A count that grows on purpose (tests, packages) is a register, not a ratchet. A slow file is split or declared. Test count is reported beside seconds. The web starting values are 15 s selected and 60 s whole for the first tier, 60 s and 3 minutes, 5 and 10 minutes, and 15 minutes. A ratchet on the count of packages over 5 s is the Go growth check. The fail-closed path (an unplaced path selects everything) may run over the tier's budget; it runs and records the time and is never refused or trimmed.
pros: A suite written by agents cannot grow unnoticed to hours. One repo's browser journeys alone are 35 minutes serial for one family (not re-timed).

rules.statement: A release aims at 15 minutes with a red line of 20 minutes, and the red line is a hard timeout on the release job.

pros: The 20 is a guess until the release is measured step by step; the web notes had set a red line of 40 minutes.

rules.statement: Report the code-to-test change share by test level, and the deletion candidates: tests with no failure in a stated window, identical coverage or a covered path that also has a stronger test; deleting one is a commit with a stated reason.

reasoning.definition: The change share per path class per release is a trigger for what to run and what to fix. Deletion stays a visible act. The reports are built from failure history and per-test coverage.
pros: Agents add and never delete; nothing lists what to delete, so nothing shrinks. The window is a guess.

rules.statement: Coverage is measured per changed file and reported at the slowest tier, and is never a threshold in the inner loop.

reasoning.definition: The record keeps the coverage figure with no floor; packages without tests count as zero percent. No land tier adds a coverage threshold, and a gate scan bans a fail-under line in the Makefile or workflows. Packages without tests count as 0% in the record.
pros: Practice; one repo reports without a threshold. Low value, kept so the cheap scan closes the row.

rules.statement: A time limit stated as a percentage or as a small number of seconds is judged on the median of at least three runs per side, with the base and the head run on the same machine in one window.

reasoning.definition: A small-seconds limit means a limit of a few seconds; a percentage or such a limit needs the median of three runs per side.
pros: On our host on 4 Nov the same tree read 55 s and 67 s plain, and 93 s and 130 s with the race detector across runs: 22 percent and 40 percent between runs of one tree, so one run per side could not tell a regression from noise.

rules.statement: A performance ceiling comes from the 99th percentile of at least twenty runs times a stated margin, with the machine's load written beside each timing.

pros: A ceiling set from one run is noise; the method is a number method, not a check.

rules.statement: Tests have a declared size class bounding what each may touch, and small tests are kept from the network, disk outside temp and the clock.

reasoning.definition: The class comes from a build tag or the test name. A tracer reports what each test touched. Go has no runner sandbox for this, so the class is reported and nothing enforces it by construction.
pros: Practice; the isolation rules hold the parts (own home, no sleep, no fixed port, named machine reads, no machine writes).
