rules.statement: A tier that passes its budget only under the loaded-host clause is a finding, not a pass, and the clause prints at the top of the report where the reader looks.

reasoning.definition: The budget is the tier's measured floor on a quiet host times a stated margin (tests.measures.2; this repository states 1.5). A run on a busy host that is over the budget is not judged, and its report says so in its first lines and counts the run as unjudged, not as green. The tier is judged on the next quiet-host run, and a tier whose last quiet-host run was over the budget fails on budget. A run that is only green because the host was busy is never recorded as the floor.
pros: Every measured push run broke its 180 second budget (206 to 301 seconds) and passed only through the clause that excuses a busy host, so the budget never pushed the heaviest member out of the tier.

rules.statement: A tier's floor is its best time on a quiet host, written with its date, machine and load; the budget is the floor times 1.5; a target such as about one minute is never a budget, and a project's budget is its own.

reasoning.definition: tests.measures.2 holds that a budget is a ceiling with a measured floor and is raised only with a new floor. This rule holds how the floor is taken and how far the budget sits above it. A floor measured on a loaded host is not a floor, and every number from a study of a busy host is a target until a quiet run is made. The margin is one number for every project, 1.5, so a report that prints the floor and the budget can be read without the file. A run over its budget on a busy host is unjudged, never green, and says so in its first lines (tests.measures.9).
pros: Every measured push of one project broke its 180 second budget and passed through the loaded-host clause printed at the bottom where nobody read it; another organisation had no budget at all, and a commit hook took 218 to 241 seconds unseen.

rules.statement: A test that takes over a third of its timeout when the host is idle is a finding, before it ever fails.

reasoning.definition: A timeout is sized for a loaded host and a test that uses a third of it when idle uses all of it at load three. The finding names the test, its idle time and its timeout, and is fixed by making the test faster (tests.runners.5, tests.runners.8) or by splitting it, never by raising the timeout alone. The tier report lists the tests over the line.
pros: One test took 9.5 seconds idle against a 30 second limit and went red at load 27; another's module took 565 milliseconds idle against a 60 second budget and still timed out nine times, and the tickets stayed open 21 to 23 days.

rules.statement: A timing assertion on a shared host is off the blocking path: it is judged against a reference taken in the same run and only on undisturbed samples, and a reading that cannot be judged gives no verdict for a bounded time, three tips of the main branch or 24 hours, and then locks.

reasoning.definition: tests.flakes.4 holds that a test asserts counted work and judges timing only on an undisturbed machine or as a ratio. This rule holds what happens when the machine is never undisturbed. The reading is inconclusive, not red, and the run is green for everything else. Inconclusive readings are counted, and after three tips of the main branch or 24 hours without a judged sample the member locks landing until someone measures on a quiet host. A rule that turns one inconclusive reading into a lock holds landing for a host it cannot control.
pros: One organisation's timing specs put 11 of 44 land logs red in one day and locked landings twice, and a rule that turned an all-inconclusive budget into a lock held landing for 8 hours 2 minutes.

rules.statement: Unit tests run in the gate from one runner, uncached, over the whole tree, or where selection is on for the packages that changed.

reasoning.definition: The default is every unit test of every package with the result cache off (tests.selection.1); a repo runs only the changed packages only when it has turned selection on.
pros: A test that is not in the gate does not exist for the agent; unit tests are the fastest tier.

rules.statement: Test and browser workers per run equal cores divided by concurrent slots, with the slot count read from the job tool and never hard-coded, applied only inside a slot.

pros: On the current host 15 cores and two heavy slots give 7 workers per run; a hard-coded number oversubscribes one run and starves another.

rules.statement: The test runner configuration is one shared preset, and race, leak and shuffle flags are set once in the shared fragment.

pros: One preset is the only place a flag is set once; the reference practice has one preset for every program.

rules.statement: A test runs in parallel with the others of its package by default, and a test that runs alone says why in its own code.

reasoning.definition: A test that needs its own process state (an environment variable, the working folder, a global) is the exception, and it carries a comment naming the state it needs. A test that only needs a variable for a child process sets it on that child's environment and stays parallel. The cases of a long table test are parallel subtests when each has its own temp folder. A package whose tests all run one at a time is a finding in the tier report, with the share of its wall time. This rule holds the tests; gates.command.17 to .20 hold the members around them. The shuffle seed (tests.isolation.10) still prints, and a test that fails only in parallel is a bug ticket, never a retry (tests.flakes.1).
pros: One push kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy because two packages ran 152 and 101 tests one after another; making them parallel removes the longest member of the tier without dropping a test.

sources.says: Parallel signals that this test is to be run in parallel with (and only with) other parallel tests.

rules.statement: Expensive setup (a build, a clone, a started program) runs once per package, in TestMain or a once, and never once per test or per case.

reasoning.definition: A case that needs a different input to the same built program reuses the build and changes the input. A case that must have its own build says so in its code. The setup writes nothing into the tree under test. This is about how many times the work is done; tests.isolation.3 holds how the shared fixture is reached (through a helper with its own temp folder and no fixed port), and both hold together.
pros: One test built the landing judge and ran the landing script four times, 38 to 47 seconds of every push, to prove four things that one build could show.

sources.says: TestMain runs in the main goroutine and can do whatever setup and teardown is necessary around a call to m.Run.

rules.statement: The race detector runs at push over the light packages, and the heavy race run is on demand; the race detector is not turned off at push.

reasoning.definition: The light packages run with the race detector on in the push tier, because a race there costs a few seconds of wall time and is found at the earliest moment. The heavy race run (the packages whose race build takes minutes) leaves every tier and runs when the owner asks for it, or when the hub asks the owner first. A change that adds shared state across goroutines to a heavy package asks for that run in its pull request. Turning the race detector off at push is not taken: it saves about 17 seconds of wall time today and about none once members run together.
pros: The heavy race tests took 6 minutes 38 seconds of a release and found no race; the light race run costs 17 seconds of wall time and keeps every race visible at push.

sources.says: The cost of race detection varies by program, but for a typical program, memory usage may increase by 5-10x and execution time by 2-20x.

rules.statement: A project that turns the race detector off at push names who runs it on the main branch each day, and an issue opens on a red.

reasoning.definition: The name is a person, a scheduled job or an agent, written in the project's test guide, and the run is daily on the default branch. A red opens an issue with the failing package and no one waits for the next day to read it. This project keeps the detector on at push (tests.runners.6), so the rule binds a project that takes the other road; a daily run that the guide asks for and nobody runs is the failure it prevents.
pros: In one project the daily race run its docs asked for was not happening, and its main branch failed the race detector on a data race in test code.

sources.says: the daily race run the docs asked for wasn't happening, and main now fails race on a data race in test code.

rules.statement: A test that waits out real time (a timeout, a retry delay, a poll) runs on a fake clock, and a real sleep in a test is a finding with its reason beside it.

reasoning.definition: The code under test takes its clock as an input, or the test runs it inside a bubble whose time package is fake, so a wait of seconds takes no wall time. A test that must observe real time, such as one of the clock adapter itself, says so in its code. The wait is not shortened by setting a smaller timeout in the test, as that tests another number.
pros: A test that waits out real time takes that time on every run however many cores it has; a fake clock takes none, and the same holds for the other time recommendations.

sources.says: Within a bubble, the time package uses a fake clock.

rules.statement: A module's whole suite is one invocation of the test tool per tier, so the runner spreads its packages over the CPUs, and a per-package timeout lives in that invocation's flags, named in the members file.

reasoning.definition: Two batches of one module run the second after the first and the CPUs idle between them. One invocation over the whole module lets the test tool schedule every package at once. A second invocation for a cover profile is the same suite run twice; one run gives the verdict and the profile. A second module in the same repository (a web folder, a tools module) is its own member with its own folder. The timeout that applies to each package is a flag of the invocation and the members file names it, so the number is in one place.
pros: One project ran its tests as two batches, 135 seconds, where one batch takes 51 seconds; another ran its Go tests then its web tests in series; a third ran the test tool twice, the second time for a cover profile sent nowhere.

rules.statement: The package whose tests read the whole tree reads it once through one shared snapshot and scans in parallel, and it may run without the race detector at push when an on-demand race member covers it.

reasoning.definition: Every project has one package of tests that read every file: names scans, repository rules, layout checks. It runs on every change whatever changed, so it sets a floor for every push and makes selection pointless for itself. Its tests share one read of the tree taken in the package's setup (tests.runners.5) and scan that snapshot in parallel (tests.runners.4). It checks text, not concurrency, so under the race detector it is 7 to 40 times slower for nothing; tests.runners.6 keeps the detector on at push for the light packages, and this package is the one exception, covered by the on-demand race run.
pros: It was the slowest package in every project of one organisation, 7 to 40 times slower under the race detector: 47 seconds to 334 seconds in one, and one test from 4.5 seconds to 72.8 seconds in another.

rules.statement: The gate's own tests run in the test member, parallel and built once, and never as a serial step of their own on every push.

reasoning.definition: A gate has tests: of its runner, its scripts, its plants (gates.plants.12). They are tests like any other and belong in the test member, where they run beside the rest and share the package's setup. A self-test step that runs each gate once more, or a sweep that runs each gate twice, is the suite run again in series, and it sets the push time.
pros: Self-tests set the push time in three repositories of one organisation, 126 of 189 seconds in one service and 221 of 254 seconds in another; the gate's tests were one project's slowest package, 126 seconds, for the same reason.

rules.statement: A change to the test runner's pool, isolation or worker settings is proved on the whole suite in the shared pool, on every host the project claims, before it lands.

reasoning.definition: Isolation off, a shared pool, a worker count: each changes what every test sees, and a test that passes alone can fail only there. The change's proof is the whole suite under the new setting on each claimed platform (gates.command.16), run where the other gates run, not on a quiet machine. A selected run proves nothing for a setting that touches every test.
pros: One organisation set isolation off on a shared pool; four specs went red only there, one at 31 seconds against 6 seconds alone, and two changes were held off the main branch for 4 hours 23 minutes.

rules.statement: Every gate run goes through one shared gate command that runs every check at each tier, from the hooks and from the land job.

reasoning.definition: The same command serves every tier (on write, commit, stop, push, land, full or after release), chosen by a flag, and it is the same in every repo: one gate script, shared, with no second entry point that runs checks. A Go repo's single `check` target and a TypeScript repo's single gate script are both this command. The hook's list is a declared subset of the land job's list: the land job calls the push tier and then the full tier, and the full tier holds what the push leaves out (the tests, the vulnerability scan, the conformance check), so every member of either runs before main.
pros: Separate entry points drift: a check is added to one and not the other. A hook that runs a fast subset of its own reports green for what the land job would refuse, so the subset is declared in the land job's list, and the land job runs every member of it and of the full tier on the merged tree before main: nothing the land job would refuse reaches main.

rules.statement: A repo enforces its rules with no helper tool installed: the gate and the hook run in a clean clone with that tool absent from PATH.

reasoning.definition: The gate and the hooks use only standard tools and the repo's Taskfile tier (the push tier for the hook). The check runs the gate in a clean clone with PATH stripped of our own helper CLIs, for example with a minimal environment. A repo does not depend on a command that a fresh checkout lacks.
pros: A gate that needs a helper nobody installed is skipped silently on a fresh machine or in a clean clone. Five of seven Go repos have a tracked pre-push hook, two have none (V-88).

rules.statement: Every rule names one home tier and its time budget in the rule data; a check that cannot meet its tier's budget moves to a later tier, never to a timer.

reasoning.definition: The tiers are on write, before commit or at the agent's stop, before push, at land, and after release. The rule data carries a tier column and a budget per rule, validated by schema (the tier column is schema-checked), and the gate runner reads the tier from the data to decide when a check runs. A test checks that each tier's measured wall time is inside its budget from the gate summary. A rule with no tier fails the schema.
pros: Tiers written as prose tables drift from what runs. A check that is too slow for its tier and is run "at most every so often" by a timer is not a gate any more.

rules.statement: Where a repo turns test selection on, what a tier runs is chosen by a planner from declared scope rules for that tier, from what changed; a full uncached run always satisfies the gate, and a repo whose full gate fits its push budget runs the full gate.

reasoning.definition: Selection is optional. The default is the whole gate on every push, with tests uncached (a cached pass is a claim about a run that did not happen). A repo turns selection on only when its full gate does not fit the push budget of gates.hooks.4. Then the scope rules are one declared file per repo (path classes mapped to checks and tests), a selector picks the packages, domains or journeys from the changed paths and the dependency graph, the runner reads tier and budget, and the plan is built by the selector from the path-class table. The tiers, scopes and targets are a written table. Whatever selection is on, a full uncached run is always accepted as passing the gate.
pros: Three target repos run the whole gate on every push, and a selector is a second program that can be wrong. Where the full gate does not fit, a hand-picked subset lets an author choose what proves their own change, so the subset comes from declared rules.

rules.statement: The planner fails closed to a full run on a global-class path, an unplaced path, a dirty tree, an unresolvable range or a failed graph build, and says why.

reasoning.definition: A change that cannot be placed runs every check and journey. Global-class paths include package manifests and lockfiles, compiler and lint and build and test configuration, shared style files, generated type declarations, infrastructure and environment files, the test kernel, API specs, generated code, the domain map and the gate scripts themselves, and also `go.mod`, `go.sum` and build files for Go. Also full: an unknown path, a file with no owner or two owners, an unresolvable range, a dirty tree at the land tiers, a failed graph build. An empty or missing input fails. A change to the selector selects everything. Message catalogues that have their own validator are not global-class, and the planner does not widen to the full suite for them.
pros: A selector that guesses on a path it cannot place proves a subset and calls it green; a lead once reported 14 chosen tests green where the package would have failed 4.

rules.statement: Checks that are global by nature run whole at every selected tier, whatever the plan selects.

reasoning.definition: Types, lint, structure, size, module hygiene, vulnerability scan, regeneration and import rules are whole-program checks and are never affected-only unless that is proven sound under caching. The list of always-full checks is written in one place and runs in full at the push, land and full tiers.
pros: An affected-only run of a whole-program check misses breakage that arrives through a file the change did not touch.

rules.statement: Tiers have written time budgets, recorded in one place; they are targets that the runner prints wall time against.

reasoning.definition: Budgets: on write about 2 s, commit 10 s, stop 60 s, pre-push 3 min, land 5 min for a selected run and 10 min for a whole run, after release 15 min. The selected and whole budgets of every tier are written in one place. They are targets and are only reported, never enforced as timers (the one enforced bound is gates.command.8).
pros: Without written budgets nobody notices a tier creeping; at one reference team the budgets were missed three to six times in the field. The first merge put 2 s on pre-commit, which belongs to on-write.

rules.statement: The release workflow's test jobs carry a stated timeout, and a run that reaches it is cancelled.

reasoning.definition: Each test and build job in the release workflow on the tag sets a `timeout-minutes` value; 20 minutes is the default red line, and a job that needs more states its number and reason in the workflow. A job without a timeout fails the workflow check. There is no after-release gate job and no hosted job on push; the slow members of gates.hooks.4 run here, before publish.
pros: A release gate that can run without bound is an outage that nobody sees until it ends.

rules.statement: A gate's cost is measured on a real workload, with an input count above zero, before the check is placed in a tier.

reasoning.definition: The rule table requires a measured block for each check (the workload, the input count, seconds and load) before a check may be assigned a tier. A measurement with 0 inputs does not count.
pros: Prices measured on an empty source mislead: the first cost figures for UI gates had no UI source at all (V-25).

rules.statement: An agent-time check finishes within 2 seconds on the edited file or runs at the agent's stop; the finding appears where the author is.

reasoning.definition: After each edit the changed file is formatted and linted by a warm, untyped, time-capped step: a long-lived lint server (one per worktree, started by the setup step and restarted when its status check fails) plus the formatter, with a hook timeout of about 15 s. If the server is unavailable it falls back to the untyped lint config rather than skipping, and it never runs the type checker. For Go, gofmt and goimports on one file take 0.02 s and need no server, so the 2 second check is the home. The hook wrapper times each check and fails the registry test when one exceeds 2 s on one file.
pros: A finding shown after the author has moved on costs a round trip; a slow edit-time check is turned off. One sample each under load: gofmt on one file 0.02 s, go vet on one package 1.76 s, golangci-lint 1.38 s.

rules.statement: The stop tier runs the fast checks, blocks on red naming the failing step, and never claims green for what it skipped.

reasoning.definition: The agent-stop hook runs the stop tier. A skip is named in the verdict and printed, and the cheap tier runs on stop. The skipped list is the one gates.plants.8 requires.
pros: A stop hook that reports green for a skipped step teaches the agent to stop early.

rules.statement: The template gate script arms the hooks first, then runs every member and accumulates the results, never stopping at the first red, and prints the cheapest failure first in its summary.

reasoning.definition: One gate script is the template for every repo. It arms the hooks, then runs every member: the structural check of the managed root files, the supply-chain config check, lint, the type check, the tests and the scans. Each member's findings print under its name. A summary line counts green, findings and could not run per member, ordered so the cheapest, most informative failure is shown first. The exit is 1 if any member found something, 2 if any could not run and none found, 0 otherwise. A member's failure never hides another member's result.
pros: One script per repo drifts. A gate that stops at the first red shows one failure per push, so a change with three faults takes three pushes; accumulating shows all of them at once, and the summary still puts the cheap failure in front.

rules.statement: A gate script that sets `pipefail` does not pipe into `grep -q`, `head` or `read`; capture the output first, or count.

reasoning.definition: With pipefail, a producer that dies of SIGPIPE when the reader exits early flips the pipeline status. Gate pipelines carry `pipefail` (the shared `check-gate-commands` check: workflow run steps declare a shell with it, or set it), and a pipeline whose consumer is `grep -q`, `head` or `read` is a finding. Shellcheck does not catch this. The structural rule is a `gatescan` rule.
pros: Latent: no shell file sets pipefail yet (0 of 36), 73 sites pipe into grep -q or head in shell files and 6 in Makefiles, so the first repo to add pipefail would flip statuses. The planted gate_bad.sh printed ok with the forbidden word present and shellcheck exited 0.

rules.statement: Gate tiers are not chained with `&&`; each tier runs and reports on its own.

reasoning.definition: Chaining tiers with `&&` lets an early failure hide the later tiers' results and lets a skipped tier read as green.
pros: A chained script reports only the first red, and a short-circuited tier never prints that it was skipped.

rules.statement: A Taskfile declares each task once, beside itself, and a generator registers its generate and check tasks in the tier lists from its own block; no shared line names every task.

reasoning.definition: A single line that lists every task is rewritten by every change that adds one, and the two tasks that run every generator are edited by every change that adds a generator. Each task carries its own declaration, and each generator adds its tasks to the tier lists (push, land, release) from its own block. A test over the Taskfile fails a task that is declared twice or listed in no tier, and a generator with a generate task and no check task.
pros: Own measure: in three days a build file changed in 24 commits, and 18 of them rewrote the phony line or the two generator recipes.

rules.statement: A program that declares supported platforms runs its tests on each of them, not only builds for them, on our own machines; the hosted machines run only at a release; a test that needs one platform says so through the platform table, never through a runtime check in the test.

reasoning.definition: The platforms a program supports are data on the program. Every test runs on our own machines, one leg for each platform, and the hosted machines run only at a release. A leg that has run on a platform is the proof for that platform only. A native run on a system the Mac cannot reach is owed to the next lent window: the change that needs it is queued, and the lent machine posts a comment whose first line is the system, the commit and pass or fail. A test that needs one platform is listed against it in the platform table, so the other legs do not run it; a test that asks the operating system at run time whether to skip itself is a finding. supply.release.7 holds the compile at push for every shipped platform and tests.isolation.11 holds that a verdict names the machine it ran on; this rule holds that the gate itself runs on each one.
pros: A build that compiles for a platform proves nothing of what runs there; the organisation's own gate ran on one platform while the program declared two.

rules.statement: The gate has tiers by moment: commit runs the check-only members in seconds, push runs the whole gate within its budget, review asks whether an independent reader accepts it in one round or two, landing proves the candidate once, release adds only what proves a release, and on demand holds the deep runs, which block nothing.

reasoning.definition: Six moments, each with one question and one budget. Commit holds only members that read and never rewrite (gates.hooks.3). Push holds every member a pushed tree must pass, and its budget is a measured number (tests.measures.9, tests.measures.2, tests.measures.10). Review is the one moment with no members: its budget is rounds, one and two at most, and its rules are agents.review.1 to .7. Landing proves the merged candidate once (gates.land.12, gates.land.16), and a pass bound to a tree is not run again for the same tree (tests.selection.7). Release is push plus the members that prove only a release: the crash-injection run and the reproducible-build dry run, with the cross-platform compile already at push. On demand holds the long fuzz run and the heavy race run (tests.generated.6, tests.runners.6); an on-demand run is asked for and reports, and no tier waits for it (gates.command.26). On demand is not a tier a member moves to: it holds only the two runs named above, and adding one is the owner's ruling. A member names its tier in data (gates.command.3), and a member that cannot meet the budget of its own moves only to a later blocking tier (push to release), never to a timer, never to on demand and never out of the gate. There is no moment below push: the builder's hand-in is the whole push tier (gates.command.31). Each moment has an owner, and a stack adds members to these moments and never a moment of its own.
pros: The release tier took 27 minutes 47 seconds, most of it fuzz and heavy race runs that found two bugs in 260 commits; cut back to the push tier plus crash injection and the dry run it is about 1 to 1.5 minutes.

rules.statement: The members of a tier run at the same time by default; a member waits only for the member it declares it needs, and that order is kept and shown, never hidden.

reasoning.definition: A member that reads what another writes declares `after` that member in the member table, and the runner keeps the edge when it runs the members in a pool. The report names each member, how long it ran and, for a member held back, the member it waited for. The pool never stops or cancels the other members at a red, so a tier still runs everything and lists every failure (gates.command.12, never stops at the first red). Results are collected and printed as the serial runner prints them (cheapest first, failures cheapest first), and the stamp and the budget are unchanged. A member that passes only because another one ran first, with no `after` declared, is a finding the first time a run orders them the other way.
pros: The pre-push tier ran fourteen members one after another and kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy; a hidden ordering (one test needing a file another member writes) is what a parallel runner would break first.

rules.statement: Tools are installed only when a pin changes, and checked once per run: the check is the guard and the install is the fix.

reasoning.definition: A run checks every tool against its pin first, and installs only when that check fails or when a pin file (the tool list, the lock files, the explorer lock) changed since the last green check, which a sum beside the tools folder records. The gate keeps its own check so it stays self-sufficient, and the build file's check target does not run a second one before it. The one check left is the whole pin check: every program's sha256 against the tool list, the refusal of a name the list does not pin, and the network-block proof with its version read-back, where the system gives a block; where it gives none (sandbox.ErrNoBlock) the check is refused by name and never passes unblocked. The sum decides only whether to install, never whether to check; it is unsealed, so it is a cache and not a verdict. A tool off its pin fails the check and nothing else runs.
pros: Every push installed the tools again and checked all eleven twice, 5 to 13 seconds of a tier whose budget is a minute, and the second check changed nothing.

rules.statement: The gate reports how many CPUs it kept busy on average beside its wall time, and a tier that keeps a small share of them busy is a finding.

reasoning.definition: The report states the busy share and the CPU count it was judged against. A tier whose members could run together but whose busy share stays low is a finding that names the serial member or package that holds the rest back. The share is read with the host's load beside it (tests.measures.1), because a busy host lowers the share a run can take, and the finding is judged on a quiet run (tests.measures.9).
pros: The gate's own report said it kept 1.7 of 15 CPUs busy while the tier broke its budget; the number was printed and nothing acted on it.

rules.statement: After the documented setup, every member passes on a fresh clone, with no file an earlier run left behind and no ordering between members that is not declared.

reasoning.definition: The proof is a run of the tier in a clone made from the remote, after the setup the README names and nothing else. A member that needs an ignored file says which member writes it (gates.command.18). A member that needs a module graph, a tool or a platform step that only the setup of an earlier run primed is a finding. The release dry run is the usual place it shows.
pros: A second machine hit two reds on its first run: the release dry run failed until a cross-platform module graph was primed, and a docs test failed until an ignored file a different member writes existed.

rules.statement: A lint step never fails or waits because another lint runs on the same host: it runs with `--allow-parallel-runners` on the one shared cache.

reasoning.definition: golangci-lint refuses to start while another copy runs as the same user, and the gate runs it with `--allow-parallel-runners`, which takes no lock, so two copies on one host both run. The cache is the same folder as before: the tool's cache code is safe for several processes on one machine to share, and it will not corrupt the cache, so no cache per run is needed and none is made. `--allow-serial-runners` is not used: it waits on a host-wide lock with no deadline, so every repository on the host queues behind one lint, and the wait counts against the tier's budget as a red that says nothing of the code. The rule does not rely on a job queue that runs one gate at a time, because a queue that allows several runs does not prevent the clash, and a second repository on the same host is outside any queue. It lands with the parallel members (gates.command.18), which make the clash likelier, and never after them.
pros: Runs of three repositories failed with "parallel golangci-lint is running", a red that said nothing of the code; the shared cache is safe for it, so no run needs to wait.

sources.says: It is safe for multiple processes on a single machine to use the same cache directory in a local file system simultaneously. They will coordinate using operating system file locks and may duplicate effort but will not corrupt the cache.
--allow-parallel-runners: Allow multiple parallel golangci-lint instances running. If false (default) - golangci-lint acquires file lock on start.
It lands with P1, not after.

rules.statement: A repo's own Taskfile lists every check as a member of one of three tasks named pre-commit, pre-push and release, each member a line of `cmds:` with its own `timeout:`, and `gragas check` verifies that contract; a repo differs from another only in which commands fill each tier, and any other difference is a recorded exemption with an expiry.

reasoning.definition: There is no shared runner and no members file: each repo runs go-task from its own Taskfile, pinned in a tool modfile, and `gragas check` reads the Taskfile and holds it to this shape. A member is a `cmd:` with a `timeout:`; the `timeout:` is read on the member, because go-task ignores one on the task and ignores any key it does not know, so a misspelt `timout:` passes in silence and the check must refuse it itself. A member that times out is killed and the run is red (go-task exit 208), but a child it started in the background can outlive it, so a member starts none. `cmds:` run in order and the run stops at the first red member; a member that may be red without stopping the run says so with `ignore_error: true`, and that line is read as an exemption with its reason. `deps:` run in parallel, and a tier uses them only for members that do not share a folder, a file or a port. A tier is verdict-true only when nothing in its environment changes the verdict, and the tier pins or clears what can: `TASK_DRY` (runs nothing and exits 0); `GOFLAGS` when it holds any flag that selects or skips tests or changes what is built (`-run`, `-skip`, `-count`, `-mod`, `-tags`: `-run=TestPass` turned a red tier green, and so did `-run=NoSuchTest`), which the tier clears or sets itself; and `TASK_CORE_UTILS`, which can switch a member from the real utilities to Go's bundled ones (a GNU flag can stop working), so the tier sets it and a member does not depend on a GNU flag. `TASK_CONCURRENCY` only serialises `deps:` and changes no colour. A repo with nothing to run says so in its Taskfile, so an empty tier and a missing tier are not the same thing. gates.command.1 holds that one command runs every check; this rule holds that the list the command reads has one shape everywhere. Evidence: a spike on Linux and on Windows; the macOS half is owed.
pros: Six projects of one organisation ran six gate shapes, and 39 repositories of another ran 39: most stopped at the first red, two kept a stamp keyed to a 24-hour age, and 36 of 38 checked nothing at commit.

sources.where: the answers to the test section
the answers to the test section and the gotchas

rules.statement: A browser, a container image and a tool that is not a module are tools: pinned by version or digest, installed per project when the pin changes, and a gate never prunes a cache it shares with another project.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.19 holds that a tool is installed when its pin changes and checked once per run. This rule says what counts as a tool. A browser the tests drive is pinned and installed by the project; a container image is pinned by digest and pulled before the lock, never inside a start call; a tool that is not a module of the project's language is pinned by checksum (supply.provenance.7). A cache shared between projects on one host is never pruned by one project's gate, because the next project's run pays the install again.
pros: One project's gate pruned browsers from the shared cache on every run, and another reinstalled its packages every push for 6 to 8 seconds; in a third organisation installs of 106 to 180 seconds sat in no budget and a stale install after a lockfile change gave 170 false lint errors.

rules.statement: A lint or test tool gets its worker count and its cache in every tier, derived from the pool's capacity, and a tool's settings never depend on which slot or host the run lands in.

reasoning.definition: The worker count comes from the capacity the job tool sets on the child process (gates.command.27, tests.runners.2), and the cache folder is the same in every tier, so a warm run is warm whether it runs at push, at land or at release. Two checks on one host never refuse each other (gates.command.22). A setting that differs by slot kind gives the same tool two speeds and a budget that cannot be set.
pros: One lint command took 394 seconds cold in one slot kind, about 128 seconds in the other, and 8.8 seconds warm with four threads; the same command, three speeds, and a push that was 65 percent that one member.

rules.statement: A run off the cycle, scheduled or on demand, exists only if someone watches it: it is named in the members file, its result is logged where the hub reads it, and a red opens an issue the same day.

reasoning.definition: The on-demand tier holds the deep runs (gates.command.17): the long fuzz run, the heavy race run, a cross-browser run, a tier that needs cloud credentials. Each is a row of the members file with the tier on demand, so the list is one list. A run is asked for by the owner or asked of the owner, and the hub's daily race run on the main branch is one such run. A run that nobody reads is not a check, and a red that waits for the next run to be noticed is a red main that nobody knows about. tests.runners.7 holds the race case; this rule holds every run off the cycle.
pros: One project's daily race run stopped silently and its main branch failed the race detector with nobody knowing; another organisation ran integration, characterisation and mutation checks by hand with no request path, no log and no issue on red.

rules.statement: The pool's capacity is the host's cores divided by its slots, set on the child process by the job tool and never written into a recipe; a member's weight is a promise and a cap, and a member heavier than the capacity runs when the pool is empty.

reasoning.definition: tests.runners.2 holds the worker count of a test or browser runner. This rule holds the pool that runs the members (gates.command.18). A member declares its weight, the pool admits members while their weights sum to the capacity, and a member that uses more than its weight is a finding. Nothing in a recipe or a script hard-codes the number: the job tool knows how many slots the host runs and sets the capacity once.
pros: One web project went red with every test passing when uncapped test workers ran beside other gates: worker timeouts rose 1, 6, 12 over three runs; capped, 9,428 of 9,428 passed. Three slots on 15 cores gave a load of 26 with no gain in total work.

rules.statement: A check never writes the tree it reads: a generator check works in a copy and compares, a formatter checks and never rewrites, and where a member must write, every member that reads its output declares that it runs after it.

reasoning.definition: Members run at the same time (gates.command.18), so a member that rewrites a file under another member is a race. The generated-files check regenerates into a temporary folder and diffs. The format check lists the files that differ and exits non-zero. A member that writes an artefact others read, such as a build, is named in the readers' after edge, and that ordering is shown in the report. A hook that formats and restages is the opposite of a check.
pros: One project's generate check rewrote the live tree, so the tests beside it failed 6 of 6 in a parallel trial; two commit hooks of another organisation ran the formatter in write mode and restaged.

rules.statement: On a shared host a heavy run takes a slot and a light command runs bare; the slots admit heavy runs by class, landings ahead of re-gates and experiments, and one heavy job in flight per agent.

reasoning.definition: A heavy run is a tier, a test suite, a build or anything that uses the pool's capacity. A light command is a type check of one file, a push, a lint of one file, a listing. Holding a slot for a light command makes the agents behind it wait for nothing. The job tool holds the slot classes; this rule says only that there are classes, that a landing comes first, and that an agent has one heavy job at a time.
pros: In one organisation a type check, a lint prune, a git push and one unit-test file held heavy slots; experiments held 360 slot-minutes in two days; and agents waited at least 2,846 minutes for heavy slots over two days.

rules.statement: Every member declares what it needs (the network, a browser, a service) and not the system it runs on; one whose need this host lacks is reported as skipped with the cause by the tier check, is listed every run and never passes quietly, and a skip is red at land and at release unless a dated exemption names the machine the gate cannot reach.

reasoning.definition: A member declares what it needs, the network included, in its entry of the repo's Taskfile; it names no operating system. A member whose need this host lacks, such as the network on a host that has none, is not run, and the tier check reports it as skipped with the reason, every time (go-task's own `platforms:` filter skips a member in silence, so the report is the check's, never go-task's). At push a skip is allowed, because the builder's machine may lack a browser or a runtime. At land and at release a skip is red, because those moments prove the whole project, unless a dated exemption names the machine that would run it; the one exemption today names Windows. No Job Object and no network-block prefix is part of the rule: how a host runs a member is the host's own affair. A vulnerability check that needs the network reports not checked when offline, never a pass. tests.admission.5 holds the test side; this rule holds the member.
pros: Browser gates inside a no-network sandbox failed 49 of 49 blocks with a network error nobody read as cannot run here; four projects had a member that needs a host the gate may not have.

sources.where: the table row gates.command.30, one dated exemption names Windows

rules.statement: Each moment of the cycle has an owner: the builder runs commit and push on their own machine, the hub lands and releases, an on-demand run is asked for, and nobody runs a later moment's tier as their hand-in.

reasoning.definition: The builder's hand-in is the push tier, run by the pre-push hook on the builder's machine. The hub runs the landing proof on the merged candidate and the release tier on a fresh clone of the tag. A builder who runs the release tier, or a full post-land run, before every push runs a moment that is not theirs and pays its cost per change. The six moments and what each holds are gates.command.17.
pros: One organisation ran 198 bare full gates in one day as its hand-in, 25.3 slot-hours, because its agent rules still named the full tier; the one push-sized run that day took 0.9 minutes against a full median of 8.7.

rules.statement: The pre-push hook is installed and runs the whole gate on the pushed tree within its measured time budget, and a range it cannot resolve fails closed.

reasoning.definition: The pre-push hook runs the one gate command (make check or its equivalent) on what is being pushed: every member, including the root-file structural check (the managed files equal their template), the tests uncached, the scans and the cross-OS builds. It is the gate, not a sample of it: no hosted job on push repeats or replaces it. Its wall time is measured against the budget of gates.hooks.4; a member too slow for that budget moves to the release workflow, never out of every gate. When the pushed range cannot be resolved the hook fails; it never falls back to "nothing to check". The hook runner reads one committed file for both pre-commit and pre-push.
pros: With no push CI a push that skips the gate moves the failure straight to main. A hook that runs a subset leaves the rest of the gate with no tier at all.

rules.statement: The hooks are installed, executable and arm themselves at the first gate run; a repo cannot be left unarmed without a check noticing.

reasoning.definition: The check (`make armed`, a make target that exists in five repos, run inside `check` and on the pre-push path; the land job runs `check-install` and the setup step `prepare` installs the hooks; the shared standing check is called `check-armed`) reads the hooks path setting, the executable bit in the index, and that the hook text names the gate. Hook installation fails closed outside a git repo or when a hooks path override is set, and hooks arm at the first gate run because package install scripts are off. The setup step (`prepare`) installs them and the land job runs the same install check (`check-install`). A hooks-path override is refused.
pros: Five Go repos have the hook and five different versions of it (V-66). An unarmed repo looks the same as an armed one until a bad push goes through.

rules.statement: The pre-commit hook is check-only and cheap: it runs the supply-chain config check, in parallel, and never rewrites files.

reasoning.definition: The commit-time hook runs only quick config checks and the staged-file lint. It writes nothing; fixing is done on write, not at commit. The setup step installs the hook, and the land job runs the install check.
pros: A commit hook that formats or runs a long list slows every commit and gets bypassed.

rules.statement: The pre-push hook runs the whole gate, its wall time is measured and reported against a budget, and a check too slow for it moves to the release workflow, never to a push or pull-request workflow or a hosted land job.

reasoning.definition: The budget is a number in the repo's gate config with its reason (the targets run their whole gate in about a minute). The pre-push wrapper measures the hook's wall time on every run and reports it with the budget, and the gate fails when the measured time stays over the budget for the recorded number of runs. The fix for an over-budget hook is to make a member faster or to move that member to the release workflow on the tag (the crash-injection run and the dry build are the usual cases), where it still blocks the release; fuzz and the heavy race run are on demand and block nothing (tests.generated.6, tests.runners.6). A member never moves to a workflow triggered by push or pull request, or to a hosted land job, and never out of every gate. The pre-commit hook stays check-only and cheap (gates.hooks.3).
pros: Heavy hooks invited `--no-verify` at a reference team, so the time is measured, not guessed. With no push CI the only place a slow check can go and still bind is the release.

rules.statement: The bypass flags are refused: no `--no-verify`, no `LEFTHOOK=0` or equivalent, and no skipped hook.

reasoning.definition: Committed agent settings deny `git commit` and `git push` with `--no-verify` or `-n` and a hook-disable environment variable (done for one repo); the land step recomputes the verdict so a push that skipped the hook still fails at land. A count of bypass attempts from the session and run log is a report. A skipped test is counted by the suppression ratchet (gates.exemptions.5).
pros: Heavy hooks invited the bypass at a reference team; a bypass that nobody can see makes the hook a suggestion.

rules.statement: A repo's hook file extends the shared hook template; its job list includes the shared jobs.

reasoning.definition: The repo's hook file may add jobs but must contain the shared ones. The check reads the hook file by meaning, not by bytes.
pros: A repo that edits the hook file removes a job and nobody sees it.

rules.statement: Secrets are scanned at commit by a shared standing gate.

reasoning.definition: One of the three standing gates shared across repos (the others are the armed hook and the pipefail check): a secret scanner runs at commit time over the staged changes.
pros: A secret reaching history cannot be removed by a later commit.

rules.statement: A builder's pre-push hook may run the commit tier plus build, vet, lint and the selected tests, with the whole push tier run on another machine when the push lands and on the train candidate.

reasoning.definition: The whole tier still runs on every pushed head and on the candidate before main moves, so nothing reaches the default branch unseen; a branch on the remote may be red for a few minutes. A pull request with a red whole run is sent back. The whole-tier proof at landing is run by the landing step itself, never read from another machine's report, as nothing at landing reads a stamp. Adopting this rule replaces the wording of gates.hooks.1 and gates.hooks.4 ("runs the whole gate"), which are retired or reworded in the same change.
pros: After the concurrency and parallelism rules a push is about 50 seconds and the hook is no longer the bottleneck of the day; a lighter hook would cut the builder's wait to about 15 seconds at the price of a red branch for a few minutes.

rules.statement: The pre-push hook runs the push tier and does nothing else, the logic lives in the runner, a push from a hosted workflow never runs the local hook, and a known hole in the bypass deny is a finding.

reasoning.definition: gates.hooks.1 and .4 hold that the hook runs the whole gate within its budget, and gates.hooks.5 that the bypass flags are refused. This rule holds the shape of the hook: one line that calls the runner with the tier's name. A loop, a substitution or a check written in the hook itself is logic the runner should hold, and it is not measured, not stamped and not shared. A tag push made by a hosted workflow does not run the local hook again, because the tag's tree is the tree the release tier proves. Where a project has no paid hosted check, the hook is the only check, and a hole in the deny (a spelling of the bypass the deny does not match) is a finding to close, not a note. The hook body is a single exec of the runner (`exec task pre-push`), so it has no shell of its own to differ by system.
pros: One hook with a quadratic shell substitution cost 374 seconds of a 391 second push and 210 seconds of every commit; four publishes ran the gates twice, 403 seconds, because the tag push re-fired the hook; and a deny written after a bypass came 9 hours 15 minutes later with a hole in it.

rules.statement: Every check has a planted violation that turns it red, a clean control and a refusal case, and the gate runs that plant at least once per tier.

reasoning.definition: A check that cannot fail is not a check. A rule with no plant is a finding, and a new rule ships with its plant and a failing-test message that names the fix. Plants lead adoption in every repo. Every registered check carries a planted-violation fixture, a clean control and a refusal case, and the gate fails when a registered check lacks one (a registry walk). For analyzers the fixture form is the analysis test package with `// want` comments; for forbidigo, ast-grep and conftest-style rules the fixture is a tiny module run through the real tool. Plants run first in the gate. The plants must exist before the check is turned on, and the plant of an old check is never deleted in the change that weakens it (that is a gate weakening, see protection).
pros: No Go repo plants one for each of its gates; one repo's drift check failed 13 of 35 entries and was not in its make check. One web repo's 82 plants never ran in `make check` because the layer check ran without its self-test flag. Another has 85 plants on main (135 on a branch). A self-test run is held in one repo (73 plants).

rules.statement: Every rule in the effective lint config is error or off, never warn, and every rule that is on has a planted fixture that fires at error severity; a clean fixture has zero findings.

reasoning.definition: The runner dumps the resolved config for a sample file per kind (for ESLint, `--print-config`) and fails on any rule at warn, including one that arrives from a plugin preset (a warn-level rule; the eslint-plugin-playwright recommended preset gave two warnings in one run). One planted fixture per rule the preset sets, each required to fire at error severity, including one for the unused-disable message. The clean fixture has zero findings, and an excluded spec file and a root tool config lint without a parse error. Every error-level lint rule has a failing fixture (a meta-check), so a rule on with no plant fails.
pros: A rule at warn is not enforced and a grid that counts it lies. A recommended plugin preset gave two warnings in one run. Hand-typed status said 3 rules enforced where the computed count was 0 at a reference team.

rules.statement: Each shared tool preset ships a test with a planted failing sample that fails naming the rule and a clean sample that passes.

reasoning.definition: Instances: a boundary test fixture that trips exactly the expected structural rules while a clean module passes; an API lint test where a bad description fails with both house rule codes and a good one passes; a spelling test where a planted misspelling fails naming the word and a good file passes; a markdown lint test where a planted skipped-heading file fails naming the rule and a good file passes. The planted and clean samples run through the real check.
pros: A preset that was never run against a bad sample can silently check nothing.

rules.statement: A rule that can fail in two directions is proved by a pair run, and cannot be at gate level without all the plants.

reasoning.definition: The pair run: the too-much case planted, the too-little case planted by a different instrument, a just-right case of the same size, the cheap cure applied to each failure, and a third result for not applicable. A row marked two-sided is refused promotion to gate with only the too-much plant. The plants need a reader who is not the row's author. Applies to rules that are balances (size, duplication, coverage, test count).
pros: Single-sided rules invite the cure that fails the other side: size rules are met by splitting, coverage floors by assertion-free tests. Argued from the evolutionary-architecture guidance; no fault of ours yet.

rules.statement: A gate fails closed on a missing tool, missing input, empty input or a pending marker unless the check declares that 0 inputs is valid, has no flag that softens a finding or an exit, and only members of the gate line count as evidence.

reasoning.definition: A zero is not an absence until a known positive proves the instrument. The runner wraps every check: an input count of 0 fails unless the check declares `zero_ok`, in which case it returns the third result (gates.plants.8). The type check runs in every gate and fails closed when its inputs, such as generated infrastructure types, are missing (for example `tsc --noEmit` after `sst install`, with the `.sst/` directory absent being red). Tools already fail on an empty glob (ESLint exits 2; a test runner with a file filter matching nothing exits 1); the runner closes the gap for custom checks and name filters. The self-test runs each check on an empty input and requires a refusal. A gate has no non-fatal mode: there is no strict, warn-only or soft flag, a finding is always exit 1, and exit 2 means could not run. A convenience hook (a phase guard, a reminder) may fail open, but it is not a gate member and is never cited as evidence that a rule holds; only members of the gate line are evidence.
pros: A pending check exited 0 at a reference team; a secrets test skips when its scanner is missing; scanners that read nothing read green; a spec that cannot fail ran against nothing. A softening flag is the switch somebody turns on the day the gate is red.

rules.statement: A lint run with fatal parse errors is a failure, not a list of findings, and no run ends with one.

reasoning.definition: The lint wrapper runs the linter with JSON output and exits 1 on any message with `fatal: true` or a null rule id. The lint wrapper (`companion lint`) matches `**/*.astro` and sets `parserOptions.parser` for those template files so TypeScript front matter in `.astro` parses; the null-rule check is on `ruleId`. The same wrapper runs the rules-loaded probe of gates.plants.7.
pros: Frontmatter TypeScript gave 23 fatal parse errors on one web repo, reported as ordinary findings.

rules.statement: A lint run proves it loaded its rules; a run that loaded none, or fewer than the pinned number, fails.

reasoning.definition: The wrapper (`companion lint`) prints the resolved config for a sample `.astro` file and a sample `.tsx` file and fails when fewer than the pinned number of accessibility rules are active. The plugin is the preset's own dependency so the working-directory (cwd-lookup) trap cannot arise.
pros: One folder ran 33 rules and another ran 0, with no error (V-34).

rules.statement: A gate proves it ran its full list, a fast tier prints what it skipped, and a check has three results: pass, fail and not applicable with 0 inputs, printed with the input count.

reasoning.definition: The gate summary lists every check run against the full registry list, with each not-applicable result and its count; a step missing from the summary compared with the rule table fails (the summary-vs-table check). The third result is allowed only where the check declares that 0 inputs is a valid state, with one known-positive run per tier that proves the check reads something. Any other empty input fails (gates.plants.5).
pros: A reference gate did not run its vulnerability scan; a gate skipping a step was a regret in the platform lane.

rules.statement: A skipped gate is named with its reason in the change.

reasoning.definition: Every skipped gate and package has a recorded reason in the gate output and in the change description. Nothing reports green for what it skipped.
pros: A skip nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a pass.

rules.statement: A gate reads a tool's output, not only its exit status, and never through a default cap.

reasoning.definition: The lint run sets `--max-same-issues=0` and `--max-issues-per-linter=0` and also `issues.uniq-by-line: false`; with the default, a second forbidigo hit on the same line was silently dropped (`http.DefaultClient` beside `*http.Client`). The formatter, import fixer and dead-code outputs are tested empty by the gate wrapper.
pros: Default caps hide findings: a second forbidden use on one line was silently dropped (verified), and 60 findings of one linter would show as fewer. No repo sets both caps.

rules.statement: A configured behaviour is checked by booting the thing and reading what it emitted, never by reading the config text: the lint config by a verify command plus a real run, and runtime settings by a probe that observes them.

reasoning.definition: `golangci-lint config verify` accepts an unknown linter name, and the run does not (verify exit 0, run exit 3). The gate self-test runs both. The same holds for every runtime setting a gate claims: middleware order, log redaction, cookie attributes, content security policy, test-runner workers and timeouts are each asserted by starting the program or tool and reading its output, headers or behaviour. A gate that reads source or config text to assert a runtime fact is a finding.
pros: A typo in the config silently disables nothing until a run proves it. A setting read from text says what somebody wrote, not what the running program does.

rules.statement: The foundation's own scripts and the shared package's own gate are linted and tested by their local gate at push.

reasoning.definition: Measure, census and page-generator scripts have tests and a lint step, with a known-positive run per script. They run in the foundation repo's own gate command (make check), which its pre-push hook runs on every push, under the budget of gates.hooks.4. The shared package's own hooks and gate run tests and a format check at push. No push or pull-request workflow runs them; a check too slow for the hook moves to the release workflow. The hook install is skipped only when the hook tool is absent, which the armed check reports.
pros: A reference team went from 10 errors to 0 once its own scripts were gated; ours had no gate on its scripts. Hosted minutes on every push are refused, so the local gate is the gate.

rules.statement: Adoption is proved end to end by a script that generates a repo from the template, edits a managed file and sees the push hook go red naming it.

reasoning.definition: The proof script packs the shared package, generates a repo from the template, runs the gate green, edits a root file, confirms the push hook goes red naming it, restores the file, confirms green, and runs each tool on a good and a bad sample. For Go, a sync self-test generates a repo, edits a managed file and requires the check to fail.
pros: A template whose generated repo was never exercised can ship a gate that does not fail.

rules.statement: A shape rule is kept with a planted hit, a clean control and a measured false-positive and false-negative rate, and a zero from a search tool means nothing until it found a known positive.

reasoning.definition: A fixture pair per shape rule, with every known bypass kept as a fixture, and a run over every clone before the rule is required. The selftest runs them; a bypass form the rule misses is recorded.
pros: The atomic-write rule had 2 of 13 hits not copies (15 percent) and 1 of 9 outside units missed. Five restructured copies planted beside a control: the rule flagged the control only (1 of 6, re-run 4 Nov), so the false-negative rate for a restructured copy is not the 1 of 9.

rules.statement: A blocking check has a measured false-positive rate under 10 percent; a check above the bar drops a level.

reasoning.definition: For every check that blocks, keep a count of hits, suppressed hits, findings later overturned, and the agent time spent satisfying a failure, from the delivery record, and report them per check. A check that is mostly suppressed is changed or dropped. A check above the bar drops a level (blocking to ratcheted to review) by a recorded decision; the reporter itself never demotes a check, because that would be a gate weakening. The 10 percent bar is a practice figure and a guess on UI gates. A failing test is never rerun to green.
pros: A check that wastes agent rounds taxes every ticket, and time spent satisfying a wrong finding is invisible unless recorded. One lint rule has 40 of 40 hits suppressed; one repo has 26 init functions each suppressed with a reason (V-55). No UI gate has an override count today.

rules.statement: A failing rule's message names its home and the fix; a failing test's first screen names the check, the expected and actual values and the one line to rerun it, and the rest goes to a file.

reasoning.definition: The rule table requires home and fix fields in every rule message; for our own lint plugin rules a plugin lint enforces the message format and docs URL. The first screen of a failing test is a review question. No line limit is set because none is measured.
pros: A message that does not say what to do is satisfied by guessing. Argued, not measured; no measured number is cited.

rules.statement: Every gate on main is green, so that a red result means something.

reasoning.definition: A failing test is never rerun to green, a blocking check has a measured false-positive rate (gates.quality.1), and the release backstop (a full run at the tag) catches what selection missed.
pros: A main that is sometimes red teaches everyone to retry, and a retry hides a real fault.

rules.statement: A new check runs on one real repo before it is required anywhere, and the trial is recorded.

reasoning.definition: Shared checks run over existing repos at pinned commits with a control run, so a result cannot pass by accident, and a dry adoption report is written per tool, before any check is required. The trial needs a known positive. The registry refuses a required check with no trial record; that a trial was real and was read is judgement.
pros: A check that has never run on real code misfires on first contact and gets switched off.

rules.statement: A gate is one you can explain in a sentence.

reasoning.definition: A required one-line `why` field on each rule row with a length cap gives presence only; a model lens checks that the sentence matches the check.
pros: A gate nobody can explain gets weakened or removed without understanding.

rules.statement: Main moves only by a reviewed change whose merged tree the checks passed: the lander runs them on the merged tree, then squash-merges; where a repo has no lander, the owner fast-forwards main to the exact tree the pre-push hook passed, or has the gate run again on the merged tree first.

reasoning.definition: The change is reviewed (the author's own included), and the owner merges it or says to. Where a repo runs the lander, the lander checks out origin/main plus the squash in a scratch clone, runs the repo's own checks there (its Taskfile's pre-push tier, or make check in gragas), and only then squash-merges. Where it does not, the pre-push hook has run the full gate on the pushed tree (gates.hooks.1), and the owner either fast-forwards main to that exact commit, so the tree that moves main is the tree that ran, or, when main has moved since or the merge is a squash, has the gate run again on the merged tree before main moves: a squash onto a main that moved is a tree that never ran. There is no stamp, no stored verdict and no hash record: a pass is the run just made on the tree about to move main, never a claim carried from another tree, another machine or the author's word. In both forms nothing else moves main: no direct push to main and no merge of a tree the checks did not pass.
pros: A merge path that skips the check is the path that gets used. With no hosted land job the binding between the tree that was merged and the run that passed it is that the run is made on that tree, just before the merge; a pass on one tree must never be claimed for another.

sources.where: the table rows gates.land.1 to gates.land.3

rules.statement: A verdict is bound to the tree it judged, the land gate runs on the tree that was pushed, and changing the tree after a gate run means a new run.

reasoning.definition: Every land carries the gate summary of its tree (the verdict carries the commit's tree id; it lists the tree id, a test count and zero skipped). The lander accepts a verdict only for the tree it merges and re-runs the top tier when a merge changes the tree. An amend that keeps the tree keeps the verdict; any change reruns, so there is no ban on amending. The lander reads the verdict from the gate's own output or from a stored record keyed by tree, never from the author's report, and never from a stamp left by a session that may be cut off; the hand-in is read from the ref, not from the message.
pros: A lead reported 14 chosen tests green where the whole package would have failed 4. The tree-keyed verdict is proven in one repo; two other repos have variants.

rules.statement: Where a repo runs the lander, it recomputes a hash over the tree, the base and the rule set, and refuses a verdict record that it cannot recompute or whose base is stale.

reasoning.definition: Applies only to a repo that runs the lander (gates.land.1); a repo whose land step is the local gate and a reviewed merge has no verdict record. The record lists what was run and why the selector, not the author, chose it. A file with plausible fields typed by hand has the same shape as one written by the gate, so the lander does the arithmetic itself. The verdict lists what was selected and why.
pros: A self-reported proof was the fault: a lead reported 14 chosen tests green where the whole package would have failed 4 (P-09 section 4 O4). Agents declare done early and prove subsets; the known way round is re-running a chosen subset through the gate, so the record lists the selection and its reason.

rules.statement: Where a repo runs the lander, the run record carries the plan with a hash over changes, rules and result, and the lander recomputes it.

reasoning.definition: Applies only to a repo that runs the lander (gates.land.1). The summary carries the plan: the base, head and merge-base ids, the rules hash, manifests hash and graph hash, the scope and its reasons, the selected domains, tests, stories and checks, and the plan hash. The lander recomputes the plan at the commit and compares the plan hash; a hand-edited plan with a stale hash is refused. For Go, the run record lists each skipped package with its reason keyed to the tree and the land step compares it (no plan hash yet).
pros: A plan that is only a file is the author's claim; a recomputed hash makes it the gate's.

rules.statement: A plan computed against a base that is not the current main tip is refused, with a message that names the rerun.

reasoning.definition: The lander refuses a plan whose base is not the main tip and merge-base of the ref, or whose head is not the gated commit, with a message like "plan computed against X, main is Y: re-run the land tier".
pros: A stale base lets a green result from an older tree stand for a newer one.

rules.statement: The land check is a runner over separate condition files, each with its own spec, and a new condition never edits the runner.

reasoning.definition: One program with conditions as separate modules; a pack adds conditions and never edits the base runner. The proven land gate with its conditions is lifted as a shared piece, and a project adds only its own rules.
pros: A runner that every new condition edits is a gate whose own changes weaken it.

rules.statement: The land tier runs tests only for what the change can reach and every whole-program check, with a full run as backstop, fail closed, each skip proved.

reasoning.definition: Selected tests and stories at land, for affected domains only; every always-full check (gates.command.6) in full. The full suite runs at least every third release, and the post-land full run is the backstop. Each skipped package has a proved reason.
pros: A full suite at every land misses the budget; selection without a backstop misses what selection missed.

rules.statement: A red release tier in the fresh checkout refuses the tag; the bad range is bisected and the miss becomes a permanent test.

reasoning.definition: The release recipe runs the release tier of the repo's own Taskfile in a fresh checkout of the commit it is about to tag, and a red run refuses the tag until the cause is fixed or reverted. There is no lock file and no record kept between runs: the next release runs the tier again on its own commit. The bad range is bisected with the full tier, the ticket that landed it is reopened, and the miss becomes a permanent test. On our side the check attaches to the release backstop, not to every land; there is no run after each land.
pros: A red nobody stops compounds; the miss that got through selection teaches the planner only if it is kept.

rules.statement: A bound on how many changes may land without a full proof.

reasoning.definition: The land check refuses a land when main is more than 3 lands (not commits) past the last full-green full run. On our side it is counted in releases: at most two tags pass between full runs (the full run at least every third release).
pros: Selection without a bound lets unproven changes pile up on main.

rules.statement: A gate check on a built artefact is accepted only when the artefact records the tree it was built from.

reasoning.definition: For the web, a story check passes only on a built storybook whose stamp records the source commit and a dirty flag, where that commit equals HEAD or the planner proves no change in the story closure (stories and their imports, tool config, global style, `package-lock.json`, environment files, the design system version) between them; the full tier always rebuilds. For Go, the binary under journey tests runs as built, and the version output prints the commit, but nothing ties the binary under test to the tree.
pros: An old build passes checks that the new tree would fail.

rules.statement: A cached result counts only when a trusted runner wrote it under a key from the tree, lockfile and platform, and a fail is never cached.

reasoning.definition: The key is recomputed from the tree ids of the gated commit, the lockfile, the runtime version, the OS and the architecture (and the browser version for stories). The summary records whether the source was a run or the cache (`result-cache`) and the key. The full tier ignores the cache. A cache is trusted only for packages that read nothing the cache cannot see; a verdict names the OS and host.
pros: A cache keyed on less lets a result from a different platform or lockfile stand in.

rules.statement: Where a repo lands trains, a train of changes is gated once, on its merged tree, before any of its changes lands; a change landed alone passes the same gate on the tree as pushed.

reasoning.definition: Applies only to a repo that lands trains of changes; a repo that merges one reviewed change at a time meets the second half through gates.land.1. The train builder compiles and vets the union of the train's trees before landing any of them. The land path comes first: many changes are not re-gated one by one.
pros: Two semantic conflicts passed every file-overlap tool and only train builds caught them (two cases in the delivery record, P-09 O5).

rules.statement: A green verdict survives a clean rebase, and landing many changes does not re-gate each.

reasoning.definition: The verdict is keyed to the change's patch id (`git patch-id`) as well as the tree, so a clean rebase keeps it.
pros: At a reference team one change ran to revision 9 when the lead wrote and revision 11 by 17:20Z; part of that is real fixes, not rebases.

rules.statement: A heavy run is refused if a verdict for the tree already exists.

reasoning.definition: The heavy-run wrapper refuses a run when the verdict store holds a verdict for the tree.
pros: At a reference team 98 of 201 heavy runs were a bare full gate repeated until the command refused.

rules.statement: A stamp is a claim keyed to the exact tree, its settings and its tools, and it only lets a rerun on the same key be skipped; it is never keyed to a commit or an age, landing and release never take it as proof, and a member that reads a moving source pins that source by digest in the key.

reasoning.definition: A stamp is plain data that any process able to write the common git folder can write, so it is trusted only to skip a local rerun. gates.land.11 holds the key of a cached result; this rule holds what the stamp may and may not do. A stamp keyed to a commit id survives an amend that changes nothing, which is fine, and one keyed to an age vouches for code nobody ran, which is not. A vulnerability database or a remote list the member reads is part of the key as a digest, or the stamp is stale the moment the source moves. The landing proof is keyed to the candidate tree (gates.land.16), which is what makes a moved main stale nothing.
pros: Two projects kept a stamp keyed to a 24-hour age; another organisation's landing read a stamp bound to the main branch's tip, so every landing staled every waiting green and 37 of 44 land commands in 8 hours landed nothing.

rules.statement: Approved, disjoint changes land as a train proved once on its merged tree; the proof is keyed to the candidate tree, so a landing that produces a tree already proved needs no rerun, landing makes one push, the next train is built on this train's squash and never on its verdict commit, and a train of one is a train.

reasoning.definition: gates.land.12 holds that a train is gated once on its merged tree. This rule holds the four things around it that cost proofs. The key is the candidate tree, not the main branch's tip, so a green that is still the same tree after main moved is still green. Landing pushes once, so there is one new tree per train. The next train starts from the squash that landed, because a verdict commit that never lands is not a base anyone can build on. A project with one builder lands trains of one with the same rule. A post-land run of the whole tree is retired where the landing proof is the whole merged tree (gates.land.12), because it proves nothing new and holds a slot.
pros: One project ran 44 checks for 13 landings, 18 of them on a verdict commit that never lands, and two landing agents threw away 9 of each other's proofs; in another organisation 44 land commands in 8 hours landed 8 changes, 5.1 runs per change.

rules.statement: Where a project has protected paths, the landing judge is built from the main branch and run on the change, so a change cannot loosen the rules it is judged by; the judge is not the tier runner, a file the judge reads changes format in two steps, expand then contract, and everything else at landing runs the head's own tier.

reasoning.definition: gates.protection.1 to .3 hold the verdicts and the list of protected paths. This rule holds which code runs the check. The judge is small and trusted, built from the base revision into its own folder; the tier runner is the head's own and runs the head's members. A format change to a file the judge reads (the members file, the protected list) lands first as a reader that accepts both forms, then as the writer of the new form, because the base's judge must still read the head's file. A project with no protected paths has no judge, and the hub lands it on the head's tier alone.
pros: A head that changed the format of a file the judge reads was judged by code that could not read it and went red at landing; five projects with no judge needed the rule only where one exists.

rules.statement: A hand-off between agents carries a notice to the agent that waits, the wait is logged, and a red proof at or after landing says in the same message which main branch commit to build on.

reasoning.definition: A hand-off is a change passed from builder to reviewer, reviewer to lander, or lander back to builder. The notice goes to the one who waits, not to a channel they may read later, and the wait is a row where the hub counts rounds (gates.measures.5). When a landing proof is red, the message that says so names the last green main, so nobody waits for someone to name one.
pros: Six engineers of one organisation waited 333 agent-minutes after a red post-land proof for someone to name a main branch commit, and four hand-offs with no notice idled 106 minutes in one day.
