rules.statement: Debt is a shrink-only list: a new rule starts with today's violations frozen, and a gate fails when a cell gets worse.

reasoning.definition: Below the milestone a gate fails only when a cell gets worse; the change that needs a higher baseline cannot raise it, because the check compares the working figure with the figure at the merge base. Lowering is free. Each metric is a committed file per entry. A list may not grow without a person typing the growth switch (`--write --grow`) and a named second reader (second-reader), the stored verdict of gates.protection.1. A bulk suppression file alone is not a ratchet: it records existing violations, fails new ones and can only shrink, but it needs the registry of gates.ratchets.4 beside it.
pros: Held in one Go repo (ratchet files, plant none recorded) and in two web repos (numeric baselines with the grow switch). A new rule that cannot start frozen is never adopted.

rules.statement: A baseline is a numeric ceiling per file that only falls, and raising it needs a stored second-party verdict.

reasoning.definition: A single count hides one file growing while another shrinks (the existing file baseline in the Go repo is the `file-baseline`), so the ceiling is per file. A baseline entry that no longer applies also fails.
pros: The first size ratchet at a reference team recorded one violation for a file that grew from 400 to 3,000 lines. The Go baseline files are 39, 40, 79 and 828 lines (V-24).

rules.statement: A baseline survives a rebase, a rename and a deletion without resetting, and a baseline entry for a missing file fails.

reasoning.definition: On a missing path the ratchet helper looks up the rename in the diff against the base: if the path was renamed the entry must move with its number not raised; if deleted the entry must be removed in the same change; otherwise fail. A structural move (renaming or moving a module, package or route) rewrites the keys of every baseline and suppression list it touches and never their counts: the sum of each baseline before and after is equal and no key names a missing path. Stale suppression keys already fail in the ESLint bulk suppression file and in dependency-cruiser's known-violation list (dependency-cruiser behaves the same) -- ESLint bulk suppression file and in known-list tools.
pros: Without this, a rename resets the baseline to zero and hides the debt. Not measured in Go; the web half rests on a stale entry failing (exit 2) until pruned.

rules.statement: Every baseline is a count made against the merge base, with an owner, a ticket and the stage by which it is zero; growth against the merge base, or any non-zero count at the stage, fails.

reasoning.definition: There is no stored list of baselines. The count is made on the merge base and on the head in the same run, so a count that grew fails however the change got there, and a baseline that nobody wrote down cannot be forgotten. The owner, the ticket and the zero-by stage sit in the config that owns the baseline, as a dated TODO which a lint rule turns into an error on the day. The zero check reads the current milestone and fails on anything non-zero at or past the stage; the last stage's gate fails while any count is above zero. One parent issue with sub-issues per rule drives the legacy debt to zero.
pros: A ratchet that never reaches zero is a permanent exemption; whether our baselines have shrunk was never measured. A reference team's countdowns to zero paid off.

rules.statement: A baseline at zero is deleted and its rule becomes a plain error; an empty registered baseline file that still exists fails.

reasoning.definition: At zero, the baseline file goes and the rule is absolute; a non-empty baseline at or past its stage fails. The check fails on the empty file so the deletion is not forgotten.
pros: An empty baseline left in place lets the rule quietly regrow.

rules.statement: No new file on a legacy path; the legacy count only shrinks and the baseline is deleted at zero.

reasoning.definition: Anything outside the declared layout is legacy, and the count of legacy files only falls. On the Go side, files outside the standard layout are counted and the count only falls. On the web side, files in no declared layer are a shrink-only list that is deleted at zero.
pros: A legacy area that can take new files never empties.

rules.statement: Each shared package has a file-count ratchet that only shrinks, and growth needs an explicit gate-change record.

reasoning.definition: A package over its size has a written reason and the count of large files only falls; raising a shared package's ceiling is a gate change (gates.protection.1).
pros: A shared package that grows without a count becomes the place everything lands.

rules.statement: A review-class item carries a fingerprint; when it changes, the gate fails until a reason that resolves to a ticket or decision is recorded.

reasoning.definition: A generated port-surface file per package, diffed in the gate like the export list of a shared package. It covers exported and unexported interfaces and the parameter structs they take; a function parameter on a port goes on the fingerprint too. A `Do(op string, args ...any)` shape would freeze the surface, so it is banned. The value is a committed diff a reviewer sees, not the reason: most landings already name a ticket, so a resolving reason costs nothing. Whether the second case (a consumer broken unseen) is real stays review.
pros: A port surface changed on 25 of one repo's 472 landings, 11 of another's 82 and 37 of 964 in a third; real changes by construction, so 0 false fires. Struct-only changes this form cannot see: 18, 11 and 1.

rules.statement: A commit that moves or renames files changes no behaviour and carries no logic edit.

reasoning.definition: A similarity check on renames at commit: for a commit marked as a move, every entry in the rename diff at 100 percent similarity must be a pure rename; a mixed commit fails. Moves are declared, because an unmarked move that changes behaviour passes. The known way round is moving, then editing, in two commits, which is the wanted result. A move commit is added to the blame-ignore list (`.git-blame-ignore-revs`). The thing moved is a separate change from the work that uses it.
pros: Mixed moves hide the real change from a reader (principles report P-02 section 5.14). Argued, no fault of ours.

rules.statement: A module move is its own change before the change that uses it: a codemod moves the files and rewrites specifiers, mocks, citations and every baseline key in one commit, and one owner makes all moves.

reasoning.definition: The codemod moves files and rewrites import specifiers, mock strings, comment citations and every registered baseline's path keys in the same commit, with zero logic change and an entry in the blame-ignore list. One mover owns every move change at a time. A move commit may rewrite baseline keys, never their count.
pros: Concurrent moves conflict, and a move mixed with logic cannot be reviewed.

rules.statement: A fingerprint covers the fact the item answers, never the bytes of the file that holds it; an answer about an import is keyed to the import set.

reasoning.definition: The item of a reviewed answer is what was asked: that package P imports I, that a function has a given length class. The fingerprint is a digest of that fact (the sorted import list of P's non-test files, the function's class), so an unrelated edit to the same file renews nothing and a change to the fact fails the gate until a reason is recorded. Two answers about one file no longer renew together. Where the fact is the file itself, as with a size class, the file digest is right. The answer's schema names the kind of fingerprint, and a file fingerprint on an answer about an import is refused. File-level review of a wiring file is a protected-path question, not a fingerprint.
pros: Own measure: 13 fingerprint renewals in three days, as many as additions, because two answers share one wiring file and every edit to it renewed both.

rules.statement: Every lint disable directive names the rule it disables and gives a reason; a blanket disable is an error.

reasoning.definition: For Go, the `//nolint` directive names its linter (`nolintlint` with require-specific and require-explanation) and gives an explanation; a bare directive is refused. For TypeScript, a disable directive must carry a description and name the rule it disables (the eslint-comments rules). The reason follows the one record format of gates.exemptions.4. nolintlint cannot check an expiry or an owner; that is the record check.
pros: 2,435 live nolint lines in Go with no exit record; the shared nolintlint is enabled nowhere (V-2, V-5). One repo has 662 suppression lines, 318 outside tests. A reference trial counted 548 and 624 nolintlint findings in two repos, mostly test files.

rules.statement: An unused lint disable directive is reported as an error, and a fixed finding makes the run fail until its suppression is pruned.

reasoning.definition: For Go, nolintlint refuses an unused directive. For TypeScript the linter setting reports unused disable directives as errors, and bulk suppressions fail on an unused entry (the flag that passes on unpruned suppressions is never used in a gate).
pros: A directive that no longer suppresses anything is dead debt and hides the next real violation at the same line.

rules.statement: A block-level lint disable is re-enabled in the same file.

reasoning.definition: Applies to TypeScript, where a block disable opens a range. A Go nolint scopes to one line or declaration, so there is no open block to close. Suppression comments are counted and only fall; an open block is the same debt.
pros: An open block silently disables the rule for the rest of the file.

rules.statement: Every exception has a recorded exit in one format, across `//nolint` disables, exemptions, allow-file entries and baselines: a reason that names an artifact, an owner and an expiry, and the gate fails on an expired entry.

reasoning.definition: The reason names an artifact (a ticket, a decision or a measurement). One parser reads all three kinds of list and fails on empty fields, a past date, a missing owner, or a reason naming a ticket that does not resolve; it prints the count of renewals. Every exemption and suppression entry (feature-flags, connector gates, lint suppressions, every exemptions file and baseline) carries a ticket and an expiry. Vulnerability ignores are entries of the same lists, with a ticket and an expiry. The expiry horizon is capped by data, and that cap is a guess; an expiry makes a gate fail with no code change, so the notice window is designed.
pros: Nolint lines, baselines and allow files have reasons but mostly no dates (none have owners). The ten other rows lean on this one format (counted exemptions, debt registry, rule-pack exemptions and others).

rules.statement: Suppressions are counted, separately inside and outside test files, and each count only falls; skipped tests count too.

reasoning.definition: The shared ratchet counts nolint and lint-ignore lines per repo (and `eslint-disable` comments, type-ignore directives and skipped tests for TypeScript), split test and non-test files by filename, with a baseline file per class that only falls. No new escape hatch: no new suppression, no skipped hook (gates.hooks.5), no skipped test.
pros: There were 1,362 suppression lines outside tests; in one repo 231 of 548 unused findings were outside test files (V-8). The built baseline split exists but no repo gate uses it.

rules.statement: An exemption names a path and a reason, is counted so it can only shrink, and an unused one is a finding.

reasoning.definition: The exemption list is held as records (gates.exemptions.4) counted in the shrink-only baseline; an exemption that matches nothing is a finding; a new exemption raises the count and is refused. Narrowing where a rule applies also takes a gate-change record (gates.protection.1).
pros: An exemption nobody counts does not shrink. A reference team's `showsRecordId` became a counted list only after a ticket (V-64).

rules.statement: Extend rather than exempt: an exemption is time-boxed with a ticket and a zero-by date, and a rule exempted repeatedly for the same kind of reason is reviewed.

reasoning.definition: When the same rule is exempted three times (a set number) for the same kind of reason, a change request on the rule is due: either the rule or the structure is wrong.
pros: Repeated exemptions mean the rule or the structure is wrong; an exemption count that nobody reads hides it.

rules.statement: A rule that is switched off in a shared config carries its measured reason beside it, and a pack states for each row the reason it narrows a base row.

reasoning.definition: For example the markdown table-alignment rule switched off for producing most of the findings on one service carries that measurement next to the setting. A check is measured on a real repo before it is required.
pros: An unexplained off switch is indistinguishable from an accident.

rules.statement: Every banned or parked item has a re-entry trigger, a recheck date and an owner, and a check fails when a recheck date passes.

reasoning.definition: A watch-list of parked or held items, each with a trigger, a recheck date, an owner and the card it reopens; a size trigger gets a measured signal. The ban covers the family of the banned library. A concern not needed yet has its owner named in advance.
pros: A ban with no way back is a permanent decision made by default.

rules.statement: Weakening a gate needs a non-author: a different session with a stored verdict tied to the content that names the weakening in words, checked at land.

reasoning.definition: Every agent pushes as one identity, so a trailer proves nothing: "non-author" means a different session with a stored verdict, content-hashed, which names the weakening in words. A named person signs only a short list: gate config, protected paths and new dependencies. The change records its reason. Weakening means raising a ceiling, removing a check, turning error to warn or off, narrowing where a rule applies, or deleting a plant. A change to a sensitive path (infrastructure and permissions, migrations, gate config, shared packages, the applies-to data) or a new dependency needs sign-off by someone other than the author. The trailer form (a `Gate-Change:` line naming a reviewer and a reason, checked by a `commit-msg` hook job) remains the record of the reason and the first, cheap check; the stored verdict is the one the land check relies on. The known way round is starting a second session to rubber-stamp, so the verdict must name the weakening in words and the list stays short enough for a person to sample.
pros: No Gate-Change trailer exists in any of seven Go repos (0, verified), and nothing stores such a verdict. A sign-off passed as a land argument stops a missing and a self sign-off but not a land-runner who names someone falsely. This row rests on the ruling of 4 November.

rules.statement: Gate paths are named in one list, and the land check requires a stored second-party verdict for any staged path on that list.

reasoning.definition: The list (a committed file) holds lint config, suppression files, hooks, dependency-boundary config, the compiler config, the package registry config, the agent instruction file and the other gate files; the list itself and test oracles, goldens and protected fixtures are on it (gates.protection.3). A commit-message job checks staged paths against the one list, and the same job runs in the land hook. Domain-edge additions are named in the trailer, and the deny list covers the bypass class only. Message catalogues carry no trailer. Other sensitive paths (shared modules, state schema, infrastructure) are not yet on the list on the Go and UI sides.
pros: 0 mentions in any repo today, no grammar and no list (V-90).

rules.statement: An agent cannot widen a rule, plant, baseline, threshold, selector map or ban list in the change it judges; test oracles, goldens, protected fixtures and the protected-path list itself are on the protected list, which takes a path, a folder or a pattern with one * segment.

reasoning.definition: A pattern such as a command folder's testdata with one * for the command name protects every feature's golden without a line per feature, and a verdict covers the one feature's files it was given for: a rebase that leaves those files byte-identical keeps the verdict valid, so another feature landing first does not cost it. The * stands for one path segment and never crosses a slash, and the pattern grammar is held by the list's schema test. The shared package and its lock are not writable by the agent that consumes them, in the same change. The agent-side deny is a committed settings rule and an OS-level write deny, which makes the stored-verdict flow the only way in. A trailer alone proves nothing, and one GitHub identity means no branch protection or CODEOWNERS: the land check is the only holder.
pros: One web repo's own check runs but its reviewer condition skips any path with no reviewer, and its scripts folder has none (V-65). Three reports asked for this with no row in the first merge.

rules.statement: A review condition never skips a protected path, including one with no named reviewer.

reasoning.definition: A path on the protected list with no named reviewer fails the condition instead of being skipped.
pros: At one reference team the reviewer condition skipped any path with no reviewer, and its scripts folder had none (V-65).

rules.statement: When a candidate conflicts only in files a generator owns, landing regenerates them and continues; a conflict in any hand-written file goes back to the builder.

reasoning.definition: A file is generator-owned when a generator in the repository's own tools writes it and gen --check holds it, and the landing step reads that list from the base revision, never from the candidate. When every conflicting path is on it, landing takes the base side, runs the generators, commits the result as the landing step's own commit, and runs the checks again; nothing is merged as text. One hand-written path among the conflicts returns the whole candidate to its builder, with the paths named. The regenerated files are never reviewed by hand, because the generator and its check are what a reviewer approved. The list of generated paths is read from the base revision's generators, built from the base, so a candidate cannot add a path to the list that judges it. A regenerate never changes a hand-written file: if running the generators would alter any path they do not own, the landing fails and the candidate returns to its builder. The regenerated tree is a new tree and gets the full proof: nothing is served from either side's stamp, and the generated-file check and the tier run on the result. A generated path that is also protected keeps needing a verdict on the regenerated bytes; landing never writes a verdict, and if the base holds none for those bytes the landing fails with the need and the digest.
pros: The organisation's run log of 8 Nov 2026 (trains 2 and 2b) shows each landing sending the waiting candidates back through a rebase, a full check run and sometimes a new verdict. A conflict in a generated file is the part of that cost with no judgement in it: the fix is the command that wrote the file, and a builder adds nothing by running it.

sources.says: Committed generated documents are held by a script that regenerates and compares.
Committed generated files are held by a script that fails when they are out of date.
A merge driver is defined in the clone's own configuration, never in the repository, and the union merge leaves added lines in an order the user must verify.

rules.statement: Gates are generic and shared by version: one lint stack, with config rendered from one shared source into each repo and checked byte for byte; a project adds only its own rules.

reasoning.definition: The gate files in each project equal the version-locked template output, and only parameters are project-owned. For Go: golangci-lint has no `extends` or `include`, so the shared config (base plus packs) is copied into each repo by a sync command and a check re-renders in memory and compares bytes, listing every stale path. Sibling repos run the same shared gates and presets published once, with the runtime floor aligned, and a parity check fails when a resolved config drifts from the preset version (one Go version across the estate).
pros: 5 distinct lint configs among 6 repos (V-25).

rules.statement: The required managed root files exist in each repo.

reasoning.definition: The structural check fails when a managed lint or hook file, or one of the one-line root config files, is absent from the repo root.
pros: A repo missing a root file silently falls back to tool defaults.

rules.statement: The managed root files are byte-equal to the template copy; an edited one fails.

reasoning.definition: The template writes a few one-line root files that only point at the shared config and are never edited. A file that must stay a copy is checked byte for byte against its origin in the gate.
pros: A root file that was edited can loosen the shared config.

rules.statement: A repo may set only a closed list of keys in its config overlay, nothing that loosens the shared base; strictness flags are never switched off.

reasoning.definition: The compiler overlay may hold only include, exclude, paths and outDir. Every override is in one parameters file read by a gate (validated with ajv-cli or check-jsonschema), "which package" decisions a human makes are written there, and a person's config refuses unknown keys (schema with additional properties false). Go lint config has no merge, so a repo may add only named fields in a separate local file that the check reads by meaning. A loosened setting fails; the strictness flags (strict compiler flags) stay on.
pros: A repo that can add keys to its overlay can turn the base off.

rules.statement: Each shared package and tool has one pinned version, and a preflight checks it is present before the gate runs.

reasoning.definition: One version file (`tools.txt` with name, version and sha256, read by `make preflight` and the `companion preflight` command; a tools file for Go tools with a separate sum file, and a plain list of name, version and checksum for the rest); the preflight exits non-zero on a missing or wrong-version tool, running each `--version`. Consumers stay within the currency window, the toolchain follows the lockfile, and one module version is used in every program. Verified 5 Nov: `go tool -modfile=tools.mod deadcode ./...` works with a `tool` directive in a separate tools module.
pros: A secret scanner is at 8.27.2 in one repo and 8.28.0 in two others (V-68, in part); 5 lint configs among 6 repos (V-25). A box check found golangci-lint at 2.14.0 with 2.15.0 the latest release.

rules.statement: A new repo starts with the pinned toolchain, hook install, lint, type-check and one gate command, and the shared package as a dev dependency.

reasoning.definition: A new TypeScript repo starts with an engines range, a package-manager pin, hook install, lint, type-check and gate scripts and the shared package as a dev dependency. A new Go repo starts with a Go version, a tools file, the hook and one make target. One package manager, pinned. The template lays down configs, scripts and gates.
pros: A repo set up by hand begins with a different gate than the next one.

rules.statement: A migration is swept within a deadline, then the old way is blocked.

reasoning.definition: The sync check compares each consumer's lock with the newest allowed shared version; a consumer older than the migration deadline in the migration record fails its own gate. It applies to code migrations and to contracts read by programs another owner deploys; it does not apply to a config key spelling, and a program whose readers all change in the same release keeps no old way to sweep.
pros: Three adoption issues were open since 27 October with no end date.

rules.statement: A check that exists is in the gate, or it is deleted, and the gate list is derived from the gate files themselves, never typed into a second list.

reasoning.definition: Every make target named as a check is reachable from the `check` target. Where a repo keeps its gates as files, each gate file declares its own metadata (name, rules held, budget, exit voice), and the gate command builds its member list by reading those files; a list typed by hand in a Makefile, a config or a doc is a second home that drifts and is a finding. A bespoke check script moves into the standard lint or import-rule tool and is then deleted: import rules go to the dependency-boundary linter or a repo test, one lint stack carries the rest, and a check that is not in the gate is deleted. Data validators of configuration files are not domain scripts and stay.
pros: A drift check that is not in the gate fails 13 of 35 entries unseen (V-27). The scan is a `gatescan` rule. A gate list typed apart from the gate files loses the gate that was added last.

rules.statement: A check replaced by a standard tool keeps a rule-by-rule parity table, and the replacement fires all the old check's plants before the old check is removed.

reasoning.definition: The table maps each old rule to a lint rule, a spec, or "dropped" with a reason; the remaining hits are then fixed or exempted with a ticket and an expiry. The replacement change runs the old plant corpus against the new config in the same change (a parity run); a plant that stops firing fails the swap. Deleting the awkward plant first is a gate weakening (gates.protection.1). Applies to home-made regex style scripts and any home-made check.
pros: A replacement silently narrows coverage, and only plants prove parity.

rules.statement: Formatting is one command.

reasoning.definition: One formatter command checks formatting in each repo; for `.astro` files that the chosen formatter cannot handle, `prettier-plugin-astro` is named in the one command, and a single wrapper command (`companion fmt`) hides the choice.
pros: Two formatters disagree, and each run undoes the other's output.

rules.statement: A banned import or code pattern is a lint error whose message names what to use instead, and the ban lists ship empty and are filled by later rules naming the owning package.

reasoning.definition: Built-in ban rules (restricted imports, restricted syntax, `no-console`, `n/no-process-env`, the eslint-comments rules) and dependency or forbidden-call linters (depguard and forbidigo for Go) forbid a named import or pattern outside its owner, each with a message that names what to use instead and the home and fix. The import and syntax ban lists exist but ship empty; each later rule fills its part naming the owning package in the message, so a ban doubles as a capability registry: each concern has one importable owner and the alternatives are banned by name.
pros: A ban without a message is satisfied by guessing the nearest bypass.

rules.statement: Rules written for the repo's own code (custom lint rules, structural patterns, domain check scripts) are checks, each with a plant and a measured error rate.

reasoning.definition: Examples that were five small rules in one source row: a call banned in one feature area, a UI primitive banned outside its owner path, with a hand-built twin counted. Each is a lint or structural rule with a planted violation and a clean control. Shape rules and generated depguard rows are kept with a planted hit and measured false rates (gates.plants.14).
pros: A domain rule written only as prose is not held.

rules.statement: Generated code is never edited by hand; regenerate it, and a check fails when the copy differs from a fresh generation.

reasoning.definition: A generated file names its version or carries a banner and regenerating leaves no diff. A derived artifact (a spec from a schema, types from a database, enums from a glossary, token output, route trees) is generated and diffed. Shapes that cross a language boundary have one source.
pros: A hand-edit is overwritten by the next regeneration, or worse, kept and drifts.

rules.statement: There is no literal service address or fallback beside the configured one.

reasoning.definition: Config is read in one package with a reader, a default and a doc row per key; a secret never comes from a flag. Variables are declared in a typed schema.
pros: A hard-coded fallback address sends traffic to the wrong place when the configured one is missing.

rules.statement: Secret-shaped keys in public environment files fail, and no secret reaches the bundle.

reasoning.definition: Public environment files hold only public values; a variable whose name looks like a secret fails the check.
pros: A secret in a public file ships to every browser.

rules.statement: A repo's own gate imports nothing from the code it judges, and reaches it only through a declared internal export or the built binary.

reasoning.definition: A gate that needs facts from the code reads them through an export declared for gates (an internal entry the package lists for that use) or by running the built program and reading its machine output. Importing the package it judges is a finding: a fault in the subject then breaks or bends the gate, and the gate passes whatever the subject's own code says. The import rule names the gate folder and the internal exports it may reach.
pros: A gate that imports its subject dies with it when the subject breaks, and judges the subject with the subject's own logic.

rules.statement: A standard is active only while it links the check that enforces it; a rule with no check is marked as an instruction and does not bind anyone.

reasoning.definition: The rule data is validated by a JSON Schema that requires either a `check` or `instruction` on every row, and the registry repo's gate (make check and the pre-push hook) fails otherwise. A rule stays unbound until its check exists, so the grid cannot lie; a changelog ledger lists rules not yet on (for example todo and skip bans, an unknown-cast comment rule, deep relative imports, and ticketed suppressions in tests).
pros: The reference team learned this the hard way; the ledger idea comes from the same team. No fault in our own record; the schema uses a standard validator, no program built.

rules.statement: Findings from a platform review are pinned as tests, so each accepted ruling is held by a check that names it, or says it is an instruction.

reasoning.definition: Examples of review tests: config shape, exact licence match, last value wins, no package runner, the skip list agrees with the byte-equal list, no rule below error. An accepted decision links the check that holds it or says instruction.
pros: A ruling with no check is forgotten by the next change.

rules.statement: Rule ids are unique, every claim in a rule resolves to a file or command that exists, and every cited rule id and ticket exists.

reasoning.definition: A rule-link checker (`companion check rule-links`) walks the rule data: unique ids, every backticked file, command or id resolves, every rule id or ticket cited (each rule row states its zero-by) in code, docs, cards and change descriptions exists (rules in the rulebook, tickets in the index). A URL link checker is a candidate for external links. A ticket names only things that exist.
pros: 52 "claim false" lines in the first review; the guides test in one repo is the model.

rules.statement: Every rule is assigned to exactly one owner or card, and a generated roster fails when a rule is unassigned or doubled.

reasoning.definition: A generator over the rule data and the cards: every rule id assigned once; unassigned or doubled fails. Where the source asks for a named owner who reads changes to sensitive paths, a CODEOWNERS file is not available (one GitHub identity), so a named non-author reviewer by trailer carries it.
pros: A donor lesson: a generated roster failing on unassigned or doubled rules. No fault of ours counted.

rules.statement: At each stage exit, list the rules whose check has not fired in a stated window and the rules with no owner, and keep each with a reason or remove it; the exemption list and extension table are reviewed too.

reasoning.definition: A silent rule may be working, so a firing count alone never removes one; the window is a guess and the output is a report that opens a review. Fire counts per rule come from gate logs. A row that no concern used in two stages is questioned, and a recurring workaround becomes a row.
pros: Rows only accumulate; the window is a guess (principles report P-02 section 7.3).

rules.statement: A shared check moves by rung (review, ratcheted, zero, enforced); its rung is a field on the rule and a move is announced.

reasoning.definition: The rung field is in the rule table. Rung adoption for a repo with debt (the adoption order is in the handbook): off, then suppress all in a no-logic change, then error for new files, then the registry stage, then zero. A firing count alone never removes a rule.
pros: A shared check that changes level silently surprises every repo that takes it.

rules.statement: Base rules apply to every project; a kind or a framework brings a rule pack of its own, a pack adds rows and never edits a base row, and an exemption is per kind with a one-line reason, as data.

reasoning.definition: The rule data has an applies-to and an exempt field per row, and a repo's rendered config equals the base plus its packs (a byte check re-renders base plus packs and compares). Exemptions are per kind, with a one-line reason, in the rule file and not a repo's choice.
pros: Operator direction (points 15 and 18): a repo cannot differ from base plus its packs.

rules.statement: Rule data stays least-powerful: the schema of rule packs and exemptions forbids expressions, conditionals and references to other rows, and a pack states for each row its level, its check, its plant and which base rows it narrows with a reason.

reasoning.definition: JSON Schema for pack files with additionalProperties false and no expression, conditional or cross-row reference keys, validated in the standards repo's gate by the front-matter validator. Free-text fields are listed so that no check reads them. Off-the-shelf validators for pure YAML or JSON packs are check-jsonschema and cue vet; not compared here.
pros: Rule data with logic in it is a second program nobody reviews.

rules.statement: A framework is not admitted until its pack exists with checks and planted violations; adding a dependency that brings a framework fails the allow-file check until the pack names it.

reasoning.definition: The module allow file has a pack field per allowed module; the check fails go.mod requires with no pack, and a pack referenced by no row. For the web, the generator refuses to list a framework with no pack directory holding a plants folder. The route in is the pilot (gates.registry.10).
pros: A two-stack foundation costs each rule a column; a framework in use has no pack today.

rules.statement: The first project on a rule pack runs a pilot list of framework-specific checks, signed by a named person, before others adopt it.

reasoning.definition: Every pack row runs on the first project with a plant before a second project on that framework starts; until then the pack is admitted by pilot. For React, the pilot list covers: a gated loader sends nothing without permission, a loader-created entry is not persisted when it must not be, search serialisation round-trips, the production build loads under the declared script policy, and the router test helper renders in the story tool and the unit runner. The list is signed by a named person; a stored signed file could be presence-checked, but who signs is the point.
pros: A rule pack that was never run on real code has unproven plants.

rules.statement: Growing the rule set is one change that adds the rule, its check, its plant and its grid cell together.

reasoning.definition: The boundary preset ships an empty extension list that later rules append to; a new shared rule lands with its check and its plant in one change. A gate check in the registry repo: a change adding a rule row must also add the check id, plant and grid cell (diff scan).
pros: A donor lesson: rows were added without their checks.

rules.statement: A status board is derived from the gate registry, not typed, and a page is generated from the rule data.

reasoning.definition: The board is generated from the registry and committed, with a generate-then-check drift gate. Generated pages show the rules, the debt and the progress. A hand edit of the board fails.
pros: Hand-typed status at a reference team said 3 enforced where the computed count was 0. Our own criteria column of checks is hand-typed, which is the same fault.

rules.statement: The rule-by-repo grid is computed from resolved configs; a rule set to warn is not counted as enforced, and a tool whose config cannot be read shows "unreadable", never "no".

reasoning.definition: The grid generator reads the resolved config (for golangci-lint, `golangci-lint linters --json`, to try) and counts error severity only. The gate fails if the committed grid differs from a regenerated one (generate-then-check).
pros: The reference team's computed grid said 0 enforced where hand-typed status said 3.

rules.statement: Every rule row states its status, the check that enforces it, its zero-by, and the failure it prevents, and has a fixture.

reasoning.definition: The rule table requires status, enforced-by and zero-by fields on every row, and a failure-prevented sentence and a fixture on every rule.
pros: A rule row without these cannot be told from a wish.

rules.statement: A number on a page, in a status page or in the rulebook is produced by a script from the baseline or gate data and never typed by hand; a frozen number only falls.

reasoning.definition: Pages are rendered from data and the committed pages are diffed; any hand-typed number fails because the rendered page differs. A scan for numerals is not used: dates, ids and versions are numerals, a page with no numbers would pass, and a hand-typed number equal to a generated one would pass. Census scripts count the debt with a fixed command and print the input count. Every number in a doc has the command that produced it.
pros: Numbers copied by hand into the criteria Today cells had wrong totals (V-28); a reference team typed 3 checks as enforced where the computed count was 0.

rules.statement: A metric that cannot be measured prints null with its reason, never 0.

reasoning.definition: The baseline format prints null with a reason; a schema test rejects a numeric 0 where the metric is unmeasurable.
pros: A failed measurement that prints 0 reads as perfect.

rules.statement: A process measure with no honest limit trips a decision-point alarm: crossing it opens a recorded decision and does not fail the build.

reasoning.definition: Each threshold is data and is labelled a guess. A crossing writes an item to the decision queue; land blocks until the decision is recorded. Examples: pipeline time, new-case fan-out, journey count. No agent is blocked at the moment of crossing, so there is nothing to game.
pros: It fills the space between a measure that nobody reads and a gate that blocks on a guess.

rules.statement: Every boolean switch has a test for its non-default value, or a ticketed exemption.

reasoning.definition: Boolean switches are listed against test references in a report first (the boolean-switch-without-test list).
pros: A switch whose non-default value is never run is dead configuration.

rules.statement: A rule that measures review rounds or refused pushes names where the count is kept, because neither leaves a record on its own.

reasoning.definition: Review by message leaves no review on GitHub, and a refused push is recorded nowhere. The count of review rounds of a pull request is kept where the reviewer's verdict is recorded: one record per round, written by the reviewer and never by the change's author. The count of refused pushes is kept by the hook that refuses them, as a field in that run's time record (one JSON file a run, in the git folder, which nothing appends to). Each count is a local claim and decides nothing: no stamp key, gate, land or release step reads it. A measure that cannot name its place prints null with the reason (gates.measures.1).
pros: A study could not say how many rounds a pull request took or how many pushes a gate refused, as no place held either number.

sources.says: Review by message leaves no review on GitHub, and a refused push is recorded nowhere.

rules.statement: A green report says how many tests, files or stories each member ran and the delta against the merge base; a member that ran nothing is red, a count that fell against the merge base fails landing, and an instrument counts as a guard only once it has been seen to fail.

reasoning.definition: gates.plants.8 holds that a check prints its input count and that zero inputs is not a pass unless declared. This rule holds the counts per member and the comparison. The count is read from the tool's own output, never from a list of files. The delta is against a count made on the merge base in the same run, not against a stored report, so a test script removed from a manifest, a target changed to do nothing, or a story set that stopped playing shows as a fall. A member that ran nothing is red whatever the tool's exit code: a Go package with no tests makes gotestsum print `EMPTY <package>` and `DONE 0 tests` and exit 0, so the tier reads that output and a member that found no test exits 1. A setting of the environment that selects or skips tests (`GOFLAGS` with `-run` or `-skip`) can hide a red test: when it leaves no test the zero count makes the member red, but when it leaves one (the Windows run's `-run=TestPass` gave `DONE 1 tests`, exit 0) only the fall of the count against the merge base shows it, and that holds only if the base ran without the flag: clearing the flag is the guard (gates.command.23), the count its backstop. A new instrument (a mutation run, a lint rule, a contrast check) is planted red once (gates.plants.1) before its green counts. Evidence: a spike on Linux and on Windows.
pros: One organisation published two versions of a design system with no test script, 4 days 20 hours with 20 spec files unrun and a green gate; a green with 18 story plays unrun passed review; 13 of 14 mutation runs tested nothing; eleven instruments were green that had never been able to go red.

a package with no tests, and GOFLAGS

rules.statement: A gate's wall time excludes the time it waited for a slot; queue wait and slot hold print on their own lines, and a timed step records the load and whether it held a slot.

reasoning.definition: tests.measures.1 holds that each tier's wall time is recorded with the load beside it. This rule holds what the wall time is: from the first member's start to the last member's end. The wait for a slot before that is a second number, and the time the slot was held is a third. A budget (tests.measures.2) is judged on the first number only. A step timed outside a slot at a high load says so, because its number is inflated by an amount nobody can state.
pros: One organisation counted 11 minutes of queue as gate time against a 1.5 times limit and landed 0 of 5; its agents waited at least 2,846 minutes for slots in two days, a floor because the wait was logged only at its start.

rules.statement: A gate or repo reader of YAML refuses a duplicate key.

reasoning.definition: The keys of a YAML mapping are unique (YAML 1.2.2, section 3.2.1.1). A reader of the gate registry, the repo checks or the dev tool's own files that takes the last of two equal keys lets a second definition override the first without a word, so the strict reader is the one every such reader calls and the permissive one is banned in those folders.
pros: A duplicate key in a gate list drops the first entry silently and the gate passes with a check missing.

rules.statement: No tracked path is a symbolic link.

reasoning.definition: A tracked entry of mode 120000 fails the check, naming the path. A link reads as a file on one system and as a text file holding a path on another, so the checkout differs by system.
pros: A repository that must check out the same on every system cannot hold an entry whose meaning depends on the system that wrote it.

rules.statement: No two tracked paths differ only by case.

reasoning.definition: Two tracked paths that are equal once case is folded fail the check, naming both. On a case-folding file system the second overwrites the first.
pros: A checkout on a case-folding system keeps one of the two files and loses the other without a message.

rules.statement: Each concern has exactly one importable owner chosen in a data file, the alternatives are banned by name, and the failure message says what to import instead.

reasoning.definition: The owner is a module, a standard-library package or a shared package. The concern table is the rulebook's list of libraries: one owner per concern with the alternatives named, and every verdict in it is a candidate until ruled. The table is data validated by a schema that requires an owner and the alternatives. A direct dependency that is not in the table fails, and a banned name in source or in a manifest fails. Existing uses of a banned library are a list that only shrinks and never gains an entry. Until the data file exists, the rule for a project is an instruction, and the check reports not applicable with the count of entries (zero) rather than passing. The first entries of a web project's table follow its framework part. Example plant: left-pad as an unlisted name and lodash as a banned one. The allow-file is the shrink-only list of existing uses. Existing uses are suppressed into a suppressions file (eslint-suppressions.json, written with --suppress-rule) that never gains an entry. The build-time cap flag is --max-issues, set to 0. Examples of banned alternatives in a web table: react-hook-form (the form pick is TanStack Form), react-hotkeys-hook, react-i18next and react-intl; the full lists belong to the framework parts.
pros: Without one owner per concern, each author picks a library and the build carries several for the same job. In the Go estate no repository had a ban list, and one would have failed the terminal-colour ban on day one; all 32 direct dependencies of the web estate hit no ban, so the cost of binding is low.

rules.statement: Each shipped binary has a declared closure of the internal packages and external modules it may link, checked per binary by a test with a shrink-only allow list, and the count of linked modules only falls.

reasoning.definition: For each binary the repository declares which internal packages and which external modules it may link, citing the concern each external module serves. A test lists each binary's real dependency closure (go list -deps for the binary's main package) and fails on any internal package or module outside that binary's list, so a helper or guest binary that links a host package fails even when the main binary may. The allow list only shrinks without a recorded exemption, and the count of linked modules per binary only falls. An empty allow file is refused with a distinct exit code, not read as a pass. The test runs in the local gate.
pros: A module can be linked without anyone having chosen it. In the Go estate, direct requires ranged from 7 to 15 per repository and linked modules from 38 to 47, and no repository had an allow file. A count per repository hides a small binary that has grown the large one's dependencies, which is where a trust line breaks.

rules.statement: A new third-party module meets a bar: a permissive licence, a release or push in the last 12 months, more than one committer or a named organisation, and a module graph small enough to read.

reasoning.definition: The change that adds the module carries a row in the concern table, one sentence on what the standard library lacks, and the weight of the dependency. The facts are measured by script; the sentence is read by a reviewer.
pros: A dependency chosen without facts is accepted on a name; the bar turns the choice into measurable items.

rules.statement: A commit that adds a dependency to any manifest section is justified in its pull request and signed off by someone other than its author; a version bump of an existing dependency does not count.

reasoning.definition: Every manifest section counts: runtime, development, optional and peer dependencies. The signature is held by a stored verdict from a different identity on changes to the protected path list. The justification text is read by a reviewer.
pros: Adding a dependency is the largest single change of supply-chain surface; one author should not make it alone.

rules.statement: The standard library comes before a new dependency or a home-made helper, before a part is written the change names the maintained tools surveyed and why none fits, and a part a maintained tool already does well is not rebuilt.

reasoning.definition: Order of preference: the standard library, then a maintained tool or library that does the job, then our own code. A change that adds a new part (a module, a command, a parser, a protocol client) names the maintained tools it looked at and the reason each was not used; "none surveyed" fails the review. Where a maintained program does the job, the program uses it through an adapter (arch.ports.6) and reads its machine output (arch.ports.20) rather than reimplementing it.
pros: A dependency or a helper for something the standard library already does is weight with no gain, and a part rebuilt where a maintained tool exists is code we now maintain alone.

rules.statement: A new library is a row of the register of libraries, which names the job, what it replaces and the alternatives it bans, and it passes the supply-chain gate and logs the replaced use as debt with a date by which it is gone.

reasoning.definition: The register is rulebook/lang/go/libraries.yaml. One concern keeps one library: the row names its job, the library to call, where an import of it is allowed, the modules and hand-written code it replaces, and the ban for the alternatives (depguard imports, forbidigo patterns). A row that is chosen and bans something becomes a row of the Go preset; a row that needs a spike, or is conditional, does not. The places still using the replaced code are listed in the debt record with a zero-by date. The replaced use may be a hand-written copy object or vocabulary.
pros: A library added beside the old one doubles the code for a concern and leaves the old one to rot.

rules.statement: A dependency that does what the platform already does is on the ban list.

reasoning.definition: Advice-only plugins that report native replacements: @e18e/eslint-plugin and eslint-plugin-depend.
pros: A package that repeats a built-in feature adds code, update work and attack surface for nothing.

rules.statement: Every banned or watched library has a named re-entry trigger, and the ban list covers the library family, not only the member in use.

reasoning.definition: A trigger is a version, a stated need or a measured threshold.
pros: A ban with no way back is either ignored or never revisited; a ban of one family member leaves the others open.

rules.statement: A dependency's API is one that models write correctly without prompting.

pros: A library whose API models misuse costs repeated rework in agent-written code.

rules.statement: A test-only module is absent from the non-test build.

pros: A module linked only for tests that reaches the shipped build enlarges what ships.

rules.statement: One package manager, pinned, installs from the lockfile only; the lockfile is the pin, it is verified, and a version conflict is never hidden.

reasoning.definition: For Go: go.sum is committed, go mod verify passes, builds use -mod=readonly, and no gate or release script uses -mod=mod or go get. For JavaScript: install with the frozen-lockfile form only, one package manager for the whole estate, and a peer mismatch fails the install instead of being silenced (a legacy-peer switch is removed). Go has no peer ranges, so that half does not transfer. The strict install form is --frozen-lockfile; peer mismatches are not hidden (legacy-peer-deps is removed). The gate scanner (gatescan) bans -mod=mod and go get in gate and release scripts.
pros: An install that resolves again can differ by day. In the web estate a package manager that honours the cooldown refused a young locked entry while another passed it, so the choice of manager is part of the defence.

rules.statement: After the dependencies are installed, the build, the type-check and the tests run with the network blocked, and generated output comes from committed inputs.

reasoning.definition: No CDN or latest-tag URL in a build config; no download at build time; a code generator's output fails the build when it did not compile. A build step that declares a fetch as its own input, such as a content build that reads a remote source, is exempt, because that fetch is the build's input. A Go build runs behind go-proc's network block (sandbox.Run) with GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly and GOPROXY=off; a JS build runs under a sandbox runtime with an empty domain allowlist. Where the system gives no block (Windows today: sandbox.ErrNoBlock) the run is refused by name and never made unblocked. Install itself needs the network and runs before. The install step is npm ci or its frozen equivalent; the build and type-check run after it with no network. A message-format plugin loads from disk through node_modules, not from a URL. The sandbox is @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime; a scan of gate and release scripts by gatescan bans -mod=mod and go get.
pros: A build that reaches the network can differ by day and is an exfiltration route. How a block is made differs by system, so the rule names the behaviour and the refusal, never one means.

rules.statement: The manifest pins the package manager by name with an error on mismatch and a minimum version, so an old tool that would ignore a setting silently refuses to install.

reasoning.definition: The settings check reads the package manager pin as part of the check-npmrc command of the reference.
pros: A package manager older than the settings file ignores the settings, so the cooldown and install-script guards vanish without a message.

rules.statement: Direct code dependencies use exact versions, ranges are allowed only for peers, and the exact-pin rule covers code dependencies, not the images a program writes into a stack it deploys.

reasoning.definition: Every direct dependency in a manifest or module file names one exact version; a peer dependency may name a range. The rule is about code the build resolves. A stack file that a program writes for its owner (a compose file, a service unit) may follow an image's release tag and update by comparing the running digest with the registry; how such stacks are written is held by the daemon and deploy rules, not here. An image the release itself builds is pinned by digest (supply.release.9). The second opinion rule is prefer-absolute-version-dependencies (and the dev form).
pros: A range on a direct dependency means two installs of one commit can differ. In the web baseline none of 32 direct dependencies was a range. Extending exact pins to the images a program deploys for its owner would forbid the update path that design chose on purpose.

rules.statement: A shared package whose peer range lags a major tool is replaced or overridden on record.

pros: A peer range that excludes the installed major forces a silenced install, which hides every other peer conflict.

rules.statement: No package runs an install script unless it is named on a reasoned allowlist.

reasoning.definition: Either of two settings blocks scripts, and the last value wins as the package manager reads it. The few packages that need a script are rebuilt by an explicit step after an install with scripts off. Go modules run nothing at fetch, and the one native build step is removed by building without cgo, so the rule has no Go check. The npm form is ignore-scripts, with the allowlisted few rebuilt explicitly.
pros: An install script runs arbitrary code on every machine that installs, which is the usual route of a package takeover.

rules.statement: Every install-script allowlist entry names the package, an owner and a reason of at least ten characters; the file must parse, and an absent file is fine.

pros: An allowlist without owner and reason becomes a list nobody can review or expire.

rules.statement: No phantom imports: the lock has exactly the declared direct dependencies, a binary run by name is a declared dependency, in a workspace the root manifest holds no dependency a package imports, and each package declares exactly the siblings its import rules allow, checked both ways.

reasoning.definition: A bare package-runner call resolves an unlisted tool to whatever has that name, so every binary used must be a declared dependency. A non-flat install layout keeps an undeclared import from resolving. The install is the frozen-lockfile form so a mismatch fails. In a workspace, a dependency in the root manifest resolves from every file, so the root holds only workspace tooling that no package imports. Each package's manifest declares exactly the packages its units may import under the layer table (arch.layers.12): a declared sibling it may not import fails, and an allowed import it does not declare fails.
pros: A package that resolves only because something else installed it breaks the day that other package changes, and a bare runner call can fetch a stranger. A root dependency hides the same phantom import inside a workspace.

rules.statement: The toolchain is at one version in every project, with the same presets, the toolchain a gate ran on is the one the lockfile names, each dependency has one version across a workspace's packages, and siblings are linked as workspace dependencies.

reasoning.definition: A preflight on every gate host compares the runtime version with its pinned file, the package manager with the manifest field, and the frozen install offline, and lists missing tools; a non-zero result stops the gate. A runtime-major file is rendered from the template answer so one major holds across declarations. One preflight serves Go and web. The preflight frozen install is install --frozen-lockfile --offline. In a workspace each third-party dependency resolves to one version across all packages, and a package depends on a sibling only through a workspace link, never a published version of it.
pros: A gate that ran on a different toolchain than the lockfile names proves nothing about the shipped build. One tool version per estate removes a class of drift.

rules.statement: Each check tool has one pinned version and runs from the pinned install, passing its exit code through; no tool is run through a package runner that could fetch a same-named stranger.

reasoning.definition: A test fails if the runner's name appears in a shipped file. No go run of a package at a version at gate time, and no go get or -mod=mod in gate or release scripts. The licence checker is one of the tools run from the pinned install (license-checker with the others such as depcruise, spectral, cspell and markdownlint).
pros: A check that fetches its own tool at run time can be replaced by whatever has that name, and a changed version gives a changed verdict.

rules.statement: The module tidy command leaves no diff, and the language version is one the estate supports.

pros: A stale unused require is a dependency nobody chose, and an unsupported language version silently skips fixes.

rules.statement: A dependency version younger than the release-age window of 7 days is refused unless the module is our own release, and the check at land reads publish dates from the lockfile.

reasoning.definition: The window is 7 days (it replaced 14 days). Our own modules are exempt: a module under the organisation's own module path, at a release tag (vX.Y.Z, never a pseudo-version or a pre-release), with no replace and a publish time that can be read, does not wait. A land check reads publish dates from go.sum and the lockfile, because an install that follows a lockfile installs a young package that is already locked. The rule states what it defends against: a bad release that is noticed quickly, not a long campaign. A maintainer change is shown in the bump. The young-version case is planted and run before the rule counts as a gate. The package manager setting is the minimum-release-age setting (min-release-age for npm). Publish times come from the proxy .info record for Go. An install that follows the lockfile, such as npm ci, installs a young locked package. The lockfile read for web is the package manager lock (pnpm-lock.yaml). The npm setting min-release-age is one line: install only versions older than N days.
pros: In the xz backdoor, version 5.6.0 was 33 days old and 5.6.1 was 19 days old at discovery, so a two-week window would have admitted both. The other supply rules (provenance, licence, scans, install scripts) do the work the window cannot. In the web estate an install that followed the lock passed a young locked entry, and one repository set the window to one day.

rules.statement: A release-age cooldown is set for the package manager at add time, numeric, and equal to the release-age window of seven days, read as the package manager reads it (the last value wins).

reasoning.definition: The estate value is 7 days (10080 minutes), the release-age window of supply.age.1, the same in every project and equal to the template and to the window the tools are held to: one number, neither under it nor over it (it replaced 14 days, 20160 minutes). The check reads the resolved setting, handles comments and quotes, and compares with the template. The setting lives in the workspace file (pnpm-workspace.yaml).
pros: A setting that is absent, non-numeric or overridden by a later line looks present and does nothing.

rules.statement: A security skip of the age window names an advisory id that resolves, and a waiver names every package it lets through, with a reason, an owner and the date all are clear.

reasoning.definition: A skip with no advisory id is refused; a skip naming a real advisory in a vulnerability database passes. A waiver for a new vendor release lists each transitive package under the window and the date by which all of them are old enough. A waiver for a new vendor major lists its transitives under the window (for example @inlang/sdk, @inlang/plugin-message-format, kysely, @napi-rs/wasm-runtime) with the date all are clear; an update-bot cooldown of seven days is the reference window. The reference waiver covered @inlang/paraglide-js 3.0.0 published that week and everything it pulls in.
pros: A fast lane for security fixes is also an attacker's route, because the second xz release arrived looking like a fix; a skip an agent can claim must therefore resolve to a real advisory.

rules.statement: The integrity and provenance signatures of every locked package are verified, and a version with weaker publishing evidence than an earlier one is refused.

reasoning.definition: Go modules are checked against go.sum and the checksum database. For packages, a trust policy that forbids a downgrade of publishing evidence is read back, and where the package manager has no signature-audit command the intent is a provenance check on the lockfile diff.
pros: A release that loses the provenance attestation its predecessors had is the signature of a stolen publishing token.

rules.statement: A vendor family updates as one group: exact pins, a stated minimum age, a provenance check on the lockfile diff, one family bump per change, and a 0.x release only through a labelled pilot with a removal path.

reasoning.definition: A bump that touches one member of a family must touch all members in one change. Each member is past the age line, and a waiver of the age rule names each package it lets through and the date all are clear. Go families, such as a terminal-UI set or a database-driver pair, move together the same way. Example family: @inlang/paraglide-js and @inlang/plugin-message-format are pinned exactly; the vendor sub-packages are neither pinned nor overridden, and there is no overrides block.
pros: A family bumped member by member leaves versions that do not fit each other, and a bump mixed with others hides which change broke.

rules.statement: A dependency is maintained: no module is archived and none has gone without a release or a push for 24 months in Go, and a web dependency has a release within 12 months or a written finished note.

reasoning.definition: An unmaintained or abandoned dependency is removed. A banned one that is already present stays on a shrink-only list. Go checks archived and last-pushed state per direct module through the host API (the network is needed, so at land or after release). The web check reads the newest release date of each direct dependency from the registry, and a finished note is an exception record. Transitive age is a report only. Examples removed in the reference: @uiw/react-json-view (alpha), @dnd-kit, zpl-renderer, and other rotting packages.
pros: A library nobody maintains carries unfixed vulnerabilities. One archived Go module was found in the baseline and nothing else.

rules.statement: No prerelease, 0.x, alpha or release-candidate major enters production except through a labelled pilot with a removal path.

reasoning.definition: For Go, v0.x is normal and the shared modules are below 1.0, so only a prerelease tag or a pseudo-version on a direct requirement needs a pilot entry in the allow file; indirect lines are left out because the module graph brings them in. For the web, a 0.x browser dependency needs a pilot record. The 0.x transitives of an accepted pilot are accepted through that pilot. Example: the 0.x transitives of @inlang/paraglide-js are accepted through one named pilot.
pros: A prerelease or an unreleased commit changes without notice and carries the same risk as a bump mixed with other edits.

rules.statement: A known-vulnerability scan of dependencies runs in the pre-push gate (in the release gate only when it does not fit the push budget), over the source for Go and over the lockfile for web, its result is read as text, and it fails on high severity.

reasoning.definition: The scan is a member of the one gate command, so the pre-push hook runs it on every push; a land tier, where a repo has one, runs it again. When the scan's network wait does not fit the hook budget of gates.hooks.4 it moves to the release workflow and still blocks the release. For Go the scan is reachability-aware and runs in source mode with the tool pinned in the shared makefile fragment. For web it is the package manager audit with --audit-level high (severity-filtered) over the lockfile, pnpm-lock.yaml, with a planted vulnerable version and a clean control; its ignore entries carry an expiry date and a reason.
pros: A dependency with a known vulnerability is the cheapest way in for an attacker. Before this rule the word vulnerability had no hit in the web catalogue, and audit appeared only as a tier-4 report. The Go scan was in six of seven repositories already. There is no hosted land job, so a scan placed only at land had no tier that runs.

rules.statement: The artifact that ships is scanned for known vulnerabilities, not only the source, and the gate reads the text of the result.

reasoning.definition: A zero exit can still print a module-level advisory, so the text is read. The scan runs on the candidate at land when release files change, and again on the shipped artifact after publish as a report. A library ships no binary, so the open question is whether a library is exempt. The command is govulncheck -mode=binary.
pros: A scan of the source can pass while the built binary carries a vulnerable module; one binary exited 0 and printed a module-level advisory.

rules.statement: A security static analyser runs, and every exclusion is named with a reason.

reasoning.definition: Four rule families are enabled by name so an exclusion cannot drop them silently: SQL built by formatting (G201), SQL built by concatenation (G202), subprocess launched with variable data (G204) and weak randomness (G404).
pros: The analyser is the largest source of suppressions, so an unnamed exclusion can quietly remove the families that matter.

rules.statement: All SQL is parameterised, so no SQL text is built from data and identifiers come from a closed list.

pros: SQL text built from data is the injection fault. In the Go estate no single-line Sprintf SQL existed in six repositories, so this pins good practice and fixes no live fault.

rules.statement: A child process starts with an argument list, never a shell string with data in it; an option terminator comes before data arguments.

reasoning.definition: A person's own pager or command line is the named exemption, with a reasoned nolint. An exempt case is a person own $PAGER or command line. The scan targets sh -c and other shell-with-data forms.
pros: A shell string with data in it is command injection. The three shell-string sites in the Go estate were all a person's own pager or command line.

rules.statement: Security randomness comes from the cryptographic generator, the non-cryptographic generator is banned for tokens, and a secret is compared in constant time.

reasoning.definition: The compare scan targets == on values with secret-named variables (token, secret).
pros: A token from the ordinary generator is guessable, and an equality compare of a secret leaks it by timing. The three imports of the ordinary generator found were a tool, a solver and a fixture.

rules.statement: A known-vulnerability scan of dependencies runs in the full gate, which the land job runs on the merged tree before main, over the source for Go and over the lockfile for web; its result is read as text, and it fails on high severity.

reasoning.definition: The scan is a member of the one gate command's full tier. The land job calls the push tier and then the full tier, so the scan runs on every change before it reaches main, and the release runs it again. The pre-push hook may leave it out: its list is a declared subset of the land job's (gates.command.1). For Go the scan is reachability-aware and runs in source mode with the tool pinned in the tools module. For web it is the package manager audit with --audit-level high (severity-filtered) over the lockfile, pnpm-lock.yaml, with a planted vulnerable version and a clean control; its ignore entries carry an expiry date and a reason.
pros: A dependency with a known vulnerability is the cheapest way in for an attacker. The scan waits on the network, which the push budget cannot carry on every push, so its home is the full tier. Before main it still runs on every change: the land job runs the full tier on the merged tree, so nothing the scan would refuse reaches main.

rules.statement: Every installed package carries a licence on one shared allowlist, weak copyleft (MPL-2.0) passes only when the package is used unmodified, and strong copyleft, unlicensed or unknown licences fail.

reasoning.definition: Allowed examples are MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC and 0BSD. MPL-2.0 is allowed for a package used as published: a patch, a vendored edited copy or a fork of an MPL-2.0 package fails until its changed files are published under the same licence and the exception is recorded. AGPL, GPL, SSPL, UNLICENSED and an unknown licence fail. What ships to the browser is held to a stricter list than the rest. Our own modules are skipped by path or scope. The policy ships once: allowed SPDX ids, the weak-copyleft list with its unmodified condition, an own-scope skip, dated exceptions and clarifications. The check runs in the gate command the pre-push hook runs. Go uses its own licence tool with the allowed list and with our modules ignored (without that, they report no licence found). Go form: go-licenses check ./... --allowed_licenses=<list> --ignore=<our modules>. Web alternative: license-checker-rseidelsohn with --onlyAllow.
pros: A strong copyleft licence in a shipped dependency can force the product's source open, and an unlicensed one gives no right to use it. Weak copyleft binds only the files of the package itself, so it is safe while those files are not changed.

rules.statement: The licence judgement is exact SPDX satisfaction of the allowlist; an empty tree, a declared but uninstalled dependency, a missing licence or non-SPDX text all fail.

pros: A licence check that passes on nothing found passes on a broken install.

rules.statement: A dated licence exception covers one named package and one licence, only as a development dependency, and fails once expired.

pros: A broad or undated exception becomes the way round the policy. A licence exception never covers shipped code.

rules.statement: A licence guessed from a file needs a clarification entry naming the same package and file; the own scope is skipped by name.

pros: A licence read from a file's text is a guess, and a clarification records who decided it.

rules.statement: Every shared module a program requires has a licence file, and its visibility is known to the check.

reasoning.definition: All packages are private for now, so the check treats every shared module as private and requires the licence file anyway. Revisit before the first repository goes public.
pros: Three released versions of the shared module had no licence file and the module is private, which the licence scan flagged.

rules.statement: LICENSE and NOTICE sit at the repository root, and every artifact that bundles third-party code ships a generated notices file equal to what it bundles, compared in the gate.

reasoning.definition: The root holds the project's own LICENSE and a NOTICE naming the project and its copyright. Each artifact that bundles third-party code (a binary, a bundle, an image, a packed package) carries a third-party notices file generated from the exact set of packages it bundles, with each package's licence text and any NOTICE it ships. The gate regenerates the notices for each artifact and fails when the committed or packed file differs. Apache-2.0 and MPL-2.0 notices travel with the code that carries them.
pros: Most permissive licences are conditional on keeping their notice; an artifact that bundles code without it breaks the licence that allowed the bundle. A hand-kept notices file drifts from what the artifact holds.

rules.statement: No secret is committed: one pinned secret scanner runs at commit and in the pre-push gate over the whole history, a land tier where one exists runs it again, and a finding is reported by rule, file and line without the value.

reasoning.definition: The scanner config is chosen explicitly and not picked up by accident. A staged-file scan runs at commit, and the gate command the pre-push hook runs scans every commit in the history and the working tree as it is. A land tier, where a repo has one, repeats the full scan; it is never the only full scan. The documentation example key is allowlisted by default and is not reported. The staged-file scan is gitleaks protect --staged (git --staged in current versions). The commit scan is one of the three standing gates shared across repos (the others are the armed hook and the pipefail check), run by the shared hook file over the staged changes.
pros: A committed secret stays in history forever and must be rotated. The scan also reaches the web bundle, which must carry no secret. There is no hosted land job, so a full scan placed only at land never ran.

rules.statement: Configuration holds a reference to a secret, never the value, and secrets are read through one required schema.

reasoning.definition: A secret never comes from a flag and is never printed. For a web page, variables it reads are in a typed schema and no secret reaches the bundle.
pros: A value in configuration is copied into logs, images and every place the configuration goes; a reference is resolved only where it is used.

rules.statement: Secret-shaped keys in public environment files fail, and no secret reaches the bundle.

reasoning.definition: Public environment files hold only public values; a variable whose name looks like a secret fails the check.
pros: A secret in a public file ships to every browser.

rules.statement: Forbidden names come from a list kept outside the repository with its words stored as hashes; every tracked file, branch name and pushed commit message is scanned against it, the check fails when the list cannot be read, and in a public repo every commit's author and committer email is a no-reply address.

reasoning.definition: The forbidden names are the private facts of the people and places a repo serves: employers, people, machines, networks, addresses, households and the software a deployment runs. The list lives outside the repository (a path set in the environment) and holds each word as a hash, so the guard does not spell what it guards. The scan reads every tracked file, the branch name and every commit message in the pushed range, matching whole words case-insensitively against the hashes. When the list path is unset or unreadable the check exits 2 (could not run), never 0. Examples, fixtures and docs use stand-in names from an explicit stand-in list and documentation address ranges. In a public repository the pre-push hook refuses a commit whose author or committer email is not the host's no-reply address.
pros: A private name in history cannot be removed without rewriting it, and a public repository publishes every word of it. In one target repository a work email reached 217 commits before the check existed. A list kept in the repo would itself publish the names.

rules.statement: A dependency bump is its own change: one direct bump per commit, no source file touched, after its cooldown, with the trial counts in the change.

reasoning.definition: The commit check compares the manifest and lockfile with the base: more than one direct dependency changed in one commit fails, a manifest or lockfile change together with non-manifest files fails, and the commit message carries a Trial line with the counts. For Go the scan is on go.mod with non-module files; indirect lines are left out because a module graph brings them in. A vendor family counts as one bump. There is no bump bot; the owner lane opens bumps. The diff scan for web reads package.json and the lockfile together with non-manifest files.
pros: A bump mixed with source edits hides the change a reader should see, and a bump can ride inside a large refactor unseen. The known way round is hiding the bump in a refactor, which the same scan catches.

rules.statement: Consumer lag behind the shared module and lockstep pairs are reported with the release as the unit, lag is not gated by a fixed window, each consumer moves its require when it is ready, and a breaking module change fixes every caller the owner keeps in the same change.

reasoning.definition: One module version in every program.
