The report compares the shared module's version in each program's go.mod with the latest tag and its date, and shows each consumer's distance from the latest shared module and the pairs that release together, with the release as the unit. Nothing fails on lag: a consumer moves its require when it is ready. A change to the shared module that breaks its surface fixes, in the same change or the same coordinated release, every caller in the repositories the owner keeps, so no kept consumer is left on a broken path. The lag is reported in minors per module, the root module and each separately versioned module on their own, and a waiver whose trigger is "until the shared module bumps" is listed beside the lag, so the release report reads "one module lags three minors; three waivers wait on it". The tag-date read needs network access to a private module.
pros: A consumer that lags keeps running code the owner has already replaced, so the lag is shown. A fixed window forces every consumer to the newest version on the owner's schedule, which arch.measures.6 itself names as a cause of coupling; fixing callers in the breaking change is what keeps a lagging consumer safe to move later. A pair that must always release together signals a misplaced boundary.

rules.statement: Related shared modules are tagged together, and a separately owned package has its own versioning.

reasoning.definition: A shared root module and its sub-module are tagged together; the design-tokens package is not in that tag and defaults to its own semver. A release check that the tags match runs in the owner repository only. The deprecate-first form is the //go:fix inline directive.
pros: The sub-module tags came about 64 minutes and two commits after the root tag, so the pair was not atomic.

rules.statement: A shared release plans who pays for each bump: consumers pay in lockstep, an upgrade comes with a codemod or a list of what changes, and a new shared rule lands as a minor with each repository recording its debt first.

reasoning.definition: A breaking tag without a changelog section that lists what consumers change is refused. A cross-repository sweep tool opens a pull request in each repository for a codemod. Debt may not grow on a bump. The changelog tool kept is git-cliff.
pros: A release that does not say what consumers must change shifts the cost silently. The changelog of an earlier shared release is the shape of such a list.

rules.statement: A shared package's version range spans minors on purpose, since a caret on a 0.x version pins one minor and could never resolve the next release.

pros: A caret range on 0.x means the next minor is a different compatible set, so the range never reaches it.

rules.statement: A shared config carries a version that consumers can read and pin.

pros: A consumer cannot pin or report the distance from a shared config that does not state its version.

rules.statement: The shared package's check tools are regular dependencies so one version bump moves all of them; lint and compiler tools are peers with declared ranges.

pros: Tools declared as peers drift apart per consumer; regular dependencies move with the one bump.

rules.statement: A library's release clock runs from the last fix merged to its consumers' main branch, the bump in each consumer has an owner, and the hand-off is logged like a review round.

reasoning.definition: supply.bumps.2 holds that consumer lag is reported with the release as the unit. This rule holds that the release is not done at publish. The release names the consumer's bump and who makes it, and the hand-off is a row where the hub counts rounds (gates.measures.5). A program's release clock runs from the last fix merged to published; a library's runs on to the consumers' main.
pros: One organisation's design-system releases reached its main web application in 2 hours 45 minutes, 5 hours 30 minutes, and once not in 5 days, because nothing linked a publish to its consumer.

rules.statement: A release is built from a clean annotated tag on main by one recipe that runs the full gate first and never pushes, an install is made only from such a build and reads the installed version back, and where something is published only the release workflow on the tag publishes it, with publish refused unless CI is set.

reasoning.definition: The release recipe (make release or its equivalent) refuses anything but a clean checkout of main, runs the full gate unless a local stamp shows that this exact tree passed it (gates.land.1), writes or checks the changelog entry (supply.release.5), tags with an annotated tag and builds. It never pushes; the person pushes the tag. An install or deploy refuses a checkout or build that is not exactly a clean release tag, and after installing reads the running program's version and commit back and compares them with the tag. Where something is published (a package, an image, a release page), only the release workflow triggered by the tag publishes it, with the publish job needing every test and build job (supply.release.6); a command refuses to publish when the CI environment variable is not set, and the first publish of a package is from the workflow too. There is no CI on every push and no run is scheduled: each release prints the age of the last whole run, and no weekly or other scheduled run is added. The recipe also runs non-blocking steps that need the network, such as the external link check (docs.links.1): each prints its findings and never stops the release.
pros: A shared package can otherwise publish from a laptop with whatever the laptop holds, and an install from an untagged tree is a version nobody can name. The invariant three target repos share is one recipe from a clean tagged main after the full gate; CI is the only place that holds the publish token.

rules.statement: A release is refused on an API break that is not declared, checked before the tag is pushed.

pros: A break the author did not declare turns every consumer's next bump into a surprise. The tag step is the last moment the check can run, because the tool refuses once the tag exists. A real break was found in the shared module.

rules.statement: A release is the same bytes from any directory: the build strips paths, and a script builds twice from two paths and compares.

reasoning.definition: It runs on the candidate at land when release files change, and again on the shipped artifact after publish as a report. The check is go build with -trimpath; a snapshot build (goreleaser build --snapshot) is made twice from two directories and compared with cmp.
pros: A build that embeds its path cannot be reproduced; two hashes from two paths prove it, and the flag that strips paths removes the difference.

rules.statement: Release artifacts carry a checksum; an SBOM or a signature is added when a third party verifies it, and not before.

pros: A checksum lets a consumer detect corruption or substitution; heavier attestations cost work with no reader until a verifier exists.

rules.statement: Every release has a plain-words changelog entry that a person writes or rewrites, a tool proposes the version with a named override allowed, a program with an API names its API number in the entry, and the release recipe never pushes.

reasoning.definition: The entry is written per change (each change adds its item under Unreleased) or as a draft the release recipe makes from the commits for a person to rewrite before tagging; either way a person writes the words, in plain language with a bold lead and no file names, function names or internal ids. A tool proposes the next version from the history since the last tag (git-cliff in the Go repos, a change-notes tool in a web workspace; the tool is chosen per repo), and the recipe accepts a named override (VERSION=vX.Y.Z) for a person's choice. A program with a versioned API names the API number in each release's entry. The release check fails a tag whose entry is missing or still the untouched draft. The recipe scan is run by a gate scanner (gatescan) and bans git push in the recipe.
pros: A tag with no entry gives consumers nothing to read, and a generated entry made of commit subjects is written for the author, not the reader. A version a tool proposes is not mistyped, and an override keeps the person's choice. A recipe that pushes releases without the person's last look.

rules.statement: After the tag build and before publish, a release step unpacks the archive, runs version and one start test and compares its digest with the one the tests saw; the publish job needs every test and build job, the workflow has no conditional or continue-on-error, and the publishing job runs no project code.

reasoning.definition: In the release workflow the publish job lists every test and build job as a need and runs only when all passed: no if: and no continue-on-error anywhere in the workflow, held by a test that reads the file. The publish job has no checkout of the project and runs none of its code; it only promotes the artifacts the build made (for example by undrafting a complete draft release). The publish job needs every job, has no if: and no continue-on-error, and runs none of the module's code. For a web project the archive's page is served and one start test is run. A page embedded in a daemon is tested through the daemon's archive. For a deployed function the bundle is unpacked, its handler invoked from the bundle, and its hash compared with the one the tests saw and with the code hash of the deployed function. A library ships no binary, so the Go rule has an exemption.
pros: A bundle can differ from the source the tests ran against through bundler options or an optional dependency resolved at build time. A last-modified time shows the function was updated, not that its bytes are the ones that passed. In one web estate 4 of 72 faults showed only on a real server after release.

rules.statement: The program is compiled and vetted at push, on the one machine the gate runs on.

reasoning.definition: One gate step runs go vet ./... at push for each system of the project's list (arch.ports.4), by GOOS on the one machine the gate runs on, as one step. It catches a compile fault only. What differs by system is the platform libraries' own proof, which is run on each system by loan and is not a leg of a product's gate.
pros: A compile fault is invisible until a later tier if the push does not vet at all. (An earlier version of this rule asked for a vet per shipped GOOS, because one program built only on Linux failed in six packages on Linux-only calls; a product now holds no such calls.)

rules.statement: Binary size is recorded as a metric, not a gate.

pros: Five standard-library imports grew a binary 4.5 percent, which a 5 percent budget passes, so a budget gate would not have caught the growth that matters; the number is the value.

rules.statement: A release carries a checksum file listing every artifact; an SBOM, provenance and a signature are added the day a repo is public, and a container image is built from a base pinned by digest and runs as a non-root user.

reasoning.definition: Every release has a checksum file listing every artifact. A repo that is not public ships no SBOM, no provenance statement and no signature, and no check asks for them; the day a repo is made public its release config adds them wherever the place a release is published supports them (a package registry's provenance statement, a build attestation, an SBOM, a signed and notarized desktop build). An image is built by the release recipe from a base image pinned by digest, runs as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem except its volumes, whether the repo is public or not. What the publisher offers is read from its documentation when the release is set up and recorded in the release config; a publisher that adds provenance later is picked up by the next review of that config. Ruling: no SBOM or signing while private; a checksum file now, and an SBOM, provenance and a signature the day a repo is public.
pros: A checksum lets a consumer detect corruption or substitution. Provenance, an SBOM and a pinned non-root base cost minutes once and age well; waiting for a third party to ask is waiting to be asked why not.

sources.where: the table row supply.release.9, a checksum file now

rules.statement: The release tier runs from a fresh clone of the tag, never from a working checkout; the release dry run is a release member with its cost listed; and a member that needs the tag says so and runs last.

reasoning.definition: supply.release.1 holds that a release is built from a clean annotated tag by one recipe that runs the full gate first. This rule holds the members: the push tier plus the release members, all at once (gates.command.17), on a clone made from the tag so no file of a working checkout reaches the build. The dry run of the release tool is a member with its cost, so a broken release config is found before the release and not at it. A member that needs the tag to exist (the changelog check, the publish) declares it and runs after the others.
pros: One project found its broken release config only at release, because the dry run was not a member; a release from a working checkout carries whatever that checkout holds.

rules.statement: A hosted release workflow maps its jobs to the members file and ends with the runner's report, installs once and never per job, and a reproducible build builds each artifact twice from two clean copies and compares byte for byte, one reproducibility proof for each artifact.

reasoning.definition: supply.workflows.5 holds that a workflow which runs gate members runs the one gate command. This rule holds the release workflow's shape: each job is a member or a group of members of the release tier, the last job prints the runner's report with its counts (gates.measures.6), and the install runs once into a cache the jobs share. supply.release.3 holds the same bytes from any directory; this rule runs that proof for each artifact, two clean copies each, the artifacts in parallel (gates.command.18).
pros: Hosted release workflows of one organisation installed per job and had no success on record in seven repositories; a release that builds once cannot say its bytes are reproducible.

rules.statement: No workflow triggers itself: workflows run only when started (manual dispatch or a call from another workflow), or on a tag push for a release, never on a schedule, a push to a branch or a pull request.

reasoning.definition: The gate runs locally: make check and the pre-push hook (gates.hooks.1) are the only gate on a push, and no workflow repeats it on push or pull request. A release workflow runs on a release tag push or by dispatch, has a dry-run option and one verify file per export, and the first publish of a package is only from the workflow. A check too slow for the hook runs in the release workflow (gates.hooks.4). The check is parse-based: it normalises the on key (a scalar, an inline list, a quoted key and a map all count) to a set of events and allows only dispatch, call and push with tags. A check in the ast-grep style passed three of five cheap restructurings and was rejected; the parse-based check passed six of six. The same check runs on Go and web repositories. A conftest policy is the alternative form. Cases the check covers: on: push: branches (the push.branches key) fails while push.tags passes. A run step with -count=N above 1 is denied. The audit named dangerous-triggers covers only pull_request_target, workflow_run and issue_comment, so it does not cover trigger sets.
pros: Hosted minutes on every push are refused: the tag is the release and the local gate is the gate. Neither the workflow linter nor the security audit checks the trigger set, so a push trigger went unseen.

rules.statement: Workflow files pass a workflow linter and a security audit, and every action is pinned to a commit.

pros: Injected faults in workflow files were found by the linter and the audit in a planted trial: three of three. One repository had two high audit findings for a token with no permission input.

rules.statement: A CI token is read-only and scoped to the repositories it needs.

exemptions.reason: A library with no CI token has nothing to scope.

reasoning.definition: Each workflow declares read-only permissions at the top. One release token covered the whole owner, and the ruling leaves it as it is, recorded as an exception with a stored verdict and an expiry tied to the shared tooling work; the release box keeps its pending mark. The permissions: key is declared at the top of each workflow.
pros: A token that can write to every repository turns a compromised job into a compromise of the estate.

rules.statement: Every shell script is linted and is found by its first line, not by its file extension.

reasoning.definition: The finder looks past the .sh name, which hid shell scripts from the extension glob.
pros: A glob on the shell extension showed one repository clean while blind to 29 files; there were 46 extensionless shell scripts against 40 tracked ones with the extension.

rules.statement: A project has no workflow that gates a push: its workflows are the release workflow on a tag and workflows started by hand, and any of them that runs gate members runs the one gate command the hook runs, plus only the members moved there for time.

reasoning.definition: The gate is make check (or the repo's one gate command), run by the pre-push hook. A workflow never holds its own list of gate steps: the release workflow runs the gate command, then the members too slow for the hook (gates.hooks.4), such as fuzzing and race tests, then builds and publishes. A dispatch workflow that checks a tree runs the same gate command. Where a shared workflow exists, a project workflow calls it rather than copying its steps. No workflow is triggered by a push to a branch or a pull request (supply.workflows.1).
pros: Hosted minutes on every push are refused, and a workflow with its own gate steps drifts from the gate the hook runs, so the release can pass a tree the hook would refuse.

rules.statement: A vendored token file equals the source at its named version, by hash, in the path agents take.

pros: One program's header said version 9 while the source tokens said 1, so a copy had drifted from what it named.

rules.statement: A part copied between sites records where it came from, with a header naming the source repository, version, path and a hash.

reasoning.definition: The header form is copied-from: <repo>@<version> <path> plus a hash.
pros: A copy with no origin cannot be updated or checked against its source.

rules.statement: Generated files name the version of the tool that made them.

reasoning.definition: Generated files start with the standard "Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT." line and a version token. Regeneration is go generate.
pros: A generated file with no banner is edited by hand and its tool version is lost.

rules.statement: If a repository has generators, regenerating leaves no diff; with zero inputs the check reports not applicable with the count.

reasoning.definition: The rule is in the gate list from the start. Its input count is the number of go:generate lines, zero today, and it declares zero a valid state: it returns not applicable with zero inputs and the count until the first generator appears. The generator lines counted are //go:generate lines.
pros: A stale generated file passes review because nobody regenerates it. No Go repository used go:generate in the seven checked, which the count shows, with the build-constraint lines as the positive.

rules.statement: There is one token file for design tokens, and every copy of it is a recorded vendored copy.

pros: Two token files drift apart; the bundled source row asked for one.

rules.statement: Build and gate recipes are Taskfile tasks that run the program's own commands, with standard tools only.

pros: A recipe written as shell for one system silently differs on another; a task that runs a program command has no shell of its own to differ, so the rule asks for no claim of which systems it works on.

rules.statement: A program fetched into an image, a tool cache or a build is pinned by version and verified before use by a signature or a checksum from its publisher's https origin, its version is read back, and a verification that cannot run stops the step.

reasoning.definition: Every fetch names an exact version. Before the fetched program is used, it is checked against the publisher's signature where the publisher signs, and otherwise against a checksum fetched from the same https origin as the program (never a checksum kept beside the download URL on a mirror). The program is then run to print its version, which must equal the pinned one. A missing signature tool, an unreachable checksum or a version mismatch stops the step with could not run; the step never continues unverified. Locked packages are held by supply.age.4; this rule covers what a package manager does not fetch.
pros: A program fetched outside the lockfile has no integrity check unless the step does one, and a step that skips a check it cannot run installs whatever the network handed it.

rules.statement: Each program owns a glossary of its terms, held to its code by a check, and a product term is defined once and linked wherever it appears.

reasoning.definition: The glossary lists each term with its definition, its aliases (prior names and outside words it translates) and the names that were retired, with what was retired when. Every schema, event or public name the program publishes is a term; every term names one of those or a retired name; every retired name in the lint configuration is in the glossary. Every page and help text links the first use of a term on it to its glossary entry, and the same thing carries the same name everywhere. A map of which program owns which concept sits beside the glossaries. An editor that shows a term's definition on hover is an aid for people only; agents read the glossary file.
pros: Fault evidence in our own repos: word faults 7, 3 and 2 in three repos, and the old organisation name found 181 times in one repo by a spell tool. Names that drift between pages and services make a reader and an agent guess which thing is meant.

rules.statement: A retired word fails where it is typed, in code, comments and docs, and the failure names the right word.

reasoning.definition: The retired-words list maps each retired word to its right word, and the failure message carries that right word. It covers identifiers, comments, strings and markdown, and a word retired in every sense fails in docs and comments as well as code. A retired identifier is not the same as a retired word: a name kept as a code name (a wire value or a compound the registry still requires) stays allowed. The list lives in one shared place and is synced into each repo, and each repo's own linter holds the names it retired so a retired name fails in the service that retired it. A write-time hook runs the scan on the edited file.
pros: A retired name that keeps appearing spreads back into new code. A spell tool found 181 hits of the old organisation name in one repo alone, and only one repo had a gate (five retired words).

rules.statement: Each word set that two programs share has one definition, and a machine-readable code is kept apart from its sentence in a closed, documented set.

reasoning.definition: For exit codes the check is the one in the code part: a documented table compared with the constants. Other shared word sets live in one data file consumed by every language through the generator, with a schema that separates the machine code from the sentence a person reads.
pros: Two programs that each spell out a code or status word drift apart, and a code that is also a sentence cannot be changed without breaking readers.

rules.statement: Printed text, the README and the how-to guides carry no code identifier, no word from a listed set of internal jargon, and no internal doc path, register, issue, rule or decision id, which belong in the register, the design notes and commits.

reasoning.definition: Printed text is every string the program shows a person: help, hints, errors, prompts and status rows. A code identifier is a package, type or function name as it appears in the code. The jargon list is one data file per repo, next to the glossary. An id is any pattern the citation resolver knows (rule, decision, ticket, register row) and any path into the docs or design folders. Design notes, the register, agent files and commits may use all of these. A word a person needs that is also an identifier is defined in the glossary and spelled the way a person says it.
pros: A person reading help or a guide cannot follow an internal name or id anywhere, so it is noise that also leaks how the code is built; the id belongs where the people who can follow it read.

rules.statement: Words on screen, in docs and in comments are spelled right against a project word list.

reasoning.definition: The spell check runs over source, docs, comments and strings, with a project dictionary for product terms. It runs on staged files at the first tier and on all files at the second. Its reach over docs and comments is set in its file globs. The first run on an untuned repository is noise: tune the dictionary once and it is then a rule with no ratchet.
pros: Untuned runs found 1,457 and 1,909 unknown words in two repos; a misspelt word in a docs page or a comment costs trust and defeats search.

rules.statement: The project picks one spelling variant, British English, and a check holds it in paths, parameters, docs, comments and text on screen.

reasoning.definition: Substitution rules turn an American spelling into the chosen one (for example color into colour). The variant applies to code names the program owns, event detail-types, docs and comments alike.
pros: Mixed variants make names fail to match (cancelled against canceled) and search miss.

rules.statement: A repository's spelling file imports the shared spelling base and adds only its own words.

reasoning.definition: The shared base sets English, allows compound words, and carries the ignore paths and a few common project words. A check fails a repository whose spelling file does not import the base and keep the import. The shared base and the shared markdown configuration ship from one place.
pros: A repo that copies the base instead of importing it drifts from every other repo.

rules.statement: No em dash in any tracked file, no semicolon in text a program prints, and headings are in sentence case; docs may use the semicolon.

reasoning.definition: The em dash scan reads every tracked text file, code and data included; a repo's own rule format uses another separator. The semicolon scan reads the strings a program prints (messages, help, errors, status rows), not docs and not code syntax. The heading scan reads markdown, HTML and .astro files. Words kept in data files are exported as text for the scan to read. In source strings a lint rule rejects string literals that contain an em dash, and a printed-string literal that contains a semicolon. ESLint form: `no-restricted-syntax` on such literals. Biome form: a GritQL plugin on the same literals.
pros: Punctuation style is checkable and drifts without a check; evidence D. An em dash is the mark that most often survives from generated text, and a semicolon in a terminal line splits one fact into two half-sentences.

rules.statement: Written output puts the point first and is honest about what it knows, text the program prints carries no joke, aside or personality and a status row is a fact, not a sentence, and a check refuses a filler-word list and the not-X-but-Y form in docs and printed text.

reasoning.definition: There are two registers. Docs may be warm and may joke. Text the program prints (help, errors, status rows, prompts) is plain fact: no joke, aside, exclamation or first person, and a status row is a value with its label. A repo keeps one list of refused filler words and phrases in its style config, and the check also refuses the not-X-but-Y construction. Point-first order and honesty stay with the reader.
pros: Printed text is read in a hurry and parsed by scripts, so personality there is noise; the filler patterns are the ones a model reaches for and a reader stops trusting. Tone, honesty and order cannot be checked by a pattern, so a reader or a model lens judges them.

rules.statement: A measured figure in a doc carries its date, the machine and whose measurement it is, a claim about outside behaviour cites a source and what it says, and a doc that generalises from one machine says so.

reasoning.definition: No figure claims more precision than its source: a source in whole units gives no decimal, an estimate is marked as one (≈), and a remainder the doc cannot explain is its own row, never spread over the rest. A doc says what it can and cannot promise. Generated figures carry the same three facts from the generator.
pros: A number without its date and machine reads as a property of the product when it is one reading on one day, and a figure with more decimals than its source is a claim nobody measured.

rules.statement: Markdown structure (headings, lists, code fences) follows one shipped lint configuration.

reasoning.definition: All default rules are on except four, line length is off, and duplicate headings are checked among siblings only. The configuration is exported from one shared place and a repository does not carry its own copy. A project's own docs, including UI projects, follow the same configuration.
pros: The default rules gave 62,000 findings on a first run (80 percent of them line length), so the configuration is the work. No repo had a doc linter configuration or front matter.

rules.statement: Every doc carries its type, status and version or as-of date, in typed front matter or in one fixed header line or status paragraph, read by one schema, and indexes are generated from it, never written by hand.

reasoning.definition: A repo declares one container for these fields: typed front matter, a fixed header line (Version, Status and Ages-with), or a bold status paragraph that opens the doc. Whatever the container, one shared parser reads it into the same fields and validates them against one JSON Schema; a doc with no type or status fails, and a doc in a container other than the declared one fails. The sidebar or index (a table of notes included) is generated from the folders and these fields, or checked against them by a test, never kept by hand. Every doc has a named owner, in the fields or in one owners file.
pros: No pinned repo had front matter; without a type, a status and an owner nobody can tell a current record from an old one or who keeps it true. The invariants are the rule; the container is the repo's choice, so a repo that already writes a header line or a status paragraph is held to the same fields without a rewrite.

rules.statement: The docs/ folder holds typed documents that are true now and marked records, and working material such as epics, handovers and run notes lives outside it.

reasoning.definition: Marked records are of three kinds, each typed so the docs check knows it is a record. A superseded decision note stays, marked at its top with its successor, keeping its old sections and its rejected alternatives with their reasons. A history log (what landed, when) is append-only and marked as history; an edit to an earlier entry fails. Unadopted proposals live in one marked folder with an index and bind nothing until a decision adopts them; nothing outside that folder cites a proposal as a rule. Nothing in docs/ is deleted to retire it.
pros: Notes mixed into the docs folder read as current fact and go stale unseen. A record that is marked is not that risk: deleting it loses the reasons behind the current design, and marking it keeps them without letting them pass for current fact.

rules.statement: A non-generated doc carries an as-of date and reads as a record of that day, a date-only change is reported, and a superseded section carries a dated note naming the note that replaced it, which links back.

reasoning.definition: A section that a later note replaces keeps its text; a dated line at its top names the replacing note, and the replacing note links back to the section. A generated doc carries no as-of date (docs.freshness.7).
pros: A date bumped with no content change makes an old claim look fresh, and a section replaced without a note reads as current.

rules.statement: A doc states a current fact only where a check holds it, and says what is built and what is only designed.

reasoning.definition: Generated reference is regenerated and diffed in the gate, numbers come from a script, paths are links that the link check follows, and every other doc is a dated record of the day it was written. A doc never says to build to a design that is frozen or to a thing that is not built.
pros: A product doc still said "Build to it today" for a frozen tree.

rules.statement: A decision is never edited in place: it is superseded by number, the superseding record names the old one, the old one is marked, and the links point both ways.

reasoning.definition: A decision has a number that is never reused. A repo declares its container: one file per decision, numbered decisions inside design notes, or entries in one append-only log amended by dated sub-entries. In every container a reversal is a new decision that names the one it replaces, the old one gains a superseded mark that names its successor, its text stays, and every cited decision number resolves.
pros: A decision that supersedes another without the back link leaves two live answers, and an edit in place loses what was decided and why. The invariants are the rule; the container is the repo's choice.

rules.statement: A stub, a placeholder return or a not-implemented body in shipped source is reported.

reasoning.definition: A syntax scan counts not-implemented throws, TODO returns and stub bodies. It is a report, not a gate.
pros: A shipped stub looks like a feature.

rules.statement: A generated doc says so in its first lines with the command that makes it, the gate regenerates and diffs it, and the help text and the doc for the same subject come from one source.

reasoning.definition: The source is the program's command registry (one declaration per command with its summary, the version it arrived in, what a second run does and who may run it); help, help --json, the README's command table, the MCP tool list, agent skill text and the generated guide are rendered from it. A generated file opens with a line that says it is generated, by which command, and not to edit it. The gate runs the command and fails on any difference. Prose about a command that is not generated links to the generated part instead of restating it. There is one registry and help prints it; MCP tools and the skill text are generated from it. Help is written once, the README's command table is generated from it, and a test fails when they differ. A guide generated from lessons beside the code says not to edit it here.
pros: A command described once and rendered everywhere cannot drift: the agent's skill, the tool list and the README are the program's own words, not a second copy of them.

rules.statement: No hand-written file carries a digest of the current state: a digest lives in the generated output, and a change to the state adds a note with a reason.

reasoning.definition: A chain whose newest line must equal the digest of the current state is wrong for every change in flight after any other lands, and the fix is a hand edit in a file nobody else should edit. The digest moves into the generated listing's header; the reason moves into a note per change, a new file with the date and at least a few words of why. The check is that when the listing's digest differs from the base's, the change adds a note. What is lost is the chain's proof that every past listing was recorded; the notes and the history give the same answer with one more command. Ratchets whose point is a hand edit that can only lower a count are not chains and stay.
pros: Own measure: a file of this kind changed in 10 commits in three days, and every one appended a line to a chain, so any two changes in flight conflicted and the second one's digest was wrong after the rebase.

sources.says: A change is one small file in a folder; the release step joins them.

rules.statement: Docs have no broken file link or anchor, checked offline in the gate, and external links are checked by a separate command that runs as a non-blocking step of the release recipe, never as a gate step and never on a schedule.

reasoning.definition: Relative links and heading anchors are checked offline, with fragments included (without --include-fragments the anchor breaks are not seen). External links are checked by their own command over the network, with a cache; the release recipe runs it and prints its result in the release record, and a dead link opens a finding but does not stop the release. The gate never reaches the network for links. A docs-site build that fails on broken links is the same rule when a site exists; no docs site is run today. Docs and agent instruction files are checked alike. Docs also have no markdown error and pass spelling.
pros: One broken file link in one repo and 36 fragment failures in one file of another, on 5,800 links of which 4,200 are remote. A site that is down for an hour is not the repo's fault, so it must not stop a push, but a dead source must still be seen before a release goes out.

rules.statement: No comment, doc or code cites a rule, decision or ticket id that does not exist.

reasoning.definition: A shared citation resolver reads comments and docs and resolves each id pattern against the rule list, the decision files and the ticket index. Citations are never required by count.
pros: Seven repos' agent files all held dangling references; of 258 backticked references in instruction files about 3 were dangling, and 4 of 26 source contradictions were knowledge-layer pointers.

rules.statement: A backticked path in a comment or doc resolves or the comment says it is a dead path and why, a dependency version named in prose equals the lockfile's, and a sentence claiming CI or a workflow runs a command is checked against the workflow files.

reasoning.definition: The resolver reads comments and docs. A version is a package name followed by a version in prose; it is compared with the lockfile (go.sum, the package lock) and fails on a mismatch. A CI claim is a sentence that names a workflow, CI or a hosted runner and a command; the command must appear in a workflow file with the trigger the sentence names, so a doc that says CI runs the gate on push fails when no workflow does.
pros: A comment that points at a path that is gone sends a reader and an agent to nothing; a version or a CI claim in prose is a second copy of a fact whose home is the lockfile or the workflow, and it goes stale first.

rules.statement: No comment restates a fact that has a home elsewhere, and no code is commented out.

pros: A restated fact goes stale in one of its two places.

rules.statement: Code in docs uses the real interfaces: every import in a documentation code fence resolves, every block compiles or type-checks, and install and upgrade steps in a guide are run as written by a test, with a step that loses its block failing.

reasoning.definition: For Go, fenced blocks are extracted into a scratch package inside the module and vetted. For TypeScript, every fence in the design-system and reference docs type-checks against the real barrels. A block marked as a fragment is skipped and counted, and that count only falls. A repository with no blocks prints not applicable. The golden path and the rule file agree. Steps under the install and upgrade headings of a guide and the changelog are written as the program's own commands, not shell lines, and are cut out by a test and run in order on a clean machine or container, from the previous release to the commit; a step heading with no block, or a block that fails, fails the test.
pros: Docs rot; the counted 41 fenced Go blocks in six clones showed no known fault from them yet, so the Go half is practice only.

rules.statement: A README keeps the shape of its kind: a directory README answers what is here, how to run it and where the rules are and points to AGENTS.md, a package README states what it is, what it exports, what it may import and how it is tested, and a CLI's product README has a fixed order of parts.

reasoning.definition: The kind follows from where the README sits: the repo root holds the product README, a package root a package README, any other folder a directory README. The product order is: a claim, what it is, install, getting started, the commands table (generated from help), longer parts, limits, where things live, documentation and contributing. A new kind adds its shape here and to the check, never a README with no kind. The package README's import line agrees with the declared import table.
pros: A README with a known shape is read in one pass by a stranger and can be partly generated; a README that does not point to the rules sends an agent and a person to guess.

rules.statement: A change in user-visible behaviour (a flag, an exit code, a --json field, a command, a config key, a written file) touches its doc in the same commit, or says docs: none in the commit.

reasoning.definition: The behaviour is read from the command manifest, the config schema and the list of files the program writes; the doc is the file under the docs folder or the README that names the changed item. A doc change in a later commit does not count.
pros: A visible choice about docs, though it buys visibility and not truth.

rules.statement: One program is kept as the worked example of every rule, linked from templates and guidance.

pros: The first file an agent opens should be a good one.

rules.statement: Each project has a profile page in the shared docs with the same fixed headings.

pros: A fixed page per project lets a reader and an agent find the same facts in the same place.

rules.statement: The instruction file is a short map that holds what a reader cannot find from the code, and a repo-wide invariant may live there as a numbered rule that code cites, each naming the check that holds it where one exists, while how a rule is checked leaves the file.

reasoning.definition: The file holds commands, traps, a where-to-look table and the repo's numbered invariants, not a repository overview, and each fact has one home. An invariant keeps its number for life and code cites it by number; its line is the rule and the name of its check, never the steps of the check. A number that code cites must exist in the file (docs.links.2). The repo-wide rules live in AGENTS.md, numbered, and code cites them by number. Its size is measured as a byte count per file that is a ratchet and only falls, and a report lists the lines whose rule id already has a check. A required list of headings is checked, and the file is size-checked. The reference organisation capped the pair of files at 12,000 characters, a figure no measurement of ours supports, so no limit is set here. The rule applies to AGENTS.md. The size check is ported from the UI repository's check-agents-md. The workflow of each repository validates its instruction file against the shared convention.
pros: One controlled study found no gain in success and over 20 percent more cost from longer files, and every line is paid for on every run. Our own files are 33,282 B, 18,492 B and 8,811 B (and 4,400 B in another repository).

rules.statement: Every backticked command and path in an instruction file resolves, and CLAUDE.md holds only the line that imports AGENTS.md.

reasoning.definition: Paths are checked against the tree with an allow list for runtime paths, make targets against the Makefile, scripts against the package manifest, and CLAUDE.md with an exact-match test for the import line. An audit also reports stale or contradictory lines and references to missing files or commands. READMEs point to AGENTS.md. AGENTS.md holds commands, traps and a where-to-look table.
pros: A scan found dangling or unverifiable references in 7 of 7 AGENTS.md files, 3 truly dangling, and the same name-exists class holds for ticket faults.

rules.statement: Rules load only when the paths they govern are touched, and an agent reads the instruction file, the ticket and every anchor it cites, in that order, before proposing or changing anything.

reasoning.definition: A nested AGENTS.md or a path-scoped rule file holds a kind's rules under that kind's directory (the closest file to the edited path wins), and the root file holds no rule id of a kind or framework pack. A pack loads its own rules. An anchor is any file, rule or decision the ticket names; the agent reads each before its first proposal, and a session-start hook can record the reads so a proposal made before them is flagged.
pros: Rules in the root file are paid for on every task and then crowd out the instruction map; unmeasured beyond the same size study.

rules.statement: A procedure an agent runs often ships as a skill that loads on use, and the instruction file points at it and does not repeat it.

reasoning.definition: An agent uses the packaged procedures and generators (add a route, add a migration, does-it-exist lookups, build a page, plan a ticket) instead of improvising the steps. New pages and parts come from a generator or a golden page.
pros: A procedure written in the instruction file is paid for every run and drifts from the generator.

rules.statement: An agent can reach the current rules with no network and no sibling clone, because they are vendored at a tag and each vendored file equals its locked hash.

reasoning.definition: Agents find standards and decisions by text search on a checkout, not by a portal. Each vendored file is hashed against a lock file, and a rule lookup in a test with no network and no clone must succeed. A rule file reachable only by URL fails. Vendored tokens for UI projects follow the same rule.
pros: Agents run in directories that are not sibling clones.

rules.statement: The first file an agent opens in an area is a good one, small and typical of how the area is written.

pros: An agent copies the first file it reads; one UI component file of 2,868 lines is the example agents copy.

rules.statement: Where a library ships its own agent instructions, take the version that does and link them from the project's instruction file.

pros: The library authors know how the library is meant to be used.

rules.statement: Before writing a helper or naming something, the agent reads the glossary and the listing of shared exports and searches the sibling repositories for what already exists.

reasoning.definition: The answer must be reachable without a network. Standards and decisions are found by text search on a checkout. Code search across the other repositories of the organisation is by local clones first, and the repository host's own search covers the rest. A new helper that duplicates an export of the shared kit is caught by the reuse scan in the code part; this rule makes the agent look first. The listing of shared exports is the registry of arch.shared.15 rendered into the instruction file, so what the agent must read exists at a path.
pros: Reinvention comes from a limited view of the repository: a name search found none of three atomic writers where the type-checked lookup found them, and the census shows 42 hand copies of shared helpers.

rules.statement: Whether agents use the lookup tools is measured, not assumed.

reasoning.definition: A question set with known answers is asked with and without the guidance and scored; the hook log of each session records whether the lookup tool answered.
pros: A tool nobody uses prevents nothing.

rules.statement: The agent's environment has a type-checked lookup and diagnostics tool for each language, and a preflight fails when it is missing.

reasoning.definition: For Go the language server is on the path with its plugin enabled; for TypeScript the language server or the native compiler server is on the path, with its version read. After each edit the agent sees type errors and can find references by type instead of text. Hosts must pass the preflight.
pros: A language server found 28 of 28 callers of one function where grep found the same plus 4 fixture strings; limited views of the repository cause reinvention.

rules.statement: Where an agent needs callers or implementations it uses a type-checked answer, and an answer is bounded in size, at about 20 KB.

pros: A language-server tool returned 112,914 bytes for one file, which fills the context for no gain.

rules.statement: A knowledge tool runs with no network and no account, is pinned to an exact version, has a licence a company may use, and never writes to the source tree.

reasoning.definition: Exact pin: the tools file names an exact version and no range. Licence: a licence check with an allow list. No writes: run the tool, then the working tree is clean. No network: a sandboxed run.
pros: A knowledge tool that reaches out or writes breaks the offline and clean-tree guarantees; one tool is pinned today by exact npm version (ast-grep 0.51.1).

rules.statement: A change that adds an exported function outside a registry owner and that calls a registry primitive or has a capability word in its name carries a trailer that names what the builder read and why none of it fits.

reasoning.definition: The trailer is `Reuse:`. It names the registry rows and the shared module's package listing the builder read, and says why none fits. The capability words are write, lock, digest, sum, walk, trust, golden and isolate. The ban half of arch.shared.8 catches the primitive; this rule catches the copy that was restructured so that the ban cannot see it, by making the builder say what they looked at. It is cheaper than a hook-log check of what the agent read, which agents.discovery.1 proposes and nobody runs. The standard line of the dispatch note, and the instruction block rendered from the registry, ask for the same three reads: the registry file, the shared module's listing at the pinned tag, and a search of the repository for the primitive.
pros: The ban on a primitive misses a helper that wraps it under another name; a sentence a builder can write without reading anything is weak evidence, but it makes the omission visible to the reviewer, which is what a Record rule is for.

rules.statement: A write by an agent to a protected path is refused where the agent writes it, and a needed change to one lands only through a second-party verdict.

reasoning.definition: Protected paths are baselines, gate config, hooks, agent settings, test oracles, plant files and the protected-path list itself. In Claude Code the deny rule is written as Edit(...), because a Write(...) rule never matches. Per-runtime write-time denies are generated from the one protected list: Claude permissions.deny, a Codex prefix_rule, a Gemini policy file and an OpenCode permission. A runtime-independent check at commit (staged paths) and at land (diff against base) fails when a protected path changes without a stored non-author verdict. A Claude Edit deny applies to built-in file tools, not to Bash subprocesses; a project-level command deny list (done for --no-verify) gives runtime-neutral command denial (the list names each denied command once and is applied to every shell an agent uses, not written per shell). The known way round is a shell redirect in place of the edit tool, so an OS-level write sandbox (denyWrite on the protected paths) is the stronger layer and the land check is the backstop.
pros: Scorer tampering was seen in 39 of 128 runs elsewhere (principles report P-09); no repo of ours committed a .claude/ file (0 tracked in seven). One Claude Code release treated a Write(...) deny as nothing, found only by a live test.

rules.statement: An agent cannot bypass the gate by command: no-verify, a hooks-path override and the hook-disabling variables are refused by committed settings, with the land check as backstop.

reasoning.definition: Refused: git commit or push with --no-verify or -n, core.hooksPath overrides, LEFTHOOK=0, HUSKY=0, and force push to the main branch. A deny rule on Bash does not match inside sh -c or an absolute path, so a push made with hooks disabled has no verdict the lander can recompute and is refused at land. A deny glob matches the command's text, not what git runs: a word split by quotes or a backslash, git's name held in a variable or a script, or in another case on a case-folding file system, a config file reached by a relative path, and a commit flag after another word get past every glob, and are tested as known gaps; the pre-push hook on each pushed tree and the land check on the merged tree are the guard. Deny lists are generated from the rule data into each runtime as the tier-0 courtesy.
pros: Own bug B-692 was a --no-verify push. A repo without the land check has only the courtesy.

rules.statement: An agent stages named paths, never sweeps in unrelated files, and never discards another person's uncommitted work.

reasoning.definition: On the deny list for agents: git add -A, git add ., git commit -a, git reset --hard, git checkout -- <path> and git clean. An agent reads git diff --cached --stat before it commits. A staged-file scope check is the second backstop, because a rule may not match a command wrapped in sh -c. The rule applies to repositories where several agents share a tree.
pros: In a shared tree an agent can lose another's work or commit scratch files (principles report P-09 section 4 O6).

rules.statement: The project commits agent settings that run the cheap check tier after an edit and at stop, a fail-closed pre-tool hook that parses each command, committed deny rules a local allow cannot lift, and refuse a planted attempt to edit a baseline with the next step named, and the pre-push gate is the wall no session mode can skip.

reasoning.definition: After an edit a hook runs the linter's autofix on the edited file; the stop hook runs the fast tier, within an agent-time budget of 2 seconds for the on-write tier. A fail-closed pre-tool hook parses each Bash command and refuses one it cannot parse. A local allow cannot lift a committed deny. Gate config itself is protected at landing by a gate-change trailer and shrink-only baselines. The session's permission mode, bypass included, is the operator's choice (agents.guards.5): the hooks, the deny rules and the pre-push gate hold in every mode, and the planted denial of agents.guards.6 is run under bypass to prove it. The Claude Code deny form was checked on release 2.1.317 and not re-run. Bypass is the default (D93): bypass is the operator's default for every session, and git push --no-verify is never used.
pros: Settings that exist only on one machine protect nothing; 0 of 11 repos committed any. A ban on a session mode is a rule the operator has chosen to set aside, while a hook, a deny rule and the pre-push gate hold whatever the mode is.

rules.statement: The guardrail set (hooks, deny rules, reviewer subagents, skills, the read-only code search tool) is delivered as managed settings that no user, project, local or command-line value overrides, the session's permission mode is the operator's choice recorded in a decision, and a doctor check shows the set applied.

reasoning.definition: One versioned agent configuration gives every agent the hooks, deny rules, reviewer subagents, skills and the read-only code search tool. The file (macOS /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json, Linux /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json), which no user, project, local or --settings value overrides. The doctor check reads the status line "Enterprise managed settings (file)" or hashes the file against the template and fails when it differs. Whether bypass mode is available is not part of the set: the operator records the choice in a decision, and the doctor prints the mode the managed file allows next to that decision. The per-agent equivalent for other runtimes is unknown. Bypass is the default (D93: bypass is available and is the default for every start a person makes; the owner keeps the bypass-disable key out of the floor).
pros: Project settings can be edited by the agent; only the managed layer cannot be switched off. The mode is a trade the operator makes with the hooks and the pre-push gate as the wall, so it is recorded, not banned.

rules.statement: Hard rules for agents are deny rules or permissions, never a hook behind an if filter, and each guardrail hook has a planted denial run from the main session and from a subagent, with an allowed control.

reasoning.definition: The if filter is best-effort and the hook runs anyway when the command cannot be parsed, so a hook is a filter and a feedback channel and not the refusal. A check parses the committed settings and fails when a refusing hook (exit 2 or a deny decision) carries an if filter with no matching deny rule. The behaviour under bypassPermissions is recorded once. The live run is scripted on each agent release (a headless run showed a deny holding under bypass and in a subagent).
pros: Only a live test shows that a deny rule is inert; a hash-keyed record would prove a record exists but not that the test ran.

rules.statement: An action that reaches outside the task's own tree needs a named permission in the ticket, the agent writes to a path the task owns by default, and a fault found outside the ticket's module becomes a ticket for that module's owner, never an edit in the current change.

reasoning.definition: Reaching outside means machine-wide hooks, service files, shared settings and another agent's state. The review question for each change is: which path outside this repository does this change write, and which ticket line allows it? Each ticket runs under a write sandbox where one can be set up. A module is a unit of the declared import table; a change whose diff touches a module the ticket does not name is refused at land unless the ticket names it, and the finding goes to that module's owner as a proposal ticket.
pros: One branch build rewrote a machine-wide hook file and 19 agents of another organisation ran it for about four minutes. A fix made in someone else's module inside an unrelated change is reviewed by nobody who owns it.

rules.statement: Text an agent reads from outside is data and never an instruction, an action that writes, publishes or reaches a secret traces to the ticket or a person, and an agent never prints the environment or reads a secret file, with a read-back comparing hashes.

reasoning.definition: Outside text is a page, an issue, a tool result or a dependency's documentation. A tool's output is read as data. A session-level gate is proposed: a session that has read outside text cannot push, publish or read a secret without a fresh gate step; a hook marks such a session and then a push or secret read needs the ticket link. The commands that dump the environment (printenv, a bare env, set, export with no arguments) and reads of secret files (.env, key files, the credentials store) are on the agent deny list. Where an agent must confirm a secret was written, it compares a hash of the value, never the value.
pros: Agents read hostile text as their job. No measurement on our estate yet; this was found by the author of the principles handbook. An environment dump puts every secret of the session into the transcript at once.

rules.statement: Before the first edit the agent checks the base is the target tip, the tree is clean and the gate is green on the base, and stops on a mismatch.

reasoning.definition: The preflight is one command the session runs first: it fetches, compares the base with the tip of the branch the change will land on, checks there are no uncommitted or untracked changes, and runs the gate (or reads a whole-run verdict for that exact tree). Any mismatch stops the session with the reason; the agent does not rebase, clean or fix the base to get past it.
pros: Work started on a stale or red base spends the session on someone else's fault and lands a change whose proof is about another tree; the land check refuses it late, after the work is done.

rules.statement: An agent that finds a rule in the way stops and escalates with options, a recommendation and a stated default, and never bends the rule to fit the ticket.

reasoning.definition: Bending includes a suppression, a lowered baseline, a skipped test, a narrowed check or a reworded rule. The escalation is a written note to the person who owns the ticket: the rule, why it blocks, two or more options, the one the agent recommends, and the default it will take if no answer comes. It does not change the rule or the check while it waits.
pros: A rule bent once to finish a ticket is gone for every later ticket, and the person who owns the rule never learns it was in the way.

rules.statement: After two identical failures the agent stops retrying and opens a read-only diagnostic step, with no restart, revert or re-baseline.

reasoning.definition: Identical means the same command failing with the same error. The diagnostic step reads (logs, the diff, the state of the tree) and writes nothing; it ends with a finding or an escalation (agents.guards.10). A third run of the same command, a reset of the tree, a revert or a refreshed baseline in that state is refused.
pros: A third try of the same thing is a rerun to green, and a restart or a new baseline hides the failure instead of explaining it.

rules.statement: A token never goes on a command line or in a brief: a tool reads it from the environment a wrapper sets or from a file, and the brief template carries the wrapper.

reasoning.definition: agents.guards.8 holds that an agent never prints the environment or reads a secret file. This rule holds the other side: a token that is written into a command, an instruction or a ticket is in the model's context and in the transcript, and a value in a transcript has left the machine. The wrapper that sets the variable is the one thing a brief names.
pros: One brief with an inline token expression led to at least 10 installs by that form and one print of the token into a transcript.

rules.statement: A missing, stale or failing reviewer verdict for a touched area blocks landing, a pass is needed but never enough alone, the reviewer is a fresh session that did not write the code and re-runs the gate from a clean checkout of the tip with a count that differs from the close a finding, and load-bearing paths need a reviewer of a different model family from the author.

reasoning.definition: The land check reads one stored verdict file per lens, holding the lens, the model family, the content hash of the diff plus the card, and the verdict, and refuses a verdict that is missing, stale (the hash names another tree) or failing for any area the change touches (the area to reviewer map). A pass never clears a change by itself: an AI review is a sensor that opens a finding, and the person or gate closes it. Load-bearing paths are the protected-path list and the area-to-reviewer map; for them the reviewer must be of a different model family from the author, and the land check refuses the same family. A block is overridden only by a second reviewer of yet another model family, with a recorded reason and ticket (a reviewer-override trailer naming the reviewer, the reason and the ticket), and every override appears in the weekly digest. Same-family review shares blind spots. The reviewer is a session that wrote none of the change; it checks out the tip into a clean tree, runs the gate there and compares its counts (tests run, checks run, findings) with the counts the author's close reported; any difference is a finding in the verdict.
pros: Argued: no study supports AI review as a verdict (principles report P-09 section 5.6). Our own evidence is that review finds faults: one project's designer agent found 31 of 72 and another's reviewers 16, and a spec-against- diff lens found a missing case that tests had not.

rules.statement: Each judgement area has a read-only reviewer lens that returns a verdict for one concern, stored tied to the content and not the sha, run on the final content and given only the diff and the card.

reasoning.definition: A lens is read-only (read, search and list tools only) and the review runner, not the lens, writes its verdict file. For Go the areas are command-line output, state and daemon safety; for the web the areas are design system, accessibility, permissions, structure and spec-vs-diff. A model gives the pass or fail on a judgement rule such as is the name accurate or is the abstraction right.
pros: A lens given more than the diff and the card can be steered by the author's account of the change, and a verdict tied to a sha goes stale on a rebase while the content is unchanged.

rules.statement: A reviewer lens has its own plant, a stored bad diff it must fail and a clean control it must pass, before its verdicts count.

reasoning.definition: At each change to the lens and at release the gate gives the lens the stored bad diff and requires a failing verdict that names the planted fault, plus a passing verdict on the clean control. Model output varies, so the run is repeated: the lens is promoted when it catches the planted fault in at least 9 of 10 runs and wrongly flags the clean control at most once, and a lens that passes the bad diff or fails the control is suspended. The stored bad diff holds a wrapper that only forwards and a swallowed error; the bad page for a web lens is a known bad page. A lens prompt reduced to always-pass is suspended. The lens itself is read-only.
pros: An instrument that cannot fail carries no information, and a lens is a prompt that can drift with a model change.

rules.statement: A change that crosses a trust boundary answers a short list of threat questions in the change: what is newly reachable, by whom, and what would an attacker try first.

reasoning.definition: This is continuous threat modelling: a full model per story is too heavy. The baseline is kept with its notable changes. Paths marked as trust boundaries force the questions; a model judges the answers, and a reader checks them on sensitive paths.
pros: An agent can invent an answer that passes any presence check, so the answer needs a reader.

rules.statement: Review reads for understanding and for the rows no check can hold: is the name accurate, is the abstraction right, and who owns the rule.

reasoning.definition: Each rule has one owner. The reviewer agent becomes a check only if its verdict blocks the land (agents.review.1).
pros: Checks hold the mechanical rules; what remains is judgement that only a reader can make.

rules.statement: When a review round finds another instance of a gap that an earlier round found, the reviewer asks for the fix to the kind of gap, with a check that fails on any new instance, and names where it belongs, not a fix of the one instance.

reasoning.definition: The fix to a kind is the one place every instance goes through: the reader, the parser, the shared helper, the check. The reviewer names it in the round, and the builder changes that place and its test; a patch of the instance in hand is sent back. The check is a test, a lint rule or a tree scan that fails on the next instance of the kind, so the class cannot return unseen. A third round on the same kind means the second round did not name it.
pros: One review went five rounds, one spelling of the same reference per round, and the fix to the kind (read the decoded data, not the raw text) came in round five; another project needed four pull requests for the same class.

sources.says: one spelling of the same token reference per round ... came only in round 5 ... needed 4 PRs for the same class.

rules.statement: A fix round reviews only the delta, and the reviewer breaks each new guard by hand; a guard that no test catches when broken is a finding.

reasoning.definition: A guard is a check, a deny, a plant or a refusal the change adds. The reviewer makes the change the guard should refuse and sees it refused, then reverts. A project may hold this in test form as a planted violation and a fixed twin (gates.plants.1); the reviewer still breaks the one guard the plant does not cover. On a fix round the reviewer reads what changed since the last round and the record of that round, not the whole change again (agents.review.2).
pros: Every security change of one project needed two or more rounds, and breaking the guards found the ones the tests did not hold.

rules.statement: A ticket names only files, commands, symbols and rules that exist at its base when dispatched, marks what it will create, and is dispatched only when its cited anchors resolve, its gates are on the line and no open decision or escalation blocks it.

reasoning.definition: Dispatch is refused while any condition fails: an anchor (file, rule, decision) the ticket cites does not resolve at the base, a gate its done-when names is not in the gate's list, or a decision or escalation the ticket depends on is still open. A ticket is dispatchable only when its anchors resolve, its gates are on the line and no open decision or escalation blocks it. A ticket lint resolves each backticked path, command, symbol and rule id against the base of the day at dispatch and fails closed on an unresolved name. A marked name that already exists fails. The ticket template defines the mark and requires names in the Files list to be backticked. A moved-path check names a path whose basename and parent now exist elsewhere. Tickets keep their original text so a later fault can be traced, and the marked share is printed for the reader. It runs at dispatch, not at intake, because a plan written against a future layout hit on 91% of 2,296 tickets at intake.
pros: The largest fault class we have: 52 of 137 faults in our run log were a ticket's false claim about the code (principles report P-09 section 4 O1). On real history it caught 11 of about 16 known name faults.

rules.statement: A ticket's scope lists the files and consumers its author expects to touch, a change that adds a method to a shared port lists every implementer, and at land the gap between the list and the diff blocks until it is answered.

reasoning.definition: Review asks at intake what the change's exported surface breaks. At land the diff's files are compared with the scope list, generated files left out, and the listed-touched share is printed. A mismatch blocks until the author answers with a recorded reason.
pros: The second 52 of the 137 faults (104 of 137 together were ticket premise or scope). Run on real tickets the gate form did not discriminate: 74% of tickets had an unlisted file, 52% of faulted ones against 65% of clean ones.

rules.statement: A done-when names a check, and the land step proves the check ran: a named test that runs zero tests fails, and the output is kept.

reasoning.definition: The land step runs the named check on the tree, reads the number of tests run and fails on zero. Evidence that the test can go red comes from the deliberate break on the tree, not from a red run on the base, because a new test cannot compile against a base that lacks what it calls. A make-line gate in a done-when is an exit code only and counts as no red evidence. A diff that changes behaviour and carries no test change states why not.
pros: Eight faults were a done-when that could not hold or turn red, and 4 of 15 drives could not turn a test red. 6 of 159 named tests never existed, and a Go run on an unknown name exits 0. Red on the base gave 0 of 12 real tickets (7 no tests, 4 compile failures, 1 green). 85 of 280 gate lines are make lines.

sources.where: sections 4 O1, 4 O3 and 9.2 items 1 and 4

rules.statement: A change arrives with its statement of purpose and the proof it was run, a change with neither is refused before anyone reads it, and tests changed in the same diff are listed first.

reasoning.definition: The land check reads the change text for a purpose line and a verdict tied to the tree. A purpose line equal to the ticket title fails, the change summary orders test files first, and the verdict hash must equal the tree. Form is a commit linter (empty body, trailer exists); the tree binding is ours.
pros: Reading cost is what agents raise, so the cost moves to the submitter; practitioner consensus, not a measurement. Nothing refuses a change for missing evidence today.

rules.statement: A change has one concern, planned as a ticket before work starts and sized for one review, an issue opens with the owner's dated words and has Today, Want, Security (when a border is touched), Done when and Design, and diff size and post-land rework are shown together per ticket.

reasoning.definition: An issue title is a claim about what should be true. The body opens with the owner's words and their date, then the sections Today, Want, Security (when the change touches a trust border), Done when and Design; the issue form holds the sections and a check refuses an issue without them. The title is a claim, and the body has the owner's dated words. A page archetype or a dialog per ticket for the web part, planned first through the issue form and the plan gate. A pull request template whose lines mirror the gates (spec regenerated, glossary term added, decision linked, what was reused, a new dependency justified) fixes the shape. No size limit is set: a ceiling would be met by splitting, which the rework count beside it exposes. A change over the size line blocks until answered, with rework shown beside it.
pros: Practitioner consensus, not a measurement; a size ceiling is a guess and splitting beats it.

rules.statement: A done claim carries an artefact naming its question; a picture decides nothing alone and measured numbers decide.

pros: Three pictures were read as fine in one repository before one was measured (in one project).

rules.statement: A fault found by a person becomes a planted check or a journey before its ticket closes.

pros: Five recurrence pairs in one record show a fault fixed without a plant returns.

rules.statement: Every bug and gap found is a row with a permanent id in one register, code, tests and docs cite it by that id, an open row links its issue, and a test checks both.

reasoning.definition: The register is one file in the repo. An id is never reused or renumbered; a closed row stays with its outcome. Nothing found lives only in a chat, a session transcript or a commit message. The test fails an open row with no issue link and a cited register id that has no row (docs.links.2 resolves the citation).
pros: A fault that lives only in a chat is found again by the next person at full cost, and an id that moves breaks every comment and test that cited it.

rules.statement: The gate writes a delivery record per ticket holding gate rounds, review rounds, rework and time, with the first-pass gate-green rate.

reasoning.definition: The record is appended by the gate to a per-ticket file, and a figure that cannot be measured prints null with its reason. A test fails if the record is missing. Coverage per changed file is reported with no threshold.
pros: The ticket is the unit that commits and pull requests cannot give: 1,739 commits in 14 days says nothing of value (principles report P-09 section 9.3).

rules.statement: A short list of measures rolls up into one line a week for the reader.

reasoning.definition: The list: first-pass gate-green rate, review rounds, rework within 14 days, files over the size line, new disables, platform-import ratio, state coverage, accessibility violations, and time to green.
pros: A weekly line shows trend without making any one number a target.

rules.statement: The reader sees the delivery numbers; the agent judged on them does not.

pros: A scorer visible to the agent invites gaming; scorer visibility is linked to hacking in an outside study (principles report P-09 section 5.5).

rules.statement: A change to guidance is measured before it spreads, by replaying closed tickets with and without it and reporting success and cost for each arm.

reasoning.definition: A replay harness runs the arms and a person reads the two arms; nothing passes or fails, so it has no plant. A guidance change must carry its replay result. Tests that give an agent a task and check that it followed the guidance are the same idea in eval form.
pros: The one controlled study shows guidance can add cost with no gain (principles report P-09 section 7.7); its figures are second-hand, from a workshop poster.

rules.statement: A commit subject states what is true after it, not what was done, its body says why, and a type and scope prefix is a repo parameter.

reasoning.definition: The subject is a sentence about the tree after the commit ("The gate refuses a stale base"), not an action ("Fix gate" or "Updated docs"). The body says why the change was needed; a body that only repeats the subject fails. A repo declares once whether subjects carry a conventional type and scope prefix, and the commit check holds whichever it declared.
pros: A log of what is true reads as the history of the program's behaviour; a log of actions says only that someone was busy. The body is the one place the reason survives.

rules.statement: A Go program starts from one layout template: programs live under cmd/<name>/ and everything else under internal/, with no pkg/ folder; adapters live under one host folder, one package per platform or per external tool, and the core lives outside it; and every package sits in a layer named in the import table.

exemptions.reason: A library has exported packages at its root and no cmd folder.

reasoning.definition: The template is rule data (the layer and import table), so a new program starts from it one to one: cmd/<name>/ (wires and registers implementations, nothing else), internal/core/ (the domain), internal/core/api/ (routes and their JSON result types), port packages (interfaces only, each with its fake), slot packages with their registries, internal/host/<platform or tool>/ (adapters, such as host/linux, host/launchd), internal/door/ (listeners), internal/config/, internal/cli/<group>/ and internal/cli/ui/ (the only terminal code), and leaf packages. A layout test walks the module tree and lists packages: it fails on any directory named pkg, on a main package outside cmd/<name>/, on a non-test package at the module root or outside cmd/ and internal/, on an adapter outside the host folder, and on a package with no layer in the table. A library repo is declared kind lib in rule data and is exempt, since a library has exported packages at its root. The popular project-layout repository (golang-standards/project-layout) is not a standard.
pros: Practice; all six of our Go repos follow cmd and internal. A shared layout makes a port, an adapter or a command findable across programs by an agent that has read one of them, and the two Go target programs already agree on the names.

rules.statement: No init functions outside the main package, or their count only falls.

pros: Own measure: init functions in our repos today: 26 in one, 1 in another, 0 in the rest. The linter is enabled in six of six configs.

sources.says: Checks that no init functions are present in Go code.
