The one surveyed command line program that registers commands from init functions through blank imports, which makes the command set depend on import side effects.

rules.statement: No replace directive in go.mod and no go.work file in a committed tree.

pros: A local replace builds on one machine only and hides the real dependency; a workspace file changes resolution for everyone who checks out.

sources.says: replace directives only apply in the main module's go.mod file and are ignored in other modules.

rules.statement: Shipped binaries are built with cgo disabled.

exemptions.reason: A library ships no binary.

pros: A cgo binary links the host's C library and breaks the static, copy-anywhere build. Own measure: set in 5 of the 7 programs today (verified); the library repo and one scraper set none.

rules.statement: Every error is handled or returned; nothing is swallowed.

reasoning.definition: The linter checks type assertions and blank assignments in non-test code; suppressions are counted by the suppression ratchet of the gates part.
pros: Own bugs: 3 of 60 sampled bugs. The linter is on everywhere with 235 suppressions in one repo.

rules.statement: An error is wrapped with %w and context saying what was being done, and compared with errors.Is or errors.As.

pros: Practice; a wrapped error compared with == silently stops matching.

rules.statement: Panic is for programmer errors only and never crosses a package's API, and an unchecked type assertion is banned.

reasoning.definition: A panic outside main and tests sits on a one-file-per-entry allow list that only shrinks. A type assertion without the ok check is an unchecked error return. Whether a panic crosses a package API is review.
pros: Own measure: panics outside main in our repos: 6 (20 in all), 8, 3, 2, 5 and 0.

rules.statement: Only main calls os.Exit or a fatal log; a command returns its ending as a value (an exit status, or a typed result or error mapped to one in one place); and every refusal is testable in process.

exemptions.reason: It has no main package.

reasoning.definition: An exit call or a fatal log call outside main is a finding; the linter's per-rule cap is off so repeats are not hidden. Test files are excluded by path (a test main may call exit). A command function is func Verb(...) int or returns a typed ending or error; either way exactly one function maps endings and errors to the exit codes of cli.exit.1, by word or type, never by message. A test calls each command in process and reads its ending.
pros: Own measure: 0 exits outside the main package everywhere today; a library that exits cannot be tested or reused. The part that protects is the lint: no exit outside main, so every path is testable in process. Both Go target programs return an ending because a refusal is a value they print on three surfaces, and forcing an error type in between adds a layer with no reader.

rules.statement: Error strings follow one style (lowercase, no trailing punctuation), and any exception is written down once.

pros: Practice. The ruling on style is open: the linter rule is disabled in three configs today, and a repo that keeps sentence-style errors lists the exception once in rule data.

rules.statement: Nil flows (a map lookup or a nil pointer followed by a field read) are checked, advisory, with a count that only falls.

pros: Practice. Findings today: 206 in one repo and 106 in another; 75 tracker issues of the tool mention false positives.

rules.statement: Each error is handled once, logged or returned and not both; a new sentinel or typed error exists only when a caller branches on it.

pros: Practice; no fault in our record. Run on two repos: 0 real hits, so adoption debt is zero where tried.

rules.statement: An error crossing a process or wire boundary travels as a word from a closed list plus detail and is typed again on the other side, and callers compare with errors.Is or errors.As, never the message.

reasoning.definition: The wire form is a word and a detail field; the receiving side maps the word back to the sentinel or typed error of the closed list, and an unknown word becomes one typed unknown error carrying it. A comparison of err.Error() or a strings.Contains on an error message is a finding.
pros: Typing an error again after a flattening joint keeps callers off message strings that change; it is the Go side of the one refusal value of cli.errors.2.

rules.statement: A daemon logs through log/slog or a handler of it, output for a person goes to stderr, and no fatal log call appears outside main.

exemptions.reason: The shared logger leaf that wraps the handler does not exist yet; go.logging.2 holds for both kinds once it is built.

reasoning.definition: A handler of slog includes a library that implements slog.Handler (for example a terminal-styled handler at a terminal and JSON without one); the program logs through the slog API either way. The standard log package is denied in the daemon kind; the logger is passed in and messages are static with key-value attributes, so a printf-built message is a finding. A fatal log call outside main is held by go.errors.4. A CLI is exempt until the shared logger leaf exists. What a daemon log holds and where it goes is daemon.logging.1; the audit record is daemon.logging.3.
pros: Own measure: only one of our repos uses slog (3 files); another has a log.Fatal. One logging API with a choice of handler keeps styled terminal output and machine logs from being two code paths.

rules.statement: Every log line from a daemon or a long CLI run carries the program version and a run id from one handler, so a CLI call and the daemon it spoke to can be joined.

exemptions.reason: It has no log output of its own.

reasoning.definition: One shared logger constructor adds the version and the run id. A matrix test runs the binary or daemon with logging on, parses every stderr or log line as JSON and asserts both fields; the default logger is banned so lines cannot bypass the handler.
pros: Practice. A run id exists in 10 files of one repo and 2 of another; a request id nowhere; 21 files write to stderr directly.

rules.statement: context.Background and context.TODO are used only at the edge, in main and tests, and their count elsewhere only falls.

reasoning.definition: contextcheck and noctx cover the missing-propagation class beside the ban on the root contexts.
pros: Own measure: uses outside main today: 70, 64, 47, 38, 14 and 6 across six repos. A root context deep in the code cannot be cancelled.

rules.statement: Every goroutine has an owner that waits for it and stops it.

reasoning.definition: A bare go statement outside an allow list of owner helpers (a run group, an error group, a wait-group go) is a finding on a shrink-only list; vet's wait-group check and the revive data-race and wait-group rules are on. A package with a go statement has a leak check in its tests (go.concurrency.6). Whether the owner stops it on cancel stays review.
pros: Own bugs: 5 of 60 sampled concurrency bugs. Bare go statements in non-test code today: 10, 13, 2, 33, 6 and 3, 67 sites to put on the shrink-only list; no error group anywhere.

rules.statement: Locks are released on every path, and each piece of shared state has one writer and one owner.

reasoning.definition: A lock is held briefly and what it guards is written beside it. The flow-aware linter reports a mutex locked and not unlocked on some path; a brief critical section with an explicit unlock passes. One writer and one owner per piece of state, and the comment naming what a lock guards, stay review.
pros: Own bugs: 5 of 60 concurrency bugs, half of the row. 0 real hits today in six repos, so adoption is free.

rules.statement: An interrupt (Ctrl-C), and SIGTERM where the system sends one, stop the program cleanly through signal.NotifyContext.

exemptions.reason: It has no main to stop.

reasoning.definition: The program ends on os.Interrupt, and on syscall.SIGTERM where the system sends one, through signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM); Go maps Windows' Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Break, close and logoff onto those two. A matrix test starts the built binary or daemon (testenv.Binary.Start), interrupts it (Running.Interrupt) and asserts exit within 5 seconds with the done or interrupted code and that a temp file or socket it owns is removed. The old signal notify call is banned in favour of NotifyContext outside the one serve helper.
pros: Own measure: used in 5 of 6 repos. A daemon that ignores the interrupt is killed by the service manager and loses its state.

rules.statement: State is cleared when its cause ends.

pros: Own bugs: 5 of 60 sampled bugs were state that outlived its cause. Cause and end are semantic: no tool knows a state has a cause.

rules.statement: A package that starts a goroutine is tested with the race detector and a leak check; the race run is in the release gate and runs locally after any change that starts or changes a goroutine; and it may sit outside the pre-push gate only when it is over that gate's measured budget.

reasoning.definition: The race run is a make target (make race) in the shared Makefile fragment. It runs in the release workflow, on a tag or by manual dispatch, and never on a push or a pull request. When a change adds or edits a go statement, the pre-push hook runs the race target for the touched packages. While the whole race run fits the pre-push budget it stays in make check. A recipe lists the packages with a go statement and greps for the leak check in their tests. Which leak check is open: the leak library's test-main verifier or the runtime's goroutine-leak profile.
pros: Practice. No repo uses the leak library; only one runs the race detector by default. The profile found one planted leak in verification. No push CI: the gate runs locally, and a check too slow for the hook moves to the release workflow, not to a hosted job.

rules.statement: Code is sequential by default: a goroutine is added only where a measured gain is cited at the go statement, an adapter adds no goroutine, poll or timer, and a slow read is cached on demand with a stated hold and bound.

reasoning.definition: The citation is a comment on the line above the go statement naming the measurement (what, how much, where it is recorded). An adapter is a plain call: a go statement, time.Ticker, time.NewTimer, time.AfterFunc or a loop around time.Sleep in a host or adapter package is a finding. A cached read states how long it holds and how many entries it keeps, and nothing reads while nobody asks.
pros: Concurrency is the largest source of bugs that show only years in, and a measured reason at the call is the cheapest guard. Keeping adapters free of polls is what keeps a program idle when nobody asks.

rules.statement: Interfaces are small, and a function accepts interfaces and returns concrete types.

pros: Practice. One repo declares 98 interfaces; their sizes were not measured; the linter flagged a 40-method port in another.

rules.statement: A concept gets a named type, the zero value is useful, and generics come only after the same code was written several times.

pros: Practice; judgement. Nothing decides that a concept needs a type.

rules.statement: No checks for states that cannot happen, and no wrapper or function that only forwards a call; pass-throughs are counted per package and read as a list, with no limit.

reasoning.definition: A types-aware analyser counts free functions that forward to a function of the same shape, and wrappers whose every method has the same signature as the call it forwards, with no type conversion. Dispatchers and adapters that convert types are exempt; an adapter that imports what the core may not is a seam and exempt; a fake alone does not earn the exemption.
pros: Practice; no fault among the 60 sampled. Free forwarders today: 48, 12, 11, 18, 2 and 2 across six repos; 39 of the first 48 forward inside our own module, in clusters left by moves, 9 are false hits.

rules.statement: The resource and context linters are on: bodyclose, noctx, and in a repo that imports the SQL package sqlclosecheck and rowserrcheck.

exemptions.reason: A program that does not import the SQL package needs neither of the two database linters; a rule-data field marks it.

pros: A leaked response body is a daemon-lifetime bug. Practice; priced in the linter trial.

rules.statement: Go tests use the standard testing package only, every test helper calls t.Helper, a table case is named by its claim, and a test checks one behaviour.

reasoning.definition: An assertion or mock library import in a test file is a finding (tests.doubles.2 bans mock libraries for every language). A function in a test file that takes a testing.TB, *testing.T or *testing.B and is not itself a test calls t.Helper first. A table case name says what holds (refuses a retired key), not an index or input. One behaviour per test is review.
pros: A helper without t.Helper reports the failure at the helper's line, not the caller's, and a case named by its claim is the failure message a person reads first. The standard package keeps tests readable by anyone who knows Go.

rules.statement: A package's tests build with every sibling package outside its declared imports unresolvable, and a suite that still passes with its subject package's non-test source removed fails as vacuous.

reasoning.definition: The Go form of the sibling-hiding resolver: a gate step lists each package's test import closure (go list -deps -test) and fails when it holds an internal package not allowed for that package's layer in the import table, so a test cannot reach a sibling the package itself may not. The subject-deleted run uses go test -overlay to replace every non-test file of the package with an empty file of the same package name; a suite that compiles and passes is vacuous. A module's tests make another module's data only through that module's exported API or their own fixtures.
pros: A suite that passes with its subject deleted is the cheapest mutation test there is, and siblings unresolvable is what makes a package extractable in fact, not only by the import table.

rules.statement: At commit, gofmt and go mod tidy run as diffs that list what differs and never rewrite the tree.

reasoning.definition: The format member runs gofmt with the list flag and fails on any file named; the tidy member runs go mod tidy with the diff flag and fails on any output. Neither writes, so both run beside the other members (gates.command.28) and inside the commit hook's seconds (gates.command.17). The fix is the same command in write mode, run by the person, not by the hook.
pros: A commit hook that rewrites files and restages them is the opposite of a check, and two hooks of one organisation did exactly that; a tidy that writes in the hook races the members beside it.

sources.says: If a file's formatting is different from gofmt's, print its name to standard output.
The -diff flag causes go mod tidy not to modify go.mod or go.sum but instead print the necessary changes as a unified diff.

rules.statement: The push lint runs vet and the shared lint preset with the parallel-test linters on, and a test that runs alone carries a serial comment that names the process state it needs.

reasoning.definition: tests.runners.4 holds that a test is parallel by default and a serial one says why. This line names the tools that hold it in Go: the linter that reports a test without a parallel call, and the one that reports a parallel call in the wrong place. The stated reason is a comment of the form `// serial:` with the state the test needs, and the linter's own disable comment is not the reason. A test that only needs a variable for a child process sets it on the child's environment and stays parallel.
pros: Four of five projects in one organisation had zero parallel tests, and one project's 152 serial tests took 136 seconds on about one CPU; the linter finds the missing call before the tier report does.

sources.says: Detects missing usage of t.Parallel() method in your Go test. ... Tparallel detects inappropriate usage of t.Parallel() method in your Go test codes.

rules.statement: The stamp key holds the Go build settings that change a verdict, the flags variable, the cgo switch, the experiment variable and the toolchain, and a run inside a workspace file gets no key.

reasoning.definition: gates.land.15 holds that a stamp is keyed to the exact tree, its settings and its tools. For Go the settings are GOFLAGS, CGO_ENABLED, GOEXPERIMENT and the toolchain version, read from the go tool, not from the shell. A workspace file changes which module code a build sees without changing the tree, so a run under one is not keyed: it runs, and nothing is stamped or served.
pros: A stamp that ignores a build setting serves a green for a build nobody ran; a workspace can point a build at a sibling checkout the tree does not hold.

sources.says: A space-separated list of -flag=value settings to apply to go commands by default
If GOWORK is set to off, the command will be in a single-module context.

rules.statement: The tools step fetches the whole module graph, so a fresh clone builds, and cross-compiles once for one other system as a smoke, with the network blocked.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.21 holds that a fresh clone passes after the documented setup, and supply.install.2 that the build runs with the network blocked after the install. A cross-compile for another system pulls modules the first never needed; the tools step downloads them once and the one cross-compile smoke runs offline. It is a smoke that no code of one system crept into the product, not a build per shipped system. One run that primed the cache is not setup.
pros: A second machine's first push was red on a module graph that only an earlier run had fetched.

rules.statement: The type check has zero errors in application and infrastructure code, under the strictest flags.

reasoning.definition: Each project runs its framework's checker: `tsc --noEmit` for plain and React code, and `astro check` (with a tsconfig extending `astro/tsconfigs/strictest`, the framework's strictest preset) for `.astro` templates, never `tsc` on `.astro` files. The check covers application code and the deployment code beside it. Strict mode is on; the full flag set is in the shared base, see ts.compiler.3.
pros: A type error that the gate lets through is a fault found at run time. At the donor project the type check refused its own lead's wrong ruling on one change, which is the evidence for a hard type gate (evidence C).

rules.statement: The compiler flags reach the strictest base one flag per change, the list of flags on can only grow, and strictness never goes down.

reasoning.definition: The sequence includes `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`, with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` last (it is the one that produces the most errors). A diff check on `tsconfig.json` fails when a flag is removed from the committed list. Project references are built with `tsc -b`. Extra flags beyond the strict base, such as unchecked indexed access and exact optional property types, are on.
pros: Turning on all flags in one change produces a wall of errors that gets suppressed; one flag per change keeps each cost small and visible.

rules.statement: One published strictest compiler core is shared by every project, in two module modes: a published library compiles with nodenext resolution, composite, and emits declarations to dist, and a bundled app uses bundler resolution with no emit.

reasoning.definition: The strict core is the same in both modes: strict on, exact optional property types, unchecked indexed access, verbatim module syntax, erasable syntax only, isolated modules, no switch fall-through and consistent file-name casing. The mode is chosen by the package's kind (published library or bundled app), never per file, and a package declares which kind it is. The base is a published package with one entry per mode; a project's own compiler file extends the base for its kind and sets only lib, types and jsx (ts.compiler.5). Copies in projects are byte-equal to the template. A third mode is added to the base, never to a project.
pros: One base changes once and reaches every project by a version bump, where per-project files drift. A library and an app are different compile targets and no single module mode serves both, while the strict flags are what the rule exists to share.

rules.statement: A strictness flag deliberately left off is recorded with its reason and pinned off by a test.

reasoning.definition: The base names each flag that is off (three in the source) with the reason beside it; a test fails when a flag recorded as off turns on without the record changing, or the reverse.
pros: A flag that is off with no recorded reason is indistinguishable from one forgotten, and nobody turns it on.

rules.statement: A project's compiler file extends the shared base and sets only lib, types and jsx, and a base option set in a project file fails.

reasoning.definition: The check reads each project compiler file and fails on any compiler option other than lib, types and jsx, so no overlay can loosen strictness or change the module mode in a corner. Where a file still lists more than one extended file, the shared base is listed last so it wins, and a test sets a flag in the overlay that the base sets the other way and asserts the base's value is the resolved one.
pros: A shared rule that a local file can silently override is not shared. Capping the overlay to three keys is the maintenance win: nobody loosens strict in a corner.

rules.statement: The native TypeScript compiler becomes the type gate once its release is stable, with the previous compiler pinned beside it, and any disagreement between the two diagnostic lists is a finding.

reasoning.definition: Stable means the native compiler's npm release is out of beta and is not a nightly. From then on the type-check step runs the native compiler as the gate and the previous major, pinned exactly, in the same step; both diagnostic lists are compared by file, code and line (project builds included), and any entry in one list and not the other fails the step as a finding until it is fixed or recorded with a reason. There is no waiting window and no scheduled tier: both run on every type check. Decorator flags are confirmed or removed first. The pinned previous compiler leaves only by a decision once the lint stack and every framework checker accept the native one.
pros: Running both compilers and failing on a disagreement is the safety; a window that depends on a scheduled tier cannot be met once gates run only at the push and the release. Until the native release is stable nothing can fail, so the rule waits.

rules.statement: No explicit `any` appears in source, and none appears in a signature.

reasoning.definition: typescript-eslint `no-explicit-any` as an error, with no exemption inside source files; the untyped rules run without type information so they work on every file kind. On `.astro` files the typed rules are switched off for the virtual script files and carried by oxlint. Use `unknown` and narrow, or a parsed type. Biome form: `noExplicitAny` at error.
pros: One `any` turns off checking for everything it touches, and spreads through inference. At the donor repo 118 non-null assertions sat in one baseline (evidence C); `any` and the empty record are the worst holes at a signature.

rules.statement: No forced type assertion (`as T`, `as unknown as T`) and no non-null assertion; narrow the value or parse it.

reasoning.definition: typescript-eslint `consistent-type-assertions` with `assertionStyle: never` (outside tests; `as const` is not flagged), `no-non-null-assertion`, and a rule against an unsafe assertion that narrows. A response from outside is never cast: it is parsed against a schema or typed by the generated client. Biome form: `noNonNullAssertion` at error and a GritQL plugin for an `as` assertion other than `as const`; the unsafe-narrowing half (`no-unsafe-type-assertion`) needs types and is ESLint-only.
pros: An assertion is a claim the compiler cannot check; one wrong claim removes the safety of a whole path.

rules.statement: No `@ts-ignore` and no `@ts-nocheck`; `@ts-expect-error` needs a description, and any suppression carries a reason and a ticket.

reasoning.definition: typescript-eslint `ban-ts-comment` as an error: every directive needs a description of at least 10 characters; a type-check suppression names a ticket and a reason of a minimum length; a file-wide suppression is banned. Counts of suppressions only fall, through ESLint bulk suppressions (see ts.lint-config.1). Biome form: `noTsIgnore` at error, plus a separate comment scan that fails `@ts-nocheck` and an expect-error comment with no ticket and reason.
pros: A suppression with no reason is a bug that has been hidden. The same rule family covers no `any` and no unchecked cast without a reason.

rules.statement: A value from outside is never cast to a type; it is parsed against a schema, or typed by the generated client.

reasoning.definition: The common form is `response.json()` cast with `as T`; it is banned. The parse happens once at the edge and the rest of the code sees the parsed type. Biome form: a GritQL plugin for an `as` assertion whose operand is a `json()` call or `JSON.parse`.
pros: A cast response is trusted without a check; a server change then breaks callers far from the call.

rules.statement: No `any`, unparsed `unknown`, raw JSON or untyped record appears in the exported signature of a core module; data is parsed at the adapter's edge into a named type.

reasoning.definition: A type-aware lint over the exported signatures of files under the core path. It resolves aliases, because the known way round is a type alias over a record, so the scan looks at the underlying type. It extends the request-validation rule (one validation by the contract) and the no-`any` rule: those cover the request and the use of `any`, and not a core function that takes `unknown` or `Record<string, unknown>`. ESLint-only as a lint rule, because the scan resolves type aliases; a Biome project holds it by a separate check that reads exported signatures through the compiler API.
pros: Argued, with no fault in the record. Parsed types at the boundary are what make a later adapter cheap (principles report P-01 section 19).

rules.statement: Ids are branded types, so one kind of id cannot be passed where another is expected.

reasoning.definition: Each id kind is a branded string derived from its schema (the schema library's brand), declared once next to the entity. A function takes the branded type; a plain string is parsed into it at the edge.
pros: Two ids are both strings; passing one for the other compiles and returns nothing or the wrong record.

rules.statement: Types are used so that a wrong program does not compile, through branded ids, exhaustive unions and parsed values.

reasoning.definition: Switches over a union are exhaustive and end in a never check; values are parsed once at the edge; ids are branded; links are typed.
pros: A guidance rule with no check of its own; its parts are held by other rules (assertions, branded ids, typed destinations).

rules.statement: A dependency ships its own types, or a matching types package exists in the lock.

reasoning.definition: After an install, each added direct dependency's manifest has `types`, `typings`, an exports entry with types, or a matching `@types` package is in the lock; otherwise the check fails. It reads the installed package manifests.
pros: An untyped dependency brings `any` in through its imports (evidence D).

rules.statement: The count of values that escape the type system (`any`, assertions, non-null assertions, suppressions) only falls.

reasoning.definition: The type-coverage tool reports the share of identifiers whose type is not `any`, and with its strict option counts casts and non-null assertions as well. The suppression counts only fall through ESLint bulk suppressions paired with a per-file count (ts.lint-config.1). In a Biome project the suppression count is the count of `biome-ignore` comments, held by the same shrink-only number.
pros: The share is the measure; without it the bans above are met by moving the hole, not closing it.

rules.statement: A function exported from a module declares its return type.

reasoning.definition: Exported functions, methods of exported classes and exported arrow functions name their return type; a local function may infer it. In library mode the compiler holds it: `isolatedDeclarations` in the library base (ts.compiler.3) fails an export whose type would need inference to emit. In app mode the lint holds it. Biome form: `useExplicitType` at error. ESLint form: `@typescript-eslint/explicit-module-boundary-types` at error.
pros: A declared return type is the contract the next reader builds on, and it stops an inferred type drifting under a refactor in a file the caller never sees.

rules.statement: Time enters through one clock port, instants are one branded type, and Date is constructed only in the clock adapter and the file reader.

reasoning.definition: Code that needs the time takes the clock port as a parameter; `new Date()`, `Date.now()` and `performance.now()` appear only in the clock adapter, and `new Date(value)` only there and in the adapter that reads file times. Every other module carries the branded instant type, never a `Date` or a bare number. Tests use the fake clock. The two allowed paths are listed in one place. Biome form: a GritQL plugin for a `Date` construction or `Date.now()` call, with an `overrides` entry for the two listed paths. ESLint form: `no-restricted-syntax` on the same calls with the same path list.
pros: A clock port is what makes every time-dependent test deterministic; a direct read of the clock is a test that passes today and fails in another timezone or at midnight.

rules.statement: Type-aware correctness rules run as errors where they are cheap: no floating promise, no misused promise and no unsafe-any flow.

reasoning.definition: The set is the strict type-checked preset: `no-floating-promises`, `no-misused-promises`, the `no-unsafe-*` family, and no needless conditions. A background task is awaited or handled. The fast tool (oxlint with its type-aware backend) runs at tier 2 on `.ts`, `.tsx` and `.astro` frontmatter and scripts; the typed ESLint run is not used below the land tier. Tests are linted without type information (see ts.lint-config.5). Biome form: `noFloatingPromises` and `noMisusedPromises` (Biome's type-aware rules) at error. The `no-unsafe-*` family is ESLint-only: Biome has no form and a GritQL pattern cannot see types, so a Biome project records the gap.
pros: A promise that is neither awaited nor handled fails silently and out of order. Typed ESLint costs 3.3 to 4.4 times the untyped run (donor measure); oxlint took 0.6 CPU seconds for the same 3,633 files.

rules.statement: Type-only imports are free across layers, and type imports are written explicitly so the exemption is checkable.

reasoning.definition: The layer rule allows `import type` across any layer (the plugin reads `importKind`), and `consistent-type-imports` makes a type-only import explicit, so a value import across layers fails while the same name as a type passes. Biome form: `useImportType` at error makes the type import explicit; the layer half is held by the boundary checker of the architecture part, a separate check that reads the import kind.
pros: A type creates no run-time dependency, so a layer rule that forbids it forbids nothing real and invites workarounds.

rules.statement: The lint engine is a project parameter (Biome or ESLint), there is one config, and every rule in it is an error, never a warning, for whichever engine is chosen.

reasoning.definition: The project declares its engine once; a second lint engine in the same project fails. The shared config for the declared engine sets each rule at error level and ships as one versioned unit. For Biome that is one `biome.json` with every enabled rule at `error` and the formatter in the same file; for ESLint it is one strict flat config with its plugin set. A rule is either at error or off and recorded on the off-list with a reason; `warn` (Biome or ESLint) and Biome's `info` level are refused. Every lint rule in this part names its Biome form (a built-in rule, a GritQL plugin or a separate check) or says it is ESLint-only; an ESLint-only rule binds only where the engine is ESLint, and a Biome project holds the same intent through the named form or records the gap. A new engine is added by naming its form on each rule, never by rewriting the rules.
pros: A warning is read by nobody; the gate must fail on it. The rules that matter (every rule at error, a plant per rule, type-aware checks) are engine-free, so tying the part to one engine would make the next engine change a rewrite.

rules.statement: Schema declarations pass the schema library's lint rules: no any-schema, no unknown-schema, strict objects, no throw inside a refinement and no schema built inside a function.

reasoning.definition: The plugin for the schema library's current major version runs as errors: `no-any-schema`, `no-unknown-schema`, `prefer-strict-object`, `no-throw-in-refine` and `no-function-scoped-schema`. Biome form: one GritQL plugin per rule (an any or unknown schema, a non-strict object, a throw inside a refinement, a schema built inside a function), registered in the one Biome config at error.
pros: A loose schema parses everything and checks nothing, which defeats the parse-at-the-edge rule.

rules.statement: Page code has no empty block, no empty catch and no swallowed rejection; a catch rethrows, returns a typed result or shows a user-visible state.

reasoning.definition: ESLint `no-empty` with `allowEmptyCatch` false as an error, plus a `no-restricted-syntax` for a catch clause whose body is a single `return <literal>` (a catch that returns a default). Tests are excluded by `files`. Typescript-eslint `no-floating-promises` and `only-throw-error` sit beside them in the typed set (ts.lint.1). Biome form: `noEmptyBlockStatements` at error and a GritQL plugin for a catch whose body is one `return` of a literal.
pros: The reader-facing rule covers what the person sees, and the runtime listener catches errors at run time; nothing covered the source.

rules.statement: A rethrown error keeps the original as its cause.

reasoning.definition: ESLint `preserve-caught-error` (core in ESLint 10) as an error: a `throw new Error(msg)` inside a catch needs the `cause` option. Biome form: a GritQL plugin for a `throw new Error(...)` inside a catch with no `cause`.
pros: A rethrow without a cause loses the stack that says where it started.

rules.statement: No catch clause only rethrows.

reasoning.definition: A catch whose only statement is `throw err` adds nothing and hides the real handling point; remove it or add context with a cause. Biome form: `noUselessCatch` at error.
pros: It is noise that reads like handling.

rules.statement: Shipped code has no console output.

reasoning.definition: ESLint `no-console` as an error in shipped source; tests and scripts are exempt by `files`. Logging goes through the program's logger. Biome form: `noConsole` at error, with an `overrides` entry that exempts tests and scripts.
pros: Console output in a page is invisible to the log pipeline and leaks internals to the browser.

rules.statement: Applies when the engine is ESLint, the bulk suppressions are paired with a per-file count of lines, because they are not a ratchet on their own.

reasoning.definition: ESLint-only. ESLint 10 bulk suppressions (`eslint-suppressions.json`, `--suppress-all`, `--prune-suppressions`) record errors per file but allow the file to grow; a per-file line-count baseline refuses growth. Biome has no bulk suppression file: each suppression is an inline `biome-ignore` comment with a reason, counted by the shrink-only suppression count of the gates part, so the line-count pairing is not needed there.
pros: In a trial a suppressed file grew by 250 lines and ESLint exited 0.

rules.statement: A new rule ships as an error, never a warning; the suppression list is seeded with every rule id of the family and pruned when code is fixed.

reasoning.definition: Bulk suppression records errors only, so a warning is never ratcheted. After code is fixed the run fails until the list is pruned (`--prune-suppressions`, exit 2 on an unpruned entry), and the flag that ignores unpruned entries is refused by the lint wrapper at the land tier. Biome form: a new rule enters the one Biome config at `error`, existing hits are suppressed with a `biome-ignore` comment carrying a reason, and Biome's unused-suppression report fails a comment left after the code is fixed. The seeding and pruning of a list file is ESLint-only.
pros: Without pruning the list keeps room for the old violations to come back.

rules.statement: Applies when the engine is ESLint, typed lint is never cached across files, and the lint cache is allowed only for a config with no typed rules.

reasoning.definition: ESLint-only. The lint wrapper refuses `--cache` when the config uses typed parser options at push and land. Lint at each gate tier runs uncached over the whole tree; where a repo turns test selection on (tests.selection.1), push and land may lint the reverse closure of the changed files instead, and the release lints everything. Biome keeps no lint cache between runs, so the rule has nothing to hold there.
pros: A typed rule's result in one file depends on its imports, so a cached result is stale when another file changes. A global check is never affected-only unless sound under caching.

rules.statement: Applies when the engine is ESLint, the edit tier lints the changed file through a warm server with an untyped config in under two seconds (2 s).

reasoning.definition: ESLint-only. An agent edit hook runs oxlint or a warm ESLint server on the changed file only. The two seconds is a measure: the donor reports a cold single-file lint of 20 seconds. Warm servers considered are eslint_d (15.1.0, MIT) and oxlint (1.91.0), not run here. Biome form: the edit hook runs `biome check` on the changed file, which needs no warm server; the same two-second ceiling applies and is recorded the same way.
pros: A cold lint is too slow for an edit loop, so the agent skips it.

rules.statement: Test files are linted without type information, and the function-length cap and the non-null assertion rule are off in tests.

reasoning.definition: The shared config has a tests override: no parser project, the function-length cap off and `no-non-null-assertion` off. The assertion style ban that applies outside tests (ts.type-safety.2) is relaxed the same way. Biome form: an `overrides` entry for test paths turns off `noNonNullAssertion`, the function-length check and the type-aware rules.
pros: Typed lint on every test file is the slowest part of the run, and tests use assertions legitimately.

rules.statement: Plain script files (js, mjs, cjs) are linted with the runtime's globals.

reasoning.definition: The config has an override for plain script files that declares the runtime's globals, so `process` or `__dirname` in a script is not flagged as undefined and the script is still linted. Biome form: an `overrides` entry for plain script files declares the runtime globals in `javascript.globals`.
pros: Without the override a script either fails with false errors or is left out of the lint.

rules.statement: Root tool config files that sit outside the compiler include are still linted, without a parse error.

reasoning.definition: Root config files (build, test and lint config) are outside the compiler's include list, so a typed parser project cannot read them. They get an untyped override or a default project, so they are linted without a parse error. ESLint-only: Biome needs no parser project, so root config files are linted with the rest and cannot hit this parse error.
pros: A parse error on a config file stops the whole lint run, or the file is silently skipped.

rules.statement: Build output, coverage, cache and infrastructure-tool output folders are excluded from lint.

reasoning.definition: The ignore list names build output, coverage, cache and generated folders (including the generated route tree). A generated file is never linted and never hand-edited. Biome form: the same folders are excluded by negated patterns in `files.includes` of the one Biome config, checked by the same test.
pros: Linting generated output produces errors nobody can fix.

rules.statement: The test lint plugin is pinned exactly, and a test confirms its TypeScript peer range accepts the project's version.

reasoning.definition: The test-runner lint plugin is pinned to an exact version in the shared config's package. A test reads its peer range and fails when the project's TypeScript version is outside it. ESLint-only: Biome has no test-runner lint plugin, so the pin and peer-range test bind only where the engine is ESLint; the Biome version itself is pinned exactly like any other tool.
pros: A plugin whose peer range excludes the project's TypeScript installs with a warning and then fails or silently skips rules.

rules.statement: The Node version is declared in the project template, and one Node major appears in every declaration: the version file, `engines`, the types package and the deploy runtime.

reasoning.definition: `package.json` carries `engines`; the version file the gate reads (not an nvm-only file) is byte-equal to the template's; `engine-strict` is on; the types package for Node (`@types/node`) and the cloud runtime setting name the same major. The check reads `engines` with npm-package-json-lint's `require-engines`.
pros: Two Node majors in one project mean the code that passes tests runs on a different runtime in production. Neither of two donor sites declared Node at all (evidence A).

rules.statement: A short list of deprecated platform core modules may not be used.

reasoning.definition: The list is data with the reason for each entry and the replacement; an import of a listed module fails. It is a boundary rule enforced by the import lint. Biome form: `noRestrictedImports` with the same list, each entry carrying its replacement in the message.
pros: A deprecated core module is removed in a later Node major and breaks the upgrade.

rules.statement: One unit test runner is used in every project.

reasoning.definition: The runner is Vitest. Jest, mocha and ava are banned entries in the manifest config; the built-in `node:test` is banned in new files by no-restricted-imports with a baseline that only falls until the existing files migrate. The rule is read per project, not per estate. Migration is ordered: the recorded-reads selector is proved on the runner first, then the files move in the same change. Biome form for the import half: `noRestrictedImports` on `node:test` with the same shrink-only baseline; the manifest ban is engine-free.
pros: Two runners double the setup and split the test selection. A donor site had 87 of the 103 built-in runner files and is the one that must migrate.

rules.statement: Exports are named, and a default export fails except in a file a framework requires it in, listed by path.

reasoning.definition: The exception list holds paths, never globs wider than the framework's own file convention, and each entry names the framework rule that needs the default export. A re-export of a default under a name (an `export` list naming `default as X`) is a named export and passes. Biome form: `noDefaultExport` at error, with an `overrides` entry for the listed paths. ESLint form: `import-x/no-default-export` (or `no-restricted-syntax` on an export-default declaration) at error, with the same path list.
pros: A default export takes whatever name each importer gives it, so a rename does not travel, search misses uses and two files can import the same thing under two names.

rules.statement: TypeScript `enum` and `namespace` are refused, and a closed set is a literal union or a schema enum.

reasoning.definition: The compiler holds it first: `erasableSyntaxOnly` in the shared core (ts.compiler.3) fails an enum, a const enum and a namespace that holds values. A type-only `declare namespace` for an outside library's types is the one form left, and only in a `.d.ts` file. Biome form: `noEnum` and `noNamespace` at error. ESLint form: `no-restricted-syntax` on an enum declaration and `@typescript-eslint/no-namespace` at error.
pros: An enum and a namespace compile to runtime objects with their own semantics, so they cannot be stripped by a type-erasing loader and differ from every other type in the program; a literal union or a schema enum says the same thing and erases cleanly.

rules.statement: Packages are ESM only and relative imports carry their file extension.

reasoning.definition: Every package manifest says `"type": "module"`; a `.cjs` file, a `require` call or a `module.exports` in source fails, and a package that must serve a CommonJS reader does so from a generated build, never from source. A relative import names the file it loads with its extension. In library mode the nodenext resolution of ts.compiler.3 makes a missing extension a type error; in app mode the lint holds it. Biome form: `useImportExtensions` at error. ESLint form: `import-x/extensions` set to always for relative imports.
pros: An import without an extension resolves only under a loader that guesses, so the same module loads under the bundler and fails under the runtime, the test runner or the next loader.

rules.statement: Importing any exported entry reads no file, network or environment and starts no timer or connection, checked by importing each entry under a hook that records such reads.

reasoning.definition: A test lists every entry of every package (the exports map, ts.packages.1, or the index of each unit), imports each one in a fresh process under a loader hook that records file reads, network sockets, environment reads, timers and child processes, and fails on any record. Work a module needs is done in a function its caller calls. This is wider than a ban on mutable package-level state: a module-level read of the environment or a connection opened at import fails here even when no state is kept. The test is engine-free, so it holds the same under Biome or ESLint.
pros: A side effect at import runs before the caller can configure, fake or refuse it, so a test, a worker or a cold start pays for work it did not ask for, and the bug shows only when the import order changes.

rules.statement: Each module's test suite runs with every sibling module unresolvable, so a test can load only its own module and what that module declares it may import.

reasoning.definition: The TypeScript form of tests.isolation.13. The test runner's resolver is configured per module from the declared import table (the architecture part's layers): an import of a sibling module that is not on the table resolves to nothing and the suite fails, whether the import is in the test or in the code under test. The configuration is generated from the table, never written by hand, so a new module is covered without a change here.
pros: A test that imports across modules passes for a module nobody could extract, so the boundary the import table claims is never exercised by the suite that should prove it.

rules.statement: A published package's exports map has one subpath per unit and no root barrel, and every entry resolves in the packed tarball.

reasoning.definition: A unit's surface is its index file; the package's surface is its exports map, with one subpath per unit pointing at that unit's built index and its types. There is no `"."` entry that re-exports every unit, and no wildcard subpath. The check packs the package, installs the tarball into a scratch folder and resolves every subpath for import and for types; a subpath that resolves only in the source tree fails. The stability mark of each export (stable, experimental or internal) lives in the surface file of the architecture part (arch.shared.9), not here. The check is engine-free.
pros: A root barrel is how a package grows a surface nobody chose, and only the packed tarball shows what a consumer sees: a file left out of the package or a types path that points into the source passes every check run on the tree.

rules.statement: One schema library holds the model, JSON Schema, types, DDL and API contracts are generated from it and held by regenerate-and-diff, no second schema library is a dependency, and what the model exports parses back to the same value.

reasoning.definition: The model is the one source. Every other shape (the JSON Schema files, the TypeScript types, the SQL DDL, the HTTP and tool contracts) is generated from it, committed, and regenerated and diffed by the gate; a hand edit to a generated file fails. The live database schema is checked against the DDL the model generates, never used to generate the model or the types. A landed migration is never edited; new SQL is appended and held to the generated DDL. The manifest names one schema library; a second one, or a query builder that owns its own schema, fails the manifest check. A round-trip test exports each model shape and parses it back to an equal value. The checks are engine-free.
pros: One model that generates every other shape is the strongest guard against a type, a table and a contract drifting apart over years, and regenerate-and-diff makes it mechanical. Naming the model as the source, and checking the live schema against it, leaves no second place where the truth can start.

rules.statement: A Node gate registers its uncaught-exception handler first, refuses an empty subject, sets process.exitCode and never calls process.exit before its last rule.

reasoning.definition: The handler for uncaught exceptions and unhandled rejections is registered before any import that can throw, and it sets a failing exit code and prints the gate's name. The gate fails when its subject (the file list, the rule list, the parsed tree) is empty. It sets `process.exitCode` and lets the event loop drain, so every rule runs and every pending write is flushed; `process.exit` is called by no gate file. The language-neutral rules (the gate list derived from the files, a gate that never imports its subject, a checker that counts what it parsed) live in the gates and architecture parts. Biome form: a GritQL plugin for a `process.exit` call in a gate file. ESLint form: `n/no-process-exit` (or `no-restricted-syntax` on the same call) for gate files. The handler order and the empty-subject refusal are held by the plant test, engine-free.
pros: A gate that exits early skips the rules after it and can cut its own output, and a gate with no handler can die on a throw and leave a zero exit code; both report green for work that did not happen.

rules.statement: At commit, the format check reads and never rewrites, and the lockfile is checked against the manifest.

reasoning.definition: The formatter runs in its check mode, lists the files that differ and exits non-zero; the fix is the same tool in write mode, run by the person. The lockfile member fails when the manifest and the lock disagree, which is the check the clean install makes before it installs anything. A hook that formats and restages is the opposite of a check (gates.command.28).
pros: Two commit hooks of one organisation ran the formatter in write mode and restaged; a stale install after a lockfile change gave 170 false lint errors and one refused landing.

sources.says: This will output a human-friendly message and a list of unformatted files, if any.
If dependencies in the package lock do not match those in package.json, npm ci will exit with an error, instead of updating the package lock.

rules.statement: Typed lint is never a commit member: at commit the staged files are linted without type information, or not at all.

reasoning.definition: Lint rules that need type information build a program over the project before the first file is read, and that cost is the same for one staged file as for all of them. The commit moment is seconds (gates.command.17). Typed lint runs at push as its own member with its threads and cache (ts.cycle.5).
pros: One staged file cost 30 seconds of typed lint at commit in one organisation's main web application, 28 of its 31.4 second commit.

sources.says: As a result, these rules are slower than traditional lint rules but are much more powerful.

rules.statement: No installed dependency folder and no build output is tracked in git.

reasoning.definition: The dependency folder is rebuilt from the lockfile and the build output from the source; tracking either makes every install or build a diff, hides the lockfile's job, and lets a hand edit to a built file reach the main branch. The ignore file names both, and a tracked file under either path fails.
pros: One package of one organisation tracks 5,460 installed files.

rules.statement: The clean install and the browser install run only when the lockfile or the pin changed, and the manifest's prepare step installs the hook and runs the framework's install step, so a fresh clone type checks.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.19 holds that a tool is installed when its pin changes; for this stack the pin is the lockfile and the browser version. The prepare step is the one script the package manager runs on a local install with no arguments, so it is where the hook install and the framework's generate or install step belong; a framework whose types come from a generated file fails the type check on a fresh clone until that step has run (gates.command.21).
pros: Eight repositories of one organisation were red on a fresh clone because a framework install step was missing from the prepare script, and installs of 106 to 180 seconds sat in no budget.

sources.says: Runs on local npm install without any arguments

rules.statement: At push the type check and the lint are their own members; the lint runs typed, on the pool's thread count, with its cache, in every tier.

reasoning.definition: The type check runs the compiler with no emit. The lint runs with type information, on as many threads as the pool gives (gates.command.25), with its cache in the same folder in every tier, so a warm push, land and release see the same speed. Each is a member, so a failure names one and both run beside the tests.
pros: One organisation's lint took 394 seconds cold and single-threaded in one slot kind and 8.8 seconds warm with four threads, and was 65 percent of a 607 second push.

sources.says: Do not emit compiler output files like JavaScript source code, source-maps or declarations.
Store the info about processed files in order to only operate on the changed ones.

rules.statement: No coverage instrumentation runs in a blocking tier; coverage runs at release or on demand.

reasoning.definition: Coverage transforms the source to count what ran, and that cost falls on every test of every push. tests.measures.5 holds that coverage is reported at the slowest tier and is never a threshold in the inner loop; this line places it: the release tier or an on-demand member (gates.command.26), never push or land.
pros: One organisation's unit tests took 215 seconds with coverage against 166 to 190 seconds without, in a blocking tier.

sources.says: coverage tracking works by transforming your source code to add instrumentation logic

rules.statement: A test that drives the project's own lint config shares one linter instance per file, built once in the file's setup.

reasoning.definition: Building a typed lint program inside a test body costs seconds per case. The file's setup builds the program once and the cases lint their samples against it (tests.runners.5). A case that needs another config says so and builds its own.
pros: Seven of the ten slowest tests in one organisation's main web application built a typed lint program inside the test body.

rules.statement: A service test imports the handler chain once per file and resets only the setting a test changes.

reasoning.definition: Re-importing the handler chain per test, or resetting every module between tests, rebuilds the service for each case. The file imports once, each test changes the one setting it is about and puts it back (tests.isolation.12 holds the list of tests that need isolation and why).
pros: Service suites of one organisation rebuilt their handler chain per test, and the tests were 126 of a 189 second push in one service.

rules.statement: A unit test never makes a real network attempt: a stub client throws a marker error, so a call that escaped the fake fails fast and names itself.

reasoning.definition: A unit test that reaches the network waits out a connect timeout on a host with no route and passes by luck on one with. The client the code under test receives is a stub whose every method throws a named marker error; a test that needs a real answer is an integration member (service.cycle.3), not a unit test. web.testing.12 holds how the network is faked where it is faked; this line holds that a unit test is never on it.
pros: Unit tests that reached for the network were among the slowest files in one organisation's services, and timed out at load.

rules.statement: At commit the formatter runs in check mode and the linter runs without fixing; neither rewrites a file.

reasoning.definition: The formatter's check mode lists the files that differ and exits non-zero; the linter reports and does not fix. Both read and never write (gates.command.28), so they run beside the other commit members inside the commit hook's seconds. The fix is the same tool in write mode, run by the person. Their cost was not measured on the host that studied the stack.
pros: A hook that rewrites files is the opposite of a check, and a formatter in write mode races the members beside it.

sources.says: ruff format --check /path/to/file.py will avoid writing any formatted files back, and instead exit with a non-zero status code
It accepts a list of files or directories, and lints all discovered Python files, optionally fixing any fixable errors.

rules.statement: The requirements are pinned with exact versions, or a lock file carries hashes; a minimum-version pin gives a fresh venv whatever is newest.

reasoning.definition: supply.install.1 holds that one package manager installs from the lockfile only and that the lockfile is the pin. For a project with a plain requirements file the pin is an exact version per line; where hashes are carried the installer refuses anything it cannot match. A line that says at least a version is not a pin.
pros: A requirements file with minimum-version pins gives every fresh venv a different tree, and a check that passed on one cannot be said to pass on the next.

sources.says: Requirements must be pinned (either to a URL, filesystem path or using ==).

rules.statement: The venv is built from the pins and rebuilt only when the pins change; a run checks it once and installs nothing when the check passes.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.19 holds that a tool is installed when its pin changes and checked once per run. The venv is this stack's install; the check compares the installed set with the pins, and the install runs when they differ or the pins file changed. The measured cost was 1.08 seconds plus 0.86 seconds warm.
pros: An install on every push is paid on every push, and an install that never checks the pin lets a stale venv pass for the pinned one.

rules.statement: At push every source file is byte-compiled, so a syntax error in a file nothing imports is found.

reasoning.definition: An import smoke (py.cycle.5) proves only the files the imports reach. The byte-compile walks the tree and compiles each file, in about 0.05 seconds, and a file with a syntax error fails it whether or not anything imports it. It is a member of its own, quiet on success.
pros: A file nothing imports can carry a syntax error for months and fail the day something imports it.

sources.says: These functions compile Python source files in a directory tree.

rules.statement: At push an import smoke imports every package in a fresh interpreter.

reasoning.definition: The smoke proves the packages import with the venv as pinned, in about 0.03 seconds. The interpreter is the one the venv pins, so its version is already in the stamp key through the pin (gates.land.15); the host's own build string is no part of the key.
pros: One organisation's desktop tool was red on import on the host that studied it, and a stamp that ignores the interpreter would have served the green of another host.

rules.statement: At push the tests run with workers from the pool and a type checker runs as its own member.

reasoning.definition: tests.runners.2 holds that the worker count comes from the pool's capacity and is never hard-coded; the test tool's automatic worker count is the tool's own reading of the host and is capped by the pool's number (gates.command.27). The type checker is a member of its own, so a type failure names it. Neither was measured on the host that studied the stack.
pros: A serial test run holds one CPU while the pool has more, and a type check inside the test command hides which one failed.

sources.says: With -n auto, pytest-xdist will use as many processes as your computer has physical CPU cores.

rules.statement: At push the program runs headless on a checked-in input and its output is compared with a checked-in expected file, read by a person.

reasoning.definition: A replay golden is the one test that runs the whole program. tests.generated.5 holds how a golden a person reads is approved; this line places one in the push tier for a program that has a headless mode. A replay that proves only that the program did not crash is a start, and the expected file grows as the output does.
pros: One organisation's desktop tool had no test that ran it; a replay was the cheapest proof that it starts and produces its output.

rules.statement: At push the requirements are scanned for known vulnerabilities, and at commit the staged diff is scanned for secrets against a reviewed allowlist.

reasoning.definition: supply.scans.7 holds the vulnerability scan in the full gate the land job runs before main, and supply.secrets.1 the secrets scan at commit; this line names the inputs for the stack: the requirements file for the first, the staged diff for the second, with the allowlist a shrink-only baseline that has an owner (gates.ratchets.1). The standard's stack line lists the secrets scan at push; this rule keeps it at commit, the earliest moment that holds it (C3). The vulnerability scan took 0.69 seconds on the measuring host.
pros: A secrets scan with no allowlist found 15 hits in three repositories of one organisation and none was a credential, so without the list the line stays red and is ignored.

sources.says: You can ignore specific findings by creating a .gitleaksignore file at the root of your repo.

rules.statement: One documented exit-code table, tested against the code and the built binary, with the estate set 0 done, 1 failed or findings, 2 usage, 3 busy, 4 not ready, 5 refused, 6 declined, in every language; a refused result, a declined one and a failed one never share a code; and a command whose port the machine lacks says not on this machine with the port's name and exits 2.

exemptions.reason: It has no exit codes.

reasoning.definition: A test parses the documentation table and the exit constants and fails on any code, name or meaning that differs, and runs the built binary through the matrix for one refused, one failed and one missing-port path and compares the exit status. A refusal is a rule holding and a failure is a bug or an outage: an agent retries one and never the other, so they never share a code. A typed refusal or error maps to its code in one place, by its word or type, never by its message (go.errors.4). A program in another language holds the same seven through its own exit owner. Declined (6) is a plan that was shown, asked for a yes, and not applied because no yes was given, whether the answer was no, no answer or the end of the input: nothing changed and nothing went wrong, and a caller never runs it again unasked, which is why it has a code of its own and does not end done (0), where a script would believe the plan was applied. It is not refused (5), where a rule held against the request, and not failed (1), where the program broke; an agent never retries a declined plan unasked. Failed shares code 1 with findings and is told apart from it by the word and by the kind in the JSON document, so a gate fails on an engine failure while a reader still sees which of the two ended the run. Whether a run that only shows a plan and asks nothing ends done (0) or declined (6) is not set here. A program that never shows a plan never exits 6, yet its table names the code, so a script reads one table across the estate. The set 0 to 5 was ruled on 4 Nov and 6 was added on 9 Nov; no meaning of 0 to 5 moved. The change is applied in lockstep: one release of the shared module sets the failed and refused codes and binds the closing word refused to 5, with the programs' tests changed in the same tag; every document that maps refused to 1 changes in one commit; the test in each program is the gate that proves it.
pros: Own measure. Today one program uses 0, 1, 2, 64, 69, 75 and 78; the shared module uses 0 to 4 with 1 for both refused and failed; three others use 1 for everything; one TypeScript program uses three codes with refusal and bad usage both 1.

rules.statement: Exit codes are imported from the one leaf package that owns them and never declared elsewhere, and a daemon imports the leaf so it does not link the terminal look.

reasoning.definition: Syntax-pattern rules flag a constant or variable named like an exit code with an integer literal, and an exit call with an integer literal argument, anywhere outside the owner package, on a shrink-only list (one file per entry). A test in the owner package asserts that the leaf's dependency list contains no terminal-library module. The owner package is the program's own exit leaf. Where a shared kit owns codes, the program imports them from it. Where the kit takes the program's table, the program's leaf is the owner and the kit only checks and draws. A daemon imports the leaf so it does not link the look.
pros: The program's own exit leaf, `internal/exit`, owns the codes, so there is one place they can change, and the shared module does not re-export them.

rules.statement: --version prints the release tag and the commit stamped at build (a build with no tag says so), the toolchain version, and, for a client of a server, the server's version; version --json gives one JSON document with the same keys plus the API number for a program with an API.

exemptions.reason: It has no binary.

reasoning.definition: The tag comes from git describe stamped at build time; a build with no tag prints v0.0.0-<commit>. In Go the commit and toolchain are compared with the binary's build information (revision, modified flag, toolchain), built with VCS stamping; another language stamps the same fields at build. A client asks its server for the server's version and prints unknown with a reason when it cannot reach it (cli.output.9). The version line is printed once, also off a terminal, and never with the banner. The matrix runs both forms, asserts exit 0, a non-empty first line and a JSON document with the keys version, commit and toolchain (plus server and api where they apply), and compares them with what was stamped. A repo-check test demands that each program has a test calling the matrix, so a program cannot skip it. The health document of the daemon repeats the same fields (see the daemon part).
pros: Own measure: the four CLIs disagree on --version, and it fails in three of them. The version line is the first thing a person pastes into a bug report and the first thing a reader checks against a provider, so it carries the tag, the commit and the API number, the same shape in any language. This rule starts the matrix helper that the output, config, environment and signal rules reuse.

rules.statement: --json prints exactly one JSON document on stdout, naming its contract version in one top-level field whose name and form the program states once, and everything else goes to stderr; a command that follows a stream prints one JSON object per line, each with the version field.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.
A daemon with no --json flag has no machine mode to hold.

reasoning.definition: The program states once, in rule data, the field name and the form (an integer such as 3, or a string such as launcher/3); a removal or a type change raises it and an addition does not. For every leaf command (the list comes from the command tree, never typed) the matrix runs with --json against a fixture, reads stdout fully, decodes it, asserts one document, end of input after it, the version field in the stated form, and empty stdout when the command fails to start; stderr may hold anything. A command annotated as following (logs -f) is read line by line instead: each line is one object with the version field.
pros: Own measure: --json exists on 11, 10, 10 and 5 leaves across four CLIs. What a reader needs is one field it can find and compare; whether it holds 3 or launcher/3 is a program's choice stated once. Marginal assertion on the matrix helper, whose cost is carried by the colour rule (cli.environment.1).

rules.statement: The output format is decided once: --json and any later machine format is a flag the shared root reads, a command returns a value the root renders, a command file holds no encoder call, and JSON result types are declared once in the API package with their tags and printed by the CLI unchanged, with no tagged struct in the command layer.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: The API package (core/api in the layout of go.layout.1) owns every result type with JSON tags; the CLI's --json and the HTTP answer print the same type. A struct with json tags in a cli/* package is a finding. TypeScript holds the same seam: result types live in the API module and a verb module declares none.
pros: Own measure; a command that encodes its own JSON drifts from the schema version rule, and result types in the API package are what make the CLI's --json and the HTTP answer one type.

rules.statement: Each command's --help and --json output has a hand-read, protected golden snapshot kept beside that command, so the shape of the JSON cannot change unnoticed; the root help, which only lists commands, is a generated document held by gen --check; and the gate cannot rewrite goldens.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: Goldens are compared with a script-test tool (its update flag only in a manual command). A repo-check fails a change that edits a golden and no source unless the commit carries the marker, and the update flag is refused whenever the gate variable is set (make check, the pre-push hook, a release workflow). Goldens are on the protected-path list, by pattern, so a verdict covers one command's files (gates.protection.3). The root help is derived text: its oracle is the per-command goldens and the generator that renders it, and a journey compares the built binary's root help with the generated document. A wrong summary in one command shows in that document's diff, which gen --check forces into the change that made it.
pros: Practice; no help snapshot exists in any repo today.

sources.says: Output is recorded as one golden file per command, in one folder beside the command tests, and none lists the whole tool.
The help of every command is checked by a test that walks the command tree, not by a snapshot of the root.

rules.statement: The command tree (commands, flags with type and default, positional words, exit codes, --json field names) is written to a committed file and compared with the file at the last tag under the program's declared reader mode: with owned readers a removed flag, field or changed exit code fails only when the contract number was not raised in the same change; with independent readers it fails unless the last tag already marked it deprecated a minor release earlier; and an addition always passes.

reasoning.definition: A program declares its readers once in rule data: owned (every reader ships with it, such as its own page and agents) or independent (a published library, a public API). With owned readers a break raises the contract number in the same change, every reader changes with it, and nothing is kept for an old reader. With independent readers a removal or change of meaning is first marked deprecated for one minor release. Once the command registry exists (cli.commands.20) the committed file is the output of help --json, not a second artefact. A daemon's published route contract is checked the same way: breaking-change diff of the OpenAPI file against the tag under the same declaration, and its error and shape claims against real answers; fuzz is added per route once the walk exists. The file is commands.json; the --json fields it records are the top-level fields of the golden output.
pros: Practice. The target programs disagree because they answer for different readers: a program that owns every reader found that a compatibility layer is where its bugs lived, and a program that ships to readers it never sees must not break them. One rule with a declared reader mode keeps the check mechanical. The shared exit-code change moves every exit code at one program's next minor; a tag diff is how that move is seen to be intended.

rules.statement: The shared flags --plain, --json, --accessible and --no-color, and --explain once lessons bind (cli.commands.18), are registered once, by the shared module, and no program defines its own.

pros: Own measure; one program defines its own colour flag today.

rules.statement: A command with no document of its own prints one shared result type under --json: the ending word, the changes made or planned, the next line, and an error with its kind.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: The type lives in the API package and every writing command without its own document returns it; a dry run fills the planned changes and an applied run the made ones.
pros: The shared result type gives every write the same ending, changes, next line and error for an agent to read.

rules.statement: Without --json the human answer goes to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, every applied or no-op line names the path it concerns, and a read command's human answer is the content itself, not a count of it.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: The render module tags each line as answer or diagnostic and routes it; a matrix test splits the streams and asserts the answer is on stdout. An applied or no-op line has a path field in its constructor. A read command's golden holds the content of a fixture, and a line such as "3 items" with no items fails.
pros: Stream discipline is what makes a pipe work in any language, a path on every applied line makes a transcript a record, and content rather than a count is the difference between an answer and a boast.

rules.statement: Every command calls one core operation and reads no store or config file itself; every operation with a route has a command or a named reason; where a command and a route show the same view their answers are one type from one function; and a test walking the route index fails on a route with neither.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands or routes.

reasoning.definition: What is left to do is computed once and handed out by both surfaces. The exceptions are a list in data with a reason each. A command package that imports a store or the config loader is a finding.
pros: Parity is what makes a page, an agent and a person see the same facts, and the walk over the route index keeps it true when a route is added years later. Two target programs wrote the same test.

rules.statement: A state or value the program could not establish is answered as unknown or null with a reason beside it, in text, in --json and in every API answer, never as 0, false, a dash, off, healthy or a default, and it never folds into ok; a field the platform has no such thing as is left out; an answer lists each source it could not read with why and never fills it from an earlier reading; a kept answer carries the time it was read; and a value known only while the program watched is omitted after a restart.

exemptions.reason: It answers no status of its own.

reasoning.definition: Good news is claimed only for what was checked; an item not checked is listed as not checked. A summary that is ok when one of its inputs is unknown is a finding. A test per answer plants an unreadable source and asserts the null, the reason, the absence of a carried-forward value and a summary that is not ok.
pros: This is the property that decides whether a status tool can be believed at 3 a.m. One rule across every surface is cheaper than three and keeps a page from showing fine over an API that said unknown.

rules.statement: A number is shown no finer than its source resolves, an estimate is marked as one, and what a model cannot explain is its own row, never spread over the measured ones.

exemptions.reason: It shows no measurements.

reasoning.definition: Each measured quantity declares its source resolution (whole watts, milliseconds); the formatter rounds to it. An estimate is printed with a mark (≈) and flagged in JSON. The remainder of a breakdown is a row of its own.
pros: A number with two decimals from a whole-watt meter is a lie with a straight face, and a remainder spread over the rest makes every row wrong.

rules.statement: A golden records one command's output and lives with that command; no hand-kept golden lists every command, and a listing of all commands is generated output.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: A command's help and --json goldens sit in a folder owned by that command (testdata beside its code, and one folder per command for the built binary's journeys). A golden that prints the root help, the menu or the command table of the whole program is not hand-kept: it is a document a generator writes and gen --check holds, so no command change edits a file another command's change also edits. A test walks the golden folders and fails on a golden that names more than one command's own output.
pros: Own measure: in one program every new command edited four cross-cutting goldens that each list every command, and each edit of a protected golden bought one reviewer verdict. A per-command golden is reviewed once, with its command. The organisation's run log of 8 Nov 2026 records the cost: each landing sent the waiting candidates through a rebase and a full gate run, and a verdict written on an earlier base was rebuilt.

sources.says: One golden per command under one folder; the root has no snapshot of its own.

rules.statement: A command that writes takes one of two declared forms: it needs an explicit --apply and its dry run writes nothing and ends by naming the apply command, or it writes only into a reviewable draft that a later, separate act makes effective. Its help says which form it has, and the list of writing commands and their form comes from the code, not from a typed list.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.
