reasoning.definition: A command registry (a walk of the command tree) carries a mutates annotation with the form (apply or draft) set by the command author. The matrix enumerates every command from the tree and runs those without the annotation expecting no write (tree hash equal before and after); an apply-form command run without --apply must leave the hash equal and end by naming the apply command; a draft-form command run once must change nothing a reader of the effective state sees until the separate act runs. A command with no declared form, or with both, fails. A repo-check analyser reports a command that calls a write helper and has no annotation. The reachability half is approximate (call graph through function values); the hash test is the real catch. The help golden must show the form line.
pros: Own bugs: a dry run that wrote (9 of 60 sampled bugs in the output-truth class). The goal is that nothing changes without a person seeing the change first: for a tool that edits a machine the dry run is the only way to show it, and for a store with change sets the draft is the dry run, so a second mode there would be code with no reader. Declaring the form per command keeps the matrix test and the help honest.

rules.statement: A command is safe to run twice: the second run changes nothing, or says it has nothing to do.

pros: Own measure; shares the fixtures and helper of cli.commands.1, so no extra build. Not measured in Go.

rules.statement: A command serialises its writes through the store's own concurrency (a transaction, an advisory lock or a file lock, declared once per store) taken before its first write, keeps a run record that can be undone, and a destructive step needs the thing's own name, typed at a terminal or given as --confirm NAME without one, which a blanket --yes never answers.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: Each store declares its one mechanism in rule data: a database's transaction, an advisory lock, or a kernel file lock through the platform's lock package for a file tree. A two-process test runs a writing command in a child holding the mechanism and starts a second: it must exit with the busy code (or the store must serialise the two with neither write lost), and the first run must be unharmed. An analyser asserts that every command with the mutates annotation acquires the declared mechanism before its first write helper. After a write a run record exists and undo restores the tree hash (record shape and undo discipline: cli.commands.24 and 25). A destructive step is one that removes data the program cannot fetch again (a drive formatted, a store or an owner's file deleted); it carries a destructive annotation. At a terminal it asks for the thing's own name typed out; without a terminal the only answer is --confirm NAME with that exact name. --yes answers only plain yes/no questions (cli.environment.8) and never a destructive step, and no other flag or environment variable answers it. A test drives each destructive command with --apply --yes and no --confirm and expects the refused code, and with a wrong name and expects the refused code.
pros: Own bugs: state and concurrency, 5 of 60 sampled. The invariant is that two writers never interleave, and a database transaction holds it better than a file lock beside the database, so the mechanism is the store's. A typed name is the one confirmation an agent cannot answer by reflex; two target programs chose the same shape independently.

rules.statement: Writes stay inside the scope the command names.

reasoning.definition: Only containment is mechanical: command tests run under a write sandbox with home, XDG folders, temp folder and working directory all inside one scratch root, and any write outside the root fails. Scope the command names is not machine readable. The test also takes a file-system snapshot (a hash of the whole parent of the scratch root) before and after, so a write the sandbox does not deny is still seen; this needs no strace-less tracing.
pros: Own bugs: 2 of 60 sampled bugs were a write beyond the command's scope.

rules.statement: A binary never rewrites shared state, and it installs or upgrades by rename, a daemon included; uninstall and removal keep user state unless told otherwise, and a test proves it.

exemptions.reason: It installs nothing.

reasoning.definition: An explicit purge flag is fine. A script test runs install, write, uninstall and looks for the data. Reverting an install is the rollback rule of the supply part.
pros: Own bugs. One repo has an install-is-a-rename test; the shared test is proposed.

rules.statement: An operation whose goal state already holds returns success, defined in the callee and documented (delete, stop, close, release, ensure); no caller needs the information.

reasoning.definition: This defines away operation semantics, never untrusted input or a typo, so the swallowed-error and exit rules stand. Each site that tolerates a not-exist error is counted per package and printed at land, so swallowing dressed as this form shows as drift. Review: does any caller need to know this state was already reached, and is the rule stated on the callee? The analyser requires a double-call test for Delete, Stop, Close, Release and Ensure methods, using one helper. The tolerated sites counted are errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist), errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) and os.IsNotExist.
pros: Practice. A count that only falls would punish legitimate idempotent deletes, so there is no number.

rules.statement: A multi-step operation that changes more than one thing says which of three it is: it rolls back, it resumes from a mark, or it is documented as having no rollback. A command that changes the machine only for the length of its run has a test that the change is undone after an error, an interrupt and a panic.

exemptions.reason: It changes no machine of its own.

reasoning.definition: Which of the three a multi-step operation is stays review. The temporary-change half is mechanical: a command annotated as changing the machine for its run (an app paused, a service stopped, a setting lowered) is driven by a test three times, once with a planted error in the middle, once with an interrupt sent mid-run (testenv.Binary.Start, then Running.Interrupt, Kill and Wait), and once with a planted panic; after each, the machine fixture must equal its state before the run. No workflow engine is adopted without a decision entry; the module allow file (S-2) refuses a workflow-engine module (temporal, cadence, argo) unless a decision entry is linked.
pros: Practice. Which of the three outcomes a function has is semantic, but what is undone after a failure is a fact a test can see, and it is what keeps a program safe to interrupt for its whole life.

rules.statement: Help is true and complete: every flag in the documents is registered and tested; every command's help has a one-line summary, usage, flags, two examples and what it writes; help has topics as well as commands; and every pointer in help or in a warning is in one form and resolves.

exemptions.reason: It has no flags.

reasoning.definition: The command tree is walked and every flag compared with the flag names in the README and docs fenced usage and flag tables; a documented flag not registered or a registered flag not documented fails. The matrix runs each flag once and a repo-check demands a test reference per flag name. Each command's help is parsed into its five parts (summary, usage, flags, examples, writes) and a missing or empty part fails; a read-only command says it writes nothing. help with no word lists commands and topics; help <command> prints the same bytes as <command> --help; help <command> <word> is a topic only when the command names that topic. A pointer has one fixed form (for example "more: <program> help <topic>"), and a test collects every pointer in help, warnings and doctor output and fails on one that names a command or topic not in the tree.
pros: Own bugs: help that lies, 9 of 60 sampled. Help with the same parts across every program lets a person or an agent learn one tool and read all of them, and the resolving pointer test keeps help from pointing at a topic that moved.

rules.statement: Output, help and docs say only what the code does. Verbs and options decided but not built are a list in data and absent from the command tree; a refused designed option names what this build has and the design that holds the slot, never a bare invalid; and a stub, placeholder return or not-implemented body in shipped source is reported.

reasoning.definition: The not-built list is one file per command, internal/cli/planned/<name>.yaml (verb or option, the design that holds it), so deciding a command adds a file and building it deletes that file in the change that adds its package. A name is built or planned, never both and never neither: the registry test fails on a name in both and on a name in neither. A test fails when a listed verb or option appears in the tree, so a stub cannot ship in its place. A refusal for a listed option exits with the refused code and prints the options this build has and the design reference; a matrix test per listed option asserts both. A syntax-pattern rule matches a panic with a not-implemented string and return-only bodies with a TODO, over non-test source; a tier-2 report fails on a rise against the committed count.
pros: Own bugs: 9 of 60 sampled bugs say what the code does not do. The list in data keeps the design and the program in step without a stub in shipped code, and naming the built alternatives turns a dead end into a next step. Wording truth cannot be judged by a program.

rules.statement: A mistyped command or flag prints the nearest match and the line to type, on stderr, with empty stdout and the usage exit code.

pros: Own measure; the command framework supplies suggestions and the test proves they are on. One program prints its version line on stdout after a typo.

rules.statement: A flag has one meaning everywhere: the same name has the same type and shorthand in every command, and one concept has one spelling. Flags are long, lowercase and hyphenated, with short forms only from one short shared list; a closed-set flag lists its accepted values in help and is checked once against them; and a duration or a size is a string with a unit, in flags, config keys and JSON alike, never a bare number.

reasoning.definition: A helper walks the command tree, groups flags by name and fails when type, shorthand or value kind differ, or two spellings of one concept exist (a list in rule data, such as dry-run and dryrun, json and output-json). It fails a flag name that is not lowercase and hyphenated and a short form not on the shared list (the base list holds -w and -f; a program adds to it only through rule data with a reason). A closed-set flag declares its set once; the parser checks the value against it before the command runs, and the help golden shows the set. A duration or size flag, config key or JSON field is typed as a duration or size and decoded from a string with a unit (15s, 2m, 64KiB); a bare integer is refused at parse time.
pros: Own measure; the check proves name and type consistency, same meaning is judgement. A unit on every duration and size stops the oldest config bug (is 15 seconds or minutes), and a short-form list keeps an agent's flags readable.

rules.statement: A bare command never hangs: at a terminal it offers a menu of what will work on this machine, off a terminal it prints help and exits with the usage code.

pros: Operator rule. Off a terminal a bare call did not do what was asked, so it is a usage outcome and a script can see it. One piped half ran in an earlier trial; the pty half needs a pseudo-terminal helper.

rules.statement: Work that takes more than 2 seconds shows progress at a terminal and plain lines in a log; a progress line redraws only when the work advances, never on a timer of its own; and a person never waits on a silent screen.

reasoning.definition: No spinner or bar ticks on its own clock: a redraw follows a work event (an item done, bytes read). Off a terminal the progress is a plain line at most once a minute, and under --json there is no progress on stdout. The test counts redraws against work events with a fake clock that never advances.
pros: Operator ruling 4 Nov, practice. A self-ticking redraw wakes the machine for nothing and hides a stall behind motion. Slow steps in the real program are found only if fixtures can slow them.

rules.statement: Every run reads the same way: a heading, what it reads, the work, a dry-run footer when nothing was written, one closing word; the banner shows only in the interactive menu.

reasoning.definition: The banner is the menu's alone; a command run, --version and --help never print it. Once lessons exist (cli.commands.18) the run also carries a two to four line why from the lesson with a more: pointer on a dry run, and after a write the commands a person can run to check the result without the program; that part binds with cli.commands.18.
pros: Operator rule; whether the run reads well is review (cli.commands.16). The banner on every run was a contradiction with the target programs, which show it in the menu only.

rules.statement: The main journeys of a CLI (first run, help, menu, one happy path, one refusal) run under a pty at 80 columns as goldens the gate cannot rewrite, and at 60 and 40 columns held to properties against them (tests.journeys.8).

pros: Operator rule; scoped by the journey rules of the tests part. A phone over ssh is 40 to 60 columns.

rules.statement: A new or changed command or menu shows its terminal transcript in the change, and a reviewer judges it.

pros: No tool decides that an experience is good.

rules.statement: The plan a dry run prints and the plan a read answer carries come from one function, a test holds them equal, and no write route or write command takes a dry-run parameter.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands or routes.

reasoning.definition: The dry-run sentence of a writing command is the plan field of the matching read (CLI --json and API answer). A test runs the dry run and the read on one fixture and compares the plan text byte for byte. A route that writes refuses a dry, dry_run or preview parameter, and an API contract check fails on one.
pros: Two code paths for one plan drift: the dry run says one thing and the page another. One function makes the preview a person sees in the terminal and on a page the same fact.

rules.statement: Every command that changes the machine has a lesson beside its code with fixed sections, every lesson cites at least one https source read before it went in, --explain prints the lesson before any command runs and writes nothing even with --apply, and a run shows the lesson's why and its check-it-yourself lines.

reasoning.definition: The fixed sections are: what it is, what was found here, why, what it does, what it does not do, how to undo it or that there is nothing to undo, check it yourself, read more, sources. A test fails on a missing or empty section and on a lesson with no https source. --explain is a shared root flag answered before any command runs; it writes nothing even beside --apply, and a command with no lesson says so in one line rather than printing nothing. A dry run opens on two to four lines of why from the lesson and a more: pointer; an applied run ends, before its closing word, on the commands a person can run to check the result without the program. The same lesson prints from help <topic> and is the source of any generated guide (cli.commands.20).
pros: A tool that changes somebody's machine and cannot say what it found, why it acts, how to undo it and where the claim comes from is a tool a person stops trusting. Fixed sections make the lesson generatable and testable, and the sources are the one defence against an agent inventing a tuning.

rules.statement: Every piece setup installs and every way a feature can fail quietly has a doctor line that names the fix when it is missing or wrong, and each subject the program manages has a help topic naming its sources.

reasoning.definition: Setup declares what it installs in data; a test fails when an installed piece has no doctor check, and when a doctor finding that is not ok has no fix line. Each subject (a managed file, service or setting group) has a help topic, and the topic lists the sources of its lesson.
pros: A feature that fails quietly is found by its owner months later; a doctor line per piece is the cheapest place to see it, and the fix line turns a finding into a step.

rules.statement: Every command is declared once, in its own package; one registry is assembled from those declarations at build time; and help, help --json, the README's command table, the MCP tool list, the HTTP contract and agent skill text are generated from that registry and held equal by a test.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: A declaration carries the summary, the version the command arrived in, what a second run does, and who may run it; a command not yet built is declared in a file of the planned folder instead (cli.commands.9), and the registry joins both. The join of the built packages is generated and held by gen --check (cli.commands.29). help --json describes every command, flag, positional word, exit code and --json field so a UI can be built from it, and is the committed command-tree file of cli.output.4. Generated files say they are generated and are refused when edited by hand (cli.commands.23). A test regenerates every surface and fails on any difference from the committed copy.
pros: A command described once and rendered everywhere cannot drift: the agent's skill, the MCP tool and the README are the program because they come from it. All three target programs already generate at least two surfaces from one source.

sources.says: Each command is built in its own package and the root adds them; no table of the commands sits in one place apart from that join.
The list of commands is data beside the code that runs them.
The command documents are generated from the command tree by a program of the repository's own.

rules.statement: A change that can lock the owner out refuses until the new access path is seen to carry an admin, keeps a whole-file undo, and a change to shared network or identity policy that reaches other devices is printed for the owner to apply, never applied by the program.

exemptions.reason: It changes no access of its own.

reasoning.definition: A lock-out change is one to access control, sign-in, the path a person reaches the machine by, or the identity source. Before writing, the command observes an admin session over the new path (seen recently, within a stated window); without it the command refuses and says what it did not see. It keeps the whole previous file and prints the one line that restores it. A policy that also binds other devices (a tailnet policy, a shared directory) is printed as the change to make, and the program holds no write credential for it.
pros: The one change a person cannot undo from outside is the one that removes their way in; a refusal before the write is the only guard that works after it.

rules.statement: A writing step reads the machine again after it runs and reports done only when the goal state holds, whatever its commands exited with; a config write is verified on a reloaded copy against the intended change before it replaces the original; and an action that asks another machine is reported by the outcome read back within a stated wait, failed with what was seen otherwise, never as sent or will retry.

exemptions.reason: It writes nothing of its own.

reasoning.definition: The first failed step stops the steps after it. A config write changes only the named table, keeps the rest byte for byte, reloads the result on a copy and refuses unless it equals the old config plus the stated change. An effect that is only a request (a packet, a message to a peer) has one attempt; success is its observed result. A test per writing command plants a step whose command exits 0 but leaves the state wrong.
pros: Exit 0 is a claim about a command, not about the machine, and a tool that says done when the state is wrong is worse than one that says nothing. Reading back is cheap, and it is the same check the lesson prints for a person (cli.commands.18).

rules.statement: A command writes every file aside, flushes it, renames it into place and flushes its folder, keeping the old mode and owner; it edits a person-written config only in the lines it owns and keeps comments and order; a change to a file another program ships goes in that program's override or drop-in; and a generated file is marked, refused when edited by hand, and regenerated to resolve a merge conflict.

exemptions.reason: It writes no files of its own.

reasoning.definition: All file writes go through one shared write helper (a link is written where it points, not replaced). A config edit is a parsed, comment-keeping edit of the owned keys; a test round-trips a commented fixture. A vendor file (a file another package or program installs) is never written; the change goes in the override file or drop-in folder that program reads. A generated file carries a do-not-edit header naming the command that writes it; a check regenerates it and fails on a difference, and a merge conflict in it is resolved by running the command again after the rebase.
pros: A half-written config after a power cut and a vendor file overwritten by an update are the two oldest ways a tool breaks a machine; two target programs wrote the same guard. The generated-file half stops a merge from silently un-generating a file.

rules.statement: Every record a program keeps (run, backup, notification, manifest) carries a version and the same fixed fields whoever did the work, backend detail sits under one passed-through field, and answers are built from the record, never from the tool.

exemptions.reason: It keeps no records.

reasoning.definition: Each record kind has one schema with a version field; the backend that did the work fills the fixed fields and puts anything of its own under one detail field the program never branches on. A status or history answer reads records only; a test runs it with the backend tool absent and expects the same answer.
pros: A versioned record with fixed fields is what lets a record written by one backend be read after that backend is replaced.

rules.statement: A run record keeps each changed file's copy and its digest after the run; undo refuses when a file no longer has that digest and names the runs that changed it since; a multi-file undo prints its way back rather than running it; and a batch of independent changes keeps one record and one undo per unit, takes the lock per unit and goes on past a failed unit.

exemptions.reason: It keeps no run records.

reasoning.definition: The way back may be a kept timestamped backup and the printed lines that restore it, with no undo command. A batch runs each unit as its own run in turn; one failed unit is reported and the rest still run.
pros: The digest check is the difference between an undo and a second accident, and per-unit records keep one bad item from blocking or tangling the rest.

rules.statement: Commands follow [group] verb [noun], with verbs from one shared base list of plain imperatives that a program extends only by declaring its domain verbs in its own single table; each verb has one documented meaning across the tool; ids and names are positional and every other input is a flag.

reasoning.definition: The shared base list holds the verbs users of common tools already know (for example list, show, add, remove, start, stop, run, logs, status, doctor, help, version); get, make and destroy are refused as command names. A program's domain verbs sit in one table in its own code with a meaning each; no second table exists. A test reads the base list and the program's table against the command tree and fails on a verb in neither, on a verb used with two meanings, and on a positional that is not an id or a name.
pros: A shared verb list lets an agent that learned one program drive another without reading its help; the base plus one declared table keeps the list extendable without each program inventing synonyms.

rules.statement: A command needing root is registered apart from owner-level ones, and which group a command sits in follows whether it needs root, never the name of the operating system.

reasoning.definition: Proposed with the privileged-helper design. A test would read the command tree and fail on a root command in the owner group or on a group split chosen by operating system.
pros: Privilege is the boundary that matters to a person deciding what to run; an operating-system split puts a root action beside an owner one on the next platform.

rules.statement: A restore writes into a fresh folder the program makes (owner-only, not existing before, no link, not a served or published folder) and refuses an existing path, a link and a served folder; an in-place restore needs its own flag with a dry run listing every file it replaces; and a restore stops before writing when space is low.

exemptions.reason: It restores nothing.

reasoning.definition: The fresh folder is made with mode 0700 by the program's own account (root for a system service). The space check compares the backup's size with the free space of the target and stops with the numbers. The in-place flag is separate from --apply and its dry run lists every path it would replace.
pros: The fresh-folder default is what makes a restore safe to run by reflex; a restore over live data is the one backup action that can destroy what it was meant to save.

rules.statement: Each command family is one package that declares its own row (name, order, summary, two examples, exit words, JSON kind, files written, menu place) next to its command; the root holds no list of commands and reads a generated join; no init function registers a command.

exemptions.reason: It has no commands.

reasoning.definition: A group of verbs that share a context and a plan screen is one package with a file per verb, not a package per verb. The row is a typed value in the package, exported with the function that builds the command; a package that exports one and not the other does not compile into the join. Order is the command's place in the spec's table and is unique; a command the spec does not name takes a high number and sorts by name. The menu place says which screen leads with the command and at what rank, so no list of leads exists in the root. A generator writes the join from the folders of command packages, sorted by name, and gen --check fails when it is stale. A test walks the joined registry for the cross-cutting rules (two examples, exit words, unique order) instead of a column each builder edits. A command package never sets a run hook that the root owns (the persistent pre-run and post-run, with or without the error return): a package that sets its own replaces the root's, which silently skips the shared refusals and the write claim, and with a join per package no shared line is left to catch it. The registry test walks the joined tree and fails on any command that sets one. A command decided and not built is a file of the planned folder (cli.commands.9).
pros: Own measure: in one program every new command edited the registry table, the root help block, the menu lists, four cross-cutting goldens, the README table and two generated command documents, so two builders on two commands collided on the same lines. The organisation's run log of 8 Nov 2026 shows each landing sending the waiting candidates through a rebase and a full gate run. Surveyed command line programs keep a command's code and help in the command's own package, and all but one keep the join by hand; the one that does not registers from init functions, which breaks arch.ports.12 and go.layout.2.

sources.says: Cross-cutting command rules (examples, help text) are tests that walk the joined tree, not columns each command edits.
The one surveyed program that registers commands from init functions through blank imports.

rules.statement: Settings come through one declared helper; a program declares which sources it reads (file, environment, flags) and documents them; where more than one source is on they resolve flag, then environment, then file, then default; and a program that runs from a rules file lets the environment name only paths and terminal variables from a short tested list, with a flag overriding only for its own run.

exemptions.reason: It takes parameters instead of reading settings.

reasoning.definition: Settings are declared once through the shared config helper (flag name, environment name, file key, default, doc line) together with the program's source declaration; precedence is implemented once with its own test table. A rules-file program (one whose behaviour an owner audits in a file, such as a tool that runs as root) declares the file as its only settings source: the environment may name the config file or the state folder and the terminal variables of cli.config.3, nothing else, and a flag changes only the run it is given to, never the file. A test sets every other environment variable the helper knows and asserts it has no effect. A repo-check bans any other reader: the environment ban (cli.config.3), the flag ban (cli.config.7) and a direct decode of a file into a config type.
pros: Practice. A setting that is not in the file of a rules-file program is a setting nobody can audit; a service in a container has no file and reads the environment by design. One helper with declared sources serves both and keeps the precedence table where two sources are on.

rules.statement: An unknown config key is refused when a person wrote the file; a renamed or retired key is refused at its file and line with the migrate command and is never read; a kept file of another shape is refused or started fresh and said so, never decoded into the current fields; a message from a peer across a trust boundary refuses unknown fields, and tolerant reading is only for a peer the reader trusts and is stated per decoder; an added field does not raise the schema number.

reasoning.definition: A person's config refuses unknown keys so a typo is seen. An old key is never read beside the new one, not for a window and not for a release: the loader keeps a list of retired keys with the command that rewrites them and refuses with file, line and that command. A state or record file whose version is not the current one is not decoded into the current type; the program either refuses naming the version or starts a fresh file and says so. Every wire decoder is declared strict or tolerant in code: strict (unknown type or field refused) for a peer the reader does not control (a guest, a route body, an archive), tolerant only for a peer the reader trusts and deploys. The loader decodes a person's file with the undecoded-keys check (or the disallow-unknown-fields option for JSON); forbidigo bans a direct decode into config types outside the loader.
pros: Own measure; the planted-key test exists in four repos. Two spellings read at once is the state two target programs measured as the source of silent misreads, and the migrate command in the refusal makes a window unnecessary. Tolerant reading is a courtesy to a peer you trust and a hole for one you do not.

rules.statement: The environment is read only in the config package, and in the terminal module for the terminal variables (NO_COLOR, TERM, COLUMNS, LESS, PAGER, ACCESSIBLE).

reasoning.definition: forbidigo with type analysis on the getenv, lookupenv, environ, expandenv and syscall getenv calls outside those two places, through path exclusions, on a one-file-per-entry shrink-only list. Passing the parent environment to a child is legitimate; list those files by path. ACCESSIBLE turns on the accessible mode of forms the same way --accessible does.
pros: Own measure; one reader is what lets precedence and the colour decision be tested once.

rules.statement: A secret never comes from a flag and is never printed; it does not reach a child through the environment unless the row that starts the child names why; every secret a program owns sits in one owner-only folder under collision-free names and is referenced by a key ending in _file; and a service receives it through the service manager's credential passing, never through group read.

reasoning.definition: The keys folder is mode 0700 and each file 0600, owned by the running account (root for a system service). A secret name cannot collide with an id the program makes. A config value is never the secret itself; a key that names a secret ends in _file and holds a path. A planted-secret test runs each command with a fixture secret in the environment and in a file and asserts the secret bytes appear in no stdout, stderr or log; an ast-grep rule flags flags whose name matches token, secret, password, passwd or apikey; a config-key check fails a key that holds a secret value and does not end in _file; a secret scanner runs on staged diffs at tier 1. Which process can read a secret once it is in a child's environment is review.
pros: Own bugs. A key in a group-readable file and a token readable from a dump are known leaks; the _file suffix makes a secret reference recognisable in any config.

rules.statement: Paths come from one helper filled by the platform's defaults for the program's kind, one key each, overridden only by --config or one environment variable naming a file or folder; the config folder holds only files the owner writes, while history, generated output and state live in their own folders and kept copies are pruned by age and count.

exemptions.reason: It has no state paths.

reasoning.definition: The defaults per kind and platform are rule data: a per-user tool follows XDG on Linux and Application Support on macOS; a system service uses /etc for config, /var/lib for state and /run for runtime files on Linux. A new platform adds a row, not a rule. forbidigo bans the home, config and cache folder lookups outside the shared paths helper, and an ast-grep rule flags string literals that start with ~/ or contain /.config/ or /.local/ in non-test code (the literal list is lint data, in the rule file). History copies go under the state folder (one folder per run, owner-only) and are pruned by age and count; generated files go in their own generated folder.
pros: Own measure; hand-built home paths in non-test code today: 19, 4, 1, 3 and 0 across five repos. The folder depends on who runs the program and on which system, and saying so is what makes the helper right on the next platform; keeping history and generated output out of the config folder keeps it readable after a year of runs.

rules.statement: Every config key and environment variable has a reader, a default, a doc row and a documented refused-when, and is refused at load naming key and reason; a key spelled in another case is refused naming its spelling; a value that becomes a path, a file name or an argument of a privileged command is held to a closed pattern and never starts with a dash; every boolean switch has a test for its non-default value; and a key meets one more question before it is added: who can pick a better value than the program?

exemptions.reason: It has no config of its own.

reasoning.definition: The doc row gives type, default and what refuses the value. Names reaching a path or argv match a declared pattern (for example lower camel case, no leading dash); a URL is https only with no login part. A refusal names the key, the file and line, and the reason. Doctor checks the rest against the machine.
pros: Own bugs: one fault in record, a parsed key read by nothing. A silently ignored key and a value that reaches an argv unchecked are two of the places a config reader lies to its owner.

rules.statement: Flags are defined in main or the command layer only; a library takes parameters.

pros: Practice; libraries that read flags cannot be reused or tested.

rules.statement: A config migration is a dry run first, proves on a copy that the new config means the same as the old before writing, moves across filesystems by copy, sync and rename, leaves no link at an old secret path, and prints its whole way back.

exemptions.reason: It has no config to migrate.

reasoning.definition: Means the same is checked field by field, for each person's effective permissions, and for every generated unit (rendered again from the new config and compared). The dry run opens on why it migrates. A secret moved to a new path is moved, not linked.
pros: The equivalence proof is what makes a migration safe to run on an owner's config, and the printed way back is its undo.

rules.statement: Each setting has one home file; a setting written in two config files is refused at load naming both places; no file overrides another; and everything about one configured thing lives in that thing's own table, with no other file keying a map by its name.

exemptions.reason: It has no config files.
A program with one config file cannot set a key in two.

reasoning.definition: The loader reads every config file, builds the set of keys per file, and refuses a key found in two with both files and lines. A configured thing (a machine, an app, a share) is named in one entry and its settings sit in its table.
pros: Override chains between files are the config bug that takes an afternoon to find, and refusing duplicates costs one loop at load. One table per thing keeps it deletable in one place.

rules.statement: A missing config file means the defaults, a config file that exists but cannot be read is an error, never the defaults, and a list key is an allowlist where an empty or absent list allows nothing.

exemptions.reason: It has no config file.

reasoning.definition: Cannot be read covers permission denied, a parse error and a read error. No key exists whose absence means everything; a program that wants allow-all needs an explicit value naming it.
pros: A default used because a file was unreadable, and an absent list that means everything, are two of the places a config reader lies to its owner.

rules.statement: A setting that can be implemented more than one way names the implementation with one key and takes its keys in a table named after it, an unknown value is refused naming the implementations this build has, and a key that may grow accepts either its value or a table holding it, both documented as the one shape, so growing it never needs a migration.

exemptions.reason: It has no config.

reasoning.definition: For example by = "ntfy" with an ntfy table beside it; a second backend is a new table, not a migration. Both forms of a growable key are read always.
pros: This is the config half of ports and adapters: a second backend is one new table, and value-or-table lets a key grow without breaking a file written years before.

rules.statement: A config file whose contents decide what runs as root is refused when anyone but root or the running account owns it, or when group or others can write it, and the refusal gives the fixing line.

exemptions.reason: It has no config file.

reasoning.definition: The check runs at every load, on the file and on each folder above it up to the root of the filesystem. The fixing line is the chown and chmod to paste.
pros: A config writable by a non-root user that a root process runs commands from is a privilege escalation.

rules.statement: An error for a person names the next step, an error in JSON is structured, a mistyped command prints nothing on stdout, an error shown to a person carries a run or request id they can quote, and every warning, as well as every error, names where to read more or what to type.

exemptions.reason: It prints no errors of its own.

reasoning.definition: The matrix runs a failing command twice with and without --json and asserts: stderr holds a next-step line (a regex for run or try followed by a command the registry knows); the JSON error is an object with a code and a next field; stdout is empty for a mistyped command; the run id differs between the two runs while a golden with the id masked is equal. Warnings (doctor findings included) are built by one constructor that takes the pointer as a required argument; a test reads the code for warnings built any other way and fails, and every pointer resolves (cli.commands.8). Whether the next step is useful is review; the check proves presence and form only.
pros: Own measure; one program prints its version line on stdout after a typo. A warning with no pointer leaves the person where an error would have; marginal assertion on the matrix helper.

rules.statement: A refusal is one value, a word from a closed list and a hint as a line to paste, built by a constructor that requires both, and the CLI, the API body and the audit line all print from that value unchanged.

reasoning.definition: Go: the refusal constructor takes the word and the hint as required parameters, so omission is a compile error; the word is a typed constant from one list, and a new refusal is a word added to the list with a test, never a new string. A golden per refusal asserts the hint is pasteable; forbidigo bans building the refusal struct literal outside the module. A test drives each word through the CLI, an API route and the audit writer and compares the word and hint in all three. TypeScript: the error table entries have a required word and next field in their type.
pros: Held in Go. One value for one refusal makes a new surface (MCP, HTTP, a page) print the right thing with no new code.

rules.statement: Go words reach a person only through the shared module and its refusal constructors; nothing writes to the terminal or decides how to paint except the module.

reasoning.definition: forbidigo on the print family, writes to stdout and stderr, and the raw write calls outside the shared terminal module (path exclusion), plus reads of NO_COLOR, PAGER and TERM through the environment calls outside the module and the program's config package (an AST helper checks the names that forbidigo cannot see in arguments), plus an AST test for string literals that look like sentences passed to writers.
pros: Forbidigo matches identifiers, not argument text; its licence shows as unasserted on GitHub, and golangci-lint bundles it.

rules.statement: Text the program did not write (agent output, file names, peer data) is safe to show: terminal output of such text strips control sequences, and a log line strips CR and LF from data.

exemptions.reason: It prints nothing.

pros: Practice. A sanitiser in the shared module with a test; the structured log handler covers logs; a raw print is cli.errors.3's to catch.

rules.statement: A command never throws past its executor: every outcome is a result the renderer prints, a failure the caller branches on is a typed result, and an exception or panic means a bug.

exemptions.reason: It has no executor.
A program with one client has no second path to keep equal; the go.errors rules hold it.

reasoning.definition: Binds a program with more than one client (CLI and MCP, HTTP or a worker) where every write runs through one executor. The executor is driven with a malformed input for every registered command and must answer with a result (the refused or failed ending and its fields), never an uncaught exception or panic. A panic or exception that reaches the executor is caught once, reported as a bug with the run id, and ends with the failed code.
pros: Typed results through one place are what make a CLI and an API print the same refusal; an exception crossing the executor is an outcome no client renders.

rules.statement: A refusal carries what was observed as the person named it, the closed set of valid choices (never the caller's own input), the rule or state in the person's terms, and the next command as a line to paste; it never holds a secret or blame, and the word invalid is refused in printed text.

exemptions.reason: It prints no refusals.

reasoning.definition: The refusal type has observed, valid, rule and hint fields; valid is filled from the set the command accepts, never echoed from input. A check over printed strings and goldens fails on the word invalid (in any case) in text a person reads; the closed word list may keep it as an internal code that is not printed.
pros: Observed plus valid plus the next line is the shape that lets an agent fix its own mistake without a second round trip; the ban on invalid is a one-word lint that forces the message to say what is wrong.

rules.statement: A non-empty NO_COLOR wins over every other setting, even when colour is forced, and so do non-TTY output, TERM=dumb and --no-color; output that is not to a terminal has no escape codes.

exemptions.reason: It prints nothing.
A daemon with no terminal has no colour to switch off.

reasoning.definition: The matrix runs every command (help and one real path) with NO_COLOR=1 together with the force variables set, non-TTY, TERM=dumb and --no-color, in a pty and a pipe, and fails on any 0x1b byte in stdout or stderr. The shared terminal module is the one reader of these variables (cli.config.3). One check holds this row, the TERM=dumb row and the pipe row.
pros: Own measure: all four CLIs print escape codes with both NO_COLOR and the force variable set (292, 150, 216 and 256 escapes); the module passes and no repo gates on it. This is the fault that earns the matrix helper.

rules.statement: Terminal width wins, else COLUMNS, never above 96; help fits and keeps the palette.

pros: Evidence M; the matrix is trialled and the copy printing 120 to 179 cells at COLUMNS=200 fails.

rules.statement: No terminal query unless rendering, and a bounded wait.

pros: The silent-pty trial fails everywhere today, the module included (fix A1 first); hold adoption order accordingly.

rules.statement: CI set means plain: no animation, no banner, no question.

pros: Held in the shared module; five shims in programs are removed by adoption.

rules.statement: Not a terminal means no colour, animation, banner or question.

pros: Matrix trialled; passes in all programs today.

rules.statement: stdout and stderr are decided separately: colour appears only on the stream that is a terminal.

pros: A test already held in the module (a warning is painted against stderr, not stdout); generalised in the matrix.

rules.statement: Accessible mode gives plain questions, plain bars, no banner and no escape byte in labels.

pros: Planned matrix; the module already has the switch.

rules.statement: Questions are never asked when nobody can answer; the refusal names the flag that answers it and ends with the refused code; and one shared --yes answers every yes/no question, so --apply --yes runs any command without a terminal, a destructive step excepted (cli.commands.3).

reasoning.definition: --yes is registered once by the shared module. It answers plain yes/no confirmations only; a choice among values is answered by its own flag (cli.environment.14), and a destructive step only by --confirm NAME.
pros: The refused code is 5. One shared --yes is what lets an agent run any command non-interactively without learning a flag per prompt.

rules.statement: Nothing animates while nobody watches.

pros: The test fails today (a live-update loop still ticks after focus-out; fix A4).

rules.statement: A pager is used only when stdin and stdout are terminals, and a failing pager never loses the page.

pros: Evidence S; the test is planned.

rules.statement: Plain output carries the same facts as coloured output.

reasoning.definition: Strip test: run a command forced to colour and again plain; strip ANSI sequences from the coloured output with a stripper library and compare byte for byte with the plain output.
pros: A status that says ok only by a green colour is invisible without colour.

rules.statement: Output downsamples to the stream's real colour depth.

reasoning.definition: Forced runs set the colour-capability variables to truecolor, 256-colour, plain xterm and dumb; the SGR parameters are parsed and the depth checked: 38;2 only under truecolor, 38;5 only under 256, 30 to 37 and 90 to 97 otherwise.
pros: One program's truecolor output under TERM=xterm fails (fix A8).

rules.statement: One conformance function runs the terminal rows against each program's real binary, and each program calls it from its own tests.

reasoning.definition: It runs the rows for colour off, width, CI, pipe, TERM=dumb, no question and depth. Trialled once; not in the shared test package yet.
pros: A program that does not call it can skip every terminal row.

rules.statement: Every interactive question names, in code, the flag or argument that answers it, and a test walks every form.

reasoning.definition: The shared form constructor takes the answering flag as a required argument and prints it beside the question; a test enumerates every form in the program and checks the named flag is registered on the command that asks.
pros: A form with no flag blocks an agent and a script; naming it in code is what lets cli.environment.8 refuse with the flag.

rules.statement: Every CLI that ships to users, in whatever language it is written, takes its look from one shared module by version; exactly one module of the program writes to the terminal or reads from it; and a program holds no copy of a module file.

reasoning.definition: The rule binds the programs that ship to users: a program a user installs and runs. A tool that only the repo's own gate or build runs is not bound, and none is named here. The seam is the same in every language: one render module is the CLI's only writer to stdout and stderr and its only reader of the terminal (raw mode, size, stdin as a terminal). Go: a depguard rule allows only the shared terminal module (and a program's cli/ui package that wraps it) to import x/term, go-isatty, fatih/color and termenv; the Charm libraries are not banned: the shared module owns its prebuilt components, and a product may import Charm directly and build its own, so the rule asks for one look, not for one importer of Charm; a repo-check lists which packages hold which adapters; a repo-check test compares every program file with the module's file list at the version in go.mod and fails on the same name at 0.8 similarity or more. TypeScript: an import rule allows the terminal and process-stdout modules only in the render module.
pros: Own measure; held in one repo with a plant, planned for the others. The rule describes a seam, not a library, so it holds the same in TypeScript. depguard is GPL-3.0 and runs inside golangci-lint as a tool, so there is no linking concern.

rules.statement: One token file is the source of every terminal colour, and every text colour is contrast-tested.

reasoning.definition: The contrast test is contrast_test.go, generated from the token list.
pros: The contrast test is held in the module and all four copies but covers 4 of 9 colours, so a colour can be added with no contrast entry.

rules.statement: Counts and sizes go through the shared module's helpers.

reasoning.definition: The module helpers are Count and Bytes, replacing literals such as %d/%d, %d B, %.1f GB and %d%%.
pros: Hand-typed count and size formats drift; planned scan.

rules.statement: No colour literal or escape string outside the shared module, and no size or spacing literal in Go outside the generated file.

reasoning.definition: An AST test over string literals fails on any ESC byte in the three spellings or a hex colour literal outside the module and the generated file; forbidigo bans the style-constructor calls that take a raw size or spacing (padding, margin, width) outside the module. Size and spacing literals are caught only through the banned constructors.
pros: The AST test fired on both escape spellings and passed with the escape only in the module. gocritic's rule engine did not load rules in three attempts.

rules.statement: The closing words are a closed set of eight (done, findings, failed, usage, busy, not ready, refused, declined), built with their next line by constructors only.

pros: Constructors only make the closed set a compile fact.

rules.statement: A dry run ends with one footer naming the flag, then the ending.

reasoning.definition: The AST helper flags the literal "dry run." and the old footer forms outside the module (18 sites); one footer function writes the footer with the flag name and the ending. The function does not exist yet (fix A5).
pros: Hand-typed footers drift; related to the command rule that a dry run ends by naming the apply command (cli.commands.1).

rules.statement: Tables keep their columns, a long cell wraps, a dropped column is marked, and piped output has no rules.

pros: The current table drops and cuts a column at 40 columns (fix A6).

rules.statement: Each component has plain and role-tagged goldens at three widths, and goldens cannot be rewritten in the gate.

reasoning.definition: The update flag refuses to run when the gate variable is set, and golden folders are on the protected-path list. A coverage assertion fails a component with only a plain golden.
pros: Eleven plain goldens are held; the tagged ones are planned.

rules.statement: Glyphs are typographic, no emoji.

reasoning.definition: The allow-list of typographic runes inside the emoji ranges is short and kept beside the helper.
pros: Planned range scan, not run.

rules.statement: Terminal use with a screen reader is held by a named person, recorded at release.

pros: No tool can do the use; only the record of it can be checked.

rules.statement: Every outward effect goes through a wrapper that records it; each external program and each verb it may run is named in one adapter's closed table; the check resolves a program name through constants and assignments and treats a name from any other source as a finding; and a test fails a program or verb run outside the table.

exemptions.reason: It starts no programs of its own.

reasoning.definition: Runs a program means a name passed to exec.Command or exec.CommandContext (or the equivalent in another language), resolved as the compiler does: a variable counts only when its value comes from a constant or from the one adapter's table. The table lists, per program, its absolute path or lookup rule and its allowed verbs; it may only shrink in the core. forbidigo on exec.Command and exec.CommandContext, and on os.StartProcess and syscall.ForkExec, outside the runner and a test (the import of os/exec is not banned: exec.LookPath starts nothing, returns exec.ErrDot for a hit in the current folder and reads PATHEXT on Windows, so a lookup is std's own and needs no wrapper), and the security analyser's rule for a variable command (gosec G204). x/sys counts as the standard library. A package-import test on net/http. The runner package, proposed, has a context, a timeout, no shell and an output cap (cli.process.2). Counts on macOS, of the former import ban: os/exec appears in 90 production files across seven repositories, and the ban found 24, 20, 11 and 13 in four of them; the call ban spares a lookup.
pros: An effect outside the wrapper is invisible to the record and to the journal that precedes effects (the outward-effect journal of the data part, store.consistency.4). One adapter per dependency is the whole value of ports: replacing a tool is one package, not a search. The resolving check and the closed table close the two ways a program name is smuggled past the import rule. Own measure.

rules.statement: An adapter runs an external program by absolute path with a fixed argv, checks each caller value against a closed shape before it enters the argv, caps the program's output and sets a deadline; a port that starts work takes a checked name, never an argv.

exemptions.reason: It starts no programs of its own.

reasoning.definition: No shell, no PATH lookup at run time (the path is resolved once and checked; the child keeps only the variables proc.Needed names for the system), the option terminator before any caller value, a value that starts with a dash refused. The output cap and the deadline are named constants per program; output past the cap is a failure, not a truncation that looks like success. A port's method takes a typed name checked against config, and the adapter builds the argv.
pros: Each of these is a known class of bug: PATH hijack, argv injection, a hung child, and a reply that grows without bound. Every program that runs another faces them, in any language.

rules.statement: A child program used as a plug-in gets a bare environment (PATH and LANG only), no secret, a timeout, one versioned request object on stdin, and a size-capped versioned reply that is refused in an unknown version, with its message length-capped and stripped of control characters.

exemptions.reason: It runs no plug-ins.

reasoning.definition: The request and the reply each carry a version field; the parent refuses a reply in a version it does not know and a reply over the cap. Text from the reply that reaches a person goes through the sanitiser of cli.errors.4.
pros: A plug-in is code the program did not write, running with the program's authority; a bare environment keeps secrets out of it, and a versioned, capped protocol keeps a new or hostile plug-in from being misread.

rules.statement: A screen has one golden per output at the width a person reads, 80 columns for a terminal, updated only by a person reading the diff, and the narrower widths are properties: no line wider than the screen, nothing cut off, the same rows in the same order.

reasoning.definition: tests.journeys.8 holds the rule for any screen; this line is its terminal form and the member that holds it at push. The 80 column golden is the hand-read oracle. The 60 and 40 column runs check the three properties and keep no file, so an output change is one diff to read, not three. For a web screen a parity check against the generated pages fills the golden. cli.commands.15 and cli.look.8 named goldens at three widths; a later ruling replaced the two narrow goldens with the properties, and this rule holds where they conflict.
pros: One project kept goldens at 80, 60 and 40 columns; each output change meant three diffs nobody read, and the 60 and 40 goldens went stale on the main branch unnoticed.

rules.statement: A pty journey reads until its expected final frame or the program's exit, never for a fixed time, and the accessible and plain modes have goldens of their own where they differ from the default.

reasoning.definition: A journey that reads for a fixed time misses its golden under load and passes with time to spare on a quiet host, which is two answers for one tree. It waits on the condition: the frame it expects, or the exit (tests.runners.8, tests.isolation.6). The accessible and plain modes change what is drawn, so each has its own golden where the output differs and shares the default's where it does not.
pros: One project's pty control missed its golden under load, at load 76 to 202 on one platform and only under load; the fix was to read until the frame, not longer.

rules.statement: Service-manager files (plist, unit) are well formed, and each comes from a template.

pros: Practice; a malformed plist is silently ignored by the manager.

rules.statement: A daemon runs with the least identity that can reach what it serves, from one template per service manager, with a sandbox wherever the manager offers one, and its notes state the trust line.

reasoning.definition: Least identity is chosen per platform, not assumed: a separate system account where the manager can give one (systemd DynamicUser= or User=), and on a single-user machine the owner's own account (a launchd LaunchAgent), never root, when a separate account would need more privilege to reach the owner's data than the owner already has. A daemon never runs as root to serve owner-level requests. Each supported manager has its own template; a manager added later adds a template and a golden, and the rule does not change. The notes name who may reach the daemon, what that caller gains, and which manager settings hold the line. The rendered templates are byte-compared to a golden; systemd-analyze verify and systemd-analyze security with a threshold run on Linux (the threshold makes the command exit non-zero above an exposure level, per a systemd commit; not run, no Linux box here); plutil -lint runs on macOS, and the plist names no UserName of root.
pros: Practice; a daemon with more identity than it needs turns any bug into a compromise of that identity. On a laptop a separate account is more exposure, not less, so the principle is least identity with the trust line written down.

rules.statement: The unit template restarts the daemon on failure only, with a backoff and a stated limit set in each manager's own terms; an idle exit is a clean exit and is never restarted; a one-shot job is never placed where the manager reruns it at load or login; and the health document counts restarts.

reasoning.definition: Under systemd: Restart=on-failure with RestartSec and StartLimitBurst plus StartLimitIntervalSec, never Restart=always, so a daemon that leaves after its idle time (daemon.lifecycle.5) stays down until its socket wakes it. Under launchd: KeepAlive with SuccessfulExit false and a ThrottleInterval, never a bare KeepAlive true for a job that exits on idle. A one-shot job (an update, a migration) has neither RunAtLoad nor KeepAlive and is not written to a folder the manager loads at login (under launchd, not in ~/Library/LaunchAgents); it is written in the program's state folder, started from there and removed when it ends, and doctor names one that is left. A manager added later states its own restart, backoff, limit and one-shot settings in the test table.
pros: A daemon that dies and stays dead is an outage no one sees; the limit stops a crash loop. A restart on a clean idle exit keeps a process awake that should sleep, and a one-shot job left where the manager loads it reruns at every login.

rules.statement: Each state file has one writer; a privileged process writes only files it alone owns, in a folder no less privileged account can write; and a daemon that runs as a person passes only requests that give a process of that person nothing it did not already have.

reasoning.definition: A test lists every state file with its one writer and its folder, and fails on a file with two writers or a privileged writer in a folder another account can write. A route or verb that would widen what a caller of the person's daemon can do (a passed write, a passed POST, a run of a command the caller could not run itself) is refused until a design rules it, and the route table marks each route as read or as ruled by a named design.
pros: A root writer in a folder a person owns can be tricked by a link into writing anywhere, and a person's daemon that passes more than the person has is a privilege raise for anyone who reaches it.

rules.statement: A program that replaces a running one keeps the previous binary and puts it back by itself when the new one does not answer healthy within a stated window; the revert is tested with a candidate built to fail.

exemptions.reason: It has no binary to replace.

pros: Own measure: of eight programs, one has a working guard, three do it manually and four have none.

rules.statement: A running old daemon is not mistaken for the new one when the command starts; the command compares the daemon's reported version.

pros: A command that talks to a stale daemon draws results from the wrong version.

rules.statement: A daemon that serves a page pairs page and server versions: the contract carries a version, the page reads it on the first answer and again on every reconnect, and a mismatch stops or reloads the page with a sentence, never draws wrong.

exemptions.reason: A daemon that declares it answers an API only has no page to pair; its readers are held by daemon.lifecycle.7.

reasoning.definition: An upgrade with a page open stops or reloads. One pairing helper is shared; one program writes a schema field and never reads it. A daemon declares whether it serves a page; a daemon that answers an API only declares so, serves no HTML, and its readers learn the API number at setup instead (daemon.lifecycle.7).
pros: Unproven in two programs (a pairing constant and a number helper); the test is not built. No target serves a page today and each makes a page a separate program, but the rule is right for the day one does.

rules.statement: A daemon that embeds a page is not silent when the page is missing: a build without the page serves a clear 404 and does not compile when the embedded folder is empty.

exemptions.reason: A daemon with no page has nothing to embed.

pros: A blank 200 for a missing page is invisible; held in part by the doctor command. It binds only a daemon that embeds a page; no target does today.

rules.statement: A daemon is asleep by default: where its service manager can start it on its socket it is started that way and exits after a stated idle time, a daemon that stays resident states why in a recorded decision with its measured idle cost, and no timer of its own runs while nothing needs it.

reasoning.definition: Under systemd a .socket unit starts the service; under launchd the Sockets key does. A Go daemon takes the socket either manager passes with go-socket's listen.Activated, by the name the unit gives it (a launchd Sockets key), and a process the manager did not start is told so (listen.ErrNotActivated) rather than handed nothing. The idle time is a named constant, and the exit after it is a clean exit (daemon.units.3 does not restart it). Where the manager cannot hand a socket over to this program, the daemon stays resident but sleeps in accept between requests, and the decision says so. A timer of the daemon's own (a watch, a refresh) starts with the work that needs it and stops when that work ends. Applies to every daemon whatever it serves; a new manager adds its socket setting to the test table.
pros: Idle power is measured on a home server and on a laptop battery; a process that keeps itself awake costs watts every hour of every day. It also keeps a daemon's behaviour explainable: nothing happens unless something asked.

rules.statement: Every start reconciles what an earlier run left (locks, units, ids, sockets, temporary files) and reclaims what nothing owns, and a test plants an orphan of each kind and proves it is reclaimed.

reasoning.definition: Reconciling is read, compare, then reclaim: a lock whose holder is gone is released, a unit or id no record names is removed, and each reclaim is logged with what was found. Remove and wipe commands reclaim the same kinds. A new kind of persisted state adds its orphan to the test table, so the rule stays true as state kinds grow.
pros: A daemon that cannot start cleanly after a crash is fixed by hand at the worst moment, and nothing may be left running unwatched.

rules.statement: A reader of a provider that answers an API only learns the provider's API number at setup and in doctor, and on a mismatch draws nothing of the provider's, names which side to update, and doctor reports it with the deploy line.

reasoning.definition: The number is the provider's one contract number (service.contract.2). A reader keeps the number it was built against, compares it with the provider's at setup and on every doctor run, and on a difference shows the sentence and the commands that bring the older side up, never a partial answer.
pros: A reader that draws a provider's answer of another shape draws wrong numbers with confidence; checking once at setup and in doctor costs nothing at run time.

rules.statement: A daemon serves one health document (ready flag, program version, commit, start time) of the same shape from one shared handler; liveness never calls a dependency and readiness does.

reasoning.definition: A deployed program alerts a person on failing health. Staged rollout is not required. The version fields repeat the CLI's --version (cli.exit.3).
pros: Practice and own measure; the shared handler is what makes the shape the same.

rules.statement: A daemon signals readiness by its service manager's own mechanism, only after it can serve; a daemon that can hang also sends the watchdog ping while it runs, or its notes say why not; and a test proves the signal follows the listen.

reasoning.definition: Under systemd a resident daemon is Type=notify and sends READY=1 after it listens; a socket-activated daemon (daemon.lifecycle.5) takes its listener from the manager, which holds the socket before the daemon starts, and still sends READY=1 once it can answer the request that woke it. Under launchd, which gives no readiness call, the daemon writes a version file in its run folder once it listens, and the install check reads that file and asks the socket for an answer. A daemon that leaves on idle stops sending the watchdog ping only as it exits. A manager added later names its mechanism in the test table; the rule does not change.
pros: Practice (systemd man page). Without a signal the manager or the install check treats a daemon that has not yet listened as up, and starts dependants or keeps a broken upgrade.

rules.statement: An observation of another machine or device changes nothing on it: the kinds of probe are a closed list in one function, a test refuses a planted new kind, and a probe that disturbs its target is dropped.

reasoning.definition: A probe that wakes a disk, wakes a sleeping machine, opens a session (an SSH or TCP connection to a service port) or asks a power state that spins a device up is a disturbance. The closed list is the only place a probe kind is added, and adding one is a reviewed change with its reason written beside it.
pros: A monitor that wakes what it watches is lying about idle and breaks idle by default (daemon.lifecycle.5) silently.

rules.statement: A daemon's logs have a level and a time; hold no secret, sign-in code, token, prompt, conversation, device or address; mark a field reported by an untrusted peer as reported; and go where the service manager reads them or to a capped, rotated file in the daemon's run folder that a caller can neither grow without bound nor forge. The log line is designed, not built.

reasoning.definition: A capped file has a stated size and rotation (for example 1 MiB) and refusals are rate-limited per peer, so a caller cannot fill the disk through the log. A value from a peer is written as a field, never spliced into the message, and control sequences are stripped. The list of things never logged is a list in the logging package that a canary test walks; a new kind of sensitive value is added to the list, not to each call.
pros: Practice; a secret in a log outlives the process that wrote it, and a program that runs agents handles prompts and conversations that are as private as a secret. A log a caller can grow or forge is an attack on the disk or the record.

rules.statement: Journal lines carry a priority prefix under JOURNAL_STREAM, and none without it.

pros: Evidence T; the test is planned (fix A9).

rules.statement: An audit record is an append-only file the program owns, the service manager's journal may hold a copy but is never the record, and a daemon answers a person in plain words, writing the underlying tool's own words only to its log.

reasoning.definition: The audit file lives in the program's state folder, is opened for append only, and survives a journal rotation. A tool's raw error (a service manager's message, a library's text) goes to the log with the command that produced it; the answer to the person says what happened and what to do in the program's own words.
pros: An audit record that rotates away with the journal is not an audit, and a raw tool message shown to a person is noise at best and a leak of internals at worst.

rules.statement: Only the expected callers can reach a daemon, and being local is never an identity: peer credentials or the gate's identity are checked on every request, never a header alone; each route and each state-changing command declares who may call it; every route and command passes one admission check; and a route or command with no entry fails.

exemptions.reason: It serves nothing.

reasoning.definition: Socket permissions or loopback bound who can reach the daemon; they decide nothing about who the caller is. A loopback or container-bridge address is anybody. A command run on the machine builds the same identity value a route builds (a local principal from the peer credentials of its own process) and passes the same admission check, with no bypass for being on the machine. A request no source vouches for is refused (service.authz.8).
pros: Practice; a bridge address is anybody, and a local bypass is the door every later surface walks through. Written as a Go test in the kit or the store test helper; no separate program.

rules.statement: Every local HTTP server, in any language, listens on loopback by default, answers only expected Host names, checks Origin against an allow list, needs a custom header for a request that changes a cookie, sets strict cookie attributes, and refuses to listen wider without TLS and a login.

reasoning.definition: A local server is any HTTP server that runs on a person's machine: a daemon, a CLI's serve command or a development tool, written in Go, TypeScript or a language added later. Strict cookie attributes are HttpOnly, Secure where TLS is on, SameSite=Strict and a Path. A wider listen address is refused at start unless TLS and an identity source are configured. Each language ships the same shared test; a new language adds its binding, the rule does not change.
pros: Held in one program already; a browser DNS-rebinding run was not done. A local server is attacked the same way whatever language it is written in.

rules.statement: A state-changing request to a local server is accepted only from the server's own origin, not merely the same site, and a change a browser sends from anywhere else is refused.

reasoning.definition: Same-site is not enough: every host under one private-network domain is one site on the Public Suffix List, so another device's page on that network would pass a same-site check. The check compares the full origin (scheme, host and port) with the server's own, and a request with Sec-Fetch-Site other than same-origin, or an Origin not its own, is refused. Applies to a local server in any language.
pros: Three programs have a cross-site refusal; a same-site rule leaves a measured hole on a private network where every device shares one site.

rules.statement: A peer's identity is believed only from the gate's own connection, on every request, and a spoofed identity header is ignored; the identity value is built only in the door packages, and the core reads no request header or URL.

reasoning.definition: A door is any way in: a route, a command, a watcher, a card. Each door builds the one identity value (who, what they may do, which door, the subject) and hands it to the core; the core decides from that value alone. An analyser over the core packages refuses any use of the request type, its headers or its URL.
pros: Held in the shared door package. A core that reads a header can be steered by any caller who can set one, and one identity value is what keeps every later door under the same check.

rules.statement: Every http.Server sets ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout and IdleTimeout, every http.Client has a Timeout or a context deadline, request bodies pass through a size cap, and all of them are constructed by the shared web package; outbound hosts come from configuration, never from a request.

exemptions.reason: A program that builds no HTTP server or client has none to time out.

reasoning.definition: A fetch that follows a user-supplied address resolves and checks it first (server-side request forgery). forbidigo with type analysis bans the default client, the bare get and post calls and the bare listen call outside the shared web package; the security scanner's G112 and G114 are on (both verified firing on 5 Nov). The scanner did not flag a client with no timeout or a server with only a header timeout, so the other timeouts and the body cap are asserted by a test on the shared constructors.
pros: A client with no timeout hangs a CLI too, so this applies to any program that builds an HTTP server or client. A construction analyzer was considered and not chosen: forbidigo on the type name also hits parameter and return types (verified false positive).

rules.statement: A daemon that serves a page gets its security headers in one place, tested, and an embedded page uses html/template or the framework's escaping, never text/template for markup.

exemptions.reason: A daemon with no page has no page to serve.

pros: Practice; a daemon test reads the headers and a depguard ban covers the template package. It binds only a daemon that serves a page; no target does today, and a daemon that answers an API only declares so (daemon.lifecycle.3).

rules.statement: A daemon that holds another program's key exposes only a named list of fixed requests, each with its address and request fixed in code, never a pass-through proxy.

reasoning.definition: A caller names a question from the list; it never supplies a path, host, method or header that reaches the other program. A new question is a new entry in code, reviewed. Values a caller may pass are typed and checked against the entry's own allow list.
pros: A proxy that forwards a key forwards it to anything a caller can name, which turns a read key into whatever the other program's API allows.

rules.statement: Proposed, promoted when the design that introduces a privileged helper is approved: a privileged helper runs only a closed list of verbs with fixed absolute command lines, checks each value against a list it builds itself, uses no shell and an empty environment, arms each mutating verb, and has a planted hostile-caller test.

reasoning.definition: The helper is its own binary with its own import closure. Each verb is an entry with a fixed absolute command line in a system-protected folder; a caller passes only values, and the helper checks each against a list it reads itself from the system, never one the caller sends. A mutating verb runs only when armed by the owner. Promotion: when the operator approves the privileged-helper part of the design named in evidence (its part 2), status becomes active, strength Hard, and the check is built; until then the rule binds nothing and is not reported as a gap.
pros: A privileged helper is the one place a bug becomes root. The shape is ruled, but the design it encodes is still proposed, and a rule ahead of its own design is what the ruling on where rules come from warns against.

rules.statement: A setting that decides whom a daemon believes has no default and is never detected, and a missing or unknown value opens no listener, believes nobody, and is named by doctor.

reasoning.definition: The trust mode (which identity source a listener believes) is written by the owner. The daemon never infers it from the platform, the network or a running process. Start with the value missing or unknown logs the reason, opens no listener, and doctor prints the key and the allowed values.
pros: A misconfigured daemon must refuse rather than believe everybody, and a detected mode changes when the machine changes, without anyone deciding.
