rules.statement: A route the machine cannot serve is absent from the route index and answers 404 with one fixed reason to every caller, never 403; a route declares its methods and any other method answers 405 with Allow; and a GET writes no state beyond one declared cache.

reasoning.definition: The route index and the 404s come from one table, so a capability the machine lacks is reported the same way to a caller who may and one who may not use it. Each refused method has a negative test. A GET may fill the one cache it declares; anything else it writes (a note, a counter, a last-seen time) is a defect, and only an operation that changes things records what a look observed. Errors follow service.errors.4: a non-2xx status with the JSON error body.
pros: These are the places a reader has to guess, and a reader that guesses breaks. 404, not 403, keeps a capability list from leaking what a caller may not see; a GET that writes makes a look change what it looked at.

rules.statement: A daemon bounds its work: a request body cap, a cap on concurrent requests and bounded queues.

pros: Practice; unbounded work turns a burst into an outage. Part of the supervision row, whose restart half is daemon.units.3.

rules.statement: A panic in a goroutine ends the process, so every goroutine recovers at its edge or the supervisor restarts it, and the restart has a stated limit.

pros: Practice. Goroutine ownership itself is go.concurrency.2.

rules.statement: Failed work parks with a reason and a redrive path (a dead letter), and a redrive filters for what can still resolve.

pros: Practice; parked work with no reason or no way back is lost work.

rules.statement: A retried path is safe twice: one helper calls any daemon route or job handler twice and compares state; a repeated idempotency key replays the stored outcome and the same key with a different request conflicts.

reasoning.definition: The list of writing routes is taken from the contract, not from the author. The same double-call helper serves the command rule (cli.commands.6) and is required for daemon routes by an analyser.
pros: Practice only; it would become a rule with a duplicate-effect fault in one of our daemons. The command-side twin is cli.commands.2.

rules.statement: Retry discipline: one constructor carries the policy; it retries only idempotent calls, at one layer, with backoff, jitter and a budget, and hand-rolled retry loops are banned.

exemptions.reason: A program that retries nothing has no policy to carry.

reasoning.definition: A syntax rule flags a sleep or timer inside a loop around a call with an error check outside the retry constructor; retry libraries are banned by depguard; a behaviour budget test checks the retry ratio, because recursion or a ticker passes the form.
pros: Practice only; only the retry-library ban is cheap. It would become a rule with a retry fault in the run log.

rules.statement: A daemon reads the machine only on a request or during a run it already pays for; a watcher waits on its source's own event stream and never polls; one short cache shares a round of reads between concurrent readers; and a timer, poll or resident sampler for a value nobody is reading needs a measured idle cost and a recorded reason.

reasoning.definition: The cache lives for a stated short time (for example 15 seconds) and serves readers that arrive while a read is in flight or fresh; it is never refreshed on a timer. A value only known while watched is left out after a restart, not carried forward. An exception names its measured cost (daemon.resilience.7) and its reason in a recorded decision.
pros: A poll costs power every hour whether anyone looks or not, and it makes behaviour depend on a clock no one set. Reading on request keeps idle cost at zero and every read explainable.

rules.statement: A recurring run or a daemon read states a processor and memory budget, measured on the real machine before it ships and again when it grows.

reasoning.definition: The budget is a number in the code or the decision beside it, with the method of the measure (for example the tree's CPU time through proc.Usage, run interleaved with and without the work, other work paused) and the date and machine it was taken on. A change that adds work to the run, a new probe or a shorter interval is measured again before it merges.
pros: A measured budget turns a preference for quiet into a check; an unmeasured run grows by small additions until the machine never sleeps.

rules.statement: A client carrying a credential follows no redirect and reports one as an error naming the callee; a request to an owner-configured address puts its token in a header, never the address, signs the body with a timestamp, resolves the name once and dials the address it checked, needs https outside loopback and private networks, and sends nothing a read permission would not show.

exemptions.reason: A program that builds no HTTP client calls nothing out.

reasoning.definition: The shared client sets a redirect policy that returns an error when the request carries a credential. A webhook or similar call uses an Authorization header, an HMAC over the timestamp and the body, a stated timeout (for example 10 seconds), and a dialer that connects to the resolved address it validated, so a DNS answer cannot change between the check and the dial. Plain http is allowed only to loopback, private or private-network addresses. The body is built from what the read permission for that subject would return, never from internal state.
pros: Each closes a real leak: a key sent on to a redirect target, a token in an address that lands in a log, a DNS rebind between check and dial, and a payload that tells a channel more than its reader may know.

rules.statement: A record or answer about an outbound channel never holds its address or token, its failure text is the program's own words, length-capped and cleaned, and a call to an outside service whose allowance is shared has a daily budget in code and uses the cheapest request that answers.

reasoning.definition: A channel is shown by name and kind only. A failure from the far side is reduced to a short sentence of the program's own with control characters stripped, and the raw text goes to the log without the address or token. A shared allowance is one the caller does not own alone (an anonymous rate limit, a public registry's quota); the budget is a constant per service and day, counted in the program's state, and a call past it is skipped with a sentence. The cheapest request is the one that reads the least (a HEAD, a digest, a conditional request).
pros: A channel address often is its credential, so any record that holds it leaks it. A shared public allowance spent carelessly is taken from everyone who shares it.

rules.statement: A daemon's outward events are one closed list with a versioned payload, pushed through channels behind an interface, and documented per event in an example file that the gate holds equal to what the daemon sends.

exemptions.reason: A daemon that sends no notification has no event list.

reasoning.definition: Each event names its subject, its data and the version of its payload. The channel interface has one adapter per kind (a push service, a webhook, a kind added later); the event list does not change when a channel is added. The example file lists every event with a sample payload, and a test renders every event through the real encoder and compares it with the file in both directions, so an event sent but not documented, or documented but never sent, fails.
pros: A notification channel is a contract nobody tests unless the list is closed and held to its document; a silent drift is found by a person who missed an alert.

rules.statement: A notification is sent only on a change; when no earlier state is readable the first run sets a silent baseline; sends are limited per subject and event; quiet hours hold back all but a bad event; and notifying rides an existing run, never a new timer.

exemptions.reason: A daemon that sends no notification has nothing to rate.

reasoning.definition: A fresh install or a lost state file sends nothing on its first pass and records what it saw. The rate limit is a stated count per subject, event and day (for example one). Quiet hours are the owner's setting; an event marked bad passes through them. The check that may notify runs inside a run the daemon already makes (a request, a scheduled job that exists for its own reason), so notifying adds no wake-up (daemon.lifecycle.5).
pros: Noise is what gets a channel muted in its second month, and a timer added only to notify costs idle power every hour for an alert that seldom comes.

rules.statement: A deployed stack the program writes names its image by tag and its update check compares the running digest with the registry; every port it opens binds loopback and is published only through the private network's serve, never publicly; and a change to shared network or identity policy that reaches other devices is printed for the owner to apply, never applied by the program.

exemptions.reason: A program that writes no deployed stack has no image, port or shared policy to place.

reasoning.definition: The tag is the image's moving tag; the update check reads the registry's digest for it (within the daily budget of daemon.outbound.2) and reports what would change. Exact pins stay the rule for code dependencies (supply.install.4); a stack's image is not a code dependency. A port bound to 0.0.0.0 or a public address, or published through a public relay, is refused when the stack is written. Shared policy is anything another device or person reads: the private network's access list, its DNS, an identity provider's groups. The program prints the exact lines and where they go.
pros: A home server that pins images never updates, which is worse than a tag plus a digest check that says what changed. Loopback plus the private network's serve makes a written stack safe by construction, and printing shared policy keeps a program from reaching past its own machine.

rules.statement: Data a program manages that cannot be fetched again has a scheduled backup through a tool behind an interface (copy, list, restore, check), a record of the last good copy, and a check that restores a sample and compares it.

exemptions.reason: Data that can be fetched again needs no backup.

reasoning.definition: The program lists which of its data can be fetched again (an image, a package, a cache) and which cannot; the second list is backed up. The interface has one adapter per backup tool, and a tool added later is one adapter. The record names the copy, its time and its check result, and status reports its age. The check restores a sample into a fresh folder (cli.commands.28) and compares it byte for byte; a failed check is a bad event. The schedule rides a run the manager already makes where it can (daemon.lifecycle.5).
pros: A backup nobody has restored is a hope, not a backup; the record of the last good copy is what tells a person how much they would lose today.

rules.statement: A service that owns job runs records each run in one shared job-run schema, through one shared recorder, and exposes them through one shared operations contract.

exemptions.reason: a service that owns no job runs has nothing to record

reasoning.definition: The shared operations contract serves the runs at /ops/job-runs, and every run validates against the shared job-runs schema.
pros: Each service inventing its own run log leaves no single answer to what ran last night and what failed.

rules.statement: Every service entry point is built by one shared bootstrap, and the plumbing libraries it wraps are imported only inside it.

reasoning.definition: The bootstrap runs a fixed sequence for every entry: contract validation, authentication context, logging with a correlation id, secrets, and the error envelope, in that order. A service writes only its own business code. The shared bootstrap is the one place a plumbing library (request middleware, logger, validator) is imported; a direct import anywhere else fails. The same shape holds in Go: each program is assembled by one shared run helper and its plumbing packages are imported only there.
pros: Many entries each wiring their own plumbing gave as many pipelines as services, each missing a different step. One owner means a step is fixed once for all.

rules.statement: No service keeps a local copy of a shared plumbing step or handler factory, and the count of copies only falls.

reasoning.definition: A step copied into a second repository moves to the shared module, and the number of copies is counted and may not rise. This covers handler factories and each plumbing step written again by hand (validation, auth context, logging, error mapping).
pros: Copies drift. The reference estate counted dozens of hand-copied plumbing steps beside a shared package that was meant to replace them.

rules.statement: No service writes its own data-layer plumbing: error tables, certificate bundles, integer parsers, outboxes or key builders.

reasoning.definition: Store opening, error mapping, number parsing and key building each have one owner in the shared data toolkit. A service that needs one imports it.
pros: Each service writing its own database error table or integer parser repeats the same bugs in a different place.

rules.statement: Every route unit has the same closed set of files: handler, contract and schema.

reasoning.definition: A route folder holds exactly the handler, its contract declaration and its schema, so a new route has a fixed shape and a generator can find all three. In Go, programs sit under one commands folder with the rest under an internal folder, so a new command has a fixed home.
pros: A route missing its contract or schema is invisible to the generated API description and the access catalogue.

rules.statement: A route contract may use only a closed set of keys (path, query, body, headers); any other key fails.

reasoning.definition: The closed set is checked by the contract builder and by a lint, so a misnamed key (for example params) cannot silently drop validation. In Go, command and config declarations refuse unknown keys and the command tree is compared with a stored file.
pros: An unknown key in a contract is ignored by the validator, so the input it was meant to constrain goes unchecked.

rules.statement: Request steps run in a pinned order, so a request without authentication never reaches the handler.

reasoning.definition: The bootstrap fixes the order of steps (origin check, authentication, authorisation, validation, handler, error mapping) and no step can be reordered or skipped by a service. In Go, a daemon checks the caller on every request before any handler, and its steps are bounded.
pros: An authentication step placed after validation or business code lets an unauthenticated request touch the handler.

rules.statement: The exposure mode of the entry origin check is an explicit code argument from the deployment tier, never ambient configuration.

reasoning.definition: A public entry passes enforce; an internal entry passes the disabled mode explicitly. No environment variable selects the mode. In Go, a daemon states its reach (socket, loopback, tailnet) as a code argument, and the peer check is never a header alone.
pros: A mode read from the environment can be switched off by a configuration slip, opening a public entry without anyone changing code.

rules.statement: The API contract is regenerated from code and diffed in the gate against the committed copy and against the contract at the merge base with the main branch, so editing or deleting the committed file does not pass a break.

reasoning.definition: The contract document is never hand-edited: the gate regenerates it from the route schemas and fails on any difference from the committed file; the file is written with LF line ends and compared byte for byte, so a checkout that changes line ends is a difference too. The same gate regenerates the contract at the merge base and applies the compatibility check of service.contract.2 between the two, so a change that edits the code and the committed file together is still compared with what main had. A missing committed file fails. In Go, the command tree and public surface are generated to a file and compared the same way.
pros: A contract written by hand drifts from the code it describes, and a generated client built from it then lies. A gate that the same change can edit is not a gate; the merge base is the copy the change cannot touch.

rules.statement: A program declares whether its readers are owned or independent, and its contract changes by that mode. With owned readers a break is allowed only when it raises the one contract number in the same change and every known reader changes with it, nothing is kept for an old reader, and a missing field is an error, never defaulted. With independent readers no change breaks the last released contract, a removal or change of meaning is deprecated for one minor release before removal, and below 1.0 such a change is at least a minor release with an entry that says what to rename.

reasoning.definition: The mode is one declared value per program, with no default: a program with no declaration fails the gate. Owned readers are readers the same owner deploys in step (its own CLI, page or sibling program); independent readers are any the owner cannot change (a published library, a public API). With owned readers the contract carries one integer raised in the change that removes a path or field, retypes a field or changes a permission; an addition does not raise it; the gate fails when the shape loses or changes anything and the number did not move. There is no deprecation window, no field marked going and no old-and-new fallback. With independent readers the gate compares the contract with the last release and fails on a change that breaks a caller (a removed field, a new required parameter, a changed type) unless the item was marked deprecated in a release at least one minor earlier. In Go, a removed flag or field or a changed exit code fails and an undeclared API break refuses the release.
pros: A silent break reaches callers that were never told. Owners of every reader found that a compatibility layer is where their bugs lived; a publisher to readers it will never see must give them notice. One rule with a declared mode stays true for both and keeps the check mechanical.

rules.statement: The contract is linted for path casing, operation identifiers, security on every operation, declared error responses and paging.

reasoning.definition: The shared lint ruleset also holds two house rules: each operation identifier is camelCase so generated client names stay stable, and every 4xx and 5xx response declares a body schema. Operation names in the contract follow one table. The ruleset applies to a daemon that publishes an HTTP description; a command-line program contract is its command tree.
pros: Names and error shapes that vary across operations make generated clients unstable and error handling per call.

rules.statement: The contract lint set extends the recommended rules, every recommended rule that defaults below error is promoted to error, and a test regenerates that list so a tool upgrade that adds a warning turns the suite red.

pros: A rule left at warn is read by nobody; a new warning arriving with an upgrade must not slip in unseen.

rules.statement: A request is validated once at the boundary against the route contract, and the handler receives only typed, validated input.

reasoning.definition: One validator checks every request, and the response, against the route contract. In Go, input is parsed once at the edge, unknown keys are refused, outside paths are confined and exit codes are tested; daemon JSON output is held by a golden and a schema test.
pros: Validation repeated or skipped inside handlers leaves paths that accept what the contract says they must not.

rules.statement: No operation returns a status code its contract does not declare.

pros: A caller written from the contract cannot handle an outcome it was never told about.

rules.statement: Every mutating request carries a version precondition (the revision it was based on) and an idempotency key.

reasoning.definition: A write based on stale state is refused as a conflict. The key lets a retry be told from a new request. In Go, a write command is safe to run twice, but there is no stale-write precondition on shared state yet.
pros: Without a precondition a late retry overwrites newer state; without a key a retry doubles the effect.

rules.statement: A repeated idempotency key replays the stored outcome; the same key with a different request conflicts (409). One shared helper proves it by calling every writing operation and every event consumer twice.

reasoning.definition: The helper walks the operationId of every operation with a write method, taking the route list from the contract and the consumer list from the subscription definitions, never from the author. It runs each operation and consumer twice against the real store with the same input and asserts the state equals one run, counting calls to test doubles at unmanaged edges (mail, a marketplace, a publish). The same key with a changed body must return the conflict. The cost decides the tier: tier 2 if the container fixture is fast enough, otherwise tier 4; it has not been timed.
pros: The middleware that implements idempotency can be satisfied by a package nobody applied. In the reference estate both toolkits had the middleware and one service did not use it. Exactly-once delivery does not exist, only at-least-once with idempotent handling.

rules.statement: No GET request changes state.

reasoning.definition: The shared twice-helper also calls every GET and checks the state is unchanged; a GET handler that appends a log line, writes a row or sends a call fails.
pros: Caches, prefetchers and retries call GET freely; a GET with effects turns each of them into a write.

rules.statement: A program declares one casing for its JSON fields, query parameters and machine values, with no implied default, and a lint on the generated contract holds every name to it; parameters are typed and defaulted in the contract, GET carries no body, an absent field is omitted, times are RFC 3339 and durations are the strings a person types.

reasoning.definition: The casing is one declared value per program (for example lowerCamelCase or lower_snake_case), read by the lint; a program with no declaration fails, and the rulebook names no default. Machine values are enum members, error codes (service.errors.2), status values (store.schemas.3), event fields (service.events.4) and permission parts (service.authz.1). A field the platform has no such thing as is omitted; null is used only for a value that could not be read, with its reason. A casing added later is one more value the lint accepts; the rule does not change.
pros: What a reader needs is consistency within one program's contract; an estate-wide casing would break working contracts for no reader's benefit, and an implied default lets a program skip the decision.

rules.statement: There is one contract document per exposure tier, each with its own access mode.

reasoning.definition: The internal document sets one internal access mode on every operation and the public document sets none, so a route cannot sit in the wrong tier by accident. In Go there is one command tree file per program and each daemon reach is stated.
pros: One document for both tiers makes the access mode a per-route guess.

rules.statement: Every operation has a one-sentence summary.

pros: The summary is what generated documentation and client method comments show; none means the operation is described by its path alone.

rules.statement: Public names (routes, operation identifiers, property keys) avoid the words the product has retired.

reasoning.definition: The check reads the retired-word list and runs over the contract paths, operation identifiers and property keys. In Go, flag, command and JSON field names are held to the same list.
pros: A retired word in a public name outlives every rename in docs and code, because callers cannot change it.

rules.statement: A consumer imports the producer type of an API or event, or translates it at its own edge; it never copies another service names or enums.

reasoning.definition: A copied enum drifts silently when the producer adds a value. In Go, one domain reaches another only through an interface the caller declares, so names are translated at that edge.
pros: A copy of another service names looks like a type but is a second source of truth.

rules.statement: A consumer of another of your programs pins the provider's published examples at a named commit, runs its real parsers over every one, checks its pin against the provider's main branch before a release, and an empty example set on a live consumer fails.

reasoning.definition: The provider publishes one example answer per path or event, generated from its own tests. The consumer copies them at a commit it names, and its tests run the same parser the program runs on each example, so a field the consumer reads that is renamed, removed or retyped fails in the consumer's own build. Before a release the consumer compares its pin with the provider's main and fails when they differ without a new pin. The provider can then retire what no one reads, and a change in what someone does read, which a plain diff reports as harmless, is caught. A field list alone is weaker than parsing the examples and does not satisfy the rule.
pros: A generated client depends on the whole response schema, so the provider cannot tell which fields anyone reads and with no window before cutover can retire nothing. Consumer-driven contracts let the provider learn what its consumers use; the article limits the idea to one enterprise or a closed community, which is the case here. Such a test runs on the other party rhythm of change and should raise a task more often than it breaks a build.

rules.statement: Delete, cancel, close, release and ensure-style commands return success when the goal state already holds, and the operation description says so; a stale revision stays a conflict and a thing that never existed stays not found.

reasoning.definition: The line drawn: define away operation semantics, never input errors. The form is callee-only, stated on the operation and not decided at the caller, so it cannot become a swallow in the caller. A measure goes beside it: a count of handlers that catch a duplicate or a not-found and continue; that count signals swallowing dressed as ensure.
pros: Without the rule each handler decides whether already-done is an error, and agents decide differently. Argued from the technique of defining errors out of existence, which works where no caller needs the information and fails on untrusted input; no case from the reference estate.

rules.statement: Where a command effects in another service complete after the response, the operation description says so and says how a caller learns it is done: an event, a status resource, or never needed.

pros: A caller reads a 200 as done; a command that writes the database first and the event second is read-after-write for its own service only, so another service may still act on stale state. Argued from the treatment of requests within an event-driven flow.

sources.where: ch. 13 (handling requests within an event-driven workflow)

rules.statement: A provider names no consumer in its shipped code, examples or config and never reads a consumer's code or tests, and a repository test holds the list of reader names out.

reasoning.definition: A consumer is named only as a reader in the provider's docs. The provider keeps a list of the names of its known readers (programs, pages, tools) in its test data, and a whole-word test over shipped code, examples and config refuses any of them. A reader added later is one more name in the list.
pros: A provider that names its consumer has made the consumer part of its contract, and every reader after the first inherits a shape made for someone else. Rules already stop a consumer naming its provider loosely; nothing stopped the reverse.

rules.statement: An answer and a config carry meaning only (a name, number, sentence, state or permission), never layout or styling, no field is named for where a reader draws it, and a whole-word test over every field name refuses place words.

reasoning.definition: Presentation is an icon, a colour, a tile, a card order or a heading. The place-word list starts with short, tile, card, heading, tab and bar, and it also refuses the word kinds that name drawn text by suffix (figure_text, phrase, text) in the program's declared casing. The list lives in one file and grows by entry; a field named after a place on a page is renamed before merge.
pros: A field named tile is a contract with one page's layout, and the page will change; meaning-only answers are what let a second reader (a CLI, an agent) use the same answer.

rules.statement: A numeric field names its unit in its key; where a reader would format it the answer also carries the formatted text from the one formatter; and a sentence in an answer travels with the numbers it was built from, with a test that fails when the two disagree.

reasoning.definition: The unit is a suffix in the program's declared casing (for example memory_mb, cpu_pct, uptime_s, power_watts), and a bare numeric key with no unit fails unless it is a count or an id. The formatted text sits beside the raw number (memory_mb and memory). The server computes order, totals, peaks and their times, sentences and downsampling; a number a reader still has to work out is a defect in the answer (web.structure.4 holds the page side).
pros: A unit in the field name is the cheapest way never to ship a number in the wrong unit, and a sentence tested against its inputs stays honest after a formula changes.

rules.statement: Only one funnel module imports the event bus client; every service publishes through it.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every outward effect goes through one wrapper that records it.
pros: A bus client imported in many places gives many publish paths, each with its own failure handling and none that can be replayed.

rules.statement: There is exactly one outbox implementation, in the shared toolkit.

reasoning.definition: In Go, one shared implementation of write-ahead intent and atomic state replace, with no copies.
pros: Each service writing its own outbox repeats the transaction, retry and replay logic and gets different gaps.

rules.statement: The outbox is written only by the toolkit call that takes the open transaction, so the event and the change commit or roll back together.

pros: An event written after the commit can be lost when the process dies between the two writes; an event written before it can announce a change that rolled back.

rules.statement: The relay publishes an outbox row idempotently and supports replay, and in production it always creates the sweep that picks up rows the live path missed.

pros: A relay that publishes twice on a retry, or cannot be told to publish again, turns every outage into manual work.

rules.statement: A failed outbox row is never deleted.

pros: A deleted failed row is an event that happened and can never be published or investigated.

rules.statement: The outbox row is the event as the public contract defines it, not a copy of the internal row, and the toolkit call that writes it validates the event against its registered schema inside the transaction, so a bad event rolls the change back.

reasoning.definition: The relay check at publish time stays as a second line. For a store whose stream forwards item images, the outbox is an explicit item written in the same transaction and shaped as the contract, and the stream forwards only those items; a plain stream of item images publishes the internal shape.
pros: Serialising after the write leaves a pile of unpublishable events that people must salvage and can reorder what was published; serialising before the write fails the business operation instead. That is the trade, and why it needs a decision and not a default. Exposing the internal model is an anti-pattern: consumers should see only public contracts.

sources.where: ch. 4 (liberating data using outbox tables; isolating internal data models; ensuring schema compatibility)

rules.statement: The event bus name is derived from the stage, never declared by hand.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every path and identifier of persistent state is made by one function from the program name.
pros: A hand-declared bus name drifts between stages and lets a stage publish onto another stage bus.

rules.statement: The derived bus exists before a service publishes to it.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a daemon signals readiness before it serves and a missing dependency is not silent.
pros: Publishing to a bus that has not been created fails silently or at first use in production.

rules.statement: Per-entry failures of a batch publish are read and retried.

reasoning.definition: A batch call can succeed as a whole and still report failed entries. In Go, every error is handled or returned and a multi-step change says rollback, resume or none.
pros: A batch publish that returns success while some entries failed loses those events with no error.

rules.statement: Every event payload is defined once, by the service that emits it, in a shared package with its schema committed beside it; consumers import the type or map it into their own words at their edge.

reasoning.definition: The package holds the schema for every event and the committed schema file is generated from it. A service defines the name and fields of its own events only; a consumer never declares a second copy. In Go, journal and message shapes are versioned in the shared module and its surface is listed, and a shape that crosses a boundary has one source.
pros: Two definitions of one event drift, and the break shows up in a consumer in production.

rules.statement: Event names (the detail-type of the event) follow one pattern: domain, entity, action and version, lowercase and dot-separated.

pros: A name that varies in shape cannot be matched by a rule or a subscription filter and hides the version.

rules.statement: A service publishes only the event families it owns.

reasoning.definition: In Go, each piece of shared state has one writer and one owner.
pros: Two publishers of one family make the schema owner ambiguous and break the consumers who trust it.

rules.statement: Every event payload extends a base envelope with schema version, event id and actor, and its fields use the casing the program declares (service.contract.10).

reasoning.definition: The rulebook names no default casing; the key-casing lint reads the program's declaration and a program with none fails. In Go, versioned files and JSON carry a version inside and journal lines are one write.
pros: Without a common envelope a consumer cannot deduplicate by id, route by version or attribute the actor.

rules.statement: An event is validated against its schema before it is published.

reasoning.definition: In Go, an effect is not run until its record is written and input is parsed at the edge.
pros: An invalid event on the bus breaks every consumer; a failure at the source is cheaper.

rules.statement: A new event family states its prospective consumers and which of them needs each field before its schema is fixed, and carries one fact: no type field that selects between meanings, and no event whose only job is to tell another team to do something.

reasoning.definition: The event carries the full result of that action, not a copy of the whole entity, so consumers need not call back. The residual risk is a discriminator inside the payload and an event used as a command.
pros: One engagement event grew a nullable field per type until no consumer could tell what it meant. The two cautions reconcile as: avoid events as semaphores or signals, and also avoid thin signals that force a call back.

sources.where: ch. 3 (designing events: single definition, narrowest types, single purpose, size, prospective consumers, semaphores)

rules.statement: Each event family catalogue entry names its owner, whether it carries personal or financial data, whether it is public or internal to its domain, and its status (active or deprecated, with a sunset); a subscription to an internal family by another domain fails.

reasoning.definition: A report of families with no subscriber (orphans) is a measure beside it. The catalogue schema requires the fields and a scan of subscriptions in the infrastructure checks them against the visibility field.
pros: Open internal streams let consumers couple to a producer internal model. Argued from the tagging of streams with owner, data class and deprecation, and restricted access to personal-data streams.

sources.where: ch. 14 (event stream metadata tagging; discovering orphaned streams and microservices)

rules.statement: Consumers deduplicate atomically and tolerate redelivery.

reasoning.definition: The processing key is written in the same transaction as the mutation. In Go, a command is safe to run twice and a torn last line is ended before append.
pros: Delivery is at least once: a consumer that cannot take the same message twice does its work twice.

rules.statement: The lifetime of a processing key (the record that stops a consumer doing the work twice) is at least the longest time a message can return: dead-letter retention, a redrive, a replay from an archive.

reasoning.definition: The key lifetime is a named constant and a test asserts it is at least the longest configured redelivery path. The key table is the consumer processing-key table. Where the store expires keys, expiry must not be the authority on whether a key still counts, because the store deletes an item only some time after its stamp (the book says up to about two days; verify against current documentation).
pros: If the key expires first, the second delivery is a first delivery again. Perfect deduplication needs an unbounded lookup, so in practice it is a bounded window kept with expiry, sized to the application sensitivity to duplicates.

rules.statement: Every subscription has a dead-letter path with redrive.

reasoning.definition: In Go, queues are bounded, but there is no park-and-redrive of failed work yet.
pros: A message that fails for good with nowhere to go either blocks the queue or is lost.

rules.statement: Work that fails for good goes to a dead-letter queue with a reason, and a redrive filters by what can still resolve (the target still exists, the state has not moved on) and does not blindly replay.

pros: A dead-letter queue is a snapshot with no expiry: a message that failed for good days ago acts on state that has since changed, and a blind redrive replays that stale intent. Silent retry forever is the default an agent writes.

rules.statement: Non-request entry points release their resources (connection pools, handles) in finally.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every goroutine has an owner that stops it and signals stop cleanly, and typed errors exist only where a caller branches.
pros: An entry that leaks a pool on the failure path exhausts connections when the runtime reuses the process.

rules.statement: A non-request entry point acknowledges a permanent refusal and throws a transient failure to the dead-letter path.

pros: Retrying a message that can never succeed wastes the queue; acknowledging one that would have succeeded loses it.

rules.statement: A queue-triggered consumer reports failure per item, so one bad message does not return the whole batch, and its batch size times its worst item time stays inside the function timeout.

reasoning.definition: The worst-case item time is a stated figure and a guess until measured. Where the platform offers to halve the batch on failure, that does not replace the per-item report.
pros: A throw from a handler holding a batch can fail every item, and the others are redelivered: harmless with deduplication but wasteful, and it hides which message is bad. A batch the function cannot finish in time fails as a whole and will fail again unless the time or the batch size changes.

sources.where: ch. 9 (batch event-processing parameters; commit offsets only after processing has completed)

rules.statement: A consumer parses an event with a reader that ignores unknown fields; a file written by a person (a config, a catalogue) refuses unknown keys.

reasoning.definition: The test is who wrote it: a typo at a keyboard must be seen, and a newer peer must not break an older one. A strict object type in a schema library rejects an extra field, which is a quiet way for an additive producer change to break an old consumer.
pros: Strictness at a person keyboard catches typos; strictness at a peer breaks independent release.

rules.statement: The catalogue entry of each event family states a policy for late and out-of-order events as a business decision, and each consumer states what a replay does to its side effects (an email resent, a marketplace call repeated).

pros: A strategy for late events is a business choice (drop, wait, or accept for a grace period): some events must be handled wherever they land and others may be discarded. A replay is something every consumer must expect, because events can be reread from a past point.

sources.where: ch. 6 (out-of-order and late-arriving events; handling late events)

rules.statement: A breaking payload change gets a new version of the event name (the detail-type), and schemas are diffed against the last release.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a versioned file says what it does with older and newer versions, and a breaking change fails the release.
pros: Consumers deployed against the old shape break silently when a field they read is removed or changes meaning.

rules.statement: Event compatibility follows the program's declared reader mode (service.contract.2). With independent readers each event family states its compatibility mode, full by default, a loosening is a recorded exit, and consumer tests are fed fixtures from every released version of the family schema. With owned readers a breaking event change raises the family's version and moves every known consumer in the same change.

reasoning.definition: Independent readers: the schema-diff step reads a compatibility field from the catalogue and tests the matching directions (old consumers read new events and new consumers read old events); a consumer test iterates the committed schema history. The backward direction matters for replay, for a redriven message in a dead-letter queue, and for a consumer deployed before its producer. Plain JSON has no built-in rules for full compatibility, so the check has to live in the diff tool. Owned readers: the gate fails a breaking change whose version did not rise or whose known consumers were not changed in the same change, and no fixture of a retired version is kept.
pros: Loosening later is easy and tightening is hard, so a publisher to readers it cannot change starts at full. An owner of every reader moves them together, and keeping old shapes for readers that no longer exist is where bugs live.

sources.where: ch. 15 (testing schema evolution and compatibility; creating mock events using schemas)

rules.statement: With independent readers a breaking change creates a new family, the old one is marked deprecated in the catalogue with a sunset date, the producer writes both during the migration, and the gate fails an old family past its date. With owned readers dual writing and sunset windows are an exception that needs a recorded reason, and a retired path or name is removed in the change that replaces it, with a test asserting it is gone.

reasoning.definition: Independent readers: a catalogue field status and sunset exist; a subscription to a deprecated family needs a recorded exit; the gate fails a deprecated family past its sunset. The sunset length is a guess and not a measurement. Owned readers: there is no old-and-new fallback, no field marked going and no grow-only promise; the replacing change deletes the old name, and a test asserts the old path, field or family no longer exists.
pros: Without a date the migration never finishes and near-duplicate families run on, and new services subscribe to the old one. Where the owner deploys every reader, a second stream is a compatibility layer with no reader to serve.

sources.where: ch. 16 (breaking schema changes; eventual migration via two event streams)

rules.statement: Every route declares who may call it and with which permission; a permission follows one grammar of three parts (owner.subject.action) written in the casing the program declares, with owner names reserved; a machine declares only permissions for subjects it has, so a grant naming an undeclared permission is refused; and a route with no entry fails.

reasoning.definition: The declaration names the auth mode and the permission. Each part of a permission is in the program's declared casing (service.contract.10); the rulebook names no default. The subject part may come from config (a named folder, a named device), and only subjects present on this machine are declared, so no grant can name an absent path. An owner name is reserved to the program that owns it. A new subject kind is one more entry in the declaration; the grammar does not change. In Go, each daemon route declares its allowed callers.
pros: A route with no declaration is open by omission; the gap is invisible until someone calls it. One grammar is what makes permissions readable by a stranger in year five, and a grant for a subject the machine lacks is a grant that waits for a path to appear.

rules.statement: The access catalogue (every route and the permission it needs) is regenerated from code and diffed against the committed copy in the gate.

reasoning.definition: The step is regenerate-and-diff. In Go, the command and route tree is generated to a file and compared so drift fails; the kit listing is generated per tag and diffed.
pros: A catalogue kept by hand drifts from the routes, and access reviews then read a list that is wrong.

rules.statement: The acting identity is never taken from the request body or a verb's input; a system actor names the job it runs as; and a bare system actor with no subject fails.

reasoning.definition: The identity comes from the verified credential or the run context only. A write made by the system (a scheduled job, a migration, a consumer) records its actor as the system with the job as subject, so every change can be traced to what made it. In Go, the caller is known from peer credentials or a secret, never from a payload or header.
pros: An identity named in a body is whatever the caller says it is, and a write by an unnamed system actor cannot be traced to the job that made it.

rules.statement: Where a door names the visitor, the server refuses what the page hides.

exemptions.reason: a door that does not identify a visitor has no hidden control to refuse

reasoning.definition: A route-list test: the daemon writes the list of routes from its contract (not hand-kept); a shared helper requests every route as a visitor with no grant and asserts 401 or 403 (or the designed denial) for each gated route; the count of routes tested equals the count in the contract. The page repository holds the front-end half.
pros: A control hidden in the page and not checked on the server is a suggestion; anyone can call the route directly.

rules.statement: Field visibility is applied only through one shared owner module.

reasoning.definition: One shared package performs permission checks, scope enforcement and field filtering, as plain functions and as middleware. In Go, redaction and secret handling of output goes through one owner and a secret is never printed.
pros: Field filtering written per route is forgotten per route; a field leaks from the route that missed it.

rules.statement: Permission mappings point only at live (active) definitions.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every reference in a rule or doc resolves and a vocabulary is declared once.
pros: A mapping to a retired permission grants nothing or, worse, something else.

rules.statement: A service keeps no accounts, passwords or login page of its own and is never an OpenID Connect client; no code verifies credentials by hand or calls the identity service on every request; and token signing exists only at the identity owner.

reasoning.definition: Identity comes from the gate in front of the service (service.authz.15). A user table with a password column, a login route, a session-cookie issuer or an OpenID Connect client library outside the identity owner is banned. Token verification code (key sets, signature checks) and symmetric-key signing are banned outside the identity owner. In Go, no home-made credential checks outside the one owner, and the security linter runs.
pros: A service with its own login is a second identity system to patch forever. Hand-rolled verification is where algorithm and expiry mistakes come from, and a per-request call to the identity service makes it a point of failure for all traffic.

rules.statement: The access catalogue passes one shared conformance test, and a request no source vouches for is refused on every route, reads and static files included, with no guest answer; a service without a catalogue refuses everything.

reasoning.definition: Deny by default covers reads as well as writes: a GET, a list, a health detail beyond liveness, and a served folder are refused without an identity. The refusal is 403 with no hint of what exists. Only routes the catalogue marks public, each with a written reason and never a writing route, answer without an identity. In Go, a shared check fails closed when a required declaration is missing.
pros: A missing catalogue that is read as nothing to check turns every route into an open one, and an open read is how a system leaks what it would refuse to change.

rules.statement: Only the identity owner touches the identity provider.

reasoning.definition: In Go, only one package touches an external identity or credential store.
pros: Every service that talks to the identity provider can change its users and credentials.

rules.statement: The identity provider drift-prone settings are pinned in code: app clients set their auth flows explicitly and the user pool keeps its schema attributes ignored on change.

pros: Provider settings that the console or the provider edits drift, and the next deploy either reverts them or breaks sign-in.

rules.statement: The cross-origin allow-list builder cannot emit a wildcard origin or a privileged header.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a daemon that serves a page is reachable only by expected callers, loopback or socket.
pros: A wildcard origin or a privileged header in the allow list lets any site act as the caller.

rules.statement: A change that adds a route, a caller class, an internal-plane grant or an outbound target answers three questions in the change: what is newly reachable, by whom, and what would an attacker try first.

reasoning.definition: It applies at boundary changes only. The paths on the gate-config list (infrastructure and IAM, migrations, gate config, shared packages) are a ready trigger.
pros: A route can declare its permission correctly and still make an internal path reachable from a new public one. Argued, not measured: a short question list per story in place of a full threat model, because a full model per story is too heavy to keep up. No case from the reference estate.

sources.where: ch. 5 (continuous threat modeling, the leading-questions table)

rules.statement: A token a program issues is stored only as a hash and shown once, and a secret that must be kept as a row is encrypted under a key that comes from the environment, never from the same store.

reasoning.definition: The plain token is returned once at issue and never again; lookup is by hash. A secret the program must use later (a connector's key) is encrypted before it is written, and the key is read from the environment or a key file named by path, so a copy of the store alone reveals nothing. A new kind of secret takes the same path.
pros: A token readable from a database dump is a live credential in every backup; hashing and encryption close that leak in every program that holds one.

rules.statement: A list read returns only the items the caller may read, an empty list when there are none; a single item the caller may not read answers as not found; and a writing route whose answer reveals state also requires the read permission for that state, with a refusal that reveals nothing.

reasoning.definition: A list is never refused with 403 for holding items the caller may not see; it is cut. An item the caller may not read is not said to exist. An action needs the read permission as well as the act permission; act without read gets the bare refusal with no detail.
pros: A 403 on one item tells the caller it exists, and an action answer that carries state leaks what the read permission would have hidden.

rules.statement: An identity source gives a person and role names only, never permissions; there is one source per server, believed only on its own socket and on no other listener; each program maps roles to its own permissions in its own file; a request carrying an identity header twice is refused; and a program never forwards identity or permissions to another tool or keeps another tool's catalogue.

reasoning.definition: A source is pluggable (the private network's login, a trusted proxy's headers, a local fallback file); a new source is one adapter. Identity headers from a proxy are believed only on the socket that proxy reaches. A duplicated identity header answers 400. Each tool reads the gate itself, so each decision has one home.
pros: A forwarded permission is a decision with two homes, and a header believed on any listener can be set by anyone who reaches another one.

rules.statement: Acts reserved to a person are an explicit list granted to no agent or system actor, pinned by a test, and every change to who may do what appends who, when, the command, the reason and the lines changed to a history only the privileged writer can write.

reasoning.definition: The person-only list names permissions in the program's grammar (service.authz.1). A grant of a listed permission to an agent or system actor is refused at write time and at load. The permissions file is written whole by one command under a lock with a revision; the history is append-only and owned by the privileged account (root on a machine, the identity owner in a service). A new act joins the list by one entry.
pros: In an estate where agents hold tokens, the person-only list is the rule that matters most, and a permission change no one can trace cannot be reviewed.

rules.statement: A new service integration enters only through the provider published contract and a generated client, with no hand-written client and no permission string copied from local code.

reasoning.definition: One change adds the contract sync, the generated client, the owning domain services list, the regenerated permission registry and the generated test handlers. Every service client is generated from a published contract, or is listed as missing with a ticket; each operation of a permissioned contract carries its permission. In Go, a provider paths, headers and fields live in one adapter and a shape that crosses a language boundary has one source.
pros: A hand-written client is a second reading of the callee contract, and it goes stale without anything failing.

rules.statement: Every outbound call has a timeout, and the timeout is non-optional on the shared client.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every HTTP client has a timeout or a context and the shared surface is listed; clients carry timeouts.
pros: A call without a timeout holds a worker for as long as the callee stays silent, and the failure spreads upstream.

rules.statement: Request signing lives in one client package.

reasoning.definition: In Go, identifiers are made in one function and the primitives are banned outside the owner.
pros: Signing code in many places is verified in none; one owner can be proved once.

rules.statement: No callee host or gateway identifier appears as a literal in source (`src`); it comes from configuration or a derived name.

pros: A literal host pins a stage and cannot be moved; it also hides which services a program depends on.

rules.statement: The shared client forwards the trace id and the caller token on every call.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a run id joins a command-line call to the daemon it spoke to.
pros: Without the trace id a request cannot be followed across services; without the caller token the callee cannot authorise the original user.

rules.statement: The shared client throws on an unresolvable callee, a signing failure and a non-2xx response; it never returns a default.

reasoning.definition: In Go, errors are returned and never swallowed.
pros: A client that turns a failure into an empty result passes the fault downstream, where it looks like missing data.

rules.statement: Retry lives in the one shared client constructor: idempotent calls only, at one layer, with exponential backoff and jitter, a bounded number of attempts and a retry budget (retries as a fraction of requests). A hand-rolled retry loop is not allowed.

reasoning.definition: The behaviour test runs the client against a handler that always fails and asserts the attempts stay under the budget; it checks behaviour as well as form because the known way round a loop ban is recursion or a timer. The attempt count (three) and the budget (about 10 percent of requests) are examples from the SRE book, not numbers measured on these services. A measure goes beside it: the retry ratio. In the reference stack the layers that can each retry are the cloud SDK, the shared client, the queue redelivery and the function async retry; whether all four are active on a given path was not checked.
pros: Three retries at each of five layers multiplies to a 243-fold load on the bottom layer. Retry traffic can keep a system overloaded after its cause is gone (metastable failure). Reasoning from incident analysis, not a measurement of the reference estate.

sources.where: timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

rules.statement: An outbound call host comes from configuration; where a feature stores a customer-supplied address (a callback, an image URL), the code resolves it and checks it against an allowlist before it fetches.

pros: A server that fetches an address an attacker chose reaches things the attacker cannot (server-side request forgery). Argued; whether any service takes an address from a request was not traced.

rules.statement: A consumer whose work includes a call to an outside API is rate-limited: it has a concurrency ceiling set below that API published limit, and a replay or redrive of its queue is throttled by the same ceiling.

reasoning.definition: A consumer marked as calling an outside API must set a maximum concurrency, and the value must come from a named constant with the third party limit beside it.
pros: A replay or backlog runs at the speed of the consumers, so an outside API can be hit at many times its normal rate after a redrive. Argued; no case from the reference estate.

sources.where: ch. 13 (third-party API replay surge) and ch. 7

rules.statement: No empty catch and no catch that returns a default.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every error is handled or returned and nothing is swallowed.
pros: A swallowed error turns a failure into missing data that surfaces far from its cause.

rules.statement: An error code is a value from the program's own closed typed list, written in the casing the program declares (service.contract.10), and a code is never reused for a new meaning.

reasoning.definition: The rulebook names no default casing: the code list is linted against the program's one declared casing, and a program with no declaration fails. In Go, exit codes are one tested table and typed errors are a closed set.
pros: A code that changes meaning breaks every caller that branches on it, and a code in a second casing is a second vocabulary for one reader to learn.

rules.statement: An error message is a developer diagnostic and is never shown to users; users see a text chosen from the code.

pros: A raw message leaks internals and changes with every refactor.

rules.statement: Each contract lists its error codes as one enum, referenced by every error response; an error is always a non-2xx status with the JSON error body, including errors raised before the handler runs or by a proxy in front of it; and a 2xx never carries an error.

reasoning.definition: Errors raised before the handler include a filtered request and a gateway 401 or 403; a proxy in front of the program is configured to answer with the same JSON body, never an empty 502 or an HTML page. A 200 with an error field, an error flag or an error sentence inside is a defect. In Go, the exit-code table and the command tree list every code and are compared.
pros: A code the contract does not list cannot be handled by a generated client, and platform codes are the ones nobody remembers. A reader that has to look inside a 200 for an error is a reader that guesses, and one that guesses breaks.

rules.statement: Every error carries a request id a user can quote, from the handler and from the gateway.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every log line carries a run id and errors name the next step.
pros: A user reporting an error with no id leaves support to search by time and guess.

rules.statement: There is no raw console output; logs are structured JSON, bare (no extra wrapper), and carry a correlation id and an event number on every line; and the set of top-level log field names is a committed contract compared with a real emitted line in the gate.

reasoning.definition: The field-name contract is a committed list of the top-level keys a line may carry. The gate runs the program, captures a real line and fails when a key is added, removed or renamed without the list changing in the same change. In Go, a daemon logs with slog, every line carries a version and run id, level and time, and there is no log.Fatal outside main.
pros: Unstructured lines cannot be searched or joined across services, and a line without a correlation id cannot be placed in a request. A log field renamed by accident breaks every dashboard and metric filter silently.

rules.statement: The logger redacts secret keys and never logs request or response bodies, and redaction is proved by planting a value in each redacted field and reading the real emitted line.

reasoning.definition: The redacted keys are one configured list (for example authorization, token, secret, key, password, cookie). The proof drives the real logger and output, not a mock, with a canary value in every listed key, and fails when the canary appears. A key added to the list is proved by the same test. In Go, a secret is never printed and no secret reaches the log.
pros: Logs are copied to more places than the data they come from, and a secret or a body in them outlives every other control.

rules.statement: A request the service rejects (validation failure, refused permission) is logged at warn, not error.

pros: A client mistake logged at error floods the alarms meant for service faults.

rules.statement: No logger is constructed outside the runtime package; one owner creates the logger.

reasoning.definition: In Go, one slog handler with version and run id, level and time.
pros: A second logger gives a second format and misses the redaction.

rules.statement: Each log metric filter matches a log line the code really emits.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every claim in a rule resolves to a file or command that exists.
pros: A filter written against a line that is never emitted counts nothing, and the alarm on it never fires.

rules.statement: The environment is read only in the config module, with a short exempt path list that only a reviewed rule change may extend.

reasoning.definition: In Go, os.Getenv is banned outside the config package, which reads with os.LookupEnv; the terminal variables sit in the shared UI package.
pros: Environment reads scattered through code mean no one can list what a service needs to run, and a missing variable fails at first use.

rules.statement: The environment is parsed once, by a schema in the config module, and the rest of the code reads the typed result.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every config key and variable has a reader, a default and a doc row, read in one package.
pros: Parsing at each use repeats the defaults and coercions, and a bad value fails late.

rules.statement: The infrastructure environment map of a service validates under the same schema the service parses at start.

pros: A variable named in the infrastructure but not in the schema (or the reverse) is found by a failed deploy or a failed start, not by a check.

rules.statement: A liveness check does not call a dependency and a readiness check does; a start test breaks a dependency and asserts liveness stays green while readiness changes.

reasoning.definition: The test is two-sided: it fails a liveness that checks the dependency and a readiness that does not. It applies only where a health or readiness route exists (a gateway check, a deploy check, a journey pre-check), because a function runtime has no liveness probe of its own. Whether the reference services expose such a route, and whether a load balancer reads it, was not checked.
pros: A readiness probe that checks a shared dependency can fail on every instance at once, so a small slowdown removes the whole service. The tension is a thorough check against the harm of a false positive across a organisation. The known way round is a shallow readiness that checks nothing, which the second plant catches.

rules.statement: Every service is born with the same alarms on errors, throttles and latency, from one shared component.

reasoning.definition: The shared alarm component is held by the infrastructure part. In Go, a daemon serves one health document, signals readiness and logs with version and run id, and its work is bounded and supervised. There is no alerting on a failing health document for a deployed program yet.
pros: Alarms added by hand per service are missing in the service that fails.

rules.statement: The suite starts one shared container per package in its global setup, and each test gets its own database cloned from a migrated template, never a container per file or a migration per test.

reasoning.definition: tests.isolation.3 holds that heavy fixtures start once and are reached through a helper; this line gives the shape for a service. The global setup starts the engine once, runs the migrations once into a template, and each test clones the template into a database of its own. A container per file costs seconds per file; a clone costs milliseconds. A bind timeout that never changes whatever the load means the knob is not connected to the pool.
pros: Four files cost 19 seconds per container per file against 7 seconds shared, and a template clone took 68 to 136 milliseconds against 210 to 322 to migrate; a container per file inside a fixed 10 second bind budget failed three tiers on the timeout.

sources.says: Testcontainers is a library that supports tests, providing lightweight, throwaway instances of common databases

rules.statement: A container image the tests use is pinned by digest and pulled in the tools step, before the lock and never inside the container's start call.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.24 holds that an image is a tool. A pull inside the start call runs under the test's bind timeout and under the heavy-test lock, so a slow pull looks like a slow container and holds the slot for the download. The tools step pulls by digest when the pin changes (gates.command.19), and the start call finds the image present.
pros: A pull inside the start call in one organisation made a constant bind timeout fire on the network, and nobody could tell the pull from the start.

sources.says: When pulling an image by digest, you specify exactly which version of an image to pull.

rules.statement: The integration tier is a member of the push or the release tier, never a command outside every hook, and a skipped database test prints as a skip and is counted, never a quiet pass.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.17 holds that a check belongs to the earliest moment where it fits the budget, and gates.command.30 that a member which cannot run here prints SKIPPED. The integration tier that needs the container runs at push where it fits and at release where it does not; it is a row of the members file either way. A test that skips because the database is absent is a skip in the report, and red at land (tests.admission.5).
pros: The integration tiers of eleven services in one organisation, 68 and 229 seconds in two of them, ran outside every hook and nothing proved them; two packages' own gates skipped 24 and 15 database tests quietly.

rules.statement: At release a cross-service end-to-end tier proves what no unit suite can: it measures the state the services hold, never the response alone, and marks the data it writes with a run marker.

reasoning.definition: A response that says accepted proves the request was read; the order, the row or the event it should have produced is the thing to read back. Each run writes its marker into the data it makes, so the tier finds its own rows and leaves the rest alone, and a teardown removes them (tests.journeys.6). The tier is a release member with a net field (gates.command.30).
pros: One real order was lost in one organisation with every unit suite green, because nothing read the state after the response.

rules.statement: The deploy is a release member run by the hub after the tier, and a package that publishes has a publish workflow that runs the push tier first.

reasoning.definition: supply.release.1 holds that a release runs the full gate first and that only the release workflow on the tag publishes. This line places the deploy and the publish in the members file: the deploy is a release member with an after edge to the tier, run by the hub (gates.command.31), and a publish is the same shape. A package that publishes with no workflow publishes from a working checkout nobody proved.
pros: Six packages of one organisation publish with no workflow, and one service has no deploy on record.

rules.statement: Exactly one module touches the network or writes a URL; views and parts take data as arguments, the hosts a page may reach come from configuration, and a fetch that follows a user-supplied address resolves and checks it first.

reasoning.definition: The one module is the generated client output plus one core client module (the gateway folder). No other file calls `fetch`, `EventSource`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `new WebSocket` or `navigator.sendBeacon`, in any form: bare, through `window`, `globalThis` or `self`, as a destructured alias, or by bracket access. Embedded page scripts and virtual files are inside the rule. No connector call (`.get`, `.post` and the like) is made outside the client layer and its gated hooks. A site that fetches at build time declares that as a parameter. The hosts a program may reach come from configuration, never from a request; a fetch whose address can come from a request resolves the address and checks it against the allowed hosts first (server-side request forgery). Embedded scripts in `.astro` files (`<script>`) are inside the rule. The destructured alias form takes `fetch` out of `window` in a `const` and the bracket form is `window["fetch"]`.
pros: A network call anywhere lets data, permissions and error handling be bypassed, and a host taken from a request is an open door. Both sites passed when counted; no fault was found in outbound hosts, and 20 outbound call sites on the Go side were counted and not traced.

rules.statement: Raw markup is written only through one funnel module, and HTML that comes from data goes through a sanitiser inside it.

reasoning.definition: Outside the funnel, no `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, `DOMParser` with innerHTML, `createContextualFragment`, `setHTMLUnsafe`, iframe `srcdoc` or computed property form of these. The framework's own raw-HTML escape (a set-html directive, a dangerously-set prop) is banned the same way. The sanitiser library is imported in the funnel only. The funnel module exposes `put()` and `raw()`. Template stack: `astro/no-set-html-directive` from `eslint-plugin-astro`. Component stack: the React form, react.components.3. Sanitiser: `dompurify`, imported in the funnel only. The computed form is `el["innerHTML"] = x`.
pros: A stray raw-HTML write is a script-injection hole; a text rule that matched only five spellings let the others pass.

rules.statement: An entry file and a route file only wire: they import from the owning module's public entry and contain no function over a small line limit, no client call, no query hook and no markup.

reasoning.definition: Entry files are the program entry and route files. A function declaration over the limit (kept in rule data) fails. The route-file form on a router stack (one page import, route group, route helper) is react.routing.11. Entry files include `app/main.ts` and route files; the function check is `no-restricted-syntax` on `FunctionDeclaration` with a body over the `thin-route` line limit kept in rule data.
pros: Logic in an entry or a route file escapes the module's tests and boundaries; both entries complied when counted.

rules.statement: A page is one orchestrator of route input, gated data and catalogued parts. Where the page reads a server of ours, the server hands over order, totals, peaks and sentences and the page only draws, and a value the page recomputes from fields beside it is refused in review. A page's own business rules, where it has any, live in the module's model folder.

reasoning.definition: The model folder is `model/`. The server side of the split is service.contract.20 (units in keys, formatted text beside the number, sentences with their inputs).
pros: A page that holds its own rules cannot be tested without rendering and drifts from the other pages. One implementation of a rule is the only one that stays right, and the server is where the test runs on real data; a page that recomputes a total is a second implementation.

rules.statement: Pure layers touch no document, window or storage; they take plain values and return decisions, and the orchestrating module holds the ports.

reasoning.definition: Scoped to pure folders: no import of DOM modules and no use of `document`, `window`, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` or `navigator`. A function that takes a port and also branches is reported, not failed. The port-and-branch report is a query of `companion shape`.
pros: A pure layer is the part that tests without a browser; once it touches the DOM it cannot be exercised in isolation.

rules.statement: A presentational part imports no data layer, query hook or client; data arrives from a page or a container.

reasoning.definition: The check declares zero part folders a valid state and returns "not applicable: 0 inputs" with the count, never a pass. Component-stack form: `components/` imports no `api/`; the plant is a part importing `../api/client`.
pros: A part that fetches for itself cannot be shown in a catalogue or reused on another page.

rules.statement: Shared presentation and utility code contains no query hook and no fetch; data access lives in modules.

pros: Shared code that fetches turns every consumer into a network client and hides the data flow.

rules.statement: Each module declares itself in one typed manifest the host reads, imports no page eagerly, and a feature flag switches off a module's surface, never its code.

reasoning.definition: The manifest holds an id equal to the module's folder, a title, a flag, its requirements, navigation, slots, query-cache roots and persistence. Dependencies and tier live in one data file, and routes come from the module's route group. A flag also switches off the closure of the modules that depend on it.
pros: Without a manifest the host imports modules by name, and a module cannot be turned off without deleting code.

rules.statement: A project uses exactly one UI framework; a second framework, or a client island directive in a single-framework project, fails with no exception route.

reasoning.definition: More than one of react, astro, preact, svelte, solid and vue in the dependencies fails. A static-site project with a React integration, or any `client:` directive, fails. The check is `companion frameworks`. The `client:` selector runs through `astro-eslint-parser` on attribute names `client:*`; the static-site plant is `<Foo client:load />` and the React integration is `@astrojs/react`.
pros: Two frameworks in one project double the toolchain and the rules that apply; the operator ruled it out.

rules.statement: A backend service of ours is a provider: every path, header name and field of its API appears in one adapter file, and no page, part or layout holds a URL path literal.

reasoning.definition: A string beginning with `/` that matches the service's path prefixes outside the adapter folder fails, scoped to include embedded page scripts, ratcheted. A path built by concatenation passes; that is accepted. The adapter folder is `src/lib/source/` (glob `src/lib/source/**`, `.astro` virtual scripts included). Plant: `fetchJSON('/api/disks')` in `lib/layout/disks.ts` fails, while the same string in `src/lib/source/disks.ts` passes.
pros: Seven files in one site held eight path literals; a changed path then breaks pages the adapter never saw.

rules.statement: A shape shared with a server has one source; the page lists the fields it reads, and that list is checked against the provider's golden or schema, so an added field passes and a renamed one fails.

reasoning.definition: The consumer list is derived from the response type where possible. Optional fields count as misses unless excepted; routes reached through a general call path must be listed; a list that shrinks without a recorded reason fails; an empty list on a live consumer fails. The check runs when the provider lands. The check is `companion contract`; where it lands for another repository (cross-repo) is unsettled.
pros: Pages read fields the server does not send (11 in one site, 6 in another, 6 pages in a third). A symmetric name check would fail on a field the server merely added, so the check is one-way.

sources.where: ch. 5 contracts and ch. 7 Postel's law

rules.statement: A new site starts from a template with default tokens, a one-page install, a catalogue that shows each primitive's accessibility state, and an upgrade path.

pros: A new site that builds its own starting point forks the design system on day one.

rules.statement: Every colour, font, shadow and size a design names comes from one token document, used by version, in which each token has a role, a meaning, a usage note and a value for every mode.

reasoning.definition: The document lives in a separate private tokens package in the house list format and generates the CSS and the Go constants; the Go terminal-look package consumes the generated Go.
