Token names follow the naming table. The check is `companion tokens check`. The alternatives `@terrazzo/cli` and `@terrazzo/plugin-lint` (and Style Dictionary) read only the interchange format.
pros: Drift between copies of a palette is the failure this prevents; it is weak as a fault weight in our record (1 of 144 faults is token drift) and strong as the operator's aim.

rules.statement: A site depends on the token source by version, the version in each lock equals the one in the project record, and a version bump is the only way to change the tokens a site uses.

reasoning.definition: The source carries generated output, a contrast test and a literal scan. The generated CSS and Go equal the tokens package output (generate-then-check). The contrast test and literal scan live in the tokens package and in the styling checks.
pros: The drift between sites is measured and small on colour; the version pin keeps it that way.

rules.statement: No colour literal appears outside the generated token file, in CSS, markup or script, in any colour notation.

reasoning.definition: Covers hex, named colours, `rgb`, `rgba`, `hsl`, `hsla`, `hwb`, `lab`, `lch`, `oklab`, `oklch`, `color` and `color-mix`, in stylesheets, embedded style blocks and script strings, class names included (no raw palette classes). Inline `style` is banned. Hex and token values live only in the token files and the per-brand token files. Current hits are fixed in the same change; there is no baseline. Stylelint 17 runs over `.css`, `<style>` blocks of `.astro` (through `postcss-html`) and CSS in `.tsx`, with `ignoreFiles` set to the generated token file only. The colour functions are `rgb rgba hsl hsla hwb lab lch oklab oklch color color-mix`. Script strings are caught by `no-restricted-syntax` on string literals that are a `#` and 3 to 8 of `[0-9a-f]`, nothing else; inline style by html-validate `no-inline-style` on templates, and on components by the React style-prop ban, react.components.4.
pros: A regex that matched only hex and five functions reported zero literals and missed named colours and four more functions, so zero was zero of the shapes it looked for. Both sites were at zero; one palette file holds 42 distinct hex values inside token definitions, which the rule allows.

rules.statement: Spacing, font size and radius come from a scale, and a literal that repeats a scale step is refused; arbitrary layout-only values pass only from an allow-list.

reasoning.definition: Hand CSS: the value of `padding*`, `margin*`, `gap`, `font-size` and `border-radius` must be a token variable; `px` is banned where a rem scale applies. Utility classes: the theme drops the default scale, and numeric steps not in the token scale are banned (the framework accepts any number as a step, so `p-13` is valid without a ban). Layout-only arbitrary values (a grid template, a calc width, a max width) pass only from a data file of allowed values. Legacy type sizes and arbitrary pixel sizes fail. Brand values arbitrary in a class string are zero. Utility side: the theme drops the default scale with `--spacing-*: initial` and `better-tailwindcss/no-restricted-classes` bans numeric steps outside the token scale. The allowed value form is `var(--space-*|--text-*|--radius-*)`.
pros: One site holds 1,172 spacing, 502 type-size and 241 radius literals as a baseline; none is traced to a fault on its own, so this is a rule held by the aim, not by a fault.

rules.statement: Shadow is a token; the framework's default shadow classes and arbitrary shadow values fail.

reasoning.definition: No default shadow utility classes (small, medium, large); use the elevation tokens. Banned classes: `shadow-sm`, `shadow-md`, `shadow-lg`.
pros: A terminal has no shadows, but a web page that picks its own loses the one elevation scale.

rules.statement: New code uses direction-neutral properties; old CSS is held by a baseline that only falls, and canvas screens are exempt.

exemptions.reason: a canvas does not mirror, so physical coordinates are the correct model

reasoning.definition: Hand CSS uses logical properties (`margin-inline-start`). Utility classes use start and end forms (`ms-`, `me-`, `ps-`, `pe-`, `start-`, `end-`, `text-start`, `rounded-s`), never `ml-`, `mr-`, `pl-`, `pr-`, `left-`, `right-`, `text-left`, `rounded-l`. Utility side: `better-tailwindcss/enforce-logical-properties` (it flagged `ml-4` and named `ms-4`, in `.tsx` and `.astro`) plus the `no-restricted-classes` regex for `left-`, `right-` and `text-left`.
pros: No fault is traced and no right-to-left language is planned; kept as a rule because every rule applies from adoption. Counts depend on the instrument.

rules.statement: `!important` and `outline: none` each need a stated reason, and an outline is never removed without a visible focus ring in its place.

reasoning.definition: The focus ring is a token applied on `:focus-visible` and never hidden. An allowed use carries a reason comment (`reportDescriptionlessDisables`). Debt is held by a count baseline. Stylelint writes `stylelint-suppressions.json`; `--prune` must run in the same change as a fix. The outline entry is `outline` mapped to `["none","0"]`; both rules also fired in `.astro` `<style>` blocks. The utility form of outline removal is `outline-none`.
pros: The counts are 9 `!important` and 102 `outline: none` in one site; hiding the keyboard position leaves a keyboard user with no way to see where they are.

rules.statement: Every text and status pair passes a contrast of 4.5 to 1, and 3 to 1 for large text and parts, on every ground it may sit on, in both modes, by a pure test computed from the tokens.

reasoning.definition: WCAG AA in both themes for every foreground and background token pair. The test iterates the token document, so a new role is covered; it also computes APCA Lc and prints it beside the ratio. It runs on any change to the token source. The generator ships the test, and the terminal side generates its own contrast test from the same table.
pros: Measured faults: a muted role at 4.29 and 4.49 on light, good 4.32, attention 4.24, white on the dark `bad` role 2.77; the Go test covers 4 of 9 colours. Colour contrast is 89.1 percent of axe WCAG failures in generated pages.

rules.statement: A text or status role says which grounds it may sit on, and the contrast check reads that list.

reasoning.definition: The schema makes the `on` field required for any role of kind text or status; a role whose `on` is wider than its checked grounds fails. The muted text role (`dim`) placed on the `web-page` ground is the case it catches.
pros: A check with an `on` list would have found the muted role placed on the page ground.

rules.statement: CSS and Go that carry a token are generated from the document and say so; nobody edits the output.

reasoning.definition: Outputs carry a "generated, do not edit" banner (header grep). The check regenerates both outputs in memory and compares with the committed files byte for byte. The loop is generate-then-check, run as `companion gen --check`.
pros: A copy of the palette was edited once in one commit of 614; 15 values lived in five places.

rules.statement: Light and dark come from the same token names, written once; an explicit choice beats the system setting and the choice is stored.

reasoning.definition: Every token name present in light is present in dark and the reverse. With no stored choice the page follows the system; a stored choice overrides it and survives a reload; the theme control is the only module touching the storage key. Browser journey details: `colorScheme: dark` with no stored choice; the theme control (`ThemeControl`) is the only module touching the `localStorage` key.
pros: Storage is byte-equal in two sites, but only one has the stored choice; the other follows the system and has no control.

rules.statement: Fonts are self-hosted and the content security policy allows no external font host.

reasoning.definition: Two nets. The built output is scanned for font-face sources and link hrefs with a host other than self; and a journey fails any request whose origin is not the app's. `font-src 'self'` is asserted from the response header. Net one is `companion dist-scan`, which reads built `dist/` for `@font-face` `src:` urls and `<link>` hrefs naming another host.
pros: One site had all 24 smoke pictures differ because of font loading; it ships 72 font files, 777.6 KB.

rules.statement: Styles are scoped by a mechanism the project declares; the mechanism is a parameter, and hand-written CSS is scoped by a class prefix.

pros: One site had 4 class-collision cases; the utility framework makes scoping moot once a site migrates.

rules.statement: A deliberate difference from the shared token source is recorded in a differences file with an owner, reason, date and way back, and goes to the owner as a proposal.

reasoning.definition: Each overridden token has one entry and each entry has an overridden token; an entry for a token no longer overridden fails. Whether the reason is good is review. Part of `companion tokens check`; the differences file is `token-differences.json`.
pros: One site has about 20 differences and its ruling to send its palette as proposals has no recipient.

rules.statement: A project styles through tokens from the token document as CSS custom properties, with one declared scoping mechanism: CSS Modules, or one utility-class framework whose theme is generated from the token document and holds no colour, size or font of its own. A second mechanism or utility framework is banned, and a colour, size or font not from the tokens fails under either mechanism.

reasoning.definition: The mechanism is the project's declared parameter (web.tokens.13); tokens are the invariant. Under CSS Modules a stylesheet lint allows only token variables for colour, size and font, and a utility-class framework in the dependencies fails. Under a utility framework the rest of this detail applies. A mechanism added later states its own lint for the same invariant; the rule does not change. Class-variant and class-merge helpers (`cva`, `clsx`, `tailwind-merge`) are allowed. A colour, size or font that is not from the theme in a class string fails (`bg-[#fff]`, `p-[13px]`, `[color:red]`); the default palette is cleared. Layout-only arbitrary values pass from a lint-checked allow-list data file. Inline style is banned. The theme file is generated and compared (generate-then-check), and a stylesheet on it allows only token variables. A new brand token is added to the brand layer with a canary value. Class-string lint covers framework templates and embedded script strings. Migrating a site's old CSS is per-repository adoption work, not a foundation rule. Lint plugin: `eslint-plugin-better-tailwindcss` with `no-restricted-classes` (arbitrary-value regex `\[.+\]`), `no-unknown-classes` and `no-conflicting-classes`; the default palette is cleared with `--color-*: initial`. Inline style: html-validate `no-inline-style` (template stack); the component-stack ban is react.components.4. Works on `.tsx` and `.astro` class strings. A calc width such as `w-[calc(100%-var(--sidebar))]` passes only from the allow-list. Layout-only arbitrary values such as `grid-cols-[...]` also pass only from the allow-list. The theme file is checked with `companion gen --check` and the `@theme` block allows only `var(--token)` values; the dependency check is `companion deps` over `package.json`, with `cva`, `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` off the ban list.
pros: No project used it at first; proposed to carry the earlier lint requirement and widened later to cover both frameworks. The targets style two ways over the same tokens, so the mechanism is a parameter and the tokens are what the rule holds.

rules.statement: Utility classes are known, non-conflicting, not duplicated and in one consistent order, with one format command.

pros: Unknown and conflicting classes fail silently in the browser.

rules.statement: Every token read is defined, and every token defined is read.

reasoning.definition: The check collects every `var(--x)` read in CSS, templates and components and every utility class that resolves to a theme variable, and compares with the token source. An undefined read fails; an unread definition fails, with a rising-count baseline. The check is `companion tokens used`, reading `.astro` and `.tsx` as well as CSS.
pros: One site has 6 unread tokens; another reads 14 defined only by a user stylesheet.

rules.statement: A new token enters the source first, with a value in every mode.

reasoning.definition: A token missing a mode fails the schema (`required` light and dark), and the vendored token names are compared with the source. The schema line is `required: [light, dark]`.
pros: A token added in the page only is the start of drift.

rules.statement: The terminal and the web read the same colour roles from one generator.

reasoning.definition: A test parses both generated outputs (CSS custom properties and Go constants) and asserts the same role names with equal resolved values; the Go side consumes the generated file only.
pros: Seven of seven spike builds imported the same CSS unchanged; the two sources disagree on whether the Go output is generated.

rules.statement: A colour keeps one meaning across the app, taken from role tokens: relation roles use their own role tokens, destructive uses the destructive token, and green means health only.

reasoning.definition: Example of a role token: the requires relation (`--color-relation-requires`).
pros: A colour that means two things in two places teaches the reader nothing.

rules.statement: Browser targets are declared once and read by the bundler, the style lint and the script lint; a feature outside them fails.

reasoning.definition: One targets file (a browser list or a Baseline year) is read by the bundler, the Stylelint baseline plugin, the ESLint CSS baseline rule and a script compatibility rule. The targets file is a `browserslist` file or a Baseline year, and the passing twin is a widely-available feature.
pros: No target is stated anywhere in the foundation today; the two-engine test checks the outcome but states no target.

rules.statement: The platform comes first: the native element, native event source, `Intl` and CSS; ARIA only fills gaps, and a primitive library that a pack names fills the rest.

reasoning.definition: A banned-package list covers packages that reimplement the platform: date libraries, polyfills for `Intl`, wrappers around the native event source, icon fonts, and UI kits that wrap native elements. It is read from the same package table as the supply-chain rule. ARIA is not used where a native element exists: a prefer-tag-over-role rule and the HTML validator's prefer-native-element and no-redundant-role rules. Plant forms: adding `moment` or `dayjs` to the dependencies; `<div role="button">`. The ban list is `companion deps`, covering wrappers of `EventSource`; template form `astro/jsx-a11y/prefer-tag-over-role`. A primitive library that a pack names is the gap-filler.
pros: The principle is supported by practice (evidence B); a reimplemented platform feature carries its own accessibility and locale faults.

rules.statement: Feature code holds no hand-built twin of a catalogued part: no raw button, input, select, textarea, table, dialog or spinner class where a catalogued part exists; the count is kept per part and only shrinks.

reasoning.definition: One element ban per catalogued part, generated from the parts catalogue and applied to feature folders only, so the part's own folder is exempt; it works on components and on templates. The input count is the number of catalogued parts; zero is a valid state and returns "not applicable: 0 inputs" with the count, never a pass. A rule added before the catalogue exists needs its plant in the same change. A conversion from a string-built element is counted too. Selector form: `JSXOpeningElement[name.name="button"]`, working on `.tsx` and on `.astro` templates. The utility spinner class `animate-spin` is also a raw-element twin.
pros: Measured: 3 twins in one site, 1 of 144 faults in another, 2 in a third; 19 buttons and 10 tables built from strings in one site, and 103 buttons from strings in 43 files in another.

rules.statement: Every screen guideline gets a lint rule, a test, or a stated reason that it stays text.

reasoning.definition: Examples to turn into checks: no card as a page root, record cells use the record field, list pages use the table component. A rule that no tool can catch is marked an instruction with its reason.
pros: A guideline that no check holds is read once and then drifts; marking it as an instruction states honestly that it is not held.

rules.statement: A page never wraps itself in a surface the shell already provides: the header sits on the canvas, a list table is its own card and record sections are section cards.

pros: A page that adds its own container around itself doubles borders and padding the shell already gives.

rules.statement: A page uses the archetype: the page shell and header, lists through the list screen and table, and records like the existing record pages.

pros: New screens built from a generator or golden page keep one folder shape and one look.

rules.statement: A shape the general part cannot express has its own catalogued part; for example a round icon-only button uses the icon button part.

pros: Bending the general part with extra props closes the catalogue's promise of few, closed props.

rules.statement: Shared parts take few, typed and closed props in one naming; a control uses one value and change contract, extra search terms go in a keywords prop, and explanations sit outside the control.

pros: A control with two value contracts forces every caller to learn which one it has.

rules.statement: Each kind of value is shown through its one part: identifiers in a monospace value, copyable values in a copyable value, secrets in a secret input, status in a status badge, permissions in a permission label, and the responsive dialog or table for phone versus desktop.

reasoning.definition: The permission label renders from a message map keyed by the permission registry id, and server text goes through the server-text part, so no literal sentence is shown.
pros: Ids, secrets and statuses shown as plain text lose copy, masking and meaning.

rules.statement: There is one notification system, a notify wrapper over the design system's toaster that takes a message result and not a literal; an actionable notice never auto-dismisses; the old toast library is gone.

reasoning.definition: The old toast library was `react-toastify`.
pros: Two toast systems stack and style differently; a literal sentence escapes the message catalogue.

rules.statement: Icons are named by meaning from one registry, and the set changes in one file; direct imports of an icon package live only in the registry.

reasoning.definition: A name like an action or object resolves through the design system's registry, which ships built-in entries; a project config extends or overrides them. No inline `<svg>` outside the registry folder, and no import of an icon package anywhere but the one icon module. Selector `JSXElement[openingElement.name.name="svg"]`; `@tabler/icons-react` only inside the icon module; `lucide-react` anywhere else fails.
pros: One site has 99 icon names; another has 3 inline shapes and 6 glyphs; the icon package is 15 minor releases behind.

rules.statement: A parts catalogue exists as data an agent can query (part, states, props, file, stack, accessibility state), every part and prop used resolves against it, a new part adds its row, and an agent looks a part's real interface up in it and never assumes.

reasoning.definition: Where a doc generator reads the stack (react-docgen for components) the catalogue is generated and a check fails on drift; where none does (templates) it is hand-written and checked against each part file's exported props. The type checker rejects an unknown prop on a typed component. A new gating primitive adds a catalogue row and tests. Without the catalogue, the checks that depend on it (twin scan, examples, kit render test) are vacuous. Command `companion catalogue` with `--check` failing on drift; template stack checked with `@astrojs/compiler` or the TypeScript API, and `astro check` rejects an unknown prop. Agents query the catalogue (the story tool's `docs-show` query) and never assume a part's props. A new gating primitive adds a row to the `authz-gates` catalogue and tests. Template-stack catalogue entries are hand-written for `.astro` part files.
pros: An audit found 22 parts declared and never drawn, and 39 drawn and never declared. Agents invent props when no queryable interface exists.

rules.statement: Every shared part has a living example in each of its states, and a new canonical part ships with an example and a catalogue row.

reasoning.definition: For every part in the catalogue and every state it declares, a story or gallery entry must exist and render; the story tool's runner (or the Vitest addon) runs each story and checks it for accessibility; the template stack's gallery is a route that lists each part and state, rendered by the land-tier browser run. Existence is compared against the catalogue. Zero shared parts is a valid state, reported as "not applicable: 0 inputs". React stack runner: `@storybook/test-runner`; check command `companion parts --examples`.
pros: The donor's story gate found 523 of 1,241 stories failing axe, which shows the net catches things, not that it prevents them.

rules.statement: Extract a part once the same part is hand-built in three or more files of a site; across sites, only at a second live consumer on the same framework and after its fault has recurred.

reasoning.definition: A report from a clone scan (a clone detector plus a JSX subtree-shape count per site) prints a shape with three or more copies as a candidate; the third copy blocks until it is moved or listed as independent. The extraction itself is judged. The exact-clone half is already enforced elsewhere. Seed: the copy census script `step-copies.py`; the clone detector is `jscpd`.
pros: Copies exist inside one site today and not across sites; thresholds are the donor's own.

rules.statement: The shared kit renders with no provider and carries its own words as plain data: a strings object with English defaults, which the host may override in part.

reasoning.definition: The kit holds no i18n library and no host config. A test renders every exported part from the catalogue with no provider and no wrapper and asserts it does not throw and its words come from the part's own defaults. Vacuous on the template stack while parts have no provider. The component-stack form, a render test with no provider, is react.testing.3. Part of the kit's own words are screen-reader-only text (`sr-only`), placeholders and default prop strings.
pros: The donor's design system added a provider and an English defaults object for this at its 0.13.0 release.

rules.statement: The shared parts package depends on no app-level library beyond its declared peers and holds no program domain.

reasoning.definition: The kit keeps no data-fetching dependency except the form peer, and no i18n library; the kit imports no program package and holds mechanism only.
pros: A kit that imports app libraries cannot be reused on a second site without that site adopting the first one's stack.

rules.statement: Every UI part comes from the design system's single entry; no second UI kit is imported, in code or in the manifest.

reasoning.definition: A second kit (a component library, a headless primitive set, a command-menu or drawer package) fails in imports and in the package manifest. A design-system source copied into the shared package counts as the package, on the primitive library chosen earlier. Plant: a named import of `Button` from `"@mui/material"` fails; the check reads `package.json` too. The reference also banned `@radix-ui/*`, `cmdk` and `vaul` as second kits.
pros: Two kits mean two focus models, two token systems and two sets of faults.

rules.statement: The design's named parts exist as `data-` attributes in the shipped page, match the design's numbers, and are what visual tests measure.

reasoning.definition: Plant attribute: `data-part="card"`. The numbers come from the design file, or from the committed parts file where no machine-readable design exists; a page with visual tests and neither file fails.
pros: A card five pixels off its design is invisible to a unit test, and a visual test needs named parts to measure instead of a picture to compare (web.testing.5).

rules.statement: Template and prop type errors are caught by a gate on every stack in use, and a stack with no typed check declares the gap in its parameters file.

reasoning.definition: Template stacks: `.astro` and `.tsx`; the tagged-template stack (`lit-html`) has no typed check (`lit-analyzer`).
pros: The weak link of the static path: a wrong prop type in a template reaches the page unseen.

rules.statement: One behaviour test written with role and test-id locators only passes unchanged on any stack.

reasoning.definition: One browser journey per behaviour; raw selectors fail the lint (`no-raw-locators`, `prefer-native-locators`) and the same spec runs against each stack's build in the admission pilot and must pass unchanged. The same spec runs in the `pack-admission` pilot. Plant: `page.locator(".card > div")`.
pros: Eight of eight spike builds passed the journey, showing the locator contract is the DOM contract between stacks.

rules.statement: A component folder has the closed shape: module, stylesheet, stories and test.

reasoning.definition: New folders only until the old ones move. The check declares zero component folders a valid state and returns "not applicable: 0 inputs" with the count. An alternative that checks names only: `@ls-lint/ls-lint`.
pros: The four text rules for the shape run against nothing, since no component folder exists at its pin; unproven on real folders.

rules.statement: Charts come from the design system; the app has no direct chart dependency.

pros: A heavy capability is owned once, so the app does not carry a second copy.

rules.statement: Every data region declares one of six states (ready, loading, empty, error, stale, disconnected) and draws each; loading is marked busy in its final boxes, empty says what is missing and what to do, and shared state parts draw them.

reasoning.definition: Loading is marked `aria-busy`, keeps its final box size (no shift) and says what it waits for after 10 seconds. Empty has text and an action. Error has Retry. Stale shows its age. Disconnected has a status region. Loading, empty and failure use the shared state parts (a section or inline loader, or a page-shaped skeleton; the empty-state part; the error-state part); no bare spinner and no bare "Checking" text. A page declares its regions in a data file (id, states); the land-tier run forces each state per region (route interception for loading, error, empty, stale and disconnected; a fixture for ready). The count of declared regions must equal the count of region elements in the page, which proves the check reads something. The state set is a closed type, and a switch-exhaustiveness lint makes a missing case a type error. The regions file is `regions.json`; the count is of `[data-region]` elements; the 10-second wait is fast-forwarded with `page.clock`.
pros: The heaviest fault class in our record: 23 of 144. No benchmark scoring this was found, which the stack report says is not proof.

rules.statement: The page ran against the real server before it is called done, on one made-up world, and the run names its build.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

reasoning.definition: The land step runs the end-to-end suite against the real binary and writes a run record (tree hash, the daemon's reported version, date, journeys run); it refuses to land unless the record's tree equals the change's tree and its build string equals the built daemon's.
pros: Faults that only a mock allowed: 8 in one site, 3 in another, 3 in a third.

rules.statement: The live transport only rings: state travels in whole answers so a missed message costs one read, and a failed stream falls back to polling and notices when open never comes.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

reasoning.definition: Stream drop uses `routeWebSocket` or a held-open event route.
pros: The browser's 6-connection limit is the reason; neither site has the fallback.

rules.statement: A failed read names the cause in plain words through one table of codes, keeps old content, offers Retry and carries an id the reader can quote; a raw server or exception message is never shown.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

reasoning.definition: Error text comes from one table typed `Record<ErrorCode, string>`, so a missing code is a type error. A backend code maps to a local message through one describer; an unknown code shows generic text with a reference id; enum labels are exhaustive maps. The error part is fed by the describer, never by the raw message. A lint bans rendering `.message` in view files; the kit asserts Retry, old content kept and a run id present, and two forced runs must show different ids. A golden of the error-state text is kept. Words are review.
pros: One site shows "500 Internal Server Error: internal error"; another stays on "Checking..." with no Retry on the shell only. The donor built this gate and it is still open.

rules.statement: A value nobody read is shown as a dash with its reason, never as 0, idle or clean.

reasoning.definition: For each nullable field in the contract schema the fixture generator sets null and the page must show a dash with a reason. The scan on `?? 0` and `|| 0` in view files is a hint that warns or needs a reason (known false positives). The hint lint is `no-restricted-syntax` on `??` with a 0 right side and on `||` with a 0 right side in view files.
pros: Two sites showed an unread value as zero; the scan hit 59 and 48 lines.

rules.statement: A response is checked against a schema where it enters, never cast; external payloads, cache hydration and URL parameters are validated at the boundary, in development and test every response is validated, and the check tolerates extra fields.

reasoning.definition: A newer server must not break an older page, so the boundary schema is non-strict and an extra field is accepted and ignored; a person's own config refuses unknown keys. Schemas come from the generated output. Type-aware lint (`no-unsafe-assignment`, `no-unsafe-argument`, `no-unsafe-return`) flags the untyped value a JSON parse returns, and `consistent-type-assertions` with `assertionStyle: never` in the api folder bans `as T` on responses. A unit test per boundary sends an extra field. Boundary library options: `zod/mini` or ajv.
pros: One site has 3 hits, the one network cast; another has 0. The test is who wrote it.

rules.statement: The page's API types and client are generated from the server's published contract (or a test proves them equal), shapes never come from local code, and no hand-written client remains.

reasoning.definition: Generate the types from the server's types or from its OpenAPI spec, commit them, and regenerate-and-diff in the check. Every service uses the generated output (client, gated query options, mock handlers). Where a project hand-keeps types, a name-comparison script is the fallback. Which generator per project is a parameter. Fallback script `drift.py`; the loop is `companion gen --check`.
pros: Today right only because people kept it so; a comparison trialled on 60 of 60 shapes found the one planted difference.

rules.statement: API specs live once in the repository, pinned by a lock file and synced by one command; per-service copies are deleted.

reasoning.definition: A vendored shared file equals its source at the named version by hash.
pros: A spec copied by hand into each service drifts from its origin without notice.

rules.statement: The page reads only fields the contract names, and a field the server stopped sending fails a test.

reasoning.definition: For each field on the consumer list the kit serves the contract body with that field deleted and asserts the page does not throw and shows a dash or an error state; the list comes from the contract, not the author. The example field is `ramBytes`, read unguarded.
pros: One site reads a bytes field unguarded and crashes when it is missing.

rules.statement: Reconnect has a bounded back-off with jitter, and a hidden tab asks nothing.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

reasoning.definition: Hidden state is `document.hidden` with a `visibilitychange` event; fake timers via `page.clock`.
pros: Both sites behave so today, unproven by test.

rules.statement: A failed refresh keeps the last good data marked stale with its age; disconnected is visible with a time and a status region, never blank; and the page never fills a value the server answered as unknown or not read.

reasoning.definition: The known unfailable spec is `hostile.spec.ts:72`; the abort is `route.abort()`. An unknown is drawn as unknown with the server's reason; a dash with a reason (web.states.5) is the empty form, never a stand-in for a value.
pros: One site tracks the link state and never draws it, and its end-to-end spec accepts either value, so it cannot fail. A page that draws 0, off or a carried-forward value for an unread one turns the server's honest answer into a false one.

rules.statement: A live update never moves what the reader is looking at: scroll, focus, open details and typed text stay.

reasoning.definition: Details element `<details>`; the kit check is `checkLiveKeepsPlace`.
pros: One site does it correctly in an unshared module; others replace whole lists.

rules.statement: The URL carries the place (page, tab, filter and open detail), and Back closes a sheet without leaving the app.

reasoning.definition: A journey per page changes the tab, filter or open detail, reloads, and asserts the same place; it then presses Back and asserts the sheet closes. On a router stack the router's typed search parameters add a type check (react.routing.3 for React). Template-stack helper: `URLSearchParams`.
pros: A tab kept only in memory loses its place on reload.

rules.statement: Search and filter act without a button, say how many match, can be cleared and survive a reload.

pros: Marked inferred in the source report; no fault in our record, so it rides on a journey that other rules already earn.

rules.statement: A derived value is computed, not stored and synced.

reasoning.definition: On the component stack the lint of react.client-state.3 holds it; the template stack has no equivalent lint and stays on the review question.
pros: Stored derived state drifts from the value it was derived from.

rules.statement: A page has a request budget, counted per page load and per journey, and fetches only what the user can see and what is not fresh.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

reasoning.definition: A counter on the browser's request event, grouped by URL path to ignore static assets, with the budget per page in the parameters file; the check fails when over. No per-row fan-out for data the user cannot see. Counter: `page.on("request")`.
pros: Marginal build on the journey runner; no fault in our record.

rules.statement: An optimistic write is undone when the request fails.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

pros: Zero optimistic handlers exist today; the rule is set ahead of the first one.

rules.statement: A write carries the version it read, and a conflict is a typed outcome distinct from not-found that the page names.

exemptions.reason: The page reads one published document and writes nothing to a server: there is no live server, reconnect, write or request budget beyond the file reads.

pros: A stale write and a missing row both read as zero rows affected unless told apart.

rules.statement: No virtualisation library is added outside the list table's virtual mode, and that mode is added only when a list mounts over about 500 rows or a profile misses a frame budget.

reasoning.definition: It is not banned; it carries a re-entry trigger. Never in a canvas list lens.
pros: A heavy library not needed yet costs bytes and behaviour; the ruling kept it watched, not banned.

rules.statement: No local-first collection library is added until a stated trigger holds: a stable (final) release, a stated offline need, a persister policy for collections, or a second screen live-joining two whole collections.

reasoning.definition: It is not banned. A prerelease major is added only as a labelled pilot.
pros: A prerelease data library locks in an unstable API.

rules.statement: There is no horizontal page scroll at 390 px or 320 px, in every state and both themes; nothing passes its box, and a wide table scrolls in its own named, focusable box that says how many rows it holds.

reasoning.definition: 390 px is the operator's width and 320 px is the WCAG reflow width. The shared check, run at both widths in both colour schemes and every forced state, asserts `scrollWidth <= clientWidth` on the document and that no element's rectangle passes its container. A wide table sits in a focusable named scroll box with a row count (axe `scrollable-region-focusable` plus a label check). The same check is the test helper for "no horizontal overflow at 390".
pros: The heaviest layout fault: 27 of 144. One site's phone table ran 352 px past the edge.

rules.statement: Text that may be long is tested at length, at the narrowest width, in every state.

reasoning.definition: The overflow check runs with a long-text fixture: a generator producing 300-character words and unbroken strings for each text field of the catalogue, in every state at 320 and 390 px, and asserts no element overflows its box or the viewport.
pros: One site had an overflow check and no state held a long question.

rules.statement: No box moves after first paint by more than 8 px, and cumulative layout shift is 0.1 or less.

reasoning.definition: The check sums the browser's layout-shift entries to 0.1 or less, and also diffs the bounding box of every landmark between first paint and settle, failing above 8 px. A report from a performance audit is kept as a report only. Observer: `PerformanceObserver`.
pros: Named 14 Oct and still failing on a PC 4 Nov. The layout-shift observer failed a 200 px late insert and did not fail an 80 px one (about 0.09), which is why the 8 px box check exists.

rules.statement: Breakpoints are three named token values, and layout is never keyed on a pointer media feature.

reasoning.definition: Media queries on width use only the token breakpoints as literals generated from the token source (a CSS variable cannot be used inside a media query); `pointer`, `hover` and `any-pointer` features are banned, and utility-class arbitrary breakpoint variants and pointer-coarse variants are banned. Utility bans: `min-[…]`, `max-[…]` variants and `pointer-coarse:` via `no-restricted-classes`; width features include `max-width`.
pros: One site uses 6 distinct widths and another 4 by one count (8 and 6 by another instrument); the direction is the same, and no fault is traced to the difference.

rules.statement: Every pointer target is at least 24 by 24 CSS px, and 44 by 44 on touch.

reasoning.definition: Axe `target-size` (24 px, WCAG 2.5.8, tag `wcag22aa`) runs on every page state, plus the kit's target check on a touch project (`hasTouch: true`) measures each interactive element's box at 44 by 44. The sizes are tokens: a minimum target and a touch target. The engine is `axe-core` 4.14.
pros: Tap targets are most of the 10 accessibility cases of 144; a select under 44 px in WebKit recurred.

rules.statement: A pointer or touch press does not move or scale the thing pressed.

reasoning.definition: For each interactive element the check reads its bounding box, presses it (mouse down; or a held tap on a touch project), reads the box again with the active style applied, and fails on any size or position change. A colour-only active state passes. The check scrolls the element into view first, otherwise the press never reaches it and the plant passes for the wrong reason. Check `checkPressStable`: `mouse.down()` or `touchscreen.tap`, `:active`; plant `transform: scale(.98)`.
pros: One case in our record; the source criterion said no check exists, and a mechanical one was built.

rules.statement: Viewport height survives browser chrome: `dvh`, never `100vh` or the full-screen height class, and the safe-area insets are honoured.

reasoning.definition: Stylelint bans `100vh` in height, min-height and max-height; the utility-class lint bans the screen-height class and arbitrary `vh` heights (the dynamic form stays). A grep of fixed-position rules without `env(safe-area-inset-*)` is review. Regexes: `/100vh/` on height properties; classes `^(min-|max-)?h-screen$` and `h-\[.*vh\]` via `no-restricted-classes`.
pros: One site has 0 uses of either unit and another 11.

rules.statement: The accessibility engine finds nothing new on any page state, in light and dark, at 1440 and 390 px, against a shrink-only known list, and an incomplete result is a finding; every story also passes it as an error in both themes.

reasoning.definition: The engine runs through the shared kit on every page state and every story. Violations are compared with a known-list file that can only shrink: an entry removed after a fix cannot be re-added. The engine's package licence is file-level copyleft, and using it unmodified is allowed.
pros: The donor's story gate found 523 of 1,241 stories (42 percent) failing. In our sites it found 3 rules on one page; one site's ratchet holds 8 written-in violations and another site's result is a null on a shell, not a zero.

rules.statement: Built HTML is valid and names every control.

reasoning.definition: The HTML validator's recommended set runs over the built output (template stacks) or over the rendered DOM (client-rendered stacks); the check lists every control without a name. Applied to built `dist` HTML; plant `<input>` with no label.
pros: The validator caught 11 of 32 planted faults, none uniquely.

rules.statement: Headings form an outline with no skipped level.

pros: Neither the HTML validator nor the template lint caught a skipped level in the trial.

rules.statement: Status is never carried by colour alone: the status part requires a text label.

reasoning.definition: A required label prop makes omission a type error; status classes and status colour tokens are banned on elements outside the part; the kit asserts every status-marked element has non-empty text. The terminal form of the rule is the strip test of the terminal-look part. Banned classes: `status-*`, `.is-ok`, `.is-bad`; plant ``; check `checkStatus`.
pros: No tool caught the planted colour-only status in the trial (the one miss of 32).

rules.statement: Under reduced motion nothing non-essential moves.

reasoning.definition: With reduced motion emulated, the page must hold no running animation except elements marked essential; transitions longer than 0.01 s on computed styles are listed. This is our rule and not a conformance floor, because the matching WCAG criterion is level AAA. Check `checkReducedMotion`: `page.emulateMedia` with `reducedMotion: "reduce"`, `document.getAnimations()`, marker `data-essential`, plant `animation: spin`.
pros: No fault in our record; held on the operator's ruling that every rule binds from adoption.

rules.statement: Text grows without loss: no clipping when spacing is raised, and zoom is not disabled.

reasoning.definition: The kit injects the WCAG 1.4.12 override (line height 1.5, letter spacing 0.12em, word spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) and asserts no text is clipped (an element with hidden overflow whose text is taller than its box); it zooms to 200 percent through a 640 CSS px viewport; axe `meta-viewport` flags disabled zoom. Check `checkTextSpacing`; override values `line-height: 1.5`, `letter-spacing`, `word-spacing`; clip test `overflow: hidden` with `scrollHeight > clientHeight`; zoom 200%.
pros: v1 gave no reason beyond its evidence grade, Evidence B.

rules.statement: Meaning has a named reader: alt text, reading order and headings are checked, and a screen-reader pass is recorded each release.

reasoning.definition: A release record `a11y-pass.json` holds the named person, date, version and tools used, valid against a schema. The tag refuses without it. The pass itself (what the alt text means, the order, a screen-reader walk) is a person's.
pros: A vendor skill raised its pass rate from 12 to 86 percent where "pass" meant automated checks only; no report of ours has run a screen reader.

rules.statement: Templates carry no image without alt text, role mismatch, click without a key, positive tabindex, empty link, untitled iframe or autofocus.

reasoning.definition: Template stack: the plugin's strict jsx-a11y set (it cannot see inside a component). Component stack: the same rules on JSX, held by react.lint.3. The built-output checks (valid HTML, the accessibility engine) cover what a template rule cannot. The lint covers key-less click handlers on `.astro` templates and, through the React rule, on `.tsx`.
pros: Eight of 32 planted faults were caught in 0.35 s; all six template plants fired in both stacks.

rules.statement: Names have a floor: no file name as alt text, no "click here", error text tied to its field, no nested interactive element, and visible labels.

reasoning.definition: Through the accessibility tree every control has a non-empty name that is not a file name or "click here"; axe `label`, `button-name`, `link-name` and `nested-interactive`; error text is tied to its field with `aria-describedby`. An icon-only control keeps an accessible name. Check `checkNames` via `page.accessibility.snapshot` or `ariaSnapshot`; plant `alt="IMG_0043.png"` (file-name alt).
pros: The check ran on 96 twins and 32 plants; its false-positive rate on real code is unknown. Above the floor it is judgement.

rules.statement: A change that does not move focus is announced, and an actionable or error notice never auto-dismisses.

reasoning.definition: After such a change a live region (`role=status`, `role=alert` or `aria-live`) must contain new text within a stated time. The notice part's timer prop is typed to forbid auto-dismiss on actionable and error variants. A `setTimeout` hiding a node in feature code is advice. Check `checkSilentUpdate`; live regions `role=status|alert`; `no-restricted-syntax` on timers hiding nodes is advice.
pros: Held on the every-rule-binds ruling.

rules.statement: An overlay keeps the dialog contract: focus goes in, stays in and comes back, Escape closes, and the overlay is modal to assistive technology.

reasoning.definition: Template stack: a native `<dialog>`, and a lint banning `role="dialog"` on a div. Component stack: the primitive library's dialog, with its lint in react.components.2. Both primitive libraries tried render a div dialog, which is why the native-element rule belongs to the template stack only. Plant `<div role="dialog">`; `role="dialog"` ban via `no-restricted-syntax`; check `checkDialog`.
pros: One site's legend popover takes no focus and the kit's "focus did not return" line there is a false positive.

rules.statement: Anything with a click handler can take focus and has a key.

reasoning.definition: The kit finds every element with a click handler and checks it is focusable and activates on Enter and Space; the static net is the template lint's click-events-have-key-events and no-static-element-interactions rules. Check `checkClickKeyboard` finds handlers with `getEventListeners`.
pros: Run on WebKit too.

rules.statement: Every control is reachable and operable by keyboard in reading order with no trap at any stop, with one focus ring token on focus-visible that is never hidden behind a sticky bar.

reasoning.definition: The kit tabs through the page and asserts every control is reached in document order, no trap, and the focused element is not covered by a sticky bar (the element at its centre is itself). The style rules (no bare `outline: none`) are in the tokens concern. Whether the order makes sense is review. Style net: `declaration-property-value-disallowed-list` for `outline: none|0`, ring token on `:focus-visible`; check `checkKeyboard` with `elementFromPoint`; axe `focus-order-semantics` is best-practice only.
pros: The kit had two defects the trial found: a false failure on a page with no controls, and a trap on the first stop that passed; the extension fixes both.

rules.statement: Contrast also holds in every reachable state.

reasoning.definition: The engine runs after each forced state of the six-states rule; the token contrast test is the earlier net.
pros: A test on the ready state passed (0 failures) while the error state failed (1).

rules.statement: Control borders and state graphics reach 3 to 1.

reasoning.definition: The kit computes the border or fill colour of each control and the focus ring against the ground at 3 to 1 (colour maths shared with the token contrast test); the text contrast rule covers text only. Engine rule `color-contrast` covers text only; check `checkControlContrast`.
pros: One site's case C5; held on the every-rule-binds ruling.

rules.statement: The declared accessibility stack catches every plant of the shared corpus, and a rule with no catcher is listed as an instruction.

reasoning.definition: A matrix runs 32 plants with fixed twins; a plant caught by no tool is listed as an instruction and the list can only fall. It runs once per kit change. Matrix script `matrix.mjs`.
pros: The corpus is the author's own, so the shape of the check is the finding.

rules.statement: APCA lightness contrast is printed beside the ratio and never gated.

reasoning.definition: The APCA package is `apca-w3`.
pros: WCAG 3's algorithm is undecided; a dark muted role measured 5.80 to 1 and Lc 41.8.

rules.statement: A Lighthouse run is a report and never a gate on score; only its byte assertion is a floor.

reasoning.definition: It runs in the release tier and its JSON is saved with the tag.
pros: One image with no alt text scored 0.84, so a score gate would pass a real fault.

rules.statement: Field markup is the design system's form field: every field has a visible label, the right input type and linked hints; an invalid field shows a linked message beside it and a summary, and what was typed stays.

reasoning.definition: Axe `label`, `aria-valid-attr-value` and `autocomplete-valid` run on every form page. The field part has a required label prop (omitting it is a type error) and linked hint and error ids; a form summary lists the errors. A journey submits invalid data and asserts each message is linked by `aria-describedby`, the summary lists them and the typed values remain. With no form the check prints "not applicable: 0 inputs" with the count. Record pages keep the record mode of the field. Counted element `<form>`; summary part `FormSummary`.
pros: No form exists to measure in either site (evidence D); the two source rules differ on where focus goes after submit.

rules.statement: On submit, focus moves to the first invalid control or to the summary.

reasoning.definition: Which of the two is a project parameter; the source reports disagree and the choice is open. Assertion on `document.activeElement`.
pros: v1 gave no reason beyond its evidence grade, Evidence B.

rules.statement: There is one form pattern and one server-to-field error mapping per project.

reasoning.definition: Template stack: native `<form>` and `FormData`, with a manifest ban on every form library. Component stack: one form library, whose import ban and field-error setter ban are react.client-state.2. A server 400 problem response maps to form and field errors through one helper that maps each field code to a message key; the server's message is not rendered, and no field error is set outside the mapping module.

rules.statement: Every affected story renders under a canary brand and a pseudo-locale and must change in both; a story with no brand or text surface takes an exemption that names a reason, a ticket and an expiry.

exemptions.reason: nothing in it can change under a canary brand or pseudo-locale; the exemption names a reason, a ticket and an expiry

reasoning.definition: This runs on the affected stories at land, never on the whole story set in the full tier. Shared words and tokens are proved by re-rendering under a different brand and an inflated pseudo-language.
pros: Without it, a word or colour that ignores the config still passes every test.

rules.statement: Component tests run in a real browser engine, and a DOM shim (jsdom, happy-dom or a later one) is not a dependency.

reasoning.definition: The test runner's browser mode (for example Vitest browser mode with Playwright) runs component and renderer tests in Chromium or another real engine. The dependency check refuses a package whose purpose is to imitate the DOM in Node; a new shim is one more name in the ban list.
pros: A shim passes layout, focus, events and styles that a browser would fail, so a green test says little about the page people see.

rules.statement: A change that alters what a person sees carries pictures of it at phone, tablet and desktop sizes (for example 390, 1024 and 1440 px) in light and dark, with links to the stories, and a done claim names its question.

reasoning.definition: The screenshot matrix of viewports and schemes is generated by the land gate, not typed into the change description; land refuses a UI change with no pictures.
pros: v1 gave no reason beyond its evidence grade, Evidence D.

rules.statement: The browser checks that find UI faults run at land for what the change can reach, not only by hand.

reasoning.definition: The land step reads the plan: a change touching a web path whose plan has no browser step fails. The picker is the reach map of the affected-gates rules; one site's habit of running its changed-journeys target is lifted into the land command.
pros: No fault in one site's record was found by its normal check; another site runs its verify target before a merge, unproven as a refusal.

rules.statement: The building agent renders and looks at its own page before asking for review.

pros: 21 of 72 faults in one site were found by the builder; the site's own check ends by saying to open the page.

rules.statement: Taste, hierarchy, tone and brand fit are judged against a written design rubric, hierarchy test first; an agent lens reads every surface, and a canvas screen that is exempt is judged by its own rubric.

reasoning.definition: Hierarchy test: one primary action, emphasis by taking away from what is secondary, labels only when needed, and no page that wraps itself in what the shell already gives. The rubric lens verdict is stored like the other lens verdicts.
pros: Faults found by the rubric in two sites (a recorded issue and a case). The rubric's content is provisional, because the book it draws on was read only in outline.

rules.statement: The operator signs a sample of surfaces plus every new surface, with a stored record.

reasoning.definition: New routes need a sign-off record entry; the check compares the route list with the sign-off file. Taste and hierarchy are judgement; only the presence of the sign-off is mechanical.
pros: The person looks at what the lens only flags.

rules.statement: Per-person state is private on a shared device.

pros: Three recorded cases in one site where one person's state showed to the next.

rules.statement: The web build output is static files where a daemon embeds it.

exemptions.reason: No daemon embeds the page: the engine embeds the built app and writes it out as files.

reasoning.definition: After the build a test asserts the output folder has no server entry, and the Go side's embed directive fails to compile when the directory is empty or absent.
pros: Held in two sites; an adapter emitting a server entry would make the embed a lie.

rules.statement: A variable a page reads is declared in a typed environment schema, secrets are reachable only on the server, only public-prefixed names reach the bundle, and a service base URL comes from one descriptor that throws when unset, never a hard-coded URL or fallback.

reasoning.definition: ESLint `no-restricted-syntax` on environment access (`import.meta.env`) outside the one schema module, with the framework's own schema as the framework side; a bundler exposes only the public prefix. An endpoint address is read from the typed schema, never hard-coded. The schema module and the public prefix are per framework: the template-stack form uses the framework's own environment schema, and the component-stack form (its bundler's public prefix) is react.config.1.
pros: And D; the outcome scan on the built output is the no-secret rule.

rules.statement: No secret reaches the bundle, and no secret sits in an environment file that the bundler inlines into the build.

reasoning.definition: gitleaks runs on the built output with redaction at land and release; findings are reported by rule and line only, never by value. An empty variable-prefix setting inlines every key into the bundle, so the rule also bans secrets in the stage environment files. A source-tree secret scan covers source. The plant fires `aws-access-token`; allow-lists must not use documented example strings.
pros: The documented AWS example key did not fire (the tool allows words like EXAMPLE), so plants must not use documented example strings. A minified single-line bundle was found. Entropy-only secrets without a known prefix may escape.

rules.statement: The built page is embedded, hashed files are immutable and the HTML entry revalidates.

exemptions.reason: No daemon embeds the page: the engine embeds the built app and writes it out as files.

reasoning.definition: A test in the shared helper asserts `Cache-Control: immutable` on hashed files and revalidation on the HTML entry; one site's web test is the lift.
pros: Held in one site.

rules.statement: A deployed page has someone listening: a health poll on its real address notifies a person when it fails, and failures per release are reported; staged rollout is not required.

exemptions.reason: The page has no address of its own, so nothing is listening for it: whoever hosts a copy owns its poll.

pros: The page shows a stale state when the server is down; this row is who hears. A page embedded in a daemon rests on the daemon's health.

rules.statement: Every story renders in a real browser with the accessibility engine at error; for a design system that is a push member, and for an application it runs at land.

reasoning.definition: web.accessibility.1 holds that every story passes the engine as an error in both themes. This line places it in the cycle. A design system's stories are its product, so they render at push, where 474 stories with the engine took 44 seconds. An application's stories are many and the render runs at land, with the plays (web.cycle.3). A story the engine skips carries an owner and an expiry (gates.exemptions.4).
pros: One organisation's design system shipped two versions with its stories unrun, and its consumer opened seven contrast tickets in eight days.

sources.where: Configure accessibility tests, the error level
sources.says: violations return a failing test in the Storybook UI and CLI/CI
test the rendering and behavior of your components in a real browser environment.

rules.statement: The story build is a member of the push tier.

reasoning.definition: A story build that fails is found at publish otherwise. It is a member with its cost listed, and the story render member declares it runs after it where it reads the built output (gates.command.28).
pros: One organisation's design system had its story build, 17.6 seconds, in no gate before the publish.

sources.where: Build Storybook as a static web application
sources.says: Storybook will create a static web application capable of being served by any web server.

rules.statement: For an application, story renders and plays run at land, the plays are counted in the report, and renders and plays share one browser page so a story is opened once per width.

reasoning.definition: gates.measures.6 holds that a green carries its counts; a play count that falls against the base fails landing. Opening a story for the render and again for the play doubles the time; the render reuses the play's page, so the verdicts of one pass serve the other.
pros: Eighteen story plays once went unrun in a green of one organisation's main web application, and renders reused 475 verdicts from the plays once they shared the page.

rules.statement: Token contrast is checked over every pair of tokens drawn together, in both themes, as one check at push.

reasoning.definition: web.tokens.8 holds the contrast ratios and that the check is a pure test over the tokens. This line holds its shape in the cycle: one member, every pair the roles allow (web.tokens.9), both themes, so a new token or a new ground is covered the day it lands and not when a consumer finds it.
pros: Seven contrast tickets in eight days came from a test that held one token pair, and one miss reached 61 stories in the consumer.

rules.statement: At push a small browser smoke set runs: the journeys that prove the page loads and the main path works, beside the other members at no wall cost; the member declares the network and its platform, and a skip is red at land.

reasoning.definition: The smoke set is a handful of journeys, chosen for what a cheaper test cannot see (tests.journeys.4), and it runs in the pool beside the build and the tests, so it adds nothing to the wall time when it is shorter than the longest member. The member carries net and os fields (gates.command.30); on a builder's machine with no browser it prints SKIPPED, and at land that skip is red. The full suite is a release member (web.cycle.6).
pros: Ten journeys of one project, 17.4 seconds, run beside its site check at no wall cost; browser gates in a no-network sandbox of another organisation failed 49 of 49 blocks with a network error nobody read as a skip.

rules.statement: At release the full browser suite runs sharded across the pool's workers, with the shards balanced by each journey's recorded duration and never by file count, and both browser engines run until the grid is green and balanced.

reasoning.definition: A shard by file puts the slow journeys in one shard and the suite waits for it. The runner records each journey's duration and the next run balances by it. The worker count is the pool's (gates.command.27); more shards on a loaded host only add contention. Both engines run at release until the grid has been green and the shards balanced; then the owner decides on the green numbers which engines stay. A release does not carry a known red journey; a tolerated red is a listed entry with an owner and an expiry (gates.exemptions.4, tests.flakes.6).
pros: One project's slowest shard fell from 1,573 seconds to about 1,261 when balanced by duration, and its grid was red three of three releases.

sources.says: To shard the test suite, pass --shard=x/y to the command line.

rules.statement: A browser journey waits on a condition through the runner's auto-wait and never on a sleep; a fixed budget scales by a printed load factor; and the page's own timers run on the runner's fake clock.

reasoning.definition: tests.runners.8 and tests.isolation.6 hold that no test waits out real time. In a browser the runner waits for the element to be ready before it acts, so a journey that sleeps is waiting twice. A budget that must be fixed (a page load) is multiplied by a factor from the host's load and the factor prints, so a red under load is read as one. The page's own timers (a poll, a toast, a debounce) run on the runner's clock, so a wait of seconds takes none.
pros: Fixed 10 and 15 second browser budgets of one organisation ran out at load 65, and a 5 second idle wait of one project was paid twice per journey.

sources.says: It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action.
Utilizing Clock functionality allows developers to manipulate and control time within tests

rules.statement: A journey's teardown removes every route handler it added, so a poll in flight cannot fail the next journey, and an action re-resolves its locator after the component's ready mark.

reasoning.definition: A route handler left on the page answers a poll that fires after the journey ended, and the failure lands on whichever journey runs next. The teardown fixture unroutes all handlers and waits for the ones in flight. A locator held across a re-render points at an element that is gone; the runner re-resolves a locator each time it acts, so the action waits for the component's ready mark and then locates.
pros: A poll left routed after one journey failed the next in one organisation, and a held element handle failed on the re-render.

sources.says: Removes all routes created with page.route() and page.routeFromHAR().
Every time a locator is used for an action, an up-to-date DOM element is located in the page.

rules.statement: At commit every link between pages and to an asset resolves offline, and for a docs repository every Markdown link too; the first run freezes a reviewed baseline of the broken links that exist, and it only shrinks.

reasoning.definition: docs.links.1 holds that docs have no broken file link, checked offline in the gate. This line places the check at commit for pages, where it took 0.16 seconds for 1,747 inputs, and gives it a baseline (gates.ratchets.1) for a repository that already breaks it, so the member is green on the day it lands and red on the first new broken link. External links are a release step, never a gate member (docs.links.1). The secrets scan of the staged diff runs at commit as for every project (supply.secrets.1).
pros: One organisation's design pages had 1,752 broken references on the first run, 1,733 of them from one file; a check with no baseline would stay red and be ignored.

sources.says: Only check local files and block network requests

rules.statement: At commit the ledger or index that lists the pages matches the pages on disk: every page is listed and every listing is a page.

reasoning.definition: A repository of pages keeps a list of them, as an index page or a data file. The check compares the list with the files both ways in 0.16 seconds. docs.freshness.1 holds that an index is generated and never written by hand; where the ledger is generated this check is the generated-files diff, and where it is written this check is what keeps it true.
pros: A page not in the ledger is a page nobody finds, and a ledger row with no page is a broken link on the index.

rules.statement: At push every page has a rendered golden at one width a person reads, updated only by a person reading the diff, a narrow-width property that the page does not overflow sideways, and the accessibility engine over it.

reasoning.definition: tests.journeys.8 holds one golden width and properties at the narrower ones for any screen; this line is its form for a page. The golden is the rendered page at the width a person reads; the property at a phone width is no horizontal overflow; and the engine runs over each page as web.accessibility.1 has it for an application. Neither was measured on the host that studied the stack, which had no browser run.
pros: A page with no rendered check changes under its author's eyes only, and a page that overflows at a phone width is read by nobody on a phone.

sources.says: Axe is an accessibility testing engine for websites and other HTML-based user interfaces.

rules.statement: A repository with no code has no push tier beyond the commit checks, and its members file says so.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.23 holds that a repository with nothing to run says so in its members file, so an empty file and a missing file differ. For a docs repository the push tier is the commit members run again on the whole tree, and the file lists them and nothing else. A push tier that runs nothing and says nothing is a green nobody can read.
pros: One repository of one organisation had no file at all and 36 of 38 checked nothing at commit; a file that says what is not run is the difference between nothing to do and nothing done.

rules.statement: At release the pack and the site index rebuild on a fresh clone, and a build that skips either on a clean clone fails.

reasoning.definition: gates.command.21 holds that every member passes on a fresh clone after the documented setup. A pages repository that bundles its pages into a pack and an index must build both from the clone alone; a build that finds no earlier output and skips is a build that never ran. The release member clones the tag (supply.release.10) and checks the two outputs exist and match the pages.
pros: One organisation's design pages skipped both the pack and the index on a clean clone, so the published set was whatever the last machine had built.

rules.statement: The generated route tree is committed, carries a no-check banner, is never edited by hand, is excluded from lint, format, import-graph and size tools, and a regenerate-and-diff check fails the gate when it is stale.

reasoning.definition: The gate runs the router's generator and then a diff of the generated file; any difference fails. The generated file starts with a banner, checked by a header grep, and sits on the ignore list of the linter, the formatter, the unused-code tool and the size tools. A generator that yields no routes fails: the number of routes in the tree must be above zero and equal the number of route files.
pros: A hand edit to generated code is lost at the next generation, and a stale tree routes to pages that no longer exist. The banner and a build with no inline script were tried on one router plugin version; the check has never run on a real React tree.

rules.statement: Links and navigation use typed destinations and params: a wrong path, a missing param or an unknown search key fails the type check, and a bare string or template-literal destination is banned.

reasoning.definition: The router's type registration is what makes a wrong path fail the compiler. A lint bans a string literal as a link destination and a navigate call without the typed form. A link to another module's route goes through the typed route reference, so it is not an import of that module. An id that looks like a number (leading zeros) round-trips through a link and the URL as the same string; a unit test holds it.
pros: A typo in a path compiles in an untyped router and fails only when someone follows the link. In a trial the typed router rejected five of five wrong usages and a second router package rejected none.

rules.statement: Every route declares a schema for its search parameters, and they are validated by the router's search validator where they enter.

reasoning.definition: The schema is declared in the route file and covers every key the route reads; an unknown key is dropped or refused, never read as a raw string. A parameter library that wraps the browser's search string may be used only through the router's adapter until the project has decided its end state.
pros: The URL is input from outside; an unvalidated search value reaches a query as the wrong type. This is the React router form of the rule that a page's place is carried in the URL.

rules.statement: The router is built by one factory where all router settings are set once, and the root route is safe to render on the server: no browser global at module scope.

reasoning.definition: Pending thresholds, preload, stale time and the default error and not-found views are set in the factory file, and a call that creates a router anywhere else fails. Gated loaders do not depend on a component being mounted. Module scope in the root route and everything it imports touches no `window` or `document`.
pros: Settings spread over route files drift apart, and a browser global at module scope breaks any non-browser render of the tree, which includes tests and static builds.

rules.statement: A route loader delegates to the query client and the router keeps no second cache; an asynchronous cache restore finishes before the router mounts, and a cache entry a loader creates carries the same flags as one a hook creates.

reasoning.definition: A raw `fetch` in a route file is banned: the loader calls the query client's ensure call (`queryClient.ensureQueryData`). A loader-created entry carries the flags a hook-created one does. A test checks that the mount happens after the persisted cache has been restored. The flags that must match are the freshness and gating settings that the hook form sets, so a loader entry is not read as stale or ungated by the component.
pros: Two caches show two answers for one resource, and a restore that finishes after mount flashes empty or stale data and can revive a gated read.

rules.statement: Every route has an error view and a not-found view, set once as router defaults, and scroll position is restored per history entry.

reasoning.definition: The factory sets the default error and not-found components (`defaultErrorComponent`, `defaultNotFoundComponent`); a lint over the route table checks that every route inherits or sets one. Three journeys hold it: a loader that throws shows the error view, an unknown URL shows the not-found view, and going Back restores the scroll position of that history entry (`scrollRestoration: true`).
pros: A route with no error view renders a blank page when its loader fails.

rules.statement: A deep link survives sign-in, so the destination is kept and restored after authentication.

exemptions.reason: No sign-in exists, so a deep link has nothing to survive.

reasoning.definition: A journey opens a deep link signed out, signs in and must land on that destination, through the router's redirect with the stored destination. The blocker form is in react.routing.8. A sign-in that always lands on the home page fails.
pros: From a research report. No project has a sign-in yet to measure.

rules.statement: A page with unsaved input blocks navigation through the router's blocker, not only tab close.

reasoning.definition: The blocker is the router's (`useBlocker`), so in-app navigation asks before it discards input; the browser's before-unload prompt covers only closing the tab. A test types into a form, navigates by the router and asserts the block.
pros: A browser prompt alone lets a link click lose a long form silently.

rules.statement: On a route change focus moves to the page heading or the main landmark and the document title changes, and the journey asserts both.

reasoning.definition: After each route change the active element is the page heading or `main`, and the title is the route's own title. The router's head management (`<Scripts>` and head tags) is tested, not assumed.
pros: A single-page route change does not move focus or announce a new page; a screen-reader user hears nothing. The words document title had no other holder in the catalogue.

rules.statement: Full-stack router features (server functions, server rendering) are not used unless a decision approves them; the default is a plain client-side router.

reasoning.definition: A heavier rendering mode is a pilot: it needs a recorded decision and its own pack of checks before the first use. The static form of the same rule for the other framework is that a static site uses no on-demand rendering.
pros: A rendering mode that is not yet needed adds a server, an adapter and a failure surface nobody has measured.

rules.statement: A route file holds route configuration plus one page import from the owning module's public entry, from its own route group only, and `main.tsx` only wires.

reasoning.definition: The router form of web.structure.3 (entry files only wire): route files and `main.tsx` are entry files. A route file declares its route with the route helper and imports exactly one page from the owning module's public entry, from its own route group; it holds no client call, no query hook and no markup. A function declaration over the `thin-route` line limit kept in rule data fails.
pros: Logic in an entry or a route file escapes the module's tests and boundaries; both entries complied when counted.

rules.statement: Server state lives in one query cache with a stated freshness, reached through gated hooks; none of it is copied to local state, and no second cache library is used.

reasoning.definition: The query lint plugin runs at error level with its exhaustive-deps, stable-client, no-rest-destructuring and no-unstable-deps rules. A lint for derived state flags server data copied into state by an effect (`no-derived-state`, `no-initialize-state` of the you-might-not-need-an-effect plugin; rule names from its README, not run). A restricted-imports rule bans the other server-state libraries (swr, apollo, rtk-query). No hand-made fetch cache exists. A gated read is never revived by a refetch, which is swept rather than linted. A hand store on a console page is an instruction, not a check.
pros: Two stores for one resource show two answers, and a copy in local state goes stale without a signal. The import ban and the lint hold the mechanical half; the gated-read half is held by a sweep.

sources.where: You Might Not Need an Effect

rules.statement: Cache freshness settings (stale and garbage-collection times) come only from one policy file, a query key's first segment comes from a key file, and a key namespace is declared once.

reasoning.definition: A literal stale time or gc time anywhere else fails; a query key built with an inline first segment fails; two key files that claim the same namespace fail. The underlying rule is that a value that decides behaviour has one home.
pros: Freshness set per call site drifts, and two key namespaces that collide invalidate each other's data.

rules.statement: Fan-out reads use the gated multi-query hook, and results are joined by id through a map, never by array position.

reasoning.definition: The combine function is hoisted so it is stable between renders. A position-based join breaks the moment the order of the requests or the responses changes.
pros: Results joined by position are silently attached to the wrong record once order changes.

rules.statement: A gated infinite query de-duplicates by id when it flattens pages, and a cursor is never put in a plain query key.
