reasoning.definition: Pages from an outside source can overlap when records are added between requests; flattening without a de-duplication shows a record twice. The cursor belongs to the infinite query's page parameter, not to the key of a plain query.
pros: A cursor in a plain key creates a new cache entry per page and loses the list; overlapping pages repeat records.

rules.statement: No `useEffect` calls fetch; data comes from the query hooks.

reasoning.definition: A lint selects an effect call whose callback holds a `fetch` call (selector with descendant). It is partial: it misses a helper called inside the effect. The stronger form is typed lint that flags a floating promise inside an effect.
pros: An effect that fetches has no cache, no dedupe, no cancel and races on fast navigation.

sources.where: You Might Not Need an Effect

rules.statement: Client state that changes lives in one store; context is only for passing values down.

reasoning.definition: One store library, no second one and no bespoke store class. The package ban lists the other client stores (redux, jotai, valtio, recoil, mobx, nanostores, zustand), and the external-store hook is restricted outside the store file. Whether a context holds changing state is a judgement that no tool makes.
pros: Two stores for client state drift apart, and state in context re-renders every consumer. Half of the rule holds by package ban; the context half is a model lens.

sources.where: scaling up with reducer and context

rules.statement: A React program uses one form library, TanStack Form, with every other form library banned, and sets field errors only in the one server-error mapping module.

reasoning.definition: `no-restricted-imports` and a manifest ban on the other form libraries: `formik`, `final-form`, `conform`, and `react-hook-form` with `@hookform/resolvers` (the replaced pick). `@tanstack/react-form` is the chosen one (before the TanStack-always ruling it was the banned one). `.setError(` calls outside the mapping module are banned, so a server 400 problem response reaches form and field errors only through the one helper of web.forms.3. Schema validation follows web.forms.4; in the form library's current major, output that differs from input is parsed in the submit handler.
pros: With no form in either site the check is vacuous until the detector sees one. Two form libraries, or field errors set by hand in pages, give two patterns for fields, validation and server errors.

rules.statement: A derived value is computed during render, never stored in state and synced by an effect.

reasoning.definition: The lint `no-derived-state` from `eslint-plugin-react-you-might-not-need-an-effect` (1.1.0) fails an effect that sets state from other state or props. This is the React form of web.states.15 (a derived value is computed, not stored and synced).
pros: Stored derived state drifts from the value it was derived from.

rules.statement: A component that fetches is a page orchestrator or a container with a marked name, never a file in the presentational components folder.

reasoning.definition: Pages orchestrate and containers carry a marked file name; leaf parts take data as props and import no data layer. The import rule is the one that holds it: the presentational folder may not depend on the api, store or query folders.
pros: A leaf part that fetches cannot be reused or tested without the network, and data access spreads into the design system.

rules.statement: Interactive parts come from one unstyled accessible primitive library; nobody hand-writes a combobox, menu or similar widget.

reasoning.definition: Widget roles written by hand (`<div role="combobox">`; combobox, menu, menuitem, listbox, option, tablist, tab, dialog, tooltip) written by hand outside the shared parts package fail. Other primitive libraries (Radix, react-aria-components, Ark, Headless UI, cmdk, vaul) and the old `@base-ui-components/react` package name are banned in the manifest; hand-written widgets are replaced by the library's. The threshold for a hand copy (more than 3) is rule data with its reason, not a project's choice. A copy-in component set is allowed on the same base when its source lives in the shared parts package. The dialog behaviour is held by the accessibility rules either way; this rule is also the component-stack lint of web.accessibility.11: the primitive library's dialog is the overlay, and a hand-rolled `role="dialog"` outside an import from the primitive fails.
pros: Hand-built widgets drift from the accessibility contract: in the source a hand-built combobox was 416 lines and a date picker 371 lines. The chosen library gave zero violations under the script and style policy.

rules.statement: HTML that comes from data renders only through a markdown renderer and a sanitiser under the trusted-types default policy; no component uses raw `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.

reasoning.definition: The renderer is react-markdown with dompurify as the sanitiser. The raw-markup funnel names the property so the React recommended lint set flags it (`react/no-danger`); the one funnel module is the only place it may appear. The policy for scripts never contains unsafe-inline.
pros: Markup built from data is the way untrusted input reaches the page as script.

rules.statement: No component passes a `style` prop to a DOM element; styling comes from token-generated classes.

reasoning.definition: `react/forbid-dom-props` with `style` as an error (`react/forbid-dom-props: style`); `forbid-dom-props` is component-stack only. This is the component-stack form of the inline-style ban in web.tokens.3 (no colour literal) and web.tokens.15 (theme from tokens); the template stack holds it with html-validate `no-inline-style`.
pros: An inline style carries colours, sizes and fonts past the token theme and the colour-literal lint; a regex that matched only some shapes reported zero and missed the rest.

rules.statement: The hooks lint pack runs as errors: rules of hooks, exhaustive dependencies, the compiler-compatibility rule and the query plugin's stable-client and key rules.

reasoning.definition: Libraries the compiler cannot memoise (a form library's `watch`, the old table hook, the virtualiser) live in one module each under a path-scoped override with an expiry date, not an inline disable. The expiry sits in a data file that a check reads; an override past its date fails.
pros: A missing dependency or a conditional hook is a bug that shows only at run time. Tried on eight planted files (three incompatible-library warnings, two query errors, four clean cases); never run on a real tree.

rules.statement: The React lint set carries the plugin's recommended rules (keys, no nested component definitions, no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`) beside the hooks and query plugins.

reasoning.definition: The set is `jsx-key`, `no-unstable-nested-components` and `no-danger`, as errors, with one plant per rule. The raw-markup funnel is the only exemption for `no-danger`. The choice between the plugin and its active alternative is made at adoption and re-planted.
pros: The hooks and query plugins alone do not catch a list without keys or a component defined inside a component. The rule was added when the catalogue's search found no holder for it (evidence D).

rules.statement: JSX meets the strict accessibility lint set, covering labels, roles, keyboard handlers, alt text, ambiguous link text and links that open elsewhere.

reasoning.definition: The jsx-a11y rules run in their strict preset as errors, through the ESLint 10 fork of the same rules (`eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y-x`) because the original plugin's peers stop at ESLint 9. The set covers no image without alt text, role mismatch, click without a key (key-less click handlers on `.tsx`), positive tabindex, empty link, untitled iframe and autofocus (web.accessibility.8). The link rules of web.forms.7 are `jsx-a11y-x/anchor-ambiguous-text` (bans "here" and "click here") and `react/jsx-no-target-blank`. The Astro form is a template lint that must prove it loaded its rules.
pros: A label, role or key handler missing in markup is found cheaply at lint time, before the accessibility run in a browser.

rules.statement: Specs and stories render through one harness; the memory router is banned outside it, stories use the shared providers with a route parameter instead of their own router, and the harness registers the router's types.

reasoning.definition: The harness builds the app with its providers and router. A test that builds a private router or imports the memory router outside the harness fails. Registration of the router types in the harness keeps typed links working in tests.
pros: A private router in a test hides provider and routing bugs that the real app has.

rules.statement: Tests do not stub the network by hand; the sanctioned mock is a request-handler mock fed by server samples.

reasoning.definition: A lint bans `vi.mock('fetch')` and `vi.stubGlobal('fetch')` in tests (the double-quoted forms `vi.stubGlobal("fetch")` and `vi.mock("...fetch")` too), and the manifest bans nock and mockttp there. The request-handler mock (msw) is the sanctioned form, with handlers fed by sample responses taken from the server.
pros: A hand stub tests the stub; a sample from the server tests the contract.

rules.statement: Every exported part of the shared kit renders with no provider and no wrapper, through the component render test, and its words come from the part's own defaults.

reasoning.definition: Component render test: `@testing-library/react`. A test renders every exported part from the catalogue with no provider and no wrapper and asserts it does not throw and its words come from the part's own defaults (a strings object with English defaults that the host may override in part). A part that reads a context must give the context a default.
pros: The donor's design system added a provider and an English defaults object for this at its 0.13.0 release. A part that needs a provider breaks every host that does not mount it.

rules.statement: Every page has a sibling story file with the stories Default, Loading, Empty, Error, NoPermission and Phone390, plus Allowed, Denied, CheckingAccess and Degraded.

exemptions.reason: There is no Allowed, Denied, CheckingAccess or Degraded state to write a story for.

reasoning.definition: The story-tool form of web.testing.8 (an example per page state): the sibling story file sits next to the page file, and the required story names are its exports. Phone390 is the phone-width story.
pros: A page with no example for a state has never been looked at in that state.

rules.statement: The story tool is the single test runner through its Vitest addon: every story renders and its play function passes in one pass, and every affected story also passes the config proof.

reasoning.definition: Runner addon: `addon-vitest`. The config proof is the canary brand and pseudo-locale (en-XA) rule. The platform's single runner is Vitest; this is the React stack's story-tool binding of web.testing.11.
pros: Two runners split the evidence and double the maintenance.

rules.statement: A budget exists for render cost under churn on any live list, counted in commits and rendered rows, not milliseconds.

reasoning.definition: A test counts commits and rendered rows for one update to a live list and asserts the count against a declared render budget. A rule-table list names each live list; a list with no matching render-budget test fails the pairing scan. The counter is the React Profiler, in a Vitest test (browser or jsdom).
pros: Solid's keyed list passed behaviour and failed churn; a count is deterministic, unlike time.

rules.statement: Route-level code splitting is on per area, and development tooling never ships in the production bundle.

reasoning.definition: The router's automatic splitting setting (`autoCodeSplitting` true) is read back from the Vite config, and the entry chunk is held at the core budget of the web part's byte budget, so an unsplit app breaches it; chunk count is a report. A test-only module, and the router and query devtools, are absent from the non-test build.
pros: No route budgets are asked for in the source; the core budget holds it.

rules.statement: A variable a page reads is declared in a typed schema module, environment access outside that module fails, and only `VITE_`-prefixed names reach the bundle.

reasoning.definition: The same `no-restricted-syntax` rule as web.delivery.8 on `import.meta.env` member access outside the typed schema module; the bundler (Vite) exposes only `VITE_` names, which is the framework side. The outcome scan of the built output (`dist/`) is the no-secret-in-bundle rule of the web part.
pros: The React twin of the template-stack rule. `VITE_` and `import.meta.env` had 0 hits in the catalogue, so the rule is held for the absence.

rules.statement: The production build is the push tier's build member, and a bundle-size budget runs after it as its own member that declares it runs after the build.

reasoning.definition: The build proves the application compiles and bundles; the budget reads its output (web.speed.1). The budget is a member of its own, so a budget failure names the budget and a build failure the build, and its `after` edge is the one ordering the pool shows (gates.command.18, gates.command.28).
pros: A build that is a step of the test command, or a budget that rebuilds, runs the same work twice and hides which one failed.

sources.says: When it is time to deploy your app for production, simply run the vite build command.

rules.statement: Heavy page mounts are spread across test files, so the workers share them instead of one file holding the path.

reasoning.definition: A file of fifty stories or page mounts runs on one worker however many the pool has, and it sets the member's time. Splitting it across files lets the runner spread the mounts (tests.runners.4). The split is by page or by story group, not by count alone, so a reader still finds the file.
pros: One file of 55 stories took 33.6 seconds in one organisation's design system, on one worker, while the others idled.

rules.statement: A large document a test reads is parsed once per file, and a scan over the whole repository belongs to the gate, not to a test.

reasoning.definition: A test that parses a token document, a route table or a schema per case does the same work per case (tests.runners.5). A test that walks the repository is the tree-reading package of this stack (tests.runners.10), and where its check is a rule of the gate, it is a gate member with a count, not a test hidden in the unit suite.
pros: Repository-wide scans inside unit tests were among the slowest files of one organisation's React applications.

rules.statement: Shared dependencies are pre-bundled and the bundler's cache is kept between runs, in every tier.

reasoning.definition: The bundler pre-bundles the dependencies once and keeps them in its cache folder; a run that starts with an empty cache pays that again for its first file. The cache folder is kept between tiers and between runs, and is never pruned by a member (gates.command.24), and the tool's settings are the same in every tier (gates.command.25).
pros: The first story of each file was 74 percent of one organisation's design-system story time, paid again on every cold run.

sources.says: Vite caches the pre-bundled dependencies in node_modules/.vite.

rules.statement: A request budget per page or story is a property checked in the same run as the render, never a second run.

reasoning.definition: The render already opens the page; the count of requests it made is read from that run and judged against the budget, as the narrow-width properties are judged on the same render (tests.journeys.8). A second run for the count is the page rendered twice.
pros: A count taken in a second run doubles the render time and can disagree with the first.

rules.statement: A static Astro project uses no actions and no server islands, because both need on-demand rendering and an adapter.

reasoning.definition: A test loads the Astro config and fails on an adapter, on an output mode other than static, and on a `src/actions` directory. A lint on `.astro` files fails on a `server:defer` island. A new rendering mode is admitted only with its own pack and a decision.
pros: On-demand rendering adds a server and an adapter to a site that was built to be a folder of files. The rule was rated C from the framework's own guides; no site uses either feature yet.

rules.statement: The framework generates the script policy, so `script-src` lists hashes and never contains `unsafe-inline`.

reasoning.definition: The Astro security.csp option is set in the config. A test parses each built page for the policy meta element and fails when `script-src` lacks hashes or holds `unsafe-inline`. Islands stay banned. An unhashed inline script in a template is in no hash list, so the browser refuses it at run time: a loud failure the violation listener catches, not a bypass.
pros: A policy that allows inline scripts gives no protection against injected ones. The option was tried on one framework version: four pages built, a policy meta element on the two counted, no script on the plain page and two inline scripts on an island page.

rules.statement: Content a page reads at build time has a schema, and a bad entry fails the build.

reasoning.definition: Each collection is declared with a collection definition and a zod schema. An entry that is missing a required field, or has a wrong type such as a date, fails `astro build`. The build itself refuses; there is no separate check, and the plant is run once to prove it.
pros: Content errors found after deploy are published errors. The rule is rated C from the framework guide; no site uses collections yet.

rules.statement: In an Astro project the inline-script attribute is used only where exempt, and style blocks are linted.

reasoning.definition: (a) ESLint no-restricted-syntax on the `is:inline` attribute in `.astro` files, through the Astro parser, with a path exemption list. (b) Stylelint with the HTML parser lints `<style>` blocks in `.astro` files with the same rule set as other styles, so a colour literal there fails.
pros: Neither hole had a row in the stack list (evidence D). Under the generated script policy an unhashed inline script fails loudly at run time, so the lint is a convenience as well as a net.

rules.statement: At commit every JSON file of the theme parses, comments allowed where the platform allows them, and every schema block in a section parses.

reasoning.definition: A theme's settings, templates and locales are JSON, and each section carries a schema block the platform reads. A file that does not parse is a page that does not render, found at publish otherwise. The check read 395 files in 0.06 seconds on the measuring host. It reads and never writes (gates.command.28).
pros: A broken JSON file or schema block reaches the live theme if nothing parses it first.

rules.statement: Every locale file has every key of the default locale; a new gap fails, and the gaps that exist today sit in a reviewed baseline with an owner that only shrinks.

reasoning.definition: gates.ratchets.1 holds that debt is a shrink-only list frozen at adoption. The parity check compares each locale's keys with the default's, and the baseline holds the missing keys per file at adoption, so the member is green on the day it lands and red on the first new gap. The baseline's length prints in the report.
pros: Eleven locale files of one organisation's theme miss 3 to 9 of 315 keys today; a check with no baseline would stay red and be ignored.

rules.statement: At push every render, include, section and asset reference resolves to a file, and every block tag is closed.

reasoning.definition: A reference to a snippet that does not exist and an unclosed conditional each render as an error on the live page. The check walks the templates, resolves each reference against the theme's folders and counts the tag pairs; a prototype did both in 0.06 seconds. It is a push member because it reads the whole theme, and it reads and never writes.
pros: A missing snippet and an unclosed conditional were both found by a prototype of this check in one organisation's theme, and nothing else would have found them before the page rendered.

rules.statement: The platform's theme linter runs at push with the repository's own config, as a member beside the reference check.

reasoning.definition: The linter knows the platform's objects, filters and deprecations, which the reference check does not; the reference check runs in milliseconds, which the linter may not. Both are members, so a failure names one. The linter's cost was not measured on the host that studied the stack, so its moment is push until a measurement says otherwise (gates.command.3).
pros: A theme with no linter in its gate ships the deprecations and the misused filters the platform's own tool would have named.

rules.statement: At push the layout files are scanned for secrets, with an allowlist that holds a third-party widget's public embed id and nothing that is a credential.

reasoning.definition: supply.secrets.1 holds the secrets scan; a theme's layout files are where a script tag with a key would sit. A public embed id of a widget looks like a secret to a scanner and is not one; it goes on the allowlist with its owner (gates.ratchets.1), and the list prints its length.
pros: A trial secrets scan found hits that were not credentials in three repositories of one organisation, and a theme's layout carries exactly the kind of public id that a scanner flags.

sources.says: You can ignore specific findings by creating a .gitleaksignore file at the root of your repo.

rules.statement: A release pushes the theme to an unpublished theme and renders the home, a product and a cart page as a preview before anything is published; a change is never deployed straight to the live theme, and the gate holds that rule, not a script alone.

reasoning.definition: The store's command line pushes to a theme by id. The release member pushes to an unpublished one, then a render member fetches the three pages from the preview and fails on an error or an empty page. The live theme changes only by publishing the previewed one. A repository script that does this is the convention; the release tier is the rule, so a push that names the live theme fails the member. The cost was not measured on the host that studied the stack.
pros: A theme deployed straight to the live store is live before anyone has seen a page of it.

rules.statement: The entry layer (command, handler, daemon route) never opens, reads or writes a store directly and never imports a storage client; it calls a typed function of the store's one package.

reasoning.definition: A repository test lists packages that import the database package, the driver or a storage client, or write to state paths, against an allow list that only shrinks. Engine parts bind this rule for their client: the DynamoDB part forbids the SDK outside the store layer, the Postgres part the database client.
pros: When entry code reaches the store directly, key building, conditions, retries and error mapping are re-implemented in each entry. One Go repository already held that only its index package imports the database package.

rules.statement: A store port is agnostic at the level of intent, not of engine: the consumer declares it, narrow, with domain verbs, domain values and typed failures, and states its guarantee; an atomic act is one named method.

reasoning.definition: The adapter uses every strength of the engine inside the method. Rule data names the store ports, and on those a type check bans the generic verbs Get, Put, Exec, Query and Do, SQL string parameters, untyped maps and the database package's types, and finds Begin, Tx, Commit and Rollback in method names. Off a store port those verbs mean nothing (6 of 8 hits in a trial were process or guest verbs). A type-based scan of core exported signatures resolves the underlying type, and a type parameter is not an untyped value. A report lists core functions that take a port and also branch. Error-text matching is a report only: it had no true hit in 10 and is beaten for free by copying the text into a variable. The review asks: name one capability of this engine the port forbids the core to use; name the second engine and where it is written down; are these domain verbs or storage verbs; what does the port say about failure. Example of a banned port method: Exec(sql: string, ...args). Typed failures are named values such as not-found and version-mismatch.
pros: A generic query method keeps the driver out of the core but carries the engine's shape. The evidence strains the ruling: seams earn their keep through testability far more than through swapping engines. SQL detection is weak because a struct field holding SQL passes.

rules.statement: A store is opened in one place that sets its modes and error mapping, and a test reads them back.

exemptions.reason: It opens no store.

reasoning.definition: For an embedded file store the modes are write-ahead log, a bounded busy timeout, foreign keys on as the connection default, immediate write transactions and one writer connection. Turning foreign keys off is banned outside the one rebuild runner, DSN strings included. A busy failure is typed (store.seams.2) and a store with a manual checkpoint says why. A store that cannot be rebuilt sets the full-sync pragmas unconditionally and the read-back asserts them. What a caller does on busy is a review question. Opening a store outside the store package is counted and is zero. The pragmas for full sync are fullfsync and checkpoint_fullfsync. The literal scan matches foreign_keys=OFF and the DSN forms foreign_keys(OFF) and foreign_keys(ON), by regex foreign_keys\s*(=|\()\s*(0|off), firing on OFF and silent on ON.
pros: One Go program lacked the immediate transaction mode and error classification. Through the pure-Go driver both full-sync pragmas read 0, unlike the command-line client, and no repository set them; the clause binds no store yet because an unrebuildable store is a plain file (store.seams.6).

rules.statement: Who writes each persisted store, and which programs a flow includes, are recorded as data and a tool walks the list.

exemptions.reason: Nothing is persisted.

reasoning.definition: A list file per program is compared with writers found by a scan. It is a measure until the list exists, then a gate: an unlisted store opening fails.
pros: Without a list, a store has writers nobody knows about. No list exists today.

sources.where: ch. 9 assigning data ownership and ch. 11

rules.statement: A schema number lives once per program; a program that reads another's schema pins the number it understands in its adapter and refuses a higher one with a typed error, never by probing help text or guessing from a field.

reasoning.definition: The scan greps a struct field matching Schema\s+int\s+ with a json:"schema" tag (regex Schema\s+int\s+`[^`]*json:"schema), silent on a field such as Name string with json:"name". The help probe is a call of the other program with --help in non-test code. The silent control is the field Name string json:"name".
pros: Eight to 19 files per program held a schema number. One program probed another's help text to learn its schema, which is the known positive for the probe scan.

rules.statement: A store says in its package comment whether it can be rebuilt, its durability setting and who runs a checkpoint; a store that cannot be rebuilt is a plain, versioned, append-only file.

pros: The choice of how to hold data depends on whether it can be re-derived, and without a stated answer backups and durability are guesses.

rules.statement: Every path, file name and identifier of persistent state is made in one function of one package, from the program's name.

exemptions.reason: It has no state of its own.

reasoning.definition: No literal for .local, Library, XDG_ or /var/lib appears elsewhere. The check is a forbidigo or AST test on those literals outside the paths package, with a shrink-only count.
pros: Seven places in one repository spelled the XDG rule and nine sites another one /var/lib; paths were resolved by five rules in at least seven places.

rules.statement: Every file a program writes, state or config, is replaced whole only by the atomic write: written to a temporary file in the same folder, flushed, renamed into place and its folder flushed, with the original mode and owner kept and a link written where it points; a bare write, rename or create onto such a path, and a new hand-written temp-then-rename, are violations.

reasoning.definition: The rule covers a person's config that a command edits as much as the program's own state: the atomic write keeps the mode and owner of the file it replaces and, when the path is a symbolic link, writes the file the link points to and leaves the link. A new kind of file a program writes goes through the same helper; the rule does not list kinds. Banned outside the owner package: os.WriteFile, os.Rename, os.Create, os.CreateTemp, os.Link, (*os.Root).Rename and unix.Renameat, with a per-file shrink-only allow list for legitimate non-state uses (counts today per repository: WriteFile 1 to 23, Rename 1 to 14, Link 0 to 9). Atomic-write libraries that do not flush the folder are not imported. An ast-grep shape rule of the same intent stays as advice, with its five known bypasses kept as fixtures. The root-confined variant stays in the Linux-only programs. Verified under golangci-lint with forbidigo: the selector is flagged where it is taken, so f := os.Rename and r.Rename on an os.Root both fire.
pros: Thirteen bodies replace a whole file and twelve of them are outside the owner; 52 non-test WriteFile sites exist and 14 replace a state file in place. A helper that makes the temp file elsewhere is caught only because CreateTemp is banned too. A config rewritten by a bare write loses its mode, its owner or the link a person made, and a crash halfway leaves half a file.

rules.statement: The atomic write keeps its promise and proves it: a unique temp name, the file flushed, rename, the folder flushed, the temp removed on failure, with a crash-injection test after each step.

exemptions.reason: Only the owner of the atomic write carries it.

reasoning.definition: A weaker promise is a named option, not a copy.
pros: A write that skips a flush looks atomic until the machine stops. One program's test already plants a bypass of the shared write.

rules.statement: A move of user data (copy, then remove the source) flushes the copy and its folder before it removes the source.

exemptions.reason: There is no source to lose.

pros: One program's copy-across removes the source after a copy it never flushed, though its comment says the copy is on disk (read, not run).

rules.statement: An append-only journal line is one write ending in a newline; a torn last line is ended before the next append, and the reader skips and counts what it cannot read.

reasoning.definition: No rotation library for a multi-writer journal. The append flag is banned outside the journal package, and a shape rule finds a seek to end followed by a write in one function. The shape rule matches $F.Seek(0, io.SeekEnd) in a function that also calls .Write(; it misses a variable such as whence := io.SeekEnd.
pros: Fourteen production files in six repositories open with the append flag (19 sites). In a trial of four append shapes, a rotation library lost records under three writers.

rules.statement: A secret is written with its final mode in a folder only the owner can list, and the program refuses a file that is wider.

exemptions.reason: There is nothing to protect.

reasoning.definition: The mode is 0600, or 0640 with a named group.
pros: One program writes a file that will hold an API key with a truncating write and an existence check, leaving a window where it is wider than intended.

rules.statement: A state file on a network or FUSE file system is refused where the format needs a local disk (a write-ahead log or a lock file).

exemptions.reason: It has no format that needs a local disk.

pros: A log or lock on a network file system gives silent corruption or no exclusion.

rules.statement: A path from outside (a flag, a config value, an environment variable or a request) is confined before use, and an archive or folder from outside is unpacked under traversal, link and size limits, with each refused entry named.

reasoning.definition: Confine with filepath.IsLocal or a rooted file system handle (os.Root), or the platform's equivalent in another language. An archive, an imported folder or a feedback bundle from outside is untrusted: an entry whose path leaves the target, a symbolic or hard link, an entry over the per-entry size limit and a total over the archive limit are each refused by name, and nothing is written for a refused archive.
pros: A path from a caller can escape its directory. The traversal word had no hits in the catalogue before this row, and the security analyser's rule for variable paths fires on every ordinary call (3 hits on 3), so it cannot gate.

rules.statement: Data files are data, so they are schema-valid, carry no logic or markup and hold only declared placeholders.

reasoning.definition: Every data file validates against a JSON Schema in strict mode with no additional properties; a string pattern forbids markup and logic delimiters except declared placeholders. The check uses the validator as a library from the shared check, because the command-line wrapper had not been published since 2023. A string in a fixture such as <b> is the plant, and the schema sets additionalProperties: false. The wrapper that was rejected is ajv-cli.
pros: A data file that carries logic or markup becomes a program nobody reviews as one.

rules.statement: A versioned file carries its version inside it and the reader says what it does with an older and a newer one; schema changes are forward-only numbered steps, each in one transaction with the version bump.

exemptions.reason: It has nothing to upgrade.

reasoning.definition: A newer file is left untouched and reported. A step marked rebuild runs only in one runner on a dedicated connection, in this order: foreign keys off before BEGIN, BEGIN IMMEDIATE, create new, copy, drop old, rename new, a foreign-key check that must be empty or roll back, version bump, COMMIT, foreign keys on and read back. Shipped steps may not be edited (a diff against the last tag). Tests use one fixture per released version plus a next fixture. The foreign-key check is the engine call foreign_key_check. The shipped-steps-unchanged half is the recipe git diff <last tag> -- <steps dir>, run against the directory of steps.
pros: One program renames a newer hours file aside, so a downgrade moves real data away. No repository tests a file written by build N against N-1 and N+1. Latent today: one program's migrations are column additions only, one has no foreign-key setting and one has no ALTER TABLE.

rules.statement: A status column's vocabulary is declared once, in the casing the program declares, and compared across the schema check list, the code constants and the doc table; the status check is generated from the same declaration; tables are strict; and every check-then-insert has a unique constraint.

exemptions.reason: It has no schema.

reasoning.definition: Each is read back from the schema by a test. The values follow the program's one declared casing (service.contract.10); the rulebook names no default. A scan flags a select followed by an insert on the same key with no unique index.
pros: In one repository 64 checks and 30 strict tables exist; another has none because its index can be rebuilt. A status written in three places drifts.

rules.statement: A store that returns a time or an integer has a round-trip test asserting the stored form and the width.

exemptions.reason: It has no stored form.

pros: A time or integer that truncates in the store reads back different from what was written.

rules.statement: Each named real engine has a contract suite pinning concurrent writers, retry on conflict, order, time and integer width, and an engine version floor.

exemptions.reason: There is no engine to pin.

reasoning.definition: With one engine in use, the suite is the store's own test set and the floor is the part that bites now. A build-time read of the linked engine version is compared with a known-bad list, which is a protected path. The suite runs once per engine named on the port.
pros: The embedded driver bundles an engine version past a write-ahead-log reset bug fixed in 3.51.3. A bug in a version below the floor corrupts data silently.

rules.statement: A lock is a kernel advisory lock, non-blocking by default, with a deadline on any blocking wait; the order of two locks is written and tested; it is taken only through the platform's lock package, and any failure other than held stops the run.

exemptions.reason: Only the owner carries the lock implementation.

reasoning.definition: forbidigo (type-aware) bans Flock and FcntlFlock calls outside the lock package, with a plain-text check for the raw system-call number and the four planted files kept as the fixture pair; a depguard row bans the third-party flock module, with an owner-lock rule that exempts the lock package's own path. A test checks that the claim fails when the lock folder is unwritable. The atomic-write package's own two calls are exempt.
pros: Fourteen production files call flock directly. In two programs the claim function treats every error except held as success. A trial planted four lock forms and the pattern flagged 2 of 4.

rules.statement: A lock that guards correctness across hosts hands out a monotonically increasing fencing token, and the store checks it on the write.

reasoning.definition: It applies where a lease or lock stands between two hosts and a double execution would corrupt data and not merely waste work. The write that follows is rejected by the store if the token is older than one it has seen. Most answers are a conditional write on a revision (store.consistency.3), which makes the question cost nothing.
pros: A lease can expire during a pause while the holder goes on writing; the same shape appears when an invocation is frozen and thawed or an at-least-once delivery runs the same work twice (inference, not measured; no case from the estate).

rules.statement: A mutation carries a version precondition; compare-and-set puts the version in the condition, and a conflict is a typed outcome distinct from not found.

exemptions.reason: There is nothing to mutate.

reasoning.definition: Both read as zero rows affected unless told apart. The test asserts the stale write's values are absent, so a retry that re-reads and overwrites fails. The request carries the revision in its body. Not-found and conflict are different typed outcomes (not-found for a missing row, a conflict for a stale one).
pros: An update without the version in its condition overwrites a newer write silently.

rules.statement: The intent is written before the effect and a record that cannot be written stops the effect; no message is published inside a database transaction (transactional outbox).

exemptions.reason: There is no effect to precede.

reasoning.definition: The run record is opened after the lock is taken, so a refused second run writes no record. The outbox writes the row in the transaction and publishes after commit; whether a message can go out for a change that then rolls back is a review question.
pros: One program opens its run record before it takes the library lock, so a refused run writes its own record.

sources.where: ch. 4 liberating data using outbox tables

rules.statement: Every outward effect goes through a wrapper that records it, and a program is run from one package.

reasoning.definition: depguard owner-exec on the process package, forbidigo on os.StartProcess and syscall.ForkExec outside the runner (both run a program without the process package, and os itself cannot be banned), and the security analyser's rule for a variable command. The runner package, proposed, has a context, a timeout, no shell and an output cap. Counts on macOS: the process package appears in 90 production files across seven repositories (24, 20, 11 and 13 in four of them).
pros: An effect outside the wrapper is invisible to the record and to the journal that precedes effects.

rules.statement: Backup uses the engine's own interface, and for every store that cannot be rebuilt a restore drill restores a backup or a point in time to a new path or instance, runs an integrity check and compares counts with the source; a file copy of a live store is not a backup.

exemptions.reason: A rebuild replaces a restore.

reasoning.definition: Counts are compared against a minimum from the fixture, so a drill over an empty store fails. The drill is started by hand or by a release, never by a timer. For a managed relational store the restore goes to a new cluster; for an embedded store a test backs up a populated store, restores it and checks. Anything you cannot re-derive from other data counts as not rebuildable. The embedded-store integrity query is the engine call integrity_check.
pros: A copy taken during writes may not be a backup. A neighbouring system found its corruption because its pipeline snapshotted and checked its backups. No row covered backup or restore before this one, and an unrebuildable store is a plain file (store.seams.6), so the embedded checks bind no store today.

rules.statement: A stateful program is crash-injected: it is killed at random points in a scripted workload, restarted, and its invariants are asserted.

exemptions.reason: There is no state to lose.
There is no state to lose.

reasoning.definition: A harness per stateful program runs at land for the affected store.
pros: No crash was injected anywhere in the estate; the atomic-write row proposes it only for the write itself. A harness that cannot break the invariant with a known flaw proves nothing.

rules.statement: Entry code never imports the database client or the query builder; only the store layer does.

pros: When handlers import the client, connection handling, error mapping and typed queries are re-implemented in each one.

rules.statement: One shared package opens the Postgres connection (pool, IAM token) and maps its errors; no new connection pool is created outside it, and one certificate bundle and one 64-bit integer parser are shared.

pros: A second pool constructor adds connections the budget does not count, and a second integer parser reads a 64-bit column differently from the first.

rules.statement: The maximum number of database connections the services can open at once is computed from the concurrency the infrastructure allows, checked to be under the cluster limit, and the session timeouts are read back.

reasoning.definition: The budget is function concurrency times pool size, summed over services that share a cluster, written as data. The connection config sets a statement timeout and an idle-in-transaction timeout, and a test reads them back with SHOW on a fresh pooled connection. A measure sits beside it: connection count and the age of the oldest open transaction, read by hand at each release. Whether a managed pooler is used was not checked.
pros: The first big surprise of a growing service is the remaining-connection-slots failure; a runtime that scales to many instances makes the sum large and spiky. Agents raise a pool size to cure a timeout and move the queue (inference).

sources.where: appendix A section A.3 use connection pooling

rules.statement: Transactions are opened only through the one shared transaction helper, which retries the serialisation and deadlock codes a bounded number of times and surfaces a typed failure after that.

reasoning.definition: The codes are 40001 and 40P01. A transaction makes no call outside the database. For a program in Go the same is one helper that retries serialisation failures, found by a scan for a transaction opened outside it.
pros: A stronger isolation level obliges the application to retry, and a helper without the retry loses the write or fails the user. A forced serialisation failure on a real container is the only ordinary test that sees it.

rules.statement: A transaction that reads a set and writes on its strength states, as arguments to the helper, which invariant it protects and the isolation level it runs at, and the anomaly the level prevents.

reasoning.definition: The default level, Read Committed, is right for a single-row read-modify-write and wrong for reading a set and then inserting on the strength of it. The review asks: which invariant does this transaction protect, which anomaly would it suffer at this level, and what does the code do on a serialisation failure.
pros: An agent copies the default level and cannot see the race, since no ordinary test produces it. The choice of level is made against a named anomaly, and the engine version matters (postgres.engine.1).

rules.statement: Optimistic concurrency uses a revision in the request body and one compare-and-set helper; a stale write is a conflict, distinct from not found, and never an entity tag or a precondition status.

pros: A stale update that overwrites silently loses a write, and a conflict read as not found hides the race.

rules.statement: Query types are generated from the program's one data model, which is the single source of every shape; the live schema is checked against the model, never the model against the live schema; and SQL is built with a typed query builder so every table and column is checked at compile time.

reasoning.definition: The model is declared once, in one schema library, and generates the table types, the DDL, the JSON Schema and the API and tool contracts; no second schema library owns a shape. The gate regenerates every derived file from the model and fails on a diff, and compares the schema after replaying every migration with the DDL the model generates (postgres.migrations.1). Types are never generated from the live database. A new derived shape (a new contract kind) is one more generator from the same model.
pros: A query written as a string fails at run time on a renamed column; types from the model fail the build instead. One model that generates every other shape is the strongest guard against a type, a table and a contract drifting apart over years, and a source chosen once cannot be argued about per change.

rules.statement: Parser behaviour (how the client reads 64-bit integers, times and decimals) is tested against a real Postgres, and generated query output is ignored by the formatter.

pros: A parser configured against a mock reads the wrong width in production; generated output rewritten by the formatter fails the no-diff regeneration check.

rules.statement: Status guards derive from the transition table through one builder, with no hand-written status condition.

pros: A hand-written WHERE on a status drifts from the transition table the moment a transition is added.

rules.statement: There is one error envelope, and storage errors (the SQLSTATE codes) are mapped to it in one place.

reasoning.definition: Local error tables are banned, and a test shows that no raw database message reaches the response.
pros: A storage error that reaches the response raw leaks the schema and gives callers a different shape per route.

rules.statement: Migrations are numbered in order and append-only: a landed migration is never edited, each carries a checksum the runner checks, and the schema after replaying every migration equals the schema file and the DDL the data model generates.

reasoning.definition: The model is the one source (postgres.queries.1): the replayed schema is compared with the DDL generated from it, and a difference fails; the model is never regenerated from the replayed schema. A change to the schema is a new migration. The runner refuses to start when a landed migration's checksum differs from the one recorded when it ran.
pros: A gap or a reorder changes what replay produces, a schema file that drifts from replay misleads the types and the review, and an edited landed migration means two databases that ran different text under one number.

rules.statement: No destructive migration (drop, truncate, destructive type change) without a written plan.

pros: A destructive step cannot be undone by a down script, so the plan is the recovery.

rules.statement: Migrations stay compatible with the running version, in the order expand, migrate, then contract.

pros: A Lambda deploy runs old and new code together for a while, and a queue can deliver an old message to new code, so a migration that breaks the old code breaks the deploy.

rules.statement: A migration that starts an expand-and-contract change records the date by which the old column or table is removed and names the readers alive during the deploy; the gate fails a leftover past its date.

reasoning.definition: The date sits in the migration header as contract-by in the same register as other exemptions. The question for the readers is which ones will be alive during this deploy. The header line reads contract-by with a date, for example contract-by: <date>.
pros: If the contract phase never runs you end up worse off, with two versions supported for good; agents add the new column and forget the old (inference). The transition is needed only when several clients are coupled to the schema.

rules.statement: Migration text has a class header and notes for renames, splits, merges and removals, no down scripts, no risky extensions, and states the delete behaviour of every reference; and a program that applies migrations at start backs up first, and restores the backup and refuses to start when a migration fails.

reasoning.definition: No CREATE EXTENSION, dblink or foreign data wrapper; every REFERENCES states ON DELETE. With no down script the way back from a failed migration is the backup taken just before it; the program names the backup in its log and exits non-zero after restoring.
pros: A down script gives false comfort for a step that cannot be reversed, and an unstated delete behaviour is a decision nobody made. A migration that fails halfway at start leaves a store no version can read unless the copy from just before is put back.

rules.statement: A migration passes a lock lint: an index is built concurrently, a constraint is added in two phases, and a lock timeout is set and read back before the step runs.

reasoning.definition: Squawk rules: require-concurrent-index-creation, require-timeout-settings, require-lock-timeout, constraint-missing-not-valid and adding-foreign-key-constraint, named from the project's documentation (exit code and config not confirmed). Atlas and eugene were considered. The pack binds a repository when it adopts Postgres. The lock timeout is the session setting lock_timeout, set and read back before the step runs.
pros: A migration on nearly empty tables cost one payment company about 15 seconds of API downtime: the ALTER waited for a strong lock behind a long read and every later query queued behind it.

rules.statement: The migration runner sets a lock timeout and a statement timeout for the session that applies a migration, and a migration that waits behind a lock aborts, shown by a test.

reasoning.definition: A deploy that hits the timeout fails and is retried. The test holds a lock from another connection and asserts the migration aborts within the timeout, and a second test reads SHOW lock_timeout in the migration session. The lint reads text; it cannot know the session setting or what runs on the table at that moment.
pros: Removing long transactions, setting a lock timeout so aborting a deploy is better than stopping the app, and splitting changes are the remedy from the payment company's incident. Its post names lock types that the current manual names differently; the queue mechanism stands.

rules.statement: Naming, check constraints, mandatory columns, primary keys, references and audit columns hold in the live schema; a reference to one of several kinds is a foreign key per kind in an exclusive arc, never a kind and an id in text; and a rule enforced in SQL is tested in SQL against the replayed migrations, never re-implemented in code to be tested.

reasoning.definition: A schema lint runs in the shared container: name casing, name inflection, mandatory columns, a primary key on every table, references and types, with ignores by identifier pattern. A status column has a check. An exclusive arc is one nullable foreign-key column per kind and a check that exactly one is set. A law the database enforces (a check, a trigger, a constraint) has a SQL test (pgTAP or plain SQL run by the test runner) on a database built from the migrations; a copy of the law in application code to test it is a second implementation and is refused in review.
pros: A convention held only in migration text drifts from what the database actually holds. A kind-and-id text reference is one the database cannot check, and a law tested only through a copy in code proves the copy.

rules.statement: After replay, the application role reads and writes every table, tables with an update time have the update trigger, actor columns are not null, and no update sets a created field.

reasoning.definition: The application role is named per service (<svc>_app); update-time tables have an updated_at trigger, and no update sets a created_* field.
pros: A table the app role cannot reach, a missing trigger or a rewritten created field is invisible until production.

rules.statement: Every if-it-does-not-exist-insert is backed by a unique index or exclusion constraint on the same key, read back from the live catalogue by a test, and a status column has a check.

reasoning.definition: A registry kept beside the repository lists the natural keys the repository layer claims; the catalogue test asserts a unique index for each. An ast-grep pattern flags a select followed by an insert on the same key in one function, to be listed or constrained.
pros: Application-level uniqueness and association validations in Rails applications were shown to be violable under concurrent requests; the finding is about where an invariant must live.

rules.statement: A generated rules catalogue is regenerated in the gate and fails on drift.

reasoning.definition: The catalogue file is named RULES-CATALOG.md in the reference, kept at a service root and regenerated by the gate.
pros: A catalogue that is not regenerated drifts from the rules it lists.

rules.statement: A table that records facts is append-only: a trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE for every role, the superuser included, and a test drives it.

reasoning.definition: The trigger raises on UPDATE and DELETE (and TRUNCATE where the engine allows a trigger on it); a grant alone is not enough because the superuser bypasses grants. A correction is a new row that refers to the one it corrects. The table is marked append-only in the model, so a new fact table gets the trigger from the same declaration.
pros: A recorded fact that can be changed is not a record, and a trigger outlasts every application that writes to the table.

rules.statement: A library that owns tables keeps them in its own schema, migrated by the library at a pinned version, and only the program's own schema is held to the DDL its model generates.

reasoning.definition: An auth library, a job queue or the migrator's ledger each get a Postgres schema of their own. The program never writes their tables by hand, and its migrations never touch them. Upgrading a library moves its pin and runs its own migrations.
pros: A library schema lets a library be upgraded without touching the product's tables, and keeps the model-equals-DDL check (postgres.migrations.1) from failing on tables the model does not own.

rules.statement: A migration that adds an index names the query it serves and the write path that pays for it, and unused indexes are listed from the engine's own statistics at release.

reasoning.definition: The measure is a count of indexes with no scans, from the statistics views, with no limit set. A two-column index is useless to a query on only its second column, and an index on every column makes every write maintain all of them. A failed concurrent build leaves an invalid index that still costs writes.
pros: A small development database hides an index that no query uses; agents add an index per query just in case (inference).

rules.statement: Tests run on the engine version production runs; an in-process build of the engine over the real migrations counts as that engine when its major version matches production; a test of roles or connections runs a server build; a version below a stated floor or on a known-bad list fails; and a contract suite pins the behaviour the data layer relies on.

reasoning.definition: An in-process build (for example PGlite) runs store tests and gates fast over the real migrations; it does not model roles, grants, connections or the superuser, so a test of those runs on a server build of the same major. The in-process major is read and compared like the container's. The container's server version equals the version declared in infrastructure and is compared with a floor file kept as data. The contract suite covers concurrent writers on one row, retry on conflict, ordering, time-zone handling and 64-bit integer width, and runs once per named engine. A container tag is never a floating one. Editing the known-bad list is a protected path.
pros: An engine version is part of the contract, and a bug fixed in a later version is a fault carried until the move. A neighbouring engine's write-ahead-log bug stood for years, and a company using it saw corruption in its backup snapshots. Agents bump an image tag to make a build pass (inference).

rules.statement: Storage keys are built only by the shared key builder; no code assembles a key string by hand.

reasoning.definition: Partition and sort keys, index keys and key prefixes come from functions in the store's key-building layer. A string that looks like a key (an entity prefix joined with an id) anywhere else fails.
pros: Hand-built keys drift between writers and readers, and a typo returns nothing instead of failing.

rules.statement: Each table has a checked-in list of its access patterns, and every query function maps to a line on it.

reasoning.definition: Each line names the question and the key or index that answers it in one request. A query function in the key-building layer that matches no line fails; a line with no query function is reported.
pros: A DynamoDB model is designed from its access patterns and cannot be made generic later: a new pattern needs a new index or a data migration. Without the list, the next pattern is found in production as a scan or a filter that reads the whole partition.

rules.statement: Each table's design note states the highest write rate one partition-key value will see and what happens beyond it, and a read that must see its own write goes to the base table, not a secondary index.

pros: Hot partitions throttle even when the table's total capacity is enough, and secondary indexes update asynchronously, serving only eventually consistent reads.

rules.statement: A change to what a table holds is additive where it can be, and otherwise a migration with a written plan whose backfill is resumable and safe to run twice.

reasoning.definition: Additive means readers default a missing attribute and writers add it as items are touched. A change that rewrites every item, or a new index that needs a backfill, is an extract-transform-load job with a written plan: a parallel scan, batched writes, resumable, idempotent.
pros: A new access pattern on existing data usually needs a full rewrite, and a one-off script run once and never retested leaves the table half migrated when it fails.

rules.statement: A Scan runs only in a migration or an export named on a short allow list, and a filter expression is never how a query gets its result.

reasoning.definition: If removing a filter expression would change the answer a user sees, the key design is wrong and the access-pattern list needs a new line. The scanned-to-returned item ratio is measured per action.
pros: A filter is applied after the items are read, so every removed item is still paid for and the response size limit is hit before the filter runs: a filter cannot save a bad model.

rules.statement: Entry code such as a handler never imports the DynamoDB SDK; only the store layer does.

pros: When handlers call the SDK directly, key building, conditions and retries are re-implemented in each one.

rules.statement: An action unit holds one storage command and imports no repository or sibling action.

pros: One command per action keeps each storage effect testable on its own and stops actions composing each other into hidden transactions.

rules.statement: Aggregate writes go only through the shared write toolkit's versioned write functions; deletes are allowed only in allow-listed short-lived actions; audit tables are append-only.

reasoning.definition: Every service that uses DynamoDB writes aggregates through the toolkit, which owns the version check and the conditional write. A delete outside the allow list fails. An audit table, such as a record of sign-in events, accepts inserts only. The toolkit has a conformance suite that every release runs.
pros: One write path is the only place where conditions, versions and retries can be proved once and trusted everywhere.

rules.statement: Every insert-if-absent and every read-modify-write uses a condition expression in the same call; uniqueness beyond the primary key is kept by a guard item written in the same transaction; a retried transactional write carries a client token.

reasoning.definition: Check-then-write is the case this rule exists for, written in one conditional call instead of a read followed by a write.
pros: Uniqueness and association checks written as read-then-write are broken by races. A transactional write with a client token is idempotent for a window, so a retry does not write twice.

rules.statement: Where an item carries a time-to-live attribute, every read that must not see an expired item checks the attribute itself.

reasoning.definition: The table's deletion of expired items is cleanup, never the moment of expiry.
pros: Expired items are deleted only eventually, typically within about two days, so a session or processing-key table that trusts deletion honours an expired token for that long.

sources.where: advanced concepts: time-to-live, and the session-store example

rules.statement: No grant uses a wildcard action or a wildcard resource, and a gate that bans wildcards runs in every service.

reasoning.definition: The gate scans the infrastructure code and the rendered policies for a star in an action or resource position. Allow lists elsewhere (modules, callers) also name entries and a wildcard fails there. In Go, the CI token is read-only and scoped, the daemon callers are checked, and the sandbox comes from a template.
pros: A wildcard grant turns any compromise or bug in one function into access to everything the account holds.

rules.statement: Event publishing, invoke and database-connect grants exist only on the declared path: publish only on the shared bus, invoke only through the one internal invoke grant, and runtime database connect only for the service own application role.

pros: These three grants are how a unit reaches other services and the data; each must come from one declared place so a reader sees every door a unit has.

rules.statement: State-bearing resources are retained on delete.

reasoning.definition: A resource that holds data that cannot be rebuilt (a database, a bucket with content, a queue holding work) carries a retain-on-delete policy so removing the stack does not remove the data. In Go, a store says whether it can be rebuilt, and state that cannot be rebuilt is append-only and kept; removal keeps user state.
pros: Deleting a stack that owns data deletes the data; one command removes it with no recovery.

rules.statement: Every storage bucket blocks public access (all four flags) and is encrypted at rest, set by the shared component, with no component option that can turn either off.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a secret is written with its final mode in a private folder and peer credentials are checked. Hosting posture for a static site (public access, encryption at rest) is a gap with no row yet.
pros: A public or unencrypted bucket is a data leak by default; removing the choice removes the mistake.

rules.statement: Concurrency caps come from shared defaults: none in development, none by default in the shared components, and a cap is never used as a queue throttle.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a daemon bounds its work with request, concurrency and queue caps from one unit template. A queue consumer that needs a ceiling sets the queue maximum concurrency instead; see the consumer rule for outside APIs.
pros: A reserved-concurrency cap used to throttle a queue starves the function other triggers need and hides the real limit.

rules.statement: A middleware or plumbing library is imported only by the one package that owns that concern.

reasoning.definition: For the handler wrapper (ordered before, after and error steps) the owner is the shared runtime package; no other package imports the middleware engine. The same holds for each concern with an owner, enforced by import rules; a direct dependency outside the list fails. In Go there is one importable owner per concern.
pros: A library imported in many packages has many configurations, and a fix or an upgrade must be found in all of them.

rules.statement: Function permissions are granted only through managed policy ARNs on the role, never through a standalone policy attachment.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a unit runs with its own identity and sandbox from one template, and CI tokens are scoped.
pros: A standalone attachment lies outside the role definition, so the role cannot be read as the full list of what a function may do.

rules.statement: Every function has a pinned role name from one table and receives the shared baseline grants.

reasoning.definition: A function with no entry in the role-name table fails, so a new function cannot be deployed with a generated role name. In Go, a daemon unit has its own identity and sandbox from one template.
pros: A generated role name changes on replacement and breaks everything that names it, and a function without the baseline misses logging and tracing grants.

rules.statement: Each function bundle has a size budget, and a built handler bundle over its byte limit fails the check.

reasoning.definition: A size-limit tool bundles each handler entry with the build bundler and compares it with the limit in the package manifest (a list of path and limit). In Go, binary size is recorded as a metric, not a gate.
pros: A large bundle slows cold start and approaches the platform package limit without anyone choosing it.

rules.statement: The infrastructure tool and its shared components package are exact-pinned to one version across the repository, and no local-path link (file: or link: protocols) reaches the main branch.

reasoning.definition: One version of the tool is in use. A local-path dependency is for experiments and fails at land. The same holds for the build tool in Go: tools pinned once and no replace directive or workspace file in a committed tree. A no-local-link rule is also supply hygiene.
pros: A range or a local link makes the deployed infrastructure depend on something the repository does not hold.

rules.statement: Services deploy only through one deploy guard, and the land check fails on the deletion or replacement of a state-bearing resource.

reasoning.definition: The guard reads the plan and refuses a plan that deletes or replaces a database, bucket, queue or identity resource without a recorded exit. In Go, an upgrade is by rename, the previous binary is kept, and it is put back by itself when the new one does not answer healthy.
pros: A replacement of a stateful resource is a deletion with a new name; the plan shows it, and only a guard stops it.

rules.statement: Infrastructure is declared only through the shared constructs, not raw cloud resources or overrides.

reasoning.definition: A raw function resource (sst.aws.Function), a raw table (aws.dynamodb.Table), raw gateway resources (aws.apigateway.*), a bundler override, function layers, local components and a bare network configuration (vpcConfig) each fail; the shared construct sets them. In Go, unit files come from a template and are checked, not hand-written.
pros: A raw resource skips everything the shared construct sets (grants, logging, retention, naming), and the gap appears in the one service that used it.

rules.statement: The program name is written in exactly one place in the infrastructure code.

reasoning.definition: In Go, every path and identifier of persistent state is made from the program name in one function.
pros: A name repeated in many places is renamed in some.

rules.statement: The log format, log groups and the stage name are set only by one shared component or file.

reasoning.definition: No logFormat: JSON option set per function, no raw LogGroup, and the stage variable ($app.stage) read only in the one stages file (stages.ts). In Go, one logging handler with version and run id, and the environment read only in config.
pros: A log format or stage read set in many places drifts: the metric filters and alarms then miss some functions.

rules.statement: Infrastructure code never imports application source.

reasoning.definition: In Go, the entry and storage layers follow a layer table, and deploy code under its own folder imports no program package.
pros: Infrastructure code that pulls in application modules runs them at deploy time and ties a deploy to application internals.

rules.statement: Imported identity, IAM and DNS resources carry retain-on-delete, so removing the stack does not remove them.

reasoning.definition: The infrastructure rule set also requires grants only through managed policies and a pinned role name for every function (the Lambda part holds those two) as one set of rules over the infrastructure code. In Go, a binary never rewrites shared state and removal must not take user data.
pros: A resource the stack only imported belongs to others; deleting the stack must not delete it.

rules.statement: One shared component gives every service the same alarms on errors, throttles and latency.

reasoning.definition: In Go, a daemon serves one health document and is bounded and supervised.
pros: Alarms written per service are missing where the failure is.
